Toast the guajillo and ancho in a dry pan for 20 seconds each side, then soak in hot water for 10 minutes. Blend with the tomato, most of the remaining onion (keep a thin slice for the slaw), the rest of the garlic, cumin, oregano and a pinch of salt. Simmer the salsa in a pan for 8 minutes, until thick and darker, then stir in the beef and let it cool.

Mix the masa harina and the rest of the salt with warm broth, a splash at a time, until it comes together. Then beat in the oil for 3 minutes, until the dough is soft and spreadable like thick hummus.
Spread a few spoons of masa over the lower two thirds of a husk, add a spoonful of beef, fold in the sides and fold the narrow end up. Stand the tamales upright, folded side down, in a steamer.
Steam, covered, for 60 to 70 minutes, topping up the water now and then, until the masa pulls away cleanly from the husk. Rest for 10 minutes.

Toss the cabbage with the lime juice, a pinch of salt and a little of the onion, sliced thin, and serve with the tamales. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: cool it, refrigerate within 2 hours and reheat it once in a steamer or microwave to 74 °C (165 °F), still in its husk.
tip: Dried corn husks are sold at Latin grocers and in many supermarkets' Mexican aisle. No husks? Use parchment squares tied with kitchen string. Traditional masa is whipped with fat; olive oil gives a denser, still tender tamale. A pressure cooker cuts the beef to 30 minutes. Tamales freeze for 3 months. Check the label on the masa harina (buy a gluten-free line if you are celiac).

name: Ajiaco with chicken, corn and potatoes
inspiredBy: Colombian ajiaco santafereño from Bogotá, with the three kinds of potato simplified and yogurt standing in for cream
about: A thick, golden Bogotá soup of chicken, corn and potatoes, perfumed with guascas and finished with creamy avocado, fresh cilantro and a spoon of cool yogurt. Some of the potatoes melt into the broth to thicken it, and the rest stay in tender chunks. Potatoes and corn bring **potassium, vitamin C and B6**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat and soften the scallion and garlic for 2 minutes. Add the chicken, the salt and enough water to cover everything by 3 cm.
Bring to a simmer and cook for 15 minutes. Add the sliced potatoes, which will dissolve into the broth, and simmer for 15 minutes more.
Add the potato chunks, the corn and the guascas and simmer for another 15 minutes, until the chunks are tender and the broth is thick and golden.
Lift the chicken out, shred it and return it to the pot for a minute.
Ladle into a bowl. Top with the avocado, cilantro and a spoon of the yogurt.
tip: Guascas is sold dried at Colombian shops; leave it out if you cannot find it. Yellow potatoes plus some russets give the classic texture. A few capers and a spoon of cream on top is how Bogotá serves it. Check the label on any boxed broth.
ingredients: half peeled and sliced thin, half in chunks
in place of cream, about ¼ cup
dried; or a pinch of dried oregano

name: Mango with lime and chile
about: Juicy mango cubes with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chile, the way Mexican street stalls sell it. It is sweet, sharp and a little hot. The mango brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Cube the mango and toss it with the lime juice, a pinch of cayenne and a tiny pinch of salt.
tip: Check the label on the chile powder if you use a blend instead of pure cayenne.

name: Orange with lime and chile
about: Juicy orange segments with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chile, the way Mexican fruit stalls serve it. It is cold, sweet and a little hot. Oranges bring **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the orange and cut it into rounds or segments, then squeeze the lime over and dust with cayenne and a tiny pinch of salt.
tip: Check the label on the chile powder if you use a blend instead of pure cayenne.

name: Chía fresca with orange and lime
inspiredBy: Mexican chía fresca, the chia agua fresca sold at street stalls, sweetened only with orange
about: Chia seeds soaked in water with fresh orange and lime juice until they plump up and turn jelly-like. It is cool, tangy and lightly sweet. Chia brings **omega-3, calcium and magnesium** in a very Mexican way.
steps: Stir the chia into a tall glass of cold water (about 250 ml) and leave it for 10 minutes, stirring once or twice, until it plumps up.
Stir in the orange juice and lime juice, add ice, and drink it right away.

name: Banana yogurt with flaxseed and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Brazilian iogurte com banana e linhaça, the everyday snack bowl
about: Thick yogurt topped with sliced banana, a spoon of ground flaxseed and a dusting of cinnamon, a very Brazilian way to snack. It is creamy, sweet and a little nutty. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the flaxseed brings omega-3.
steps: Slice the banana into the yogurt, then sprinkle with the ground flaxseed and cinnamon.

name: Grilled queijo coalho with orange
inspiredBy: queijo coalho na brasa, the grilled cheese sold on skewers on Brazilian beaches
about: Squares of queijo coalho seared until golden and squeaky, with juicy orange segments to cut through the salt. It is the Brazilian beach snack, done in a pan. The cheese brings **calcium and protein**, and the orange brings vitamin C.
steps: Cut the coalho into thick squares and sear them in a dry nonstick pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes a side, until golden and spotty.
Peel the orange, split it into segments and eat them with the warm cheese.
tip: Halloumi works the same way.

name: Black bean dip with carrot and red pepper sticks
inspiredBy: Mexican frijoles negros mashed with lime and cumin, served like a dip
about: Creamy mashed black beans with lime, garlic, cumin and a little olive oil, scooped up with crunchy carrot and red pepper sticks. It is savoury, tangy and filling. Black beans bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Use beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Mash them with a fork or blitz with the lime juice, grated garlic, cumin, oil and salt, adding a splash of water for a creamy texture. Stir in the cilantro.
Serve with the carrot and red pepper for dipping.
tip: Make a double batch on Sunday; it keeps 4 days.

name: Guacamole with red pepper strips and baked tortilla wedges
inspiredBy: Mexican guacamole, scooped with crisp baked tortilla and raw red pepper
about: Chunky avocado mashed with lime, onion, cilantro and a little tomato, scooped up with crisp baked corn tortilla wedges and sweet red pepper strips. It is creamy, fresh and very filling. Avocado brings **vitamin E, potassium and healthy fat**, and the red pepper brings vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Spread the tortilla wedges on a tray and bake for about 8 minutes, until crisp.
Mash the avocado roughly with the lime juice and salt, then fold in the tomato, onion and cilantro, all finely chopped.
Scoop with the warm wedges and the red pepper strips.
tip: Check the tortillas say 100% corn, nothing else.

name: Roasted chickpeas with lime and chile
about: Chickpeas roasted until crunchy and tossed with lime, cumin and a pinch of cayenne. They are salty, tangy and very moreish, the kind of snack you can carry in your pocket. Chickpeas bring **protein, fibre and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas very dry with a towel, then toss them with the oil, cumin and salt.
Spread them on a tray and roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crunchy and deep golden.
Toss with the lime juice and cayenne while hot.
tip: Roast a double batch if you like, and re-crisp the second half in a hot oven for 5 minutes before you eat it.
ingredients: canned, drained, rinsed and dried well

name: Chicken anticuchos with ají amarillo
inspiredBy: Peruvian anticuchos, the street-corner skewers usually made with beef heart, here with chicken thigh
about: Chicken thigh cubes marinated in ají amarillo, garlic, cumin and lime, threaded on skewers and grilled until charred at the edges. They are smoky, juicy and mildly hot. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**.
steps: Stir the ají amarillo paste with the grated garlic, cumin, lime juice, oil and salt. Toss the chicken in it and leave for at least 20 minutes, or all day in the fridge.
Thread the chicken on skewers (soak wooden ones in water first).
Grill or broil about 10 cm from the heat for 8 to 10 minutes, turning once or twice, until charred in spots and cooked through.
tip: Marinate in the morning and it takes 10 minutes at snack time. Check the label on the ají paste.

name: Hard-boiled eggs with lime and chile
inspiredBy: Mexican huevos duros with lime, salt and chile, the bar and street-stall snack
about: Hard-boiled eggs sprinkled with lime juice, a pinch of salt and chile, a simple Mexican snack. They are creamy, sharp and a little hot. The eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the eggs into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes. Cool them in cold water, then peel.
Halve the eggs and sprinkle with the lime juice, salt and cayenne.
tip: Boil a few extra on Sunday; they keep 5 days in the shell. Check the label on the chile powder if it is a blend.

name: Black bean and corn cup with lime
inspiredBy: Mexican ensalada de frijol y elote, the bean and corn salad
about: Black beans and sweet corn tossed with tomato, onion, cilantro, lime and a little olive oil in a cup. It is cool, savoury and bright, and easy to carry. Beans and corn together bring **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Use beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Toss the beans with the corn, tomato, onion, cilantro, lime juice, oil and salt.
Let it sit for 10 minutes so the flavours settle, then eat it cold.
tip: It keeps 2 days in the fridge, so make a double batch.

name: Sardines with lime, tomato and onion
inspiredBy: Mexican sardinas a la mexicana, made here as a no-cook salpicón with lime, tomato and onion
about: Canned sardines, with their soft bones, dressed with lime, diced tomato, onion and cilantro. It takes five minutes and tastes bright and briny. Sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin B12**.
steps: Mix the tomato, onion, cilantro, lime juice, salt and a pinch of cayenne in a small bowl.
Break the sardines into big chunks, spoon the tomato mixture over and eat right away.
tip: Add a sliced serrano for more heat. Buy sardines in oil or water, not in a sauce.

name: Buckwheat porridge with cinnamon pear, walnuts and yogurt
inspiredBy: Northern Italian grano saraceno, the buckwheat of Valtellina, here cooked as a creamy porridge with pear and walnuts, the way buckwheat is eaten in colder places
about: Toasted buckwheat simmered in milk until it turns soft and nutty, with sliced pear, a spoon of Greek yogurt, a drizzle of honey and toasted walnuts. Buckwheat is not wheat at all, so it is **naturally gluten-free**, and it gives you magnesium and fibre while the walnuts add omega-3.
steps: Rinse the buckwheat in a sieve. Tip it into a small dry pot and toast over medium heat for 2 minutes, until it smells nutty.
Pour in the milk, add the cinnamon and salt, and bring to a gentle simmer.

Cook uncovered on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the groats are tender and the porridge is thick and creamy. If it gets stodgy before the groats are soft, add a splash of water; if it is still loose, give it a few minutes more.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry pan for a couple of minutes, until golden and fragrant.
Spoon the porridge into a bowl, fan the pear on top, add the yogurt and walnuts and drizzle with honey.
tip: Cook a double batch on Sunday night and it keeps 3 days in the fridge. Loosen it with a splash of milk and reheat for 2 minutes.
ingredients: toasted (kasha) or plain, certified gluten-free if you are celiac

name: Greek yogurt with orange, walnuts and crunchy buckwheat
inspiredBy: Greek yogurt with honey and walnuts (yiaourti me meli), a favourite breakfast and dessert, with orange and toasted buckwheat for crunch
about: Thick Greek yogurt topped with juicy orange segments, toasted walnuts and a spoon of crunchy toasted buckwheat, finished with honey and a pinch of cinnamon. It takes five minutes, and the yogurt and walnuts bring **protein, calcium and omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for a couple of minutes, until fragrant. Use buckwheat from your Sunday jar, or make it now: soak the groats in cold water for 15 minutes, drain well and toast them in a dry pan over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until dry and crisp.
Peel the orange, cut away the white pith, and slice it into segments, saving the juice.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, arrange the orange on top and pour over the juice.
Scatter the toasted buckwheat and walnuts, drizzle with honey and finish with the cinnamon.
tip: Toast a jar of buckwheat on Sunday as in step 1; it keeps 5 days in a sealed jar, and breakfast takes 5 minutes. For a change, swap the orange for pomegranate seeds or a chopped pear.

name: Tortilla de patatas with spinach and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish tortilla española, the thick potato and onion omelette, with spinach folded in as in tortilla de espinacas
about: A thick, tender Spanish omelette of slowly cooked potato, sweet onion and a handful of spinach, held together with eggs and sliced like a cake. It is **gluten-free by nature**, and the eggs bring protein and choline while the potato adds potassium. It is just as good cold, so one pan covers two breakfasts.
steps: Warm most of the olive oil in a 22 cm nonstick frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the potato and onion with a pinch of the salt, cover with a lid and cook gently for 15 to 18 minutes, with a splash of water if they stick, turning now and then, until soft. Stir in the chopped spinach for the last 2 minutes, until it wilts.
Beat the eggs in a big bowl with the rest of the salt. Tip the potato, onion and spinach into the eggs and let it sit for 5 minutes.
Wipe the pan, warm the last of the oil over medium heat and pour in the mixture. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, shaking the pan now and then, until the edges are set and the underside is golden.
Put a large plate over the pan, flip the whole thing over, then slide it back and cook for another 5 minutes, until the middle is set and a knife comes out clean.
Serve a wedge of tortilla with the lemon squeezed over it and a scatter of parsley.
This makes two portions. Keep the second wedge for tomorrow; it is lovely cold or warmed for a minute.
tip: Slide a thin spatula around the edge before you flip. Cook it until the middle is set all the way through; a lower heat keeps it tender.

name: Salade niçoise with tuna, potatoes and green beans
inspiredBy: Salade niçoise from Nice, here in the home version with warm potatoes and green beans
about: Warm new potatoes, crisp green beans, ripe tomato, tuna, a boiled egg and olives, all tossed in a sharp lemon and sherry vinegar vinaigrette scented with basil. The tuna and egg bring **plenty of protein**, and the potatoes and beans carry the potassium.
steps: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water, bring to the boil and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slips in easily. Add the green beans for the last 4 minutes and the egg for the last 10 minutes.
Drain everything. Run the beans and egg under cold water to stop the cooking, then peel and quarter the egg.
Whisk the olive oil, vinegar, lemon juice, herbes de Provence and a pinch of salt in a big bowl. Toss the warm potatoes (halved or thickly sliced) in it so they soak up the dressing.
Add the beans, tomato, onion and olives and toss gently. Tear in the basil.
Flake the tuna over the top, arrange the egg on the side and finish with a grind of pepper.
tip: Cook the potatoes, beans and egg the night before and lunch is a 5 minute assembly. Oil-packed tuna is more traditional and keeps better; drained, it fits the numbers. Check the label on the tuna: plain is fine, but some flavoured cans contain hydrolyzed wheat protein.

name: Lemon-oregano chicken with potatoes and Greek salad
inspiredBy: Greek chicken souvlaki with potatoes and horiatiki salad
about: Chicken thigh marinated in lemon, garlic and oregano and seared until golden, piled onto a crunchy tomato, cucumber and olive salad with a warm parsley potato salad, chickpeas and a crumble of feta. The chicken and feta make it **high in protein**, and the lemon helps you absorb the iron in the chickpeas.
steps: Slice the chicken into chunky strips. Toss with half the lemon juice, the crushed garlic, half the oregano, a little of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Leave it to marinate while you do the rest, or for up to a few hours in the fridge.

Boil the potato chunks in salted water for 12 to 15 minutes, until tender. Drain, then toss with a few slices of the onion, half the parsley and a little of the olive oil while they are still warm, like a Greek patatosalata.
Mix the tomato, cucumber, onion, olives, chickpeas and parsley in a bowl. Dress with the rest of the lemon juice, oregano and olive oil.
Heat a heavy pan over medium-high heat and sear the chicken for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until golden and cooked through. Rest it for a minute.
Spoon the potatoes into a bowl, pile on the salad and chicken, and crumble the feta over the top.
tip: Marinate the chicken in the morning and it takes 15 minutes at lunch. For a packed lunch, cook it the night before; it is good cold.

name: Soupe au pistou with white beans and summer vegetables
inspiredBy: Provençal soupe au pistou, finished with a basil, garlic and cheese paste; the pasta is left out and the beans carry the soup
about: A thick, fragrant soup of white beans, zucchini and green beans, finished with a spoon of fresh basil, garlic and parmesan pounded into olive oil. The beans give you **protein, fibre and folate**, and the basil swirled in at the end is what makes it smell like Provence.
steps: Drain the soaked beans and put them in a pot with the bay leaf and enough fresh water to cover by 5 cm. Simmer gently for 45 to 60 minutes, until tender. Salt them near the end.
In a large pot, warm a little of the olive oil and soften the onion for 5 minutes. Add the tomato and cook for 3 minutes more.
Add the beans with their cooking water, plus enough water to make it soupy. Simmer for 10 minutes, then add the zucchini and green beans and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, until just tender.
Make the pistou: pound the basil, garlic and a pinch of salt in a mortar (or blitz briefly), then work in the parmesan and the rest of the olive oil until you have a loose green paste.
Ladle the soup into a bowl and stir a big spoonful of pistou in at the table, so the basil stays bright.
tip: Soak the beans Thursday night, simmer them on Friday evening and keep them in their water; Saturday's soup then takes 25 minutes. Short on time? Use canned white beans, drained, about two and a half times the dry weight in the list. The soup freezes well, but stir in the pistou fresh.

name: Escalivada with chickpeas and sardines
inspiredBy: Catalan escalivada, eggplant, red pepper and onion roasted until smoky and silky, here with chickpeas and sardines to make a full lunch
about: Eggplant, red pepper and onion roasted until soft and slightly charred, then dressed with garlic, sherry vinegar and olive oil. Chickpeas and sardines turn this smoky Catalan side into a lunch with **protein, fibre and plenty of vitamin C**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the eggplant, pepper and onion with most of the olive oil and a pinch of salt on a large tray, in a single layer.
Roast for 30 to 35 minutes, turning once, until the eggplant is soft and golden and the edges of the pepper and onion are charred.
Whisk the vinegar, lemon juice, crushed garlic, smoked paprika and the last of the olive oil in a bowl.
Toss the vegetables and the chickpeas in the dressing while still warm and let them sit for 5 minutes so they soak it up.
Spoon onto a plate, break the sardines into big pieces over the top and scatter with parsley.
tip: The vegetables are just as good cold the next day, so roast a double tray and keep half in the fridge for up to 3 days. Sherry vinegar is the classic choice. Buy sardines in oil or water, not in a sauce.
ingredients: most of a small can, drained, bones and all

name: Fasolada, Greek white bean soup with spinach and olives
inspiredBy: Greek fasolada, the everyday bean soup often called the national dish, with a handful of greens added
about: Creamy white beans simmered with carrot, onion and tomato until the broth turns velvety, with spinach wilted in at the end and lemon, Kalamata olives and a drizzle of olive oil on top. The beans cover **lots of fibre, iron and folate**, and the lemon helps you absorb that iron.
steps: Drain the soaked beans, cover with fresh water in a large pot, bring to the boil and boil hard for 5 minutes. Drain and rinse. This keeps the soup clean tasting.
Return the beans to the pot with the bay leaf and fresh water to cover by 5 cm. Simmer gently for 30 minutes.
In a pan, warm most of the olive oil and soften the onion and carrot for 6 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste for 1 minute, then tip everything into the beans.
Simmer for another 30 to 40 minutes, until the beans are very soft and the broth has thickened. Mash a few beans against the side of the pot to make it creamy. Salt at the end.
Stir in the spinach and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until wilted. Take off the heat and add the lemon juice, oregano and parsley.
Ladle into bowls and top with the olives and the last of the olive oil. This makes two portions, so pack the second for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Soak the beans on Sunday night. In a pressure cooker the beans take 20 minutes. In a hurry, use canned white beans, drained, about two and a half times the dry weight in the list, and simmer for 25 minutes. It freezes well for 3 months.

name: Roast salmon with lemon-oregano potatoes and shaved fennel
inspiredBy: Greek patates lemonates, potatoes roasted in lemon and oregano, with fish in the Aegean style
about: Tender roast salmon over golden potatoes soaked in lemon, garlic and oregano, with a crisp shaved fennel salad on the side. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the potatoes bring a good hit of potassium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potato wedges on a tray with half the olive oil, half the lemon juice, the crushed garlic, the oregano, a splash of water and half the salt. Roast for 25 minutes, turning once.
Meanwhile, shave the fennel as thin as you can and toss with parsley, a spoon of lemon juice, a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of salt. Leave it to soften slightly.

Rub the salmon with the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Push the potatoes to one side, put the salmon on the tray skin side down and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until it just flakes and is still a little translucent in the middle.
Squeeze the last of the lemon over the salmon and potatoes, and serve with the fennel salad.
tip: Cook the salmon fresh rather than keeping it as leftovers. Wedges pale a little with so little oil; the lemon and a hot oven give them their crust. Mackerel or trout work the same way.

name: Gemista, peppers and tomatoes stuffed with herby rice and beef
inspiredBy: Greek gemista, summer vegetables stuffed with rice and herbs, in the version with minced meat (gemista me kima)
about: Sweet peppers and tomatoes baked until soft around a filling of rice, beef, almonds, parsley and cinnamon that soaks up the tomato juices, with spinach folded into the filling. It is **gluten-free by nature**: the beef brings iron and zinc, and the peppers a good dose of vitamin C. Even better the next day.
steps: Heat the oven to 190°C (375°F). Cut the tops off the peppers and tomatoes and keep them as lids. Scoop the tomato flesh into a bowl and chop it roughly, leaving a sturdy shell.

Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes and chop them. Warm half the olive oil in a pan and cook the onion for 5 minutes. Add the beef and garlic and brown for 5 minutes, breaking it up. Stir in the tomato paste, cinnamon, oregano and the chopped tomato flesh and cook for 3 minutes, then fold in the chopped spinach for the last 2 minutes, until wilted, as in Greek spanakorizo.
Off the heat, stir in the raw rice, toasted almonds, parsley, lemon juice and salt. The rice cooks in the oven, so leave it raw.

Stand the peppers and tomatoes close together in a deep baking dish. Fill each about three quarters full, because the rice swells. Put the lids on and pour 200 ml of water around them, with a drizzle of the last of the olive oil.
Cover with foil and bake for 40 minutes, then uncover and bake for 20 minutes more, until the rice is tender and the tops are blistered.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch, because gemista tastes better the next day.
tip: To keep a weeknight easy, stuff the vegetables in the morning and keep them covered in the fridge, then just bake. Pine nuts are the classic crunch, and almonds do the same job. For a vegetarian version, swap the beef for a can of drained chickpeas.
ingredients: 1 large, tops cut off and saved
2 medium, tops cut off and saved

name: Lentejas, Spanish lentil stew with carrots, spinach and smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Spanish lentejas, the everyday lentil stew, here built on pimentón and a splash of vinegar
about: A comforting pot of brown lentils stewed with carrot, onion, garlic and plenty of smoked paprika, finished with wilted spinach, a splash of sherry vinegar and a firm-yolk fried egg. The lentils and egg carry **protein, iron and folate**, and the vinegar at the end lifts the whole pot.
steps: Warm most of the olive oil in a pot over medium heat and soften the onion and carrot for 7 minutes, until the onion is translucent.
Stir in the garlic, tomato paste and smoked paprika for 1 minute, until the oil turns red and smells smoky. Do not let the paprika scorch.

Add the rinsed lentils, the bay leaf and enough water to cover by 3 cm. Bring to the boil, then simmer gently for 25 to 30 minutes, until the lentils are tender but not falling apart. Top up with water if it gets dry.
Stir in the spinach and the salt and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until wilted.
Finish with the vinegar and taste. Fry an egg in a little olive oil until the white is set, flipping it for the last minute so the yolk is firm, and set it on top of tonight's bowl.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch, and fry its egg fresh when you reheat it, or boil one for 10 minutes the night before and halve it on top.
tip: Use pimentón de la Vera if you can find it. Smoked paprika gives the smoky depth here, so no cured sausage is needed. The stew freezes well for 3 months.
ingredients: brown or green lentils, no need to soak

name: Socca with roasted mackerel and a tomato, olive and parsley salad
inspiredBy: Niçoise socca, the thin chickpea flour pancake baked in a very hot oven, with fish in the Provençal style
about: A golden, crisp-edged chickpea flour flatbread (socca) topped with roasted mackerel and a bright tomato, olive and parsley salad. The chickpea flour is **naturally gluten-free** and high in protein, and the mackerel adds omega-3, vitamin D and B12.
steps: Whisk the chickpea flour with water, about twice the flour's weight, a pinch of salt, black pepper and a spoon of the olive oil until completely smooth. It should be thin, like pouring cream. Let it rest for at least 20 minutes, or all day in the fridge, skimming off any foam.

Heat the oven to 240°C (475°F) with a heavy 25 cm ovenproof pan or a baking tray inside. Mix the tomato, cucumber, olives, onion, parsley, oregano, half the lemon juice and a spoon of olive oil in a bowl.

Rub the mackerel with a little olive oil and the herbes de Provence. Take the pan out, add a spoon of olive oil and swirl it, then pour in the batter (it should be thin, 3 to 4 mm). Bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until the top is spotted brown and the edges are crisp.
While the socca bakes, lay the mackerel skin side up on a small oiled tray and roast it on the shelf below for 6 to 8 minutes, until it just flakes. Squeeze over the rest of the lemon.
Slide the socca out, break it into pieces, and serve with the mackerel and the salad piled on top.
tip: Mix the batter in the morning and the evening is 20 minutes. Socca is best eaten hot and crisp, so bake it right before you sit down. Buy chickpea flour from a gluten-free line if you are celiac, since cross-contact with wheat flour is common in bulk bins.

name: Saffron risotto with shrimp and mussels
inspiredBy: Italian risotto ai frutti di mare, a weekend risotto of the Adriatic and Ligurian coasts
about: Creamy arborio rice stirred slowly in a saffron and mussel broth, finished with sweet shrimp, tender mussels, tomato, lemon and parsley. It is a **weekend dish worth the stirring**, and the shellfish bring zinc, iodine and B12.
steps: Scrub the mussels and pull off any beards. Put them in a wide pot with 150 ml of water, cover and steam over high heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until they open (throw away any that stay shut). Strain the liquid through a fine sieve into a jug, top it up with hot water to about four times the volume of the rice, and keep it warm. Pick the meat from the shells.
Steep the saffron in a few spoons of the hot broth.
Warm half the olive oil in a wide pan and soften the onion and garlic for 5 minutes. Add the rice and stir for 2 minutes, until the grains turn translucent at the edges.

Add the saffron broth, then the hot liquid a ladle at a time, stirring often and letting each addition mostly absorb. Keep going for 18 to 20 minutes in all, until the rice is tender with a little bite and loose and creamy like a thick soup. Stir in the diced tomato for the last 5 minutes, for a sweet, fresh note.
In a hot pan, sear the shrimp in the last of the olive oil for 1 to 2 minutes a side, until pink. Fold the shrimp and mussel meat into the risotto for the last minute.
Take off the heat, stir in the lemon juice, salt to taste and parsley, and let it rest for 1 minute. Serve right away, because risotto does not wait.
tip: Risotto is naturally gluten-free, but check the label if you use boxed fish or seafood stock, since many contain wheat. The mussel broth is plenty here. No fresh mussels? Use clams or a larger handful of shrimp.
ingredients: meat only, about 500 g in the shell

name: Soft polenta with chicken and mushroom ragù and garlicky spinach
inspiredBy: Northern Italian polenta poured onto a wooden board (polenta sulla spianatora), here with a quick ragù of chicken and mushrooms
about: Creamy cornmeal polenta stirred with parmesan and spread under a rich ragù of chicken thigh and mushrooms, with garlicky spinach alongside. It is **comfort food that is gluten-free by tradition**, and the spinach and mushrooms add folate, vitamin K and B vitamins.
steps: Season the chicken with a pinch of salt, pepper and half the herbes de Provence. Brown it in half the olive oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat for 5 minutes, then lift it out.
In the same pan, cook the mushrooms in a single layer until the liquid cooks off and they turn golden, about 8 minutes. Add half the garlic and the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute.
Return the chicken, add 150 ml of water and simmer, covered, for 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender and the sauce is thick and glossy. Finish with a splash of sherry vinegar and taste.

Meanwhile, bring about 4 times the cornmeal's volume of salted water to the boil. Pour the cornmeal in a thin stream, whisking constantly. Turn the heat to low and cook for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring every few minutes and adding a splash of water if it tightens, until thick and creamy. Stir in the parmesan.
Wilt the spinach in a pan with the last of the olive oil and the rest of the garlic for 2 to 3 minutes, until it collapses.
Spread the polenta on a warm plate or board, spoon the ragù over, add the spinach on the side and finish with parsley.
tip: Polenta that is left over sets firm, so slice it and pan-fry in olive oil the next day. Check the label on the cornmeal (buy a gluten-free line if you are celiac). Pre-cooked tube polenta is a fine shortcut, but check its label too.

name: Orange and toasted almonds
inspiredBy: Spanish oranges with almonds, a simple end-of-meal plate
about: A juicy orange and a small handful of toasted almonds. The vitamin C in the orange and the **vitamin E and magnesium** in the almonds make it a snack that really works.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until fragrant, then let them cool.
Peel the orange, cut it into wedges and eat with the almonds.
ingredients: 1 large orange, peeled and cut in wedges

name: Tzatziki with carrot and cucumber sticks
inspiredBy: Greek tzatziki, the garlicky cucumber and yogurt dip
about: Thick yogurt with grated cucumber, garlic, lemon and olive oil, scooped up with crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the vegetables give you something to crunch.
steps: Grate half the cucumber and squeeze it hard in a clean tea towel to get rid of the water.
Stir it into the yogurt with the crushed garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and salt.
Cut the rest of the cucumber and the carrot into sticks and serve with the dip.
ingredients: half grated and squeezed dry, half cut in sticks

name: Crunchy roasted chickpeas with cumin and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish bar snacks, garbanzos fritos, baked rather than fried
about: Canned chickpeas dried and roasted until crisp, tossed in olive oil, cumin and a little lemon. They give you **fibre and plant protein** in a crunchy bite.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Drain the chickpeas and pat them very dry with a towel, because dry chickpeas get crunchy.
Toss with the olive oil, cumin and salt on a tray and roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crisp.
Squeeze over the lemon while they are warm. They are best the same day, and keep crisp for 2 days in a jar left open a crack.
tip: Roast a double batch and eat them over two days.

name: Olive tapenade with fennel and carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Provençal tapenade, the olive paste from Provence
about: A quick tapenade of Kalamata olives, garlic, lemon and olive oil, spooned onto crunchy vegetable sticks. It tastes of Provence, and the olives and oil bring **vitamin E**.
steps: Blitz the olives with the garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and parsley into a rough paste, or chop everything finely by hand.
Spoon into a small bowl and serve with the fennel and carrot sticks.
tip: Use pitted Kalamata or Niçoise olives, rinsed, rather than canned ripe olives. A teaspoon of capers is traditional if you have a jar. Make a small jar on Sunday, it keeps a week in the fridge.

name: Greek yogurt with honey and walnuts
inspiredBy: Greek yiaourti me meli, thick yogurt with honey and walnuts
about: Thick yogurt with a drizzle of honey and crunchy toasted walnuts. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein** and the walnuts bring omega-3.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes and chop them roughly.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, drizzle with honey, scatter over the walnuts and dust with cinnamon.

name: Quick romesco with cucumber and zucchini sticks
inspiredBy: Catalan romesco, the red pepper and almond sauce, made here without the usual bread
about: Roasted red pepper blitzed with almonds, garlic, smoked paprika and vinegar into a smoky dip for crisp vegetable sticks. The pepper brings **vitamin C** and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Roast the pepper halves under a hot grill or at 230°C (450°F) for about 20 minutes, until blackened in places. Cover for 5 minutes, then peel off the worst of the skin. Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 minutes.
Blitz the pepper with the almonds, garlic, vinegar, olive oil, paprika, salt and a splash of water to loosen it into a thick, rough sauce.
Serve with the cucumber and zucchini sticks.
tip: Roast a few extra peppers on Sunday. The sauce keeps 4 days in the fridge.

name: Boiled egg with olives, tomato and smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Spanish tapas, huevo duro with olives
about: A boiled egg dusted with smoked paprika, with olives and tomato wedges on the side. The egg brings **protein and choline**, in a snack you can make ahead.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes, until the yolk is firm. Chill in cold water, then peel.
Halve the egg and dust with smoked paprika and salt, then serve with the olives and tomato.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday; they keep 5 days in the shell.

name: Sardines with shaved fennel, lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish and Portuguese tinned sardine tapas
about: Good canned sardines laid over crisp shaved fennel with lemon, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil. The soft bones are edible and a real source of **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Shave the fennel as thin as you can and pile it on a plate.
Lay the sardines on top, then squeeze over the lemon, drizzle with olive oil and add parsley and a grind of pepper.
tip: Buy sardines in oil or water rather than a flavoured sauce. Not a sardine fan? Mackerel or anchovies from a tin work too.

name: Tomato with parmesan and basil
inspiredBy: Italian tomato and cheese plates, like a caprese with parmesan
about: Ripe tomato slices with shavings of parmesan, torn basil and olive oil. It tastes like summer, and the parmesan brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Lay the tomato slices on a plate and sprinkle with a pinch of salt.
Shave the parmesan over the top, tear on the basil and drizzle with olive oil.

name: Tuna and chickpea salad with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Italian tonno e ceci, a quick pantry salad
about: Canned tuna and chickpeas tossed with red onion, parsley, lemon and olive oil. It is a small, savoury snack with **plenty of protein and fibre**.
steps: Tip the chickpeas into a bowl and mash a few with a fork so the dressing clings.
Add the tuna, onion and parsley, then dress with the lemon juice, olive oil, salt and pepper and toss gently.
tip: It keeps a day in the fridge.

name: Garlic shrimp with lemon (gambas al ajillo)
inspiredBy: Spanish gambas al ajillo, sizzling garlic shrimp from the tapas bar
about: Shrimp seared in a little olive oil with plenty of garlic, smoked paprika and parsley, finished with lemon. They are quick, low in saturated fat and full of **protein, iodine and selenium**.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan over medium heat and soften the garlic for 1 minute, until fragrant but not brown.
Add the shrimp and the paprika and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until pink and curled.
Take off the heat, squeeze over the lemon, add the parsley and salt, and eat straight away.
tip: Keep a bag of frozen peeled shrimp and thaw it in cold water for 10 minutes.

name: Pear with walnuts and honey
inspiredBy: Italian and Greek fruit and nut plates
about: A ripe pear cut in wedges with toasted walnuts, a drizzle of honey and a pinch of cinnamon. Simple, sweet and crunchy, with **fibre and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Fan the pear wedges on a plate, scatter the walnuts, drizzle with honey and dust with cinnamon.

name: Besan chilla with kale, tomato and green chutney yogurt
inspiredBy: Gujarati and Maharashtrian besan puda (chilla), the everyday chickpea-flour pancake, with kale in place of the usual spinach or methi
about: Savoury chickpea-flour pancakes, golden and a little crisp at the edges, with finely chopped kale, onion and green chili folded into the batter. They come with a cool cilantro and lemon chutney yogurt and fresh tomato on top. The besan and yogurt together bring **a good dose of protein** to the first meal of the day, and the kale adds calcium and folate.
steps: Whisk the besan with the turmeric, ajwain, Kashmiri chili and about half the salt. Pour in enough cold water, a little at a time, to make a smooth batter about as thick as thin pancake batter. Leave it for 10 minutes so the flour swells.

Stir the sesame seeds, kale, onion, green chili, ginger, half the cilantro and half the tomato into the batter. It looks like a lot of kale, but it wilts into the batter; chop it very fine so the chillas hold together when you flip them.
Make the chutney yogurt by blitzing the rest of the cilantro with a little green chili, the lemon juice, the cumin and the remaining salt and a splash of water, then stirring it into the yogurt.

Heat a nonstick pan over medium heat and brush it lightly with oil. Pour in a ladle of batter and spread it into a round about 15 cm wide. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until the edges lift and the underside is golden and speckled.
Drizzle a little oil around the edge, flip, and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more, until cooked through with no raw patches. Repeat to use all the batter (you will get 2 or 3 chillas).
Pile the rest of the tomato on the chillas and serve them with the chutney yogurt.
tip: Whisk the batter the night before and keep it in the fridge, and breakfast takes 10 minutes: stir in the kale just before you cook. Kale stands in for the fenugreek (methi) leaves that are traditional. Buy besan that lists only chickpeas on the label, and a gluten-free line if you are celiac, since some mills share equipment with wheat.
ingredients: stems out, about 2 big handfuls, chopped very fine
half in the batter, half chopped on top
finely chopped, a little saved for the chutney
half in the batter, half in the chutney yogurt
plain, for the green chutney yogurt
white sesame, stirred into the batter

name: Vegetable ven pongal with pepper, cashews and peanut-sesame chutney
inspiredBy: Tamil ven pongal, the temple and tiffin-shop breakfast of rice and moong dal, made here with whole green moong and grated carrot, so it is heartier and a little greener than the white original
about: A soft, ghee-scented pot of rice, whole moong and grated carrot cooked down until creamy, then crowned with a sizzling tempering of black pepper, cumin, cashews and curry leaves. The coconut, peanut and sesame chutney gives it a bright, nutty edge. The moong, peanuts and sesame make it a **breakfast with protein that lasts** to lunch.
steps: Dry-roast the moong in the dry pot for 2 minutes, until it smells nutty (skip this if you soaked it overnight), then rinse it with the rice until the water runs mostly clear.

Add the carrot, the ginger, half the salt and about 3 times as much water as rice and moong. Pressure cook for 4 whistles, or simmer covered for about 40 minutes, until everything is soft. Stir in the milk and simmer for 3 minutes, mashing lightly with the back of a spoon, until creamy and porridge-like. Loosen with hot water if it feels stiff.

While it cooks, dry-roast the peanuts and the sesame seeds in a small pan until they smell toasty. Blitz them with the coconut, green chili, lemon juice, the rest of the salt and a splash of water into a coarse chutney.

Warm the ghee in your smallest pan or a tadka ladle over medium-low heat and fry the cashews and almonds until golden. Add the pepper, cumin and curry leaves and let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then pour the whole thing over the pongal.
Serve the pongal hot, with the chutney.
tip: Soak the moong and cook the rice and dal in a pressure cooker or rice cooker the night before, then warm it with a splash of water while you make the tempering, and breakfast takes 10 minutes. Traditional ven pongal often has a pinch of hing; if you want it, buy a gluten-free brand, since most hing is cut with wheat flour.
ingredients: short or long grain white rice
whole green moong, soaked if you can
fresh or frozen, for the chutney
dry-roasted in a pan, for the chutney
skim milk, stirred in at the end

name: Idli with vegetable sambar and coconut-sesame chutney
inspiredBy: Tamil idli with sambar and chutney, the weekend tiffin
about: Soft, steamed idlis from a fermented rice and urad batter, with a tangy, spiced sambar full of carrot, kale and tomato and a green coconut and sesame chutney. This is the classic Tamil tiffin and naturally gluten-free; kale stands in for the greens many families add to sambar. The urad and toor dal bring **protein, folate and iron**, and the long fermentation makes the idlis light.
steps: Start the batter the day before. Rinse the rice with the fenugreek seeds and soak it in plenty of water for 4 to 6 hours. Soak the urad dal separately for the same time.

Drain and grind the urad dal with a little cold water until it is light, fluffy and pale. Grind the rice a little coarser, so it feels slightly gritty between your fingers. Mix the two with half the salt, cover loosely and leave in a warm spot for 8 to 12 hours (in a cool kitchen allow 18 to 24 hours, or put it in the oven with only the light on), until the batter has risen, smells pleasantly sour and is full of bubbles.
Meanwhile, cook the toor dal with plenty of water until completely soft, about 12 minutes in a pressure cooker or 35 minutes in a pot, and mash it.

Simmer the carrot, kale, onion and tomato with the tamarind, sambar powder, the remaining salt and about 2 cups of water for 12 minutes, until the vegetables are tender. Stir in the mashed dal and simmer for 5 more minutes.
Warm the oil in a small pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the hing and curry leaves, and pour the sizzling oil into the sambar.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until they smell nutty. Blend them with the coconut, green chili, cilantro, a pinch of salt and a splash of water into a smooth chutney.

Lightly grease the idli moulds, fill them with batter (do not stir the batter first, or you will lose the air) and steam for 12 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean. Rest for 2 minutes before unmoulding.
Serve the idlis with the sambar and chutney. Keep the second portion of idlis, sambar and chutney for tomorrow: re-steam the idlis for 3 minutes and loosen the sambar with a splash of water.
tip: Make two or three times the batter: a single batch is too little for most blenders and ferments less reliably. Soak the rice and urad on Friday morning, grind them after work and leave the batter in the oven with the light on overnight. Cooked idlis freeze well for a month. Check the label on the sambar powder and the hing, since both can be cut with wheat flour; skip the hing if you are unsure, and the sambar is still good.
ingredients: whole or split white urad dal
sambar powder, check the label for wheat

name: Gujarati tuvar dal with brown basmati, cabbage-carrot sambharo and chaas
inspiredBy: a Gujarati dal-bhat plate, with tuvar dal, sambharo and chaas
about: A tangy Gujarati dal with tomato and peanuts, spooned over nutty brown basmati and served with a quick, crunchy cabbage and carrot sambharo and a glass of spiced chaas. The sambharo is lightly sizzled in a mustard seed tempering and finished with lemon. The dal and chaas together bring **protein, folate and calcium** in one plate.
steps: Rinse the dal and simmer it with the turmeric, the tomato, the peanuts and plenty of water until completely soft, about 12 minutes in a pressure cooker or 35 minutes in a pot. Whisk it smooth.
Cook the brown basmati in plenty of salted water until tender, about 25 minutes, then drain.
Return the dal to a low heat. Stir in half the lemon juice, half the salt and a splash of water if it is too thick. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Warm half the oil in a small pan. Add the cumin, cloves, cinnamon, Kashmiri chili, hing and curry leaves, let them sizzle for 20 seconds and pour over the dal.

For the sambharo, warm the rest of the oil, add the mustard seeds and the green chili and let them pop. Toss in the cabbage and carrot for 1 to 2 minutes, only until the colour brightens and they are still crunchy. Season with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Whisk the yogurt with a glass of cold water, a pinch of salt and the cilantro to make the chaas.
Serve the dal over the rice, with the sambharo alongside and the chaas to drink.
tip: Use a pressure cooker and the dal takes 12 minutes. A pinch of jaggery gives the Gujarati sweet and sour. Hing is often cut with wheat flour, so buy a gluten-free brand or leave it out of the tempering; add a little more cumin instead.

name: Neer dosa with Kerala egg roast
inspiredBy: Mangalorean neer dosa, served with a Kerala-style egg roast
about: Paper-thin, lacy rice crepes that need no fermenting, with a dark, glossy Kerala egg roast of onion, tomato, pepper and curry leaves. The dosas are soft and a little chewy, ideal for mopping up the masala. The eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel. Cut a few shallow slits in each so the masala gets in.
Blitz the coconut with a little water, then whisk it into the rice flour with a pinch of salt and enough water to make a very thin batter, like milk. Rest it for 15 minutes.
For the roast, warm the oil in a wide pan and fry the onion with a pinch of salt for 8 to 10 minutes, until deep golden. Add the garlic, ginger, green chili and curry leaves for a minute.

Stir in the Kashmiri chili, coriander, pepper, fennel, turmeric and garam masala, then the tomato. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until it breaks down into a thick, dark masala and the oil shows at the edges.
Add the eggs, turn them in the masala for 2 minutes and finish with the cilantro and a grind of pepper.

Heat a nonstick pan over medium heat. Stir the batter (it settles) and pour a ladle in a thin swirl, tilting the pan to coat it. Cover for about 1 minute, until the dosa is set and lacy. Do not flip. Fold it and repeat to make 3 or 4.
Serve the dosas hot, with the egg roast.
tip: The batter should pour like milk: if the first dosa tears, whisk in a spoonful more water. Check the label on the garam masala, or use a pinch each of cinnamon and black pepper instead. Make the egg roast the night before (it tastes better the next day), and lunch is just the dosas, about 10 minutes.

name: Maharashtrian egg bhurji with jowar bhakri
inspiredBy: Maharashtrian anda bhurji with jowar bhakri
about: Soft scrambled eggs with onion, tomato, green peas and ginger in the Maharashtrian dhaba style, scooped up with a hot, rustic til-flecked jowar bhakri, a crunchy peanut chutney and a squeeze of lemon. Jowar is a naturally gluten-free millet with a sweet, nutty flavour. The eggs, peas and peanuts bring **protein, choline and fibre**.
steps: Make the bhakri dough first. Stir the jowar flour with the sesame seeds and a pinch of salt and pour in just-boiled water a little at a time, stirring with a spoon, until it comes together. Cover for 5 minutes, then knead with wet hands until smooth and soft. Divide into 2 balls.
Crush the peanuts coarsely with the garlic, a little of the Kashmiri chili and a pinch of salt in a mortar or blender for a quick shenga chutney, and set it aside.

Pat each ball into a thin round about 12 cm wide, with wet fingers on a sheet of parchment or a damp cloth. Cook on a hot dry pan for 1 minute, flip, sprinkle the top with a few drops of water, flip again and cook until the bhakri puffs in places and is speckled. Wrap in a clean towel to keep soft.
Warm the oil in a pan and add the cumin. When it sizzles, add the onion, green chili and ginger and cook for 5 minutes, until the onion is soft and golden.
Stir in the turmeric, Kashmiri chili, tomato and peas. Cook for 4 minutes, until the tomato softens and the peas are tender.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt, pour them in and stir slowly until just set but still soft and glossy, about 2 minutes. Fold in the cilantro.
Serve the bhurji with the bhakri, the chutney, the raw onion slices and the lemon wedges.
tip: Bhakri is best fresh, but it keeps wrapped in a towel for a few hours, and you can re-crisp it on a dry pan. If your bhakri cracks at the edges, the dough was too dry: add a splash of hot water and knead again.
ingredients: jowar flour (whole sorghum, ground), certified gluten-free if you are celiac
two thirds finely chopped, the rest sliced raw for serving
white sesame, kneaded into the dough

name: Kolhapuri-style chicken with jowar bhakri and onion-cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Kolhapuri tambda rassa, the red chicken curry of southern Maharashtra, with a lighter masala
about: A red, fragrant chicken curry in the Kolhapuri style, with roasted coconut, onion and a toasted spice paste, eaten the Maharashtrian way with a hot jowar bhakri and a cool salad of raw onion, cucumber and lemon. The chicken and jowar bring **protein, iron and B vitamins**, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Toss the chicken with the turmeric, half the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and half the ginger and garlic. Leave it for 15 minutes.

Toast the coconut in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until it browns at the edges. Add the sesame seeds, Kashmiri chili, coriander, cumin, pepper, cinnamon and cloves for 1 minute more, until fragrant, then tip it all into a blender with a third of the onion and a splash of water and blend into a thick, red paste.

Warm the oil in a heavy pot and cook most of the rest of the onion, keeping a handful for serving, for 8 to 10 minutes, until deeply golden. Add the remaining ginger and garlic for a minute, then the paste. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the oil separates and it smells toasted.

Add the tomato and cook for 5 minutes, then the chicken. Brown it for 3 minutes, pour in about 2 cups of hot water and the rest of the salt, cover and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until the chicken is tender and the gravy is thin, red and glossy.

While it simmers, stir the jowar flour with a pinch of salt, add just-boiled water a little at a time until a dough forms, cover for 5 minutes, then knead with wet hands until smooth. Divide into 4 balls (2 per portion). Press each ball into a thin round between oiled sheets of plastic, or use a tortilla press, cook on a hot dry pan for 1 minute, flip, sprinkle with water, flip again and cook until it puffs in places. Wrap in a towel.
Toss the cucumber and the raw sliced onion with the remaining lemon juice, a pinch of salt and half the cilantro. Finish the chicken with the rest of the cilantro.
Serve the chicken with 2 bhakri and the salad. Pack the second portion, with its bhakri, for tomorrow: warm the curry, and re-crisp the bhakri on a dry pan with a sprinkle of water.
tip: Toast and blend the spice paste on Sunday and it keeps 3 days in the fridge, which takes about 10 minutes off a weeknight. Kashmiri chili gives the red colour more than heat; for real Kolhapuri fire, add a fresh green chili or a pinch of hot red chili powder. If you are celiac, buy jowar flour from a gluten-free line and check any ready-made Kolhapuri masala for wheat fillers.
ingredients: jowar flour (whole sorghum, ground), certified gluten-free if you are celiac
a handful sliced raw for serving

name: Goan-style mackerel curry with brown basmati and okra
inspiredBy: Goan xitt kodi (fish curry rice), with brown rice and okra
about: Mackerel pieces gently poached in a tangy Goan curry with a little coconut with Kashmiri chili, tamarind and okra, over nutty brown basmati. It is bright, red and well balanced, and the fish stays soft because it only simmers for a few minutes. The mackerel carries **omega-3 fats, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Rinse the brown basmati and cook it in plenty of salted water until tender, about 25 minutes. Drain and keep warm.
Blend the coconut, half the onion, the garlic, ginger, Kashmiri chili, coriander, cumin, turmeric and pepper with a splash of water into a smooth red paste.

Warm the oil in a wide pan and cook the rest of the onion for 6 minutes until golden. Add the okra and cook it on medium-high heat for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the stickiness cooks off.
Stir in the paste and cook for 4 minutes, until it deepens in colour. Add the tomato, the tamarind and about a cup and a half of water and simmer for 8 minutes.

Season the fish with the salt and lower the pieces into the gravy. Cover and simmer very gently for 6 to 8 minutes, until the fish is just opaque. Shake the pan instead of stirring, so the pieces do not break.
Let it rest for 5 minutes, scatter the cilantro on top and serve with the rice.
tip: Goan curry tastes better after a rest, so you can make it before you shower. Any firm fish works if you cannot find mackerel, but you lose the omega-3.
ingredients: fillets or steaks, bones out, cut in pieces

name: Gujarati kadhi with foxtail millet and moong khichdi
inspiredBy: Gujarati kadhi khichdi, the Sunday-supper comfort bowl, with foxtail millet in place of some of the rice
about: A soft, comforting pot of foxtail millet and moong dal khichdi with peas and carrot, under a tangy, silky Gujarati kadhi of yogurt and besan tempered with mustard, cumin and curry leaves. A few drops of ghee on top is how it is eaten. The moong and yogurt bring **protein, folate and calcium**, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the millet and moong together (soak the moong overnight if you can). Put them in a pot with the peas, carrot, half the turmeric, half the salt and about 4 cups of water per cup of grain. Pressure cook for 3 whistles (5 or 6 if the moong was not soaked), or simmer covered for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring now and then, until everything is soft and porridge-like.
For the kadhi, whisk the yogurt, besan, the rest of the turmeric, the rest of the salt and about 2 cups of water in a pot until completely smooth, with no lumps of besan.
Warm the oil and half the ghee in a small pan. Add the mustard seeds, cumin, cloves, cinnamon, fenugreek, ginger, green chili and curry leaves and let them sizzle for 30 seconds.

Stir the tempering into the kadhi and heat gently over medium-low heat, stirring often, for 15 to 20 minutes, until it thickens slightly and loses its raw besan smell. Do not boil hard or it can split.

Spoon the khichdi into bowls, ladle the kadhi over, add the remaining ghee and the cilantro. Pack the second portion for tomorrow: the kadhi thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: A pinch of jaggery and a squeeze of lemon at the end gives the sweet and sour balance that Gujarati kadhi is known for. Whisk the besan into cold yogurt before it ever goes near the heat. The khichdi simmers while you make the kadhi, so both are ready together.

name: Kerala kadala curry with puttu
inspiredBy: Kerala puttu and kadala curry, the classic Kerala breakfast, made as a dinner
about: Chickpeas simmered in a roasted-coconut gravy with fennel, pepper and curry leaves, served with a little puttu, steamed rice flour and coconut that soaks up every drop. The chickpeas bring **protein, fibre, iron and folate**, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Soak the kala chana overnight, then pressure cook them with a little salt until completely tender, about 30 minutes under pressure or 1 to 1½ hours in a pot. If you soaked the week's batch, cook it all now and keep the rest in the fridge for the sundal and roasted chickpeas. Canned chickpeas work too, though they are softer, at about 2.5 times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Keep a cup of the cooking water, or use plain water.

Toast most of the coconut in a dry pan for 4 to 5 minutes, until golden brown and fragrant. Add the Kashmiri chili, coriander, fennel, pepper, cinnamon and clove for the last minute. Blend with the ginger, garlic and a splash of water into a thick, dark paste.
Warm half the oil in a pot and cook the onion for 8 minutes until golden. Add the turmeric and the tomato and cook for 5 minutes, until the tomato breaks down.

Stir in the paste, the chickpeas, the salt and the reserved cooking water. Simmer for 15 minutes, until the gravy is thick and clings to the chickpeas, mashing a few against the pot to thicken it. Stir in the kale for the last 3 minutes, until just wilted.
Warm the rest of the oil in a small pan. Add the mustard seeds and curry leaves, let them crackle for 20 seconds and pour over the curry.

For the puttu, dry-roast the rice flour in a pan for 5 minutes, stirring, until it smells nutty and feels dry, then cool it and rub in a pinch of salt and just enough water, sprinkled in a little at a time, to make damp, crumbly flour that holds together when squeezed. Rub it through a sieve. Layer the flour and the last of the coconut in a puttu maker, or a small steaming basket lined with a clean cloth, and steam for 8 to 10 minutes.
Serve the puttu with the kadala curry. Pack the second portion for tomorrow: re-steam the puttu for 3 minutes and warm the curry with a splash of water.
tip: The puttu is a small side here and the kala chana are the meal; at the Light size it is a few spoonfuls, so steam it in a cup. Kala chana (brown chickpeas) is the traditional bean; soak it overnight, since it takes a little longer than the pale kind. No puttu maker? Press the damp flour and coconut into a heatproof cup and steam it in a large pot with a lid.
ingredients: soaked overnight and cooked (see the steps)
fine white rice flour, for the puttu
fresh or frozen, most for the gravy, a little for the puttu

name: Kerala sardine roast with kappa and kale thoran
inspiredBy: Kerala mathi fry with kappa, the toddy-shop pairing, with a kale thoran in place of cheera (amaranth leaves)
about: Fresh sardines marinated in tamarind, pepper and Kashmiri chili and roasted until crisp at the edges, with kappa (mashed cassava) and a quick kale thoran with coconut. It is robust and sour-hot, the kind of plate eaten in toddy shops. The sardines bring **omega-3 fats, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Peel the cassava, cut it into chunks and cut out the woody core. Boil in salted water for 15 to 20 minutes, until a fork goes in easily. Drain well.

Mash the garlic, ginger, tamarind, Kashmiri chili, turmeric, pepper, fennel and half the salt with a teaspoon of the oil into a paste. Rub it over the sardines, inside and out, and leave for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Lay the sardines on a lined tray, brush them with a little more of the oil and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, turning once, until the skin is browned and the flesh flakes. Or pan-fry them in a hot pan for 3 minutes a side.
Crush the hot cassava coarsely with a fork, with a quarter of the coconut, a pinch of salt and the green chili, finely chopped, until it is rough and fluffy rather than smooth.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the oil, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the onion and curry leaves for 4 minutes. Add the kale and stir for 3 to 4 minutes, until just tender and still bright green. Stir in the rest of the coconut and a pinch of salt.
Serve the sardines with the kappa, the thoran and a squeeze of lemon.
tip: Cassava is sold peeled and frozen in many supermarkets, which saves the work. Frozen whole sardines from a Portuguese, Italian or Asian grocer work well; allow 4 to 6 small ones. If you cannot find sardines, mackerel works with a little more roasting time.
ingredients: whole, cleaned and gutted by your fishmonger

name: Chicken dum biryani with brown basmati, egg and cucumber raita
inspiredBy: Hyderabadi dum biryani, with brown basmati and a lighter hand with the ghee
about: Marinated chicken layered with brown basmati, golden fried onion, almonds, mint and saffron, sealed and steamed on the lowest heat until the grains drink up the juices. It is the weekend showpiece, fragrant with whole spices, with a cooling cucumber raita on the side. The chicken, egg and yogurt bring **protein, choline and B vitamins**, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Mix the chicken with most of the yogurt, the ginger, garlic, lemon juice, Kashmiri chili, turmeric, garam masala and half the salt. Leave it for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool and peel them. Soak the saffron in 2 tablespoons of warm water. Rinse the rice and parboil it in a large pot of salted water with the bay leaf, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon for 18 to 20 minutes, until it is about three-quarters cooked and still has a firm bite. Drain.

Warm the ghee and oil in a heavy pot and cook the onion over medium heat for about 20 minutes, with a splash of water if it catches, until deep golden and soft. Lift half of it out, along with the almonds fried for the last minute, and set aside for the top.
Add the chicken and its marinade to the pot and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, until the chicken is half cooked and the sauce has thickened.

Spread the parboiled rice over the chicken. Top with the reserved onion and almonds, the cilantro and mint and the saffron water, then sprinkle 3 tablespoons of hot water over the rice. Cover with foil and a tight lid and cook on the lowest heat for 25 minutes, then rest off the heat for 10 minutes without opening.
Meanwhile, stir the grated cucumber, the last of the yogurt, the cumin and a pinch of salt together for the raita.

Fold the rice up from the bottom to mix the layers, halve the eggs and set them on top, and serve with the raita. Pack the second portion for tomorrow: biryani reheats well in a covered pan or the microwave with a splash of water.
tip: This is a chicken-forward biryani, so the raita and egg complete the plate. Use whole spices rather than a packet biryani masala if you can, since masala mixes sometimes carry wheat fillers. Parboil the brown basmati until it is just firm; it finishes in the steam. A flat pan or tawa under the pot keeps the bottom from catching during the dum.
ingredients: plain, about two thirds for the marinade, the rest for the raita
one hard-boiled egg per portion, for the top

name: Salmon curry with beetroot curry, kale mallung and pol sambol
inspiredBy: a Sri Lankan rice and curry plate: a mild fish curry in coconut milk, beetroot curry, kale mallung and pol sambol
about: A gently spiced Sri Lankan-style coconut curry with tamarind and curry leaves, here with salmon in place of the usual tuna or white fish, beside a deep-pink beetroot curry, a quick kale mallung and a punchy fresh coconut sambol. A small plate of rice soaks up the gravy. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats, vitamin D and B12**, and the beets and kale add folate.
steps: Rinse the rice and cook it in plenty of salted water until tender, about 25 minutes, then drain.

Toast the coriander, cumin, fennel and fenugreek in a dry pan for a minute, then grind with the pepper, cinnamon and cardamom into a rough curry powder. Blitz most of the coconut with half a cup of warm water, then strain or leave as is, for a quick coconut milk.

For the beetroot curry, warm half the oil in a small pot and add the mustard seeds. When they pop, add half the curry leaves and a third of the onion, then the beet, a pinch of turmeric, a pinch of salt and about half of the coconut milk with a splash of water. Simmer, covered, for 15 to 18 minutes, until the beet is tender and the sauce is thick and pink.

For the pol sambol, a small, fiery condiment for the rice, mash the coconut with the raw onion you set aside, half the green chili, the lemon juice, the Kashmiri chili and a pinch of salt using your fingers until it is crumbly and rust-red.

For the fish curry, warm the rest of the oil in a wide pan and cook the remaining onion, garlic and curry leaves for 5 minutes. Stir in the ground spices, the turmeric and the tamarind, then add the rest of the coconut milk, the rest of the chili and about half a cup of water. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Slip in the salmon, season with the salt, cover and cook gently for 6 to 8 minutes, until just opaque. Do not stir; tilt the pan to baste.

For the kale mallung, toss the kale in a hot dry pan with a pinch of salt, a pinch of turmeric and the rest of the green chili for 2 minutes, until bright and just wilted, then fold in a spoonful of the sambol.
Serve the fish curry with the rice, the beetroot curry, the mallung and the rest of the sambol.
tip: Salmon is not a traditional Sri Lankan fish, so treat this as a friendly twist: skipjack or mackerel are the usual choices. A sprig of pandan, if you find it, makes the curry smell like home. Eat the sambol the day it is made.
ingredients: skinless fillet, cut in large chunks
stems out, shredded very fine, for the mallung
fresh or frozen, a spoonful for the sambol, the rest blended into coconut milk
sliced, about a third kept raw for the sambol

name: Guava and pomegranate chaat
inspiredBy: Indian street-cart guava chaat, with pomegranate
about: Crisp guava chunks and ruby pomegranate seeds tossed with lemon, chaat masala and a little roasted peanut for crunch. It is sweet, sour, salty and hot in one bite. Guava brings **more than a day of vitamin C** in one bowl.
steps: Toss the guava and pomegranate seeds with the lemon juice, the chaat masala and a pinch of salt.
If your peanuts are raw, toast them in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes. Scatter the peanuts and cilantro over the top just before eating, so they stay crunchy.
tip: Check the label on the chaat masala, or make your own with a pinch of ground cumin, black salt and a little amchur.

name: Boiled peanut sundal with coconut
inspiredBy: Tamil sundal, the temple and beach-stall snack of boiled legumes
about: Warm boiled peanuts tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and green chili, with fresh coconut and a squeeze of lemon. It is the Chennai beach snack, soft and savoury and surprisingly filling. The peanuts bring **protein and vitamin E**.
steps: Soak the peanuts overnight in water. Drain, then pressure cook with salted water for 3 whistles, or simmer for 40 to 45 minutes, until tender with no raw bite, and drain.
Warm the oil, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the green chili and curry leaves for 20 seconds.
Toss the peanuts in the tempering with the coconut and lemon juice.
tip: Soak and boil the peanuts the night before; they keep 4 to 5 days in the fridge. Temper them fresh.

name: Oven-roasted masala chickpeas
inspiredBy: roasted chana, the everyday crunchy snack of North and West India
about: Chickpeas roasted in the oven until crisp outside and soft inside, tossed with chaat masala, Kashmiri chili and lemon. They are the crunchy snack that stands in for packaged namkeen. The chickpeas bring **protein, fibre and iron**.
steps: Use the kala chana you cooked for Friday's kadala curry, or canned chickpeas at about 2.5 times the dry weight, drained, rinsed and patted very dry.
Toss them with the oil, the Kashmiri chili, the cumin and a pinch of salt and spread them on a tray in a single layer.
Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp and golden. Toss with the chaat masala and the lemon juice while still warm.
tip: They are crispest on the day. Dry the chickpeas well before roasting, and leave them in the turned-off oven for 10 minutes for extra crunch.

name: Masala chaas
inspiredBy: Gujarati chaas and South Indian neer mor
about: Thin, cooling buttermilk-style yogurt whisked with roasted cumin, ginger, curry leaves and cilantro. It is the Gujarati and South Indian answer to a heavy meal. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with about a cup of cold water until smooth and pourable.
Stir in the ginger, green chili, cilantro, cumin and salt.
Tear in the curry leaves and serve very cold.
tip: Add a squeeze of lemon in summer, or a pinch of black salt for a stronger, funkier finish.

name: Saffron and cardamom shrikhand with papaya and pomegranate
inspiredBy: Gujarati and Maharashtrian shrikhand, lighter and sweetened with fruit
about: Thick Greek yogurt sweetened with ripe papaya, scented with saffron and cardamom and topped with ruby pomegranate seeds. It is the Gujarati and Maharashtrian dessert, lightened. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the almonds add a little crunch.
steps: Soak the saffron in a spoonful of warm water.
Whisk the yogurt with the mashed papaya, cardamom and saffron water until smooth and creamy.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the pomegranate seeds and almonds.
tip: Sweeten with a teaspoon of honey or jaggery if the papaya is not very ripe.

name: Masala boiled eggs
inspiredBy: Indian street-stall masala eggs
about: Hard-boiled eggs halved and dusted with Kashmiri chili, black pepper and a few drops of lemon, with cilantro on top. It is the simplest road-side snack, and it keeps you full. The eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel.
Halve the eggs and sprinkle with the Kashmiri chili, pepper, salt and lemon juice, then top with cilantro.
tip: Boil a few on Sunday; they keep 5 days in the shell.

name: Cabbage and carrot kosambari with toasted sesame
inspiredBy: Karnataka kosambari, here made with sesame instead of soaked dal
about: Crisp shredded cabbage and sweet grated carrot tossed with lemon, mustard seeds and toasted sesame, in the spirit of a Karnataka kosambari. It is crunchy, tangy and refreshing. The carrot brings **plenty of vitamin A**, and the toasted sesame adds crunch.
steps: Toss the cabbage, carrot and green chili with the lemon juice and salt.
Dry-roast the sesame seeds in a small pan, then dry-fry the mustard seeds for 20 seconds until they pop.
Fold the sesame, mustard seeds and cilantro into the salad just before serving.
tip: Dress it just before serving so the cabbage stays crunchy.

name: Tandoori-style chicken bites
inspiredBy: North Indian chicken tikka
about: Little chunks of chicken thigh marinated in yogurt, lemon, ginger, garlic and Kashmiri chili, roasted until browned at the edges. They are the high-protein snack for a hungrier day. The chicken brings **protein, zinc and B6**.
steps: Mix the chicken with the yogurt, ginger, garlic, lemon juice, Kashmiri chili, turmeric, cumin, salt and oil and leave it for at least 20 minutes.
Thread onto skewers or spread on a tray and roast at 230 C (450 F) for 15 to 18 minutes, turning once, until browned and cooked through.
Rest for 3 minutes and serve warm.
tip: Marinate in the morning and it takes 15 minutes in the oven at snack time.
ingredients: skinless thigh, cut in small chunks

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil sundal
about: Soft chickpeas tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and green chili, with fresh coconut and lemon. It is the humble protein snack of Tamil festivals. The chickpeas bring **protein, fibre and iron**.
steps: Use the kala chana you cooked for Friday's kadala curry, or canned, drained and rinsed.
Warm the oil, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the green chili and curry leaves.
Toss the chickpeas through the tempering with the coconut and lemon juice.
tip: A pinch of black pepper wakes it up.

name: Haldi doodh with almonds and cardamom
inspiredBy: North Indian and Gujarati haldi doodh, with ground almonds as in badam doodh
about: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, black pepper and cardamom and whisked with finely ground almonds until it is silky. It is the Gujarati and Maharashtrian bedtime cup, and a snack that feels like a hug. The milk brings **calcium and B12** to the day, and the almonds add a little vitamin E.
steps: Grind the almonds as fine as you can, with a spoonful of the milk, into a smooth paste.
Warm the rest of the milk with the turmeric, pepper and cardamom over medium-low heat for about 5 minutes, until steaming, without letting it boil over.
Whisk in the almond paste and heat for 1 more minute. Pour into a mug.
tip: Stir in a teaspoon of jaggery or honey if you like it sweet. Skip the pepper for children.

name: Egg chaat with onion, tomato and lemon
inspiredBy: Indian street-stall anda chaat
about: Chopped hard-boiled eggs tossed with red onion, tomato, cilantro, lemon and chaat masala, with a few roasted peanuts for crunch. It is tangy, salty and fresh, and it takes ten minutes. The eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool them in cold water, peel and chop roughly.
Toss the eggs gently with the onion, tomato, cilantro, lemon juice, chaat masala, pepper and salt.
Scatter the peanuts (toasted in a dry pan if raw) on top just before eating.
tip: Boil the eggs a day or two ahead and the chaat takes 3 minutes.

name: Black bean and egg breakfast plate with avocado, lime crema and tomato salsa
inspiredBy: Inspired by Mexican huevos and frijoles breakfasts
about: Two firm-cooked eggs on a plate with warm black beans, creamy avocado, a spoonful of lime yogurt crema and a quick tomato salsa. It is a proper breakfast with **protein, fibre, folate and choline**.
steps: The night before, put the eggs in a small pot, cover with cold water and bring to the boil. Simmer for 10 minutes so the yolks are completely firm, cool under cold running water and keep them in their shells in the fridge. Peel them in the morning.
In the morning, warm the black beans in a small pan with the cumin and a splash of water for 3 to 4 minutes, until steaming hot.
Wash the tomatoes, cilantro and avocado. Stir the tomatoes, onion, cilantro, half the lime juice and salt together for the salsa.
Slice the eggs and the avocado. Plate them with the warm beans and the salsa. Stir the yogurt with a squeeze of the lime juice and a pinch of salt and spoon it over the beans as a quick crema.
tip: Boil the eggs the night before and this is a 10-minute weekday breakfast.

name: Yogurt and fruit breakfast plate with toasted oats and walnuts
about: A bowl of thick Greek yogurt with sliced kiwi, blueberries and a handful of toasted oats and walnuts for crunch. It is cool, quick and brings **protein, calcium, vitamin C and omega-3**.
steps: Toast the oats and walnuts with the cinnamon in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, stirring, until golden and fragrant. Tip them onto a plate to cool.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl. Peel and slice the kiwi, and rinse the blueberries.
Arrange the fruit around the yogurt and scatter the toasted oats and walnuts over the top.
tip: Toast a few days of oats and walnuts at once and keep them in a jar.

name: Cinnamon buckwheat porridge with stewed apple and walnuts
about: Creamy buckwheat simmered in milk with cinnamon, finished with a spoonful of Greek yogurt and topped with soft stewed apple and crunchy walnuts. Buckwheat is an intact grain, and with the milk, yogurt and nuts it gives you **protein, magnesium, calcium and omega-3**.
steps: Rinse the buckwheat in a sieve. Put it in a small pot with the milk and half the cinnamon, and bring just to the boil.
Turn the heat down, cover and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the groats are tender. Add a splash of water if it thickens before they are done.
Meanwhile, wash and dice the apple. Cook it in a small pan with a splash of water and the rest of the cinnamon for 5 minutes, until soft.
Take the porridge off the heat and stir in the yogurt. Spoon it into a bowl and top with the apple and the chopped walnuts.
tip: Cook it fresh. Cooked grains keep no more than 3 days, so do not batch this for the whole week.

name: Lemon-garlic chicken bites with kale and quinoa tabbouleh and tahini sauce
inspiredBy: Inspired by Lebanese shish taouk and tabbouleh, with quinoa in place of bulgur and kale chopped in with the parsley
about: Juicy lemon-garlic chicken pieces with a herb-heavy quinoa tabbouleh, made greener with finely chopped kale and spinach, and a lemony tahini sauce. The parsley and greens bring **vitamin K, vitamin C and calcium**, and the second portion makes tomorrow's lunch plate.
