Beat the egg and egg whites with the oregano and pepper, pour them over the vegetables and stir gently, folding as it sets. Cook until just set but still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Fold the omelette onto a plate, scatter with parsley and add a squeeze of lemon. Serve with the toast.
tip: A spoonful of crumbled feta on top is traditional and adds about 110 mg of sodium. Save it for Sunday.

name: Tuscan-style white bean and tuna salad with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Tuscan tonno e fagioli
about: Creamy white beans tossed with unsalted tuna and a boiled egg (a modern addition), sweet red onion, ripe tomato and a big handful of parsley in a sharp lemon and red wine vinegar dressing. **Beans and tuna** make it a filling lunch with no salt needed, because the acid does the seasoning.
steps: Put the egg on to boil for 9 minutes. Rinse the beans well and let them drain. Slice the onion as thin as you can and let it sit in the lemon juice and vinegar for 5 minutes to soften and mellow.
Whisk the olive oil and garlic into the onion mixture to make the dressing.
Fold in the beans, tomato, flaked tuna and most of the parsley. Add plenty of black pepper.
Cool the egg under cold water, peel and quarter it.
Pile the salad onto a plate, tuck in the egg and scatter with the last of the parsley.
tip: Taste before serving. If it seems flat, it needs more lemon, not more salt. No unsalted tuna? Rinse a regular can well and use a little less.

name: Greek village salad with chickpeas, tuna and a little feta
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki
about: The classic tomato, cucumber and red onion salad, bulked up with chickpeas and flaked unsalted tuna and finished with oregano, a few rinsed Kalamata olives, a drizzle of good olive oil and just a spoonful of crumbled feta. It's crunchy, juicy and **full of potassium and fibre**.
steps: Rinse and drain the chickpeas really well. Put them in a bowl with the cucumber, tomato, red onion and flaked tuna.
Whisk the olive oil with the vinegar and oregano, and pour it over. Toss and let it sit for 5 minutes so the tomatoes give up their juice.
Crumble the feta over the salad, scatter with the rinsed olives and the parsley.
Tear the bread over the salad or serve it alongside to mop up the juices.
tip: Rinse the feta under cold water for a few seconds first to wash off some of the surface salt. Mopping up the tomato juices with the bread is the best part.

name: Parsley tabbouleh with lentils and tuna
inspiredBy: Lebanese tabbouleh, with lentils and tuna added for a full meal
about: A parsley-heavy Levantine tabbouleh with a little bulgur, lentils and flaked unsalted tuna for substance, mint, lemon and a drizzle of pomegranate molasses. It's **lemony, herby and very green**, and it eats like a full meal.
steps: Cover the bulgur with boiling water, about double its volume, and let it sit for 15 minutes until tender. Drain well and squeeze out any extra water.
Toss the bulgur with the parsley, mint, tomato, cucumber, lentils and flaked tuna.
Whisk the lemon juice with the olive oil, allspice and pomegranate molasses, then toss it through. It should taste sharp and fresh.
Add a crack of pepper and serve.
tip: Chop the parsley dry. Wet parsley turns the salad soggy.
ingredients: finely chopped, the bulk of the salad
no-salt-added canned or cooked from dry, drained

name: Greek lemon and oregano chicken with roast potatoes and tomatoes
inspiredBy: Greek kotopoulo lemonato me patates
about: Skinless chicken breast, potato wedges and carrots roasted on one tray with garlic, lots of lemon and oregano, with red onion and tomatoes that collapse into a sauce. It makes **two portions**, so tomorrow's lunch is already cooked.
steps: Heat the oven to 220C (425F). Toss the potato wedges and carrot with half the olive oil, half the lemon juice and half the oregano on a large tray. Roast for 15 minutes.
Rub the chicken with the rest of the oil, the garlic, the pepper, the salt and the rest of the oregano. Slice thick breasts in half so they cook evenly.

Add the chicken, onion and tomato to the tray and pour over the rest of the lemon juice and a splash of water. Roast for 20 to 25 minutes, checking the chicken at 20, until it is cooked through and the potatoes are golden at the edges.
Spoon the pan juices over everything, and finish with parsley.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Slice the chicken and eat it cold or warm it gently.
tip: Reheat the leftover gently with a squeeze of lemon, or eat it cold, sliced thin, over salad.

name: Roasted salmon with lemony whole-wheat pasta, tomato and kale
inspiredBy: Southern Italian pasta with cavolo nero and roasted tomatoes
about: A salmon fillet roasted with tomatoes, garlic and thyme, served over whole-wheat pasta tossed with garlicky kale, lemon juice and good olive oil. **Salmon is the omega-3 star**, and the tomato juices make the sauce.
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (400F). Put the tomato, half the garlic and the thyme on a small tray with half the oil and roast for 10 minutes.
Nestle the salmon into the tomatoes, season with pepper and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until it flakes but is still a little translucent in the middle.
Boil the pasta in plenty of unsalted water until al dente. Scoop out a mugful of the cooking water before draining.

While it cooks, warm the rest of the oil in a pan with the remaining garlic and the Aleppo pepper for 30 seconds. Add the kale, the lemon zest, the salt and a splash of water and cook until tender and glossy, about 6 minutes.
Toss the pasta with the kale, the lemon juice and a splash of pasta water until glossy.
Serve the pasta with the salmon and roasted tomatoes on top, scattered with parsley.
tip: Pasta cooked in unsalted water is fine here because the kale and lemon carry the flavour.
ingredients: from a lemon; zest it before you squeeze it

name: Fakes, Greek lentil soup with greens and a splash of vinegar
inspiredBy: Greek fakes, the everyday lentil soup
about: A thick, comforting Greek lentil soup with carrot, tomato, bay and oregano, with spinach stirred in and a splash of red wine vinegar and a raw drizzle of olive oil at the end. **The vinegar is the secret**, since it wakes up every spoonful. It makes two bowls and tastes better tomorrow.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a large pot and soften the onion, carrot and potato over medium heat until sweet, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic, oregano and bay for a minute, until fragrant.

Stir in the lentils, the tomato and about three and a half times as much water as lentils. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered, until the lentils are completely soft and the soup is thick, 30 to 35 minutes.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, then take the pot off the heat.
Add the vinegar, salt and pepper, and taste. It should be bright and a bit sharp.

Ladle into bowls, scatter with parsley and finish with a drizzle of the remaining olive oil. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so loosen it with water and add a fresh splash of vinegar when you reheat it.
tip: In a hurry? Use no-salt-added canned lentils and simmer for 15 minutes.
ingredients: a bay leaf or two for the pot

name: Grilled sardines with fennel, tomato and white beans
inspiredBy: Italian pesce azzurro with fennel and beans
about: Fresh sardines roasted until their skin crisps, laid over white beans simmered with sweet fennel, tomato, garlic and lemon. **Fresh sardines are rich in omega-3**, with far less salt than the canned kind.
steps: Heat the broiler. Pat the sardines dry and rub them with a little of the oil, the oregano, the salt and a squeeze of lemon.
Warm the rest of the oil in a pan and cook the fennel and garlic over medium heat until soft and just golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the tomato and Aleppo pepper and cook until jammy, about 4 minutes. Stir in the beans with a splash of water and simmer for 5 minutes.
Broil the sardines on the top rack for 3 to 4 minutes per side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Spoon the beans onto a plate, top with the sardines and finish with lemon juice and parsley. Serve with the toast.
tip: Can't find fresh sardines? Use two small mackerel fillets instead. Chili flakes work if you can't find Aleppo pepper.

name: Espinacas con garbanzos, Spanish chickpeas and spinach
inspiredBy: Andalusian espinacas con garbanzos
about: A smoky, garlicky Seville tapas classic of chickpeas and spinach, thickened with ground almonds, brightened with sherry vinegar and topped with a chopped egg. It's a **chickpea and spinach feast** for folate and fibre, and it makes two portions.
steps: Put the eggs on to boil for 10 minutes, then cool them in cold water and peel them. Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and fry the torn bread until golden, 2 to 3 minutes. Lift it out and set aside.
In the same oil, soften the onion for 5 minutes, then add the garlic, paprika and cumin for 30 seconds, until it smells smoky.
Add the tomato and cook for 4 minutes until thick.
Pound or blitz the fried bread with the almonds and a splash of water to a rough paste. Stir it in with the chickpeas and a splash more water. Simmer for 8 minutes.
Add the spinach in handfuls and stir until wilted. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the sherry vinegar and salt. It should taste warm and tangy.
Chop an egg over your bowl. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch with its egg whole on the side, and chop it over just before you eat. The stew reheats well with a splash of water.
tip: Hard-boiled egg is the classic finish for the Lenten chickpea and spinach potaje, and it adds protein and choline. The stew freezes well, but freeze it without the egg.

name: Gemista, Greek stuffed peppers with lean turkey and bulgur
inspiredBy: Greek gemista, normally made with rice
about: Sweet red peppers stuffed with lean turkey, bulgur, a few chickpeas, onion, tomato, mint and parsley, scented with cinnamon and allspice and baked with potato wedges until they collapse into their own sauce. It's the **weekend project**, and it makes two big portions so Sunday's lunch is sorted.
steps: Heat the oven to 190C (375F). Slice the tops off the peppers and scoop out any seeds. Stand them in a snug baking dish with the potato wedges around them.
Warm half the olive oil in a pan and soften the onion for 6 minutes. Add the garlic and turkey and cook, breaking it up, until no pink remains, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the bulgur, the crushed tomato, the grated fresh tomato, the chickpeas, cinnamon, allspice and pepper. Simmer for 5 minutes, then stir in the mint and most of the parsley.
Spoon the filling into the peppers without packing it tight, because the bulgur will swell. Put the tops back on.

Drizzle everything with the remaining olive oil and add a splash of water to the dish. Cover with foil and bake for 40 minutes. Uncover and bake for 20 minutes more, until the peppers are soft and the potatoes are golden.
Finish with the lemon juice and the last of the parsley. Let the peppers rest for 10 minutes before serving, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Eat the potatoes with the juices.
ingredients: whole, tops cut off and kept

name: Sumac roasted trout with tahini sauce, bulgur and lemony kale
inspiredBy: Levantine samke with tahini, and a pomegranate-tart greens salad
about: A trout fillet roasted with sumac, garlic and lemon, with a nutty lemon-tahini sauce, fluffy bulgur and garlicky kale with fresh tomato, finished with pomegranate molasses. **Trout is an oily fish** that cooks in minutes, and the sumac gives it a lemony zing with no salt.
steps: Heat the oven to 200C (400F). Rub the trout with half the olive oil, the sumac, half the garlic and a squeeze of lemon. Lay it on a lined tray.
Cover the bulgur with boiling water, about double its volume, cover and let it sit for 20 minutes, until tender and fluffy.
Roast the trout for 10 to 12 minutes, until it flakes easily.
Whisk the tahini with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice and about 3 tablespoons of cold water until pale and pourable.
Warm the kale in a pan with the rest of the oil and a splash of water until tender, about 5 minutes. Toss it with the tomato, onion, parsley and the pomegranate molasses.
Serve the trout over the bulgur with the kale and tomato alongside, drizzled with tahini and a pinch of Aleppo pepper.
tip: Swap in a salmon fillet if trout is hard to find.

name: Orange and unsalted walnuts
about: A juicy orange and a small handful of unsalted walnuts. **Sweet, crunchy and quick**, with vitamin C and plant omega-3.
steps: Peel the orange and split it into segments.
Eat it with the walnuts, a few at a time.

name: No-salt hummus with carrot and cucumber
inspiredBy: Levantine hummus bi tahini, without the salt
about: A lemony, garlicky homemade hummus made with no added salt, with crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks to dip. The **tahini and lemon** carry the flavour.
steps: Make the hummus as a batch of two portions, about 140 g of chickpeas and double the tahini, lemon juice, garlic and cumin, so the blender can catch it. Blitz with a few tablespoons of cold water until smooth and creamy, adding more if it's stiff.
Spoon half into a bowl, make a well, pour in the olive oil and dust with sumac or smoked paprika.
Dip the carrot and cucumber sticks in it. Keep the other half covered in the fridge for up to 4 days, for another snack or spread thick on toast.

name: Greek yogurt with chopped dates and toasted walnuts
about: Thick yogurt with sticky chopped Medjool dates and toasted walnuts, a little like a Greek dessert. The **dates sweeten it**, so no honey is needed.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, then chop them.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and stir in most of the dates.
Top with the walnuts and the remaining dates and dust with cinnamon.

name: Greek yogurt with chopped dates and toasted almonds
about: Thick yogurt with sticky chopped Medjool dates and toasted almonds, a little like a Greek dessert. The **dates sweeten it**, so no honey is needed.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, then chop them.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and stir in most of the dates.
Top with the almonds and the remaining dates and dust with cinnamon.

name: Apple slices with walnuts and cinnamon
about: Crisp apple slices with a handful of unsalted walnuts and a dusting of cinnamon. **A sweet, crunchy snack** with plant omega-3.
steps: Slice the apple and toss it with a little lemon juice so it stays bright.
Dust with cinnamon and eat with the walnuts.

name: Medjool dates stuffed with almonds and a dab of tahini
inspiredBy: Middle Eastern stuffed dates
about: Soft Medjool dates stuffed with almonds and a dab of tahini, with a few more almonds on the side. It's a **chewy, caramel-like treat** with no added sugar.
steps: Slit the dates open and remove the pits.
Tuck two or three almonds into each date with a little dab of tahini and press it closed. Eat the rest of the almonds alongside.

name: Crunchy smoked paprika chickpeas
inspiredBy: Spanish tapas
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp with smoked paprika, garlic and a squeeze of lemon, like a Spanish tapas nibble. **Crunchy and savoury** with no salt.
steps: Heat the oven to 210C (410F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a clean towel. This is what makes them crisp.
Toss them with the olive oil, paprika, cumin and garlic, and spread them on a tray in one layer.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp and deep red.
Squeeze over the lemon and let them cool a few minutes. They'll crisp up as they cool.
tip: Roast a double batch if you like: they keep for a day or two in an open container, since a sealed lid softens them.
ingredients: no-salt-added canned, drained, rinsed and dried well

name: Cucumber rounds with lemony tuna and parsley
inspiredBy: Italian tonno al limone
about: Thick cucumber rounds piled with flaked unsalted tuna, lemon, parsley and a little olive oil and black pepper. It's **cool, sharp and protein-rich**, a bit like a tiny salad you eat with your hands.
steps: Flake the tuna into a small bowl and stir in the lemon juice, parsley, olive oil and pepper.
Spoon it onto the cucumber rounds and eat right away.

name: Garlicky yogurt and cucumber dip with carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Greek tzatziki
about: A quick tzatziki of thick yogurt, grated cucumber, garlic, mint and lemon, for dipping carrot sticks. **Cooling and garlicky**, and it counts as calcium and protein too.
steps: Squeeze the grated cucumber in a clean towel until it's quite dry.
Stir it into the yogurt with the garlic, mint and lemon juice.
Dip the carrot sticks. It's even better after 20 minutes in the fridge.

name: Lemony white bean dip with cucumber and carrot
inspiredBy: Tuscan white bean purée
about: A creamy Tuscan-style white bean dip with garlic, lemon, olive oil and parsley, for dipping cucumber and carrot. **Beans make it filling**, and it's as good as hummus.
steps: Mash or blitz the beans with the lemon juice, garlic, most of the olive oil and a few spoonfuls of cold water until creamy.
Spoon into a bowl, drizzle with the last of the oil and scatter with parsley and pepper.
Dip the vegetable sticks.

name: Pan con tomate with garlic and walnuts
inspiredBy: Catalan pa amb tomàquet
about: Toasted whole-wheat bread rubbed with garlic and ripe tomato, with a drizzle of olive oil and a few walnuts on the side. **Simple Spanish tapas** that tastes like summer.
steps: Toast the bread until crisp and golden.
Rub the cut side of the garlic over the hot toast, then rub with the cut tomato until the bread is pink and the skin is left behind.
Drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle with oregano and eat with the walnuts.

name: Greek yogurt with orange segments and toasted walnuts
about: Thick yogurt topped with juicy orange segments and toasted walnuts, with a pinch of cinnamon. **Cool, sweet and crunchy**, and the yogurt brings calcium and protein.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, then chop them.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and tuck in the orange segments.
Scatter with the walnuts and dust with cinnamon.

name: Bran flakes with strawberries, ground flax and a boiled egg
about: A crunchy, not-too-sweet bowl of fortified bran flakes with toasted pumpkin seeds, ground flax and a pile of ripe strawberries, with a few spoonfuls of plain yogurt and a boiled egg on the side, a hearty Canadian-style breakfast bowl. The cereal and seeds bring **iron**, and the strawberries bring the vitamin C that helps your body absorb it. Have your coffee or tea an hour or two later, not with the bowl.
steps: Lower the egg into gently boiling water and cook for 10 minutes until the yolk is firm. Cool it in cold water, then peel it.
Meanwhile, toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they start to pop, about 3 minutes. Tip them onto a plate to cool.
Rinse the strawberries under cold water, then hull and slice them.
Put the bran flakes in a bowl, scatter over the toasted seeds and the ground flax, and pile the strawberries on top. Dust with cinnamon.
Spoon the yogurt over just before eating so the flakes stay crisp, and eat the egg alongside.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday (they keep in the shell up to 7 days in the fridge) and toast a jar of seeds, and breakfast takes two minutes. Any ripe berry will do in place of the strawberries.

name: Huevos a la mexicana with black beans and orange
inspiredBy: Mexican huevos a la mexicana, with black beans and an orange on the side
about: Eggs scrambled with tomato, onion and fresh jalapeño, the red, white and green breakfast of a Mexican morning, with warm corn tortillas and black beans. The eggs and beans bring **iron and protein**, and the tomato, lime and a juicy orange on the side bring the vitamin C that helps you absorb the iron from the beans.
steps: Rinse the black beans and warm them in a small pot with the cumin and a splash of water, mashing about half with a fork, for 4 minutes. Keep them warm.
Wash the tomato, onion, jalapeño, cilantro and orange. Dice or chop the first four, and cut the orange into segments.
Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and soften the onion and jalapeño with a pinch of the salt for 3 minutes. Add the tomato and cook until the juices mostly cook off, about 3 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt, pour them in and stir gently until they are set with no liquid left, about 2 minutes. Squeeze over the lime and scatter the cilantro.
Warm the tortillas in a dry pan, about 30 seconds a side. Serve the eggs with the beans, the tortillas and the orange. Wash your hands, the board and the knife after handling the raw eggs.
tip: Leave out the jalapeño for a milder plate and pass hot sauce at the table.

name: Tofu bhurji with peppers and spinach on whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: North Indian paneer bhurji, with crumbled tofu in place of paneer
about: Crumbled tofu cooked with onion, ginger, green chili and red pepper in the style of a Punjabi paneer bhurji, with a handful of spinach wilted in and a squeeze of lemon, piled on whole-wheat toast. The tofu carries the **iron**, and the red pepper and lemon bring the vitamin C that helps you absorb it.
steps: Press the tofu between a few layers of paper towel for 5 minutes, then crumble it into small pieces with your hands.
Wash the pepper, spinach and cilantro. Dice the pepper, chop the spinach and cilantro, and chop the onion, ginger, garlic and chili.

Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the cumin and let it sizzle for 15 seconds, then add the onion and a pinch of the salt and cook until soft and golden, about 5 minutes. Stir in the ginger, garlic and chili for 1 minute.
Add the red pepper and cook 3 minutes, then stir in the turmeric, the crumbled tofu and the rest of the salt. Cook, stirring, until the tofu is hot and dry-looking with golden edges, about 5 minutes.
Fold in the spinach until it wilts, about 1 minute, then take the pan off the heat and finish with the garam masala, lemon juice and cilantro. Serve on the toast.
tip: Use a milder green pepper in place of the chili, or leave it out. Leftover bhurji also fills a warm whole-wheat pita.

name: Warm lentil salad with roasted red pepper, spinach and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: a French-style lentil salad, with roasted red pepper, spinach and an orange dressing
about: Tender lentils tossed warm with sweet roasted red pepper, spinach softened in the dressing and toasted pumpkin seeds, topped with a boiled egg and dressed with a light orange and lemon vinaigrette. The lentils bring **iron and protein**, and the pepper, orange and spinach bring the vitamin C that helps your body absorb it.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Wash the pepper, toss the strips with half the oil and a pinch of the salt on a tray, and roast until soft and charred at the edges, about 20 minutes.
Lower the egg into a pot of gently boiling water and cook for 10 minutes until the yolk is firm. Cool it in cold water, then peel and halve it.
Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes. Wash the spinach and the orange.
Whisk the juice of half the orange with the lemon juice, the rest of the oil, the cumin and the rest of the salt. Cut the remaining orange into segments.
Rinse the lentils and warm them in a small pot with a splash of water until steaming, about 4 minutes. Drain well and toss with the dressing, the spinach and the onion so the spinach softens.
Fold in the roasted pepper and orange segments, top with the egg halves and seeds, and serve with the toast.
tip: It is just as good cold the next day; add the egg and seeds fresh.

name: Egg and chickpea pita with parsley, tomato and lemon-tahini
inspiredBy: Israeli sabich, with chickpeas and a boiled egg in the pita
about: A pita packed with garlicky chickpeas, sliced boiled egg, a big handful of parsley, tomato and crisp red pepper, drizzled with a lemony tahini dressing. The chickpeas and parsley bring **iron**, the egg and chickpeas bring protein, and the red pepper, tomato and lemon bring the vitamin C that helps you absorb it.
steps: Lower the egg into gently boiling water and cook for 10 minutes until the yolk is firm. Cool it in cold water, then peel and slice it.
Rinse the chickpeas well. Wash the parsley, tomato and red pepper, then chop the parsley and dice the tomato and pepper.
Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, garlic and a pinch of the salt into a loose, tangy dressing, adding a spoonful of cold water only if it is too sharp.

Warm the olive oil in a small pan, stir in the cumin for 15 seconds and add the chickpeas and the rest of the salt. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until hot and lightly golden, crushing a few with the back of a spoon.
Toss the chickpeas with the parsley, tomato, red pepper and onion. Warm the pita, split it open and stuff it with the salad and the egg slices. Drizzle with the tahini sauce.
tip: Warm the pita for a minute in a dry pan, or wrap it in a damp towel and microwave for 15 seconds.

name: Smashed sardines on rye with tomato, spinach and lemon
inspiredBy: Portuguese and Sicilian sardines on toast
about: Canned sardines mashed with lemon, parsley and onion, piled onto toasted rye with juicy tomato, baby spinach and strips of red pepper. Sardines are an **oily fish rich in omega-3, with iron**, and the lemon, tomato and pepper bring the vitamin C that helps you absorb it.
steps: Wash the tomato, spinach, pepper and parsley, then slice the tomato, cut the pepper into strips and chop the parsley.
Mash the sardines in a bowl with a fork, leaving some chunks, with the lemon juice, parsley, onion, half the olive oil and a grind of pepper.
Toast the rye until crisp. Drizzle the rest of the oil over it, then layer on the tomato slices and the spinach.
Pile the smashed sardines on top and serve the pepper strips alongside. Eat it straight away; the sardines are not a good leftover.
tip: A few capers or chopped olives are lovely in the sardine mix, but rinse them well since they are salty.

name: Beef and black bean chili over a baked potato
inspiredBy: Canadian-style beef chili, served over a baked potato
about: A smoky, deeply spiced chili of lean ground beef, black beans and tomatoes with plenty of red pepper, spooned over a baked potato and finished with lime and cilantro. The beef and beans bring **heme and plant iron together**, and the tomatoes, peppers and lime bring the vitamin C. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Prick the scrubbed potatoes with a fork and bake on a tray until very tender, about 50 minutes, while you make the chili.

Wash the pepper, cilantro and onion. Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and soften the onion and pepper with a pinch of the salt until golden at the edges, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic for 1 minute.

Add the beef, breaking it up with a spoon, and cook until no pink is left, about 6 minutes. Wash your hands, the board and the knife after the raw beef. Stir in the cumin, paprika, cinnamon and cayenne and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.

Add the crushed tomatoes with their juice, the rinsed beans, the rest of the salt and a splash of water. Simmer, partly covered, for 25 minutes until thick. Check that the beef is cooked through, 71 °C (160 °F) on a thermometer.
Split the potatoes, spoon the chili over them and finish with the lime juice and cilantro.

Cool the second portion of chili in a shallow container within 2 hours, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat once until steaming, 74 °C (165 °F), and bake or microwave a fresh potato to go with it.
tip: The chili freezes well for up to 3 months: cool it within 2 hours in a shallow container first, and freeze it without the potato. Thaw in the fridge overnight, eat within 2 days and never refreeze. Reheat once to 74 °C (165 °F). Short on time? Prick the potatoes and microwave them for 8 to 10 minutes, and the chili needs only about 35. A squeeze of lime on top brightens it.
ingredients: whole canned tomatoes in juice, crushed by hand

name: Whole-wheat spaghetti with sardines, kale and apricot
inspiredBy: Sicilian pasta con le sarde, with kale and dried apricot in place of raisins
about: A quick take on Sicily's pasta con le sarde: sardines melted into garlic and olive oil with fennel seed, sweet dried apricot, kale and lemon, tossed through whole-wheat spaghetti. The sardines bring **omega-3**, and their soft bones add calcium, while the pasta and kale add iron and the lemon and kale bring the vitamin C.
steps: Bring a large pot of water to the boil for the pasta. Wash the kale and parsley, slice the kale and the onion, and chop the apricot.

Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the fennel seed and onion with a pinch of the salt and cook until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, apricot and chili flakes for 1 minute.
Cook the spaghetti in the boiling water until just tender, about 10 minutes, adding the kale for the last 2 minutes. Save a cup of the pasta water, then drain.
Add the sardines to the pan and break them up with a spoon.
Toss in the pasta and kale with a splash of pasta water, the lemon juice and the rest of the salt until glossy, adding more pasta water if it looks dry. Heat until steaming hot.
Serve topped with the parsley. This is a one-sitting dish, not a leftover.
tip: Pasta con le sarde is traditionally finished with toasted breadcrumbs for crunch; a spoonful of coarse breadcrumbs fried in the pan works too.

name: Palak masoor dal with brown basmati
inspiredBy: North Indian dal palak, made with red lentils
about: A thick, golden red lentil dal with plenty of spinach, tomato, ginger and a sizzling cumin tadka, finished with lemon and served with nutty brown basmati rice. The lentils bring **plant iron**, with the spinach adding a little, and the tomato and lemon bring the vitamin C that helps you absorb it. It makes two portions.
steps: Rinse the lentils and put them in a pot with the turmeric, a pinch of the salt and about three times their volume of water. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, then simmer, partly covered, until soft and falling apart, about 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, rinse the rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes. Drain and keep it covered.

Wash the spinach, tomato and cilantro. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the cumin and let it sizzle for 15 seconds, then add the onion and cook until golden, about 7 minutes. Stir in the garlic, ginger and cayenne for 1 minute.

Add the tomato and cook until it collapses, about 5 minutes. Stir this tadka into the lentils with the spinach and the rest of the salt and simmer until the spinach is soft and the dal is thick, about 5 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and finish with the garam masala, lemon juice and cilantro. Serve over the rice.
Cool the rice within 1 hour and the dal within 2 hours in shallow containers, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat once until steaming, 74 °C (165 °F), with a splash of water.
tip: Frozen spinach works if fresh is a hassle. The dal freezes well for up to 3 months: cool it within 2 hours first, freeze it without the rice and cook the rice fresh. Thaw in the fridge overnight, eat within 2 days and never refreeze. Reheat once to 74 °C (165 °F).
ingredients: rinsed until the water runs clear

name: Mussels in tomato and paprika broth with kale and whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Spanish-style mussels steamed in tomato, garlic and smoked paprika
about: Mussels steamed open in a garlicky tomato and smoked paprika broth with kale softened in and a lot of parsley, with whole-wheat toast for mopping. Mussels are one of the best **iron-rich seafoods**, and the tomatoes, parsley and a squeeze of lemon bring the vitamin C that helps you absorb it. It is ready in about 40 minutes.
steps: Buy live mussels from a seller who keeps them on ice: the shells should be closed, or snap shut when tapped, and smell of the sea. Use them within 1 day of buying, 2 at most. Wash the kale and parsley, and slice the kale. Scrub them under cold running water and pull off the beards. Farmed mussels only need a scrub; if they feel gritty, soak them for 20 minutes in cold, lightly salted water, never fresh water. Throw away any that are cracked, that stay open when tapped, or that smell off. Wash your hands, the board and the knife after the raw mussels.
Warm the olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat and soften the onion with a pinch of the salt for 5 minutes. Add the garlic, paprika and chili flakes for 1 minute.
Add the crushed tomatoes with their juice, the kale and a splash of water and simmer for 10 minutes, until the kale is tender and the sauce is slightly thickened.

Add the mussels, cover tightly and steam over medium-high heat, shaking the pot once or twice, until the shells open, about 5 minutes. Throw away any that stay closed. Shellfish is safe at 74 °C (165 °F); in practice the shells are wide open and the flesh is firm, so give them one more minute after they open.

Stir in the lemon juice and most of the parsley. Ladle into a bowl, leaving any sandy liquid at the bottom of the pot, scatter over the rest of the parsley and serve with the toast. Eat it fresh; shellfish is not a good leftover.
tip: Keep mussels in the fridge in an open bowl covered with a damp cloth, never in a sealed bag or in fresh water, and cook them the day you buy them, or the next day at the latest.
ingredients: shelled weight; buy them in the shell, about 3 to 4 times this weight
whole canned tomatoes in juice, crushed by hand

name: Tofu and broccoli stir-fry with red pepper and cashews
inspiredBy: Chinese-style tofu and broccoli stir-fry, with brown rice
about: Golden tofu with crisp broccoli and red pepper in a garlicky ginger, soy and lemon sauce, finished with toasted cashews and served over brown rice. The tofu and cashews bring **iron**, and the broccoli and red pepper bring plenty of vitamin C to help you absorb it. It makes two portions.
steps: Rinse the rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes. Drain and keep it covered.
Press the tofu between paper towels for 10 minutes, then cut it into cubes. Wash the broccoli and pepper, then cut them up.
Whisk the soy sauce and lemon juice with a splash of water in a small bowl.
Warm half the oil in a large non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Fry the tofu, turning once or twice, until golden on most sides, about 8 minutes. Lift it out.
Add the rest of the oil, then the broccoli with a splash of water, cover and steam for 2 minutes. Add the pepper and stir-fry 2 minutes, then the garlic and ginger for 30 seconds.
Return the tofu, pour in the sauce and toss until the tofu and vegetables are coated, about 1 minute. Scatter over the cashews and serve over the rice.
Cool the rice within 1 hour and the stir-fry within 2 hours, refrigerate in shallow containers and eat within 3 days. Reheat once until steaming, 74 °C (165 °F).
tip: Toast the cashews in a dry pan for 3 minutes first for more flavour, and a teaspoon of toasted sesame oil on the rice is lovely.

name: Slow lamb, chickpea and apricot stew with spinach
inspiredBy: a Moroccan-style lamb tagine with apricots and chickpeas
about: A fragrant weekend stew of lean lamb leg simmered with cumin, ginger and cinnamon, chickpeas, carrots, dried apricots and tomatoes, with spinach wilted in at the end and brown rice on the side. The lamb is a **source of iron your body absorbs easily**, and the tomatoes, lemon and parsley bring the vitamin C. It makes two portions.
steps: Heat the oven to 160 °C (325 °F). Wash the spinach, carrots and parsley, and peel the carrots. Pat the lamb dry and season with the paprika, cumin and half the salt.
Warm the oil in a heavy ovenproof pot over medium-high heat and brown the lamb in batches, about 5 minutes a batch. Lift it out. Wash your hands, the board and the knife after the raw lamb.
Lower the heat, add the onion and a pinch of the salt and cook until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, ginger, cinnamon and turmeric for 1 minute.

Return the lamb with the carrots, the crushed tomatoes and their juice, the apricots and enough water to just cover. Bring to a simmer, cover and braise in the oven until the lamb is very tender, about 75 minutes. The lamb is cooked through at 71 °C (160 °F), well before it is tender.

Stir in the chickpeas and the rest of the salt and simmer, uncovered, on the stovetop for 10 minutes. Meanwhile cook the rinsed rice in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, and drain.
Stir the spinach into the stew until it wilts, about 1 minute. Finish with the lemon juice and parsley and serve over the rice.
Cool the rice within 1 hour and the stew within 2 hours in shallow containers, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat once until steaming, 74 °C (165 °F).
tip: A pressure cooker does the braise in 30 minutes. Ask the butcher for leg steaks and cube them yourself to keep it lean. The stew freezes well for up to 3 months. Thaw in the fridge overnight, eat within 2 days and never refreeze; cool the rice and the stew first (1 hour for rice, 2 hours for the stew) before freezing, and reheat once to 74 °C (165 °F).
ingredients: lean leg, trimmed of visible fat and cut into cubes
whole canned tomatoes in juice, crushed by hand

name: Pan-seared mackerel on warm lentils with garlicky kale and parsley salsa verde
inspiredBy: Italian salsa verde over mackerel and lentils
about: Crisp-skinned Atlantic mackerel on warm lentils with garlicky kale, sweet roasted red pepper and a bright parsley and lemon salsa verde. Mackerel is an **oily fish with omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the lentils bring plant iron, with the kale, peppers and lemon bringing plenty of vitamin C alongside.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Wash the peppers, kale and parsley. Toss the pepper strips with a third of the oil and a pinch of the salt on a tray and roast until soft and charred at the edges, about 20 minutes.
For the salsa verde, stir the parsley, garlic, lemon juice, chili flakes, half the remaining oil and a pinch of salt together in a bowl and leave to sit for 10 minutes.

Warm the rinsed lentils in a small pot with the onion, a splash of water and a pinch of the salt until steaming, about 5 minutes. Cook the kale in a covered pan with a splash of water and a little of the garlic from the salsa until tender and bright, about 6 minutes.

Pat the mackerel dry and season with the paprika and the rest of the salt. Heat the rest of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and cook the fillets skin side down, pressing gently, until the skin is crisp, about 4 minutes. Flip and cook 2 minutes more, until the flesh flakes and reaches 70 °C (158 °F). Wash your hands and board after the raw fish.
Spoon the lentils and kale onto a plate, lay the mackerel on top, add the peppers and spoon over the salsa verde.
tip: Salsa verde keeps for 2 days in the fridge but loses its colour; make it fresh when you can.
ingredients: fillets, skin on, pin bones removed

name: Yogurt with strawberries, pumpkin seeds and ground flax
about: Thick plain Greek yogurt with sliced strawberries, a crunch of pumpkin seeds and a spoonful of ground flax. Dairy sits at a snack, away from the big iron meals, and the strawberries bring **vitamin C along with the seeds' iron**.
steps: Rinse the strawberries, then hull and slice them.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the strawberries and scatter over the pumpkin seeds and flax.

name: Smoky roasted chickpeas with an orange
about: Crunchy chickpeas roasted with smoked paprika and cumin, with a juicy orange on the side. The chickpeas bring **iron and fibre**, and the orange brings the vitamin C that helps you absorb it.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Rinse the chickpeas and pat them very dry with a towel.
Toss them on a tray with the oil, paprika, cumin and salt and roast, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp, about 25 minutes. Let them cool a few minutes to crisp up further.
Wash the orange, cut it into wedges and serve with the chickpeas. Keep leftovers in an open container; they soften in a day.

name: Dark chocolate with strawberries
about: A few squares of dark chocolate with a bowl of strawberries. Dark chocolate brings a little **iron** along with its flavour, and the strawberries bring vitamin C. It is a treat that happens to be useful.
steps: Rinse the strawberries.
Break the chocolate into squares and eat with the berries.

name: Dried apricots and cashews with an orange
about: Chewy dried apricots, creamy cashews and juicy orange wedges. The apricots and cashews bring **iron and copper**, and the orange brings vitamin C.
steps: Wash the orange and cut it into wedges.
Serve the apricots, cashews and orange together in a small bowl.

name: Tahini hummus with red pepper sticks
inspiredBy: Levantine hummus bi tahini
about: A quick lemony hummus whirled from chickpeas and tahini, for dunking raw red pepper sticks. The chickpeas and tahini bring **iron and fibre**, and the red pepper brings plenty of vitamin C.
steps: Wash the pepper and cut it into sticks.
Blend the chickpeas with the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, cumin, salt and a splash of cold water until very smooth, about 2 minutes. Add more water for a looser texture.
Serve the hummus with the pepper sticks. Keep any extra in the fridge for up to 3 days.
tip: A mini chopper or a stick blender in a tall jar copes with this small amount, or make a bigger batch and keep it up to 3 days.

name: Orange and strawberry cup with toasted pumpkin seeds
about: Juicy orange segments and strawberries with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds for crunch. The seeds bring **iron and zinc**, and the fruit brings plenty of vitamin C.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.
Wash the orange and strawberries. Cut the orange into segments and slice the strawberries, then scatter the warm seeds on top.

name: Orange yogurt with crunchy bran flakes
about: Thick plain yogurt with orange segments and a handful of crushed fortified bran flakes for crunch. The orange brings **vitamin C**, and the cereal brings a little iron. It keeps the dairy at a snack, apart from the bigger iron meals.
steps: Wash the orange and cut it into segments.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange and scatter over the bran flakes just before eating.

name: Smoky lime pumpkin seeds and cashews
about: A warm, savoury mix of pumpkin seeds and cashews toasted in a dry pan with smoked paprika and finished with lime. The nuts and seeds bring **a little iron**, with magnesium and copper, and the lime brings a little vitamin C.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds and cashews in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat, toss with the paprika, salt and lime juice, and let cool a few minutes. Eat warm or at room temperature.

name: Yogurt with chopped apricot, cashews and orange
about: Thick plain yogurt with chopped dried apricots, a few cashews and orange segments. It keeps the dairy at a snack, apart from the bigger iron meals, with **vitamin C from the orange** and a little iron from the apricots and cashews.
steps: Wash the orange and cut it into segments.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the orange, apricots and cashews.

name: Nasi lemak-inspired plate with sardine sambal, egg and peanuts
inspiredBy: Malaysian nasi lemak, with brown rice, only a little coconut milk and tinned sardines in sambal (sambal sardin)
about: Gingery pandan and coconut rice with a hot, tangy sardine sambal, a boiled egg, crunchy peanuts and cool cucumber, the classic Malaysian breakfast plate. The sardines come with their soft bones, so this plate brings **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of simmering water for 10 minutes, until the white and the yolk are both firm. Cool it under cold water, then peel and halve it.

While the egg cooks, put the rice in another small pot with the coconut milk, the pandan, the ginger, a splash of water and the salt. Cover and warm over low heat for 5 minutes, until it's hot and the grains look glossy. Fish out the pandan and ginger.
Soften the shallot and garlic in the oil in a small pan, about 4 minutes. Stir in the sambal oelek for a minute, until the oil turns red and it smells sweet and sharp.
Add the sardines with their sauce and the tamarind, break them up with a spoon and simmer for 3 minutes, until thick and jammy.
Pile the coconut rice on a plate with the sambal, egg, cucumber and peanuts. Eat everything together.
tip: Boil the eggs and make the sardine sambal the night before, and the plate takes 5 minutes. The sambal keeps 3 days in the fridge, so a double batch covers both nasi lemak mornings. Skip the pandan if you can't find it.
ingredients: full-fat, just enough to scent the rice
a knotted pandan leaf, fresh or frozen
tinned in tomato sauce, bones and all

name: Tapsilog-inspired garlic rice with beef tapa, fried egg and atchara
inspiredBy: Filipino tapsilog (tapa, sinangag, itlog), with lean beef, brown rice and a quick carrot atchara
about: Thin slices of beef cured in soy, calamansi and garlic and seared hot, with garlicky fried brown rice, a fried egg and a quick sweet-sour carrot pickle. It's the Filipino all-day breakfast, and the beef and egg bring **iron, zinc and choline**, while the atchara keeps it bright instead of heavy.
steps: Toss the beef with the soy sauce, calamansi, half the garlic, half the palm sugar and the pepper. Leave it to cure while you make the atchara, or overnight in the fridge.

For the atchara, toss the carrot and ginger with the vinegar, the rest of the palm sugar and a pinch of the salt. Squeeze it with your hands for a minute, then leave it for 15 minutes to turn tangy and a little sweet.

Heat a little of the oil in a wide pan and fry the rest of the garlic until pale gold, about 1 minute. Add the cold rice, breaking up any clumps, and stir-fry for 4 minutes, until hot with a few crisp grains. Season with the rest of the salt and tip it into a bowl.
Wipe the pan, heat it hard with a little more oil and sear the beef for 1 to 2 minutes per side, until browned and sticky at the edges. Pile it on the rice.
Fry the egg in the remaining oil until the edges are crisp, then flip it for the last minute so the white and the yolk are both firm. Serve with a spoonful of atchara.
tip: Do steps 1 and 2 the night before and breakfast is 12 minutes. Green papaya is the traditional atchara, so use it in place of the carrot if you have it. A small dish of vinegar with chopped chili and garlic is how most Filipino tables finish it.
ingredients: lean round steak, sliced about 3 mm thick against the grain
minced, half for the beef and half for the rice
half for the beef, half for the atchara

name: Bubur ayam, Indonesian chicken rice porridge with fried shallot
inspiredBy: Indonesian bubur ayam, made with brown rice, mustard greens (sawi) and the chicken liver (ati) that tops the Jakarta version
about: A silky, turmeric-yellow rice porridge with shredded ginger chicken, a little tender chicken liver, mustard greens, crushed peanuts and crisp fried shallots, finished with sweet soy, sambal and a squeeze of lime. It's warm, gentle and the way a lot of Indonesia starts the day. The little bit of liver brings **vitamin A, B12 and iron**.
steps: Fry the shallot rings in the oil over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes. Lift them out onto a paper towel and keep the flavoured oil in the pot.

Add the garlic, ginger and turmeric to the oil for 30 seconds. Add the rice, the chicken thigh and about 4 times as much water as rice by volume. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring now and then, for 25 minutes.
Add the liver and simmer for 5 minutes more. Mash about a third of the rice against the side of the pot, so the porridge turns thick and creamy.
Lift out the chicken and liver, shred the chicken with two forks and chop the liver. Stir the mustard greens into the porridge for 1 minute, until bright, then season with the salt and white pepper.
Ladle into a bowl and top with the chicken, liver, fried shallot and peanuts. Drizzle over the kecap manis, add the sambal and squeeze the lime over.
tip: On weekdays, simmer the porridge with the chicken the night before, then reheat it in the morning with a splash of water and add the liver, greens and toppings fresh (about 10 minutes). A pressure cooker does the whole porridge in 15 minutes. Leave the liver out and use 150 g of chicken if you prefer.

name: Gado-gado with tofu, egg, lontong and peanut sauce
inspiredBy: Indonesian gado-gado, with pan-fried tofu and a lontong-style pressed rice cake made from the batch rice
about: Blanched long beans and bean sprouts with a slice of pressed rice, golden tofu, a boiled egg and crisp cucumber, all under a warm, garlicky peanut sauce with sambal, sweet soy and tamarind. The tofu is calcium-set, so this one lunch brings **lots of calcium and protein**.
steps: Pack the cold rice firmly into a small container lined with plastic wrap, or roll it tightly in the wrap, and chill it while you cook. Slice it into thick squares to serve.

Lower the egg into a pot of boiling water for 10 minutes, then lift it out into cold water. In the same water, blanch the long beans for 3 minutes and the sprouts for 20 seconds. Drain well and let them cool a little.
Pan-fry the tofu cubes in the oil over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side, until golden and crisp at the edges.

Blitz the peanuts with the garlic, salt, sambal, kecap manis, tamarind, palm sugar and about 4 tablespoons of hot water in a mini chopper, until it pours like thick cream. Add a splash more water if it's too thick.
Arrange the vegetables, the rice slices, tofu, cucumber and the halved egg on a plate and spoon the sauce over.
tip: The sauce keeps 4 days in a jar in the fridge, thinned with a splash of water. Swap the tofu for tempeh if you like, or add a handful of blanched spinach for more greens.
ingredients: long beans, cut into 4 cm pieces
cold rice from your batch, pressed into a lontong-style block
calcium-set, check the label, cut into cubes

name: Chicken adobo with garlic, bay leaf and wilted mustard greens
inspiredBy: Filipino adobo, braised in cane vinegar, soy sauce and garlic, with mustasa (mustard greens) wilted in at the end
about: Chicken thighs braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaf and black pepper until the sauce is sticky and tangy, with mustard greens wilted in at the end and fresh tomato wedges to cut the richness. Adobo tastes better the next day, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The chicken and greens bring **protein, vitamin K and calcium**.
steps: Put the chicken thighs, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaf, pepper and about ½ cup (125 ml) of water per serving in a wide pot. Marinate for 15 minutes if you have the time.
Bring to a boil, then simmer without stirring for 5 minutes, so the sharp smell of the vinegar cooks off. Cover and simmer gently for 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender.
Lift the chicken out. Boil the sauce hard, uncovered, for 5 to 6 minutes, until it has reduced to a glossy glaze.

Heat the oil in a wide pan with the shallot and brown the chicken for 2 to 3 minutes per side, then pour the sauce back over it. Add the mustard greens and cook for 2 minutes, until just wilted and still bright green.
Serve over rice with the tomato wedges. Pack the second portion, with its rice and a little of the sauce, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Add a thinly sliced chili to the sauce for heat. Some cooks add a splash of coconut milk at the end (adobo sa gata). To freeze, do it before the greens go in.
ingredients: mustasa (mustard greens), cut into 5 cm pieces

name: Tumis tempeh, tofu and kangkong with chili and kecap manis
inspiredBy: Indonesian orek tempe and tumis kangkung, a sticky, sweet and hot stir-fry
about: Browned tempeh and tofu cubes with plenty of water spinach, stir-fried with shallot, garlic, galangal and plenty of fresh chili, then glazed with sweet soy. Tempeh is a **complete plant protein with iron**, and the calcium-set tofu adds **a lot of calcium**. The leftovers are just as good the next day.
steps: Fry the tempeh cubes in the oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until golden. Add the tofu and fry for 3 minutes more. Lift them out.
In the same pan, stir-fry the shallot, garlic, chili and galangal for 2 minutes, until it smells wonderful.
Add the kangkong stems with 2 tablespoons of water for 1 minute, then the leaves for 1 minute more, until bright green and just wilted.
Add the tomato and kecap manis, return the tempeh and tofu to the pan and toss over high heat for 2 minutes, until glossy and sticky. Add the salt.
Serve over rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The leftover won't be crisp, but it's just as good in a rice bowl with cucumber. Make it milder by seeding the chili. No water spinach? Use spinach, added at the very end.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Sinigang with mackerel, kangkong and okra
inspiredBy: Filipino sinigang sa sampalok, the sour tamarind soup, made with mackerel (as with hasa-hasa) in place of the usual bangus
about: A bright, sour tamarind broth with tender mackerel, tomato, okra and a big handful of water spinach (kangkong), with a long chili for gentle heat. It's one of the Philippines' great comfort soups, and the mackerel brings **omega-3**, while the greens add folate and vitamin K.
steps: Bring about 2 cups (500 ml) of water per serving to a boil with the shallot, tomato and ginger. Simmer for 8 minutes, until the tomato has softened into the broth.
Stir in the tamarind paste until it dissolves, then the fish sauce. Add the okra and the whole chili and simmer for 3 minutes.
Lay the mackerel in the broth and simmer very gently for 5 minutes, until it's just opaque and flakes. Try not to stir it, or it will break up.
Add the kangkong, stems first, and the leaves for the last 30 seconds, until just wilted. Taste: it should be sour first, then salty. Add more tamarind or fish sauce if it needs it.
Ladle into a deep bowl and eat with the rice on the side.
tip: Bangus (milkfish), salmon belly or a firm white fish all work too, but mackerel is very rich in omega-3. Fish like this doesn't keep well, so it's cooked fresh and doesn't make a leftover lunch.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Pancit bihon with chicken, shrimp, tofu and mustard greens
inspiredBy: Filipino pancit bihon guisado, with tokwa (tofu), extra vegetables and a lighter hand with the noodles
about: Thin rice vermicelli stir-fried with chicken thigh, shrimp, golden tofu, long beans, mustard greens, carrot and garlic in a light soy, fish sauce and calamansi sauce. It's the Filipino party noodle turned into a quick lunch, and the calcium-set tofu and mustard greens bring **calcium and protein**.
steps: Soak the vermicelli in hot water for 5 to 6 minutes, until it's pliable but still has some bite. Drain it, keeping about ⅓ cup (80 ml) of the soaking water. Toss the chicken with half the soy sauce and keep the shrimp in the fridge.
Heat half the oil in a wide pan or wok over high heat and fry the tofu for 4 minutes, turning, until golden. Lift it out.

Add the rest of the oil, then the shallot and garlic for 1 minute, then the chicken for 4 to 5 minutes, until no longer pink and cooked through to 74 °C (165 °F). Add the carrot, long beans and shrimp and stir-fry for 3 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and curled, then add the mustard greens for 1 minute.
Add the noodles, the tofu, the rest of the soy sauce, the fish sauce and the reserved soaking water. Toss with tongs for 2 to 3 minutes, until the noodles have soaked up the liquid and are tender.
Finish with pepper and the calamansi, and put extra calamansi on the table.
tip: Cut everything before you start, since stir-frying goes fast. Chicken breast works in place of the thigh. Wash your hands and the board after the raw chicken and shrimp.
ingredients: boneless skinless chicken thigh, sliced thin
sitaw (long beans), cut into 4 cm lengths

name: Pinakbet with chicken, squash, okra and long beans
inspiredBy: Tagalog-style pinakbet, with shrimp paste (belacan) in place of the softer bagoong alamang
about: A one-pot Filipino vegetable stew of squash, okra, long beans and tomato, built on chicken breast and a spoon of salty shrimp paste. The vegetables steam in their own juices, so it tastes deeply of vegetable, and it covers **lots of fibre, vitamin A and potassium**. It reheats beautifully for lunch.
steps: Soften the shallot, garlic and ginger in the oil in a wide pot over medium heat, about 3 minutes. Add the chicken and brown it for 4 minutes.
Stir in the shrimp paste for 1 minute, until it smells fragrant, then add the tomato and cook for 3 minutes, until it breaks down into a sauce.
Add the squash and about ¼ cup (60 ml) of water per serving, cover and simmer for 8 minutes.
Lay the beans on top, cover and cook for 8 minutes. Add the okra for the last 5 minutes. Give the pot a shake now and then instead of stirring, so the vegetables stay whole.

Season with pepper, but taste first: the shrimp paste is the salt here. Check that the chicken has reached 74 °C (165 °F). Serve with rice, and pack the second portion into a shallow container for the fridge within 2 hours; it keeps until tomorrow's lunch, reheated until steaming hot.
tip: Eggplant (talong) and bitter melon (ampalaya) are the classic extras: add a few chunks of eggplant with the beans, and salt a few slices of bitter melon for 10 minutes, squeeze them and add them too. A wedge of calamansi on top is nice.
ingredients: boneless skinless chicken breast, cut into 2 cm cubes
shrimp paste, standing in for bagoong
kalabasa, seeded, cut into 3 cm chunks

name: Lighter beef rendang with garlicky kangkong
inspiredBy: Minangkabau rendang, cooked to the saucier kalio stage with much less coconut milk, served with a quick kangkong stir-fry
about: Lean beef chuck simmered slowly in coconut milk, lemongrass, galangal, chili and tamarind until the sauce cooks down to a thick, dark gravy that clings to the beef, with a quick garlicky stir-fry of water spinach on the side. It uses a fraction of the usual coconut milk, so it's rich and spicy but low in saturated fat, and **high in iron and zinc**. Rendang gets better overnight, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Blitz the shallot, 6 g of the garlic, galangal, lemongrass, chili, turmeric, coriander, cumin, clove and cinnamon with 2 tablespoons of water into a thick paste.

Spoon the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk into a heavy pot over medium heat and fry the paste for 4 minutes, until it smells wonderful and the oil starts to separate. Add the beef and stir to coat.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk, the tamarind and about ½ cup (125 ml) of water per serving. Simmer, partly covered, for 75 to 90 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beef is very tender.

Uncover, turn the heat up and cook for 15 to 20 minutes more, stirring often, until the sauce is thick and dark, clings to the beef and a little oil shows at the edges. Stir in the palm sugar and most of the salt.
While it reduces, fry the rest of the garlic in the oil for 30 seconds, then toss in the kangkong with a splash of water and the last pinch of salt for 2 minutes, until just wilted.
Serve the rendang with the rice and the kangkong. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: For a weeknight, cook it in a pressure cooker: 25 minutes on high, then reduce uncovered for 15 minutes. Or do the paste and the long simmer the day before and finish the reduction while the rice reheats.
ingredients: lean beef chuck (or shin), trimmed and cut into 3 cm cubes
peeled, 6 g for the paste and 3 g for the kangkong
water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Laksa-inspired noodle soup with shrimp, tofu and bean sprouts
inspiredBy: Malaysian curry laksa, with a fresh paste, a little coconut milk, a shrimp-shell stock and plenty of sprouts and herbs
about: A fragrant, gently spicy coconut broth built on a fresh paste of lemongrass, galangal, chili, shallot and shrimp paste, with a stock made from the shrimp shells, ladled over rice vermicelli, shrimp, golden tofu, mustard greens and crunchy bean sprouts. It's the weekend project, and the shrimp and calcium-set tofu make it **high in protein and calcium**.
steps: Peel the shrimp and put the shells in a pot with about 1½ cups (375 ml) of water per serving. Simmer for 10 minutes, then strain and keep the stock. Keep the peeled shrimp in the fridge.
Soak the vermicelli in hot water for 5 minutes, until pliable, then drain and rinse. Put one portion in a deep bowl with the bean sprouts, and keep the rest of the noodles and sprouts for tomorrow.
Blitz the shallot, lemongrass, galangal, chili, shrimp paste, turmeric and coriander with 3 tablespoons of water into a smooth paste.
Sear the tofu sticks in the oil in a hot non-stick pot for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until golden. Lift them out.

In the same pot, spoon in the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk and fry the paste over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens, smells toasty and the oil begins to separate. Add the rest of the coconut milk and the shrimp stock and simmer for 10 minutes. Season with the salt and white pepper.
Add the shrimp and the mustard greens and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and curled. Taste: it should be fragrant, salty and a little hot.

Ladle the broth, shrimp and mustard greens over the noodles and sprouts in the bowl, then top with the tofu, the Thai basil and a squeeze of lime. For the second portion, keep the broth, the noodles and the raw shrimp and mustard greens separate, then add the shrimp and mustard greens to the reheated broth for 2 minutes.
tip: If the paste catches, add a splash of water. The paste freezes well, so make a double batch for an even faster laksa another night. A few candlenuts or raw macadamias blitzed into the paste make it richer, if you can find them.
ingredients: raw, peeled weight; buy about 180 g shell-on and keep the shells for the stock
Thai basil, standing in for laksa leaf (daun kesum)

name: Ikan bakar, grilled mackerel with sambal belacan and ulam
inspiredBy: Malay and Indonesian ikan bakar, with a hot, sour sambal belacan and a plate of raw herbs and vegetables (ulam)
about: Mackerel marinated in turmeric, garlic, tamarind and sweet soy, grilled until the skin blisters and crisps, with a fiery sambal belacan and a plate of cucumber, raw long beans and Thai basil to eat alongside. Mackerel is one of the richest sources of **omega-3** you can buy, and the sambal and lime keep it fresh and light.
steps: Mash the garlic, the shallot, the turmeric, tamarind, kecap manis, half the lime juice and a pinch of the salt into a rough paste. Rub it over the fish and leave it for 15 to 20 minutes.

For the sambal, toast the shrimp paste in a dry pan for 1 minute, until crumbly and fragrant (open a window). Pound or blitz it with the chili, the tomato, the rest of the lime juice and the rest of the salt into a coarse sambal. Taste: it should be hot, salty and sour.

Heat a grill, grill pan or the broiler until very hot and brush with the oil. Cook the fish skin-side down for 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin blisters and crisps, then flip it for 3 to 4 minutes, until it just flakes with a fork.

Serve the fish with the rice, a spoonful of sambal, and the cucumber, raw long beans and Thai basil on the side. The raw vegetables and herbs (ulam) are meant to be eaten with the fish and sambal, a bite at a time.
tip: Spanish mackerel or sardines work too. On a barbecue, wrap the fish in a banana leaf for the real thing.
ingredients: fillets with the skin on, or a butterflied whole fish
about 1 lime, split between marinade and sambal
raw long beans, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Ripe papaya
about: Sweet, soft ripe papaya eaten plain, the way it's enjoyed across the islands. It brings **vitamin C, vitamin A and folate**.
steps: Cut the papaya into chunks and eat it just as it is.
tip: A squeeze of lime helps if the papaya isn't very sweet.

name: Bubur kacang hijau, sweet mung beans in ginger coconut milk
inspiredBy: Indonesian bubur kacang hijau, lighter on coconut milk and sugar
about: Whole mung beans simmered until they burst, in a sweet, gingery coconut milk scented with pandan. It's a classic Indonesian snack that brings **fibre, folate and plant iron**, with only a spoon of coconut milk per bowl. The recipe makes 2 bowls.
steps: Soak about ½ cup (110 g) of mung beans overnight if you can. Put them in a pot with about 1¾ cups (440 ml) of water, the ginger and the pandan. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 35 minutes if soaked, or 50 minutes if not, until most of the beans have split and the mixture is thick. Top up with a splash of hot water if it thickens before the beans split.

Fish out the ginger and pandan. Stir in the palm sugar, the coconut milk and the salt, and simmer for 5 more minutes. Serve warm, and keep the second bowl in the fridge to reheat tomorrow with a splash of water.
tip: Not eating it tomorrow? Freeze the second bowl. It reheats well.

name: Rujak-style papaya with tamarind-chili dip
inspiredBy: Indonesian rujak buah
about: Sweet, soft papaya with a sweet, sour and hot tamarind dip, the Indonesian fruit salad called rujak. The papaya brings **vitamin C and folate**, and the tamarind and chili wake it right up.
steps: Stir the tamarind, palm sugar, sambal oelek and 1 tablespoon of warm water into a smooth dip.
Arrange the papaya on a plate and dip each piece.
ingredients: peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Roasted peanuts with chili salt
about: A handful of unsalted roasted peanuts tossed with a pinch of salt and a little fresh chili, the kind of snack you'd find at any warung or sari-sari store. It brings **protein, vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toss the peanuts with the chopped chili and salt, and eat them right away while they're still crunchy.

name: Tempe goreng, crisp tempeh with sambal kecap
inspiredBy: Indonesian tempe goreng
about: Thin slices of tempeh rubbed with garlic and coriander, pan-fried until crisp and golden, with a quick dip of sweet soy and fresh chili, a favourite Indonesian snack. Tempeh brings **plant protein, fibre and iron**.
steps: Crush the garlic with the salt and coriander, rub it over the slices and leave them 5 minutes.
Heat the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and fry the tempeh slices for 3 minutes per side, until golden and crisp.
Stir the kecap manis and chili together in a small dish and dip the tempeh in it.

name: Cucumber and tomato with sambal
about: Cool cucumber and ripe tomato with a spoon of sambal and a squeeze of lime, a fresh, lively snack you'd eat alongside almost any Malaysian or Indonesian meal. It adds **vitamin C and potassium** for very few calories.
steps: Stir the sambal and lime juice together. Dip the cucumber and tomato in it.

name: Steamed kalabasa with palm sugar and pandan
inspiredBy: Filipino and Indonesian steamed squash
about: Soft steamed squash mashed with a little palm sugar and a pinch of salt, scented with pandan, a comforting sweet snack in the Philippines and Indonesia. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Steam the squash with the pandan leaf for 12 to 15 minutes, until very soft.
Discard the pandan, then mash the squash lightly with the palm sugar and the salt, and eat it warm.
ingredients: kalabasa, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Boiled egg with chili vinegar
inspiredBy: Filipino sawsawan
about: A boiled egg dipped in cane vinegar with fresh chili and a pinch of salt, the sawsawan on every Filipino table. It gives you **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into simmering water for 10 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel it.
Stir the vinegar, chili and salt together, halve the egg and dip it.

name: Blanched okra and tomato with sambal belacan
inspiredBy: Malay ulam with sambal belacan
about: Tender blanched okra and ripe tomato with a hot, tangy sambal belacan to dip in, the way a Malaysian table serves raw and blanched vegetables (ulam). It brings **fibre, vitamin C and vitamin K** for very few calories.
steps: Blanch the okra in boiling water for 3 minutes, until bright green and just tender, then drain.
Toast the shrimp paste in a dry pan for 1 minute, until crumbly and fragrant. Mash it with the chili and lime juice into a coarse sambal, then eat the okra and tomato dipped in it.

name: Blanched kangkong with sambal and lime
about: A big handful of blanched water spinach with a spoon of sambal and a squeeze of lime, a simple Malaysian and Filipino side that makes a fine snack. It's **rich in vitamin K and folate**, and very light.
steps: Blanch the kangkong stems in boiling water for 1 minute, then the leaves for 20 seconds, and drain well.
Stir the sambal and lime juice together and toss with the kangkong.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Ginataang kalabasa, squash simmered in coconut milk
inspiredBy: Filipino ginataang kalabasa
about: Soft squash simmered in a little coconut milk with garlic and ginger, a gentle Filipino merienda. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**, and the coconut milk is only a spoonful.
steps: Put the squash, coconut milk, garlic, ginger, salt and a splash of water in a small pot. Cover and simmer gently for 12 to 15 minutes, until the squash is very soft.
Mash a few pieces against the side of the pot to thicken the sauce, and eat it warm.
ingredients: kalabasa, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Japanese breakfast set: tofu and wakame miso soup, tamagoyaki and brown rice
inspiredBy: a classic Japanese asa-gohan breakfast, with brown rice and a walnut furikake on top
about: A proper Japanese morning: miso soup with tofu and wakame, a rolled omelette (tamagoyaki), warm brown rice under a sprinkle of toasted sesame, nori, bonito and walnuts, and a quick cucumber pickle. With rice from your batch it is about 15 minutes. The **eggs bring protein and choline**, and the soup is warm and easy on the stomach.
steps: Reheat a portion of your batch rice with a splash of water, covered, until steaming. A couple of minutes in the microwave is fine.
Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds. Leave it to soften while you cook.

Bring about 220 ml (a scant cup) of water to a gentle simmer, add the bonito flakes and steep for 2 minutes, then strain them out and squeeze them dry. Add the wakame (a pinch swells into a lot) and the tofu to the broth, and simmer for 2 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Whisk the miso with a ladle of the broth until smooth, then stir it back in. Don't boil it once the miso is in, which keeps the flavour mellow. Sprinkle with half the scallion.

Start the eggs while the dashi steeps. Beat the eggs with the sugar, the rest of the tamari and the rest of the scallion, finely sliced. Warm the oil in a small non-stick pan over medium-low heat, pour in a thin layer of egg, and roll it up when the layer is set. Push the roll to one side, pour in more egg under it, and roll again until the egg is used up. Give the finished roll a minute on each side so no runny egg is left inside.

Toast the squeezed bonito flakes in a dry pan with the chopped walnuts and the rest of the sesame seeds until the flakes are dry and crisp, about 2 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and crumble in the nori. Sprinkle over the rice, and serve with the sliced tamagoyaki, the soup and the pickle.
tip: Short on time? Scramble the eggs with the sugar and tamari instead of rolling them, until no runny egg is left. Same flavour, half the fuss.

name: Korean banchan breakfast: soy-braised tofu, soybean sprouts, kimchi, fried egg and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-jorim and kongnamul-muchim, set out the way a home breakfast table has a few small side dishes
about: Golden pan-seared tofu in a garlicky soy, gochujang and gochugaru glaze, with sesame soybean sprouts, a little kimchi, a crisp-edged fried egg and brown rice. The tofu and sprouts are made once and last two mornings, so each breakfast takes about 10 minutes. The **tofu and sprouts bring plant protein and folate**.
steps: The evening before, make the banchan for two mornings (cook double the amounts for 2 portions). Cut the tofu into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick and pat them dry. Warm half the canola oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side.

Mince the garlic and scallion. Stir most of them into the tamari, gochujang, gochugaru and a splash of water, pour it over the tofu, and simmer, spooning the sauce over, until it is thick and glossy, about 3 minutes.
Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes, until they no longer taste raw. Drain, and toss with the rest of the garlic and scallion, the sesame oil and the sesame seeds.
Cool the tofu and the sprouts and keep them in separate containers in the fridge. They keep for 3 days.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water, and warm the tofu in the microwave or a small pan for a minute.
Fry the egg in the rest of the canola oil until the white is set and crisp at the edges, then flip it and cook for the last minute so the yolk is firm.
Serve the rice with the tofu and its sauce, the sprouts, the egg and the kimchi.
tip: The evening batch takes about 20 minutes once, and you get two quick mornings out of it.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Dak-juk, Korean chicken and vegetable rice porridge with walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean dak-juk, made from cooked rice and barley, with walnuts on top like hodu-juk
about: A silky, gently savoury porridge of rice and barley with tender chicken, carrot and zucchini, finished with toasted sesame oil, nori, scallion and crunchy walnuts. It is slow weekend comfort food that makes two bowls, so Sunday's breakfast is already done. The **chicken and barley keep you full** for hours, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Mince the ginger and garlic, dice the carrot and zucchini, slice the scallion, and cut the chicken into small pieces.
Warm half the sesame oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the chicken with the ginger and garlic until it turns white, about 3 minutes.
Add the carrot and the cooked rice and barley, and pour in water to cover the grains by about 3 cm (1 inch). That is roughly 3 parts water to 1 part cooked grain.

Bring to a boil, then simmer over low heat, stirring often and pressing some of the grains against the side of the pot, for about 20 minutes. Add water as it thickens, until the porridge is thick and creamy. Stir in the zucchini and tamari for the last 5 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then chop them roughly.

Ladle one portion into a bowl and finish with the sesame oil, scallion, walnuts and crumbled nori. Chill the second portion of porridge on its own, and keep its walnuts and nori separate so they stay crisp. Loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A spoonful of kimchi on the side is very Korean, and wakes the porridge up.

name: Cold soba with chilled tofu and edamame, with a ginger dipping sauce
inspiredBy: Japanese zaru soba, turned into a fuller lunch bowl
about: Chilled buckwheat noodles with cool tofu, edamame and crisp cucumber, dunked in a light, gingery bonito and soy sauce and finished with shredded nori. It is fresh, filling and ready in about 20 minutes. The **tofu and edamame carry the protein**, and the buckwheat gives it a nutty flavour and a little extra fibre.
steps: Make the dipping sauce first so it can chill. Simmer about 60 ml (¼ cup) of water with the bonito flakes, tamari and sugar for 2 minutes, then strain. Stir in the vinegar and half the grated ginger, and cool it quickly in a bowl set over ice, or the night before in the fridge.
Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, drain and cool them under cold water.

Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Drain, then rinse really well under cold running water, rubbing gently, until the noodles are chilled and no longer slippery.
Pile the noodles on a plate with the tofu, the cucumber cut into matchsticks and the edamame. Scatter over the sesame seeds, the sliced scallion and the nori cut into thin strips with scissors.
Serve with the sauce and the rest of the ginger for dunking.
tip: Stir a little hot noodle water into the leftover sauce and drink it at the end, the Japanese way.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate, chilled, cubed

name: Tofu steak and onigiri bento with broccoli goma-ae and carrot-daikon pickle
inspiredBy: a Japanese bento of onigiri and kohaku namasu, with a soy-glazed tofu steak for the protein
about: Two small rice balls seasoned with bonito flakes and sesame, wrapped in crisp nori, with a sweet-soy tofu steak, broccoli in a sesame dressing and a bright carrot and daikon pickle. It is the lunchbox you can eat cold at your desk. The **tofu brings plant protein**, the broccoli adds vitamin C and folate, and the pickle adds crunch.
steps: The night before, make the tofu, the broccoli and the pickle. Peel the carrot and daikon and cut them into thin matchsticks. Toss with the vinegar and half the sugar, squeeze lightly, and leave to pickle.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley until steaming hot. The barley makes it sticky enough to shape.

Pat the tofu dry and cut it into two slabs. Sear it in the oil over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Add most of the tamari and most of the remaining sugar to the pan and turn the tofu in the sizzling glaze for a minute, until it is sticky and dark.

Cut the broccoli into small florets and boil for 2 minutes, then drain and cool under cold water. Toss with a few drops of the tamari, a pinch of the sugar and half the sesame seeds, to make the goma-ae.

Stir the bonito flakes with the last of the tamari until damp, and mix them into the warm rice with the rest of the sesame seeds. Wet your hands and press the rice firmly into 2 triangles or balls, or press it in plastic wrap and twist.
Pack the onigiri with the tofu, broccoli and pickle, and keep the nori separate. Wrap each onigiri in a strip of nori just before eating so it stays crisp.
tip: Everything except the onigiri can be made the night before. Shape the rice in the morning and wrap the balls in plastic wrap.

name: Natto soba with grated daikon, scallion, nori and kimchi, with bok choy ohitashi
inspiredBy: Japanese natto soba, with kimchi for crunch and a simple ohitashi side
about: Cold buckwheat noodles topped with sticky, savoury natto, sharp grated daikon, scallion and nori, with a spoonful of kimchi for crunch and bok choy dressed in soy and sesame on the side. It is a fast, very Japanese lunch if you like natto. **Natto is rich in iron and fibre**, and the bok choy adds calcium.
steps: Simmer about 50 ml (3 tbsp) of water with the bonito flakes, half the tamari and the sugar for 2 minutes, then strain and cool it in the fridge or over ice. This is the noodle sauce.

Boil the bok choy for 1 to 2 minutes, until just tender and still bright green. Drain, cool under cold water, squeeze lightly and cut into chunks. Toss with a few drops of the tamari and the sesame seeds.
