Add a little more oil and the zucchini to the pan. Cook until golden at the edges and tender, about 4 minutes. Add the kale with a splash of water and cook until silky, about 3 minutes, then put the vegetables with the rice.
Add the rest of the olive oil and the garlic to the pan and let it sizzle for 30 seconds, until fragrant but not brown.
Add the shrimp, paprika, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt. Cook until pink and curled, about 2 minutes a side.
Spoon the shrimp and the garlicky oil over the rice. Add sliced avocado, parsley and the remaining lemon juice.
tip: Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphate.
ingredients: grated or pulsed into rice-size pieces

name: Chicken cacciatore with mushrooms, peppers and olives
inspiredBy: Italian pollo alla cacciatora, with no pasta or bread alongside
about: Chicken thighs braised with plenty of mushrooms, a little red pepper, black olives and capers in a light tomato and herb sauce, a hunter-style stew from Italy. It is even better the next day, and the mushrooms bring **B vitamins and potassium** while the spinach stirred in at the end adds folate.
steps: Pat the chicken dry and season with salt and pepper. Warm half the olive oil in a wide pan or Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the chicken well on both sides, about 8 minutes. Set it aside.
Add the rest of the olive oil, the mushrooms and a pinch of salt. Cook until they lose their water and turn golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the onion, red pepper and garlic and cook until soft, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the vinegar, scraping up the browned bits, then add the crushed tomatoes, thyme, rosemary and about ⅓ cup (80 ml) of water.
Return the chicken to the pan, cover and simmer gently for 20 minutes, then take the lid off for the last 5 minutes so the sauce thickens.
Stir in the rinsed olives and capers and the spinach, and cook 2 more minutes, until the spinach wilts.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well and keeps for 3 days in the fridge.
tip: Bone-in thighs make an even richer sauce. Brown them the same way and simmer 35 minutes instead of 20.

name: Eggplant and lamb moussaka with zucchini and a yogurt topping
inspiredBy: Greek moussaka, with zucchini for the potatoes and a yogurt and egg topping in place of flour béchamel
about: Layers of roasted eggplant and zucchini under a cinnamon-scented lamb and tomato sauce, finished with a golden yogurt and egg topping. It is the Greek weekend classic with no potato or flour, and the second portion is even better tomorrow. The eggplant brings **fibre and potassium** for very few carbs.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Lay the eggplant and zucchini on lined trays, brush both sides with about half the olive oil (a thin coat is enough on a lined tray), season with salt and roast until soft and golden, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Meanwhile, warm the remaining oil in a large pan. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic and lamb. Break the lamb up and brown it well, about 8 minutes.

Stir in the cinnamon, oregano, bay leaf, crushed tomatoes, about ½ cup (125 ml) of water for the dish, salt and pepper. Simmer for about 20 minutes, until thick but still saucy. Discard the bay leaf and stir in the parsley.
Lower the oven to 190°C (375°F). In a baking dish, layer half the eggplant and zucchini, then all the meat sauce, then the rest of the vegetables.
Whisk the yogurt with the egg, nutmeg and a pinch of salt. Spread it over the top.
Bake until set and golden in patches, about 30 minutes. Let it rest for 10 minutes before cutting, or it will slump.
Cut it into two portions. Keep the second for tomorrow's lunch; it reheats well and keeps for 3 days.
tip: Ask the butcher to mince a lean leg of lamb. It keeps the moussaka light and not greasy.
ingredients: for the two portions, 1 jumbo egg

name: Roast trout with tomatoes, olives and lemony greens
inspiredBy: Greek plaki, fish baked with tomato, garlic and olive oil
about: Trout fillets roasted on a bed of cherry tomatoes, olives, capers and garlic, served with kale braised until silky in lemon and olive oil, the way Greek horta are served. It is a Greek-island plaki dinner, and the trout brings **omega-3 and vitamin D** while the kale adds calcium and vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Toss the tomatoes, onion, sliced garlic, olives and capers on a tray with about half the olive oil, the oregano and a pinch of salt.
Roast for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes start to burst.
Pat the trout dry, rub it with a little olive oil, salt and pepper, and lay the fillets skin side up on the tomatoes.
Roast another 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.

While it cooks, strip the kale from its stems and chop it. Warm a little olive oil in a pan with a splash of water and cook the kale with a pinch of salt until silky, about 6 minutes. Take it off the heat and dress with half the lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.
Plate the kale, then the trout and tomatoes, and spoon the tomato juices over the fish. Finish with parsley and the remaining lemon.
ingredients: leaves only, most of a small bunch

name: Warm olives with rosemary and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Spanish tapas bar olives and nuts
about: Black olives and whole hazelnuts warmed in olive oil with rosemary and a squeeze of lemon, which makes them taste like a bar snack in Catalonia. The hazelnuts give you **vitamin E and magnesium** with very few carbs.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan over medium heat. Add the hazelnuts and rosemary and toast for 2 minutes, stirring, until the hazelnuts smell nutty.
Add the rinsed olives and warm through for 1 minute.
Tip into a bowl and squeeze a little lemon over the top.

name: Garlic mushrooms with parsley and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo
about: Mushrooms sautéed hard in olive oil until golden, then tossed with sizzling garlic, parsley and a squeeze of lemon. It is a classic Spanish tapa, and mushrooms are a surprisingly good source of **B vitamins and potassium**.
steps: Heat the olive oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer with a pinch of salt and cook, without stirring too much, until golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, just until fragrant.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with parsley and a squeeze of lemon.

name: Avocado with lemon, olive oil and oregano
inspiredBy: Spanish and Greek avocado with lemon, olive oil and herbs
about: A whole ripe avocado, halved and dressed with generous olive oil, lemon, oregano and Aleppo pepper. It is simple and creamy, and avocado is a great source of **potassium, folate and fibre**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Drizzle with the lemon juice and olive oil, then sprinkle over the oregano, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt.
Eat it straight from the skin with a spoon.

name: Olive and caper tapenade with cucumber dippers
inspiredBy: Provençal and Ligurian olive tapenade
about: A coarse tapenade of black olives, capers, garlic and lemon, scooped up with crunchy cucumber. The olives and olive oil are the Mediterranean fats at their purest, and they bring **vitamin E**.
steps: Rinse the olives and capers under cold water and pat them dry. Chop them with the garlic and parsley until they make a coarse paste, or pulse them a few times in a food processor.
Stir in the lemon juice, olive oil and pepper.
Cut the cucumber into dippers and serve with the tapenade.

name: Raspberries and walnuts with cinnamon
inspiredBy: Greek fruit and walnuts, without the honey
about: Juicy raspberries with a handful of toasted walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. It is sweet-tart and crunchy, with plant omega-3 from the walnuts and plenty of **fibre** from the berries.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Put the raspberries in a bowl, add the warm walnuts and dust with cinnamon.

name: Toasted hazelnuts with rosemary and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish and Piedmontese toasted hazelnuts
about: Whole hazelnuts toasted in a dry pan until golden and fragrant, then tossed with rosemary, a pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon. Hazelnuts are grown across Spain and Italy, and a small handful gives you **vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fats** with hardly any carbs.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking now and then, until golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with the olive oil, rosemary and salt.
Add a squeeze of lemon and let them cool for a couple of minutes so they crunch.

name: Avocado filled with tuna and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish and Italian tuna with avocado and lemon
about: A ripe avocado half filled with flaked tuna, lemon, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil. It is rich, creamy and filling, with **protein and potassium** in one easy bite.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Flake the tuna with the lemon juice, chopped parsley, olive oil, pepper and a pinch of salt.
Pile the tuna into the hollow of the avocado and eat with a spoon.

name: Poached shrimp with lemon and smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Spanish gambas cocidas
about: Shrimp poached in a pot of lemony water for a couple of minutes, then tossed with olive oil, smoked paprika and parsley and eaten cold, like a plate of Spanish gambas cocidas. It is a cold plate of shrimp to pick at, with plenty of **protein** for almost no carbs.
steps: Bring a small pot of salted water to a boil with a squeeze of the lemon.
Add the shrimp and cook until pink and curled, about 2 minutes. Drain and cool under cold water.
Toss with the olive oil, paprika, parsley and the rest of the lemon juice.
tip: Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphate.

name: Tuna-stuffed eggs with capers and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish huevos rellenos de atún
about: Hard-boiled egg halves filled with a creamy mash of the yolk, flaked tuna, capers, parsley and lemon, a classic Spanish tapa. It is a small, salty, filling snack, and the egg and tuna bring **choline and protein**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes. Cool it under cold water, then peel and halve lengthwise.
Pop out the yolk and mash it with the drained tuna, chopped capers, parsley, lemon juice and olive oil until creamy.
Spoon the filling back into the whites and dust with the paprika.

name: Marinated olives with oregano, garlic and lemon
inspiredBy: Greek meze marinated olives
about: Black olives tossed with olive oil, a little garlic, oregano and lemon and left to sit for a few minutes, the way every meze table in Greece starts. They are salty, fruity and satisfying, and a handful of olives is a classic Mediterranean source of **healthy fats and vitamin E**.
steps: Rinse the olives under cold water, pat them dry and put them in a small bowl.
Add the olive oil, lemon juice, finely grated garlic, oregano and chopped parsley, and toss well.
Leave them to marinate for 10 minutes if you can, then eat with a fork or toothpicks.

name: Almonds fried in olive oil with pimentón
inspiredBy: Spanish almendras fritas
about: Whole almonds fried in olive oil until golden, then tossed with smoked paprika and a pinch of salt, the kind of snack a Spanish bar puts out with a cold drink. They are warm, crunchy and rich, and bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small frying pan over medium heat.
Add the almonds and fry, stirring, for about 3 minutes, until they are golden and smell toasty.
Tip them and the oil onto a plate, toss with the pimentón and salt, and let them cool for a couple of minutes so they crisp up.

name: Shakshuka with kale and parsley, and sliced avocado
inspiredBy: the shakshuka of Tunisia and Libya, now cooked all over the Levant, with kale folded into the sauce and avocado in place of the bread
about: Eggs poached in a cumin and paprika tomato sauce thick with sweet red pepper and a good handful of kale, with cool avocado on the side for the yolk. It is a favourite Middle Eastern breakfast, minus the bread, and the eggs and kale bring **choline, calcium and vitamin K** before nine in the morning.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide, deep frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, cumin, paprika and Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Add the tomato, a splash of water, the salt and the pepper. Simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, until the tomato has broken down and the sauce is thick but still saucy.
Stir in the kale and cook until it wilts and turns bright green, about 3 minutes.
Make a dip in the sauce for each egg with the back of a spoon and crack the eggs in. Cover and cook over low heat until the whites and yolks are both firm, 5 to 6 minutes.
Scatter the parsley over the pan. Slice the avocado alongside and squeeze the lemon over it.
tip: Cook the tomato sauce (without the kale and eggs) in a big batch on Sunday. It keeps for 4 days, and a weekday shakshuka is then ready in 10 minutes.

name: Turkish poached egg, cooked firm, on garlic yogurt with Aleppo pepper oil and a crisp cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Turkish çılbır, poached egg on garlicky yogurt, with olive oil in place of the butter and a cucumber salad in place of the bread
about: A firm poached egg on a cool bed of thick garlic yogurt, with a spoonful of warm olive oil blushed red with Aleppo pepper and fresh dill. A crunchy cucumber and radish salad with olives sits alongside. It is ready in about 15 minutes, and the egg and thick yogurt bring **protein, choline and calcium**.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the grated garlic and a pinch of the salt. Spread it on a shallow plate and let it come to room temperature while you cook the egg.

Bring a deep pan of water to a bare simmer. Crack each egg into its own cup, swirl the water gently and slide them in one at a time. Cover and poach for 5 minutes, until the whites and yolks are both firm.
Meanwhile, toss the cucumber, radish, parsley and olives with the lemon juice and the rest of the salt.
Warm the olive oil in a small pan for about 1 minute, until it shimmers, then take it off the heat and stir in the Aleppo pepper so it turns brick red.
Lift the egg (or eggs) out with a slotted spoon, blot on a towel and set on the yogurt. Spoon the hot pepper oil over, scatter with the dill and serve with the salad.
tip: No Aleppo pepper? A pinch of paprika with a pinch of chili flakes does the same job.

name: Labneh plate with a hard-boiled egg, za'atar oil, olives and cucumber
inspiredBy: the Levantine morning labneh plate, with a boiled egg as on a Turkish kahvaltı table and no bread, with chia stirred through for fibre
about: A thick swoop of labneh under a pool of olive oil and za'atar, with a hard-boiled egg, peppery arugula, cool cucumber and tomato, plenty of olives and fresh mint, with a spoon of chia stirred through the labneh for a little texture. It is how a Lebanese breakfast looks, minus the bread. The egg, labneh and chia bring **choline, calcium and fibre**.
steps: Lower the egg (or eggs) into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes, until the white and yolk are firm. Cool under cold water, then peel.

Stir the chia seeds and a spoonful of water into the labneh and let it stand for 5 minutes, so the seeds soften. (Stir it together the night before if you like it smoother.) Spread it on a plate with the back of a spoon, leaving a little dip in the middle.
Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and pour it into the dip.
Arrange the arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish and olives around it and set the egg halves on the labneh. Scatter with the mint and squeeze the lemon over the vegetables.
tip: Labneh is sold at Middle Eastern shops and many supermarkets. If you can't find it, strain thick plain yogurt in a cloth overnight.

name: Sumac beef on a bread-free fattoush with avocado
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush without the fried pita, with seared beef on top
about: Thin slices of seared beef over a big, sharp fattoush of romaine, kale, arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish and mint, dressed with plenty of lemon, olive oil and sumac, with creamy avocado alongside. The crunch comes from the radish and cucumber instead of fried bread. The salad is full of **vitamin C, folate and calcium**.
steps: Toss the sliced beef with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Heat a third of the olive oil in a heavy frying pan over high heat and sear the beef in two batches, about 1 minute per side, until browned but still a little pink inside. Set aside.
For the dressing, whisk the rest of the olive oil with the lemon juice, the rest of the sumac and a pinch of salt.
Rub the kale with a spoonful of the dressing for a minute to soften it. Toss it with the romaine, arugula, cucumber, tomato, radish, parsley and mint and the rest of the dressing.
Pile the salad onto a plate and lay the beef and the avocado cubes over it.
tip: Slicing the beef very thin while it is half frozen is easiest.
ingredients: lean round steak, sliced thin against the grain
stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

name: Circassian chicken in walnut and garlic sauce, on crisp romaine
inspiredBy: Turkish çerkez tavuğu, poached chicken in a rich walnut sauce, here without the bread that usually thickens it
about: Tender poached chicken breast shredded into a creamy walnut and garlic sauce, served cool over crisp romaine with cucumber and radish and a drizzle of red paprika oil. It is a Turkish and Syrian celebration dish that eats beautifully cold, and it makes two portions. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3, copper and magnesium**.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with the onion chunk, bay leaf, a pinch of the salt and enough water to cover. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 14 to 16 minutes, until cooked through. Lift the chicken out and keep about 1 cup (250 ml) of the broth.

While it cooks, toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until fragrant. Let them cool, then blitz them in a food processor with the garlic, lemon juice, the rest of the salt then add the warm broth a spoonful at a time until you have a thick, creamy sauce, like hummus.
Shred the chicken into thick pieces with two forks and toss it with about two thirds of the walnut sauce.
Warm the olive oil with the paprika and Aleppo pepper in a small pan for 30 seconds, until it turns a deep red.
Arrange the romaine, cucumber and radish on a plate. Pile the chicken on top, spoon over the rest of the sauce, drizzle with the red oil and scatter with the parsley and the pepper.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It is meant to be eaten cool or at room temperature, with the greens packed separately.
tip: Cooked chicken keeps well, so you can poach it on Sunday. Save the broth for soup.
ingredients: a chunk, for the poaching water

name: Chicken shawarma lettuce bowls with garlic-tahini sauce, avocado and pickles
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian chicken shawarma, served over crisp romaine with the pickles and garlic sauce but no flatbread
about: Thinly sliced chicken marinated in lemon, garlic and warm spices, roasted until the edges char, then piled over crunchy romaine with cucumber, tomato, pickles, avocado and a punchy garlic and tahini sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The chicken, tahini and parsley bring **protein, magnesium and calcium**.
steps: Mix the sliced chicken with the olive oil, half the lemon juice, half the garlic (crushed), the baharat, cumin, turmeric, cinnamon, salt and pepper. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or up to a day in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) and line a tray with parchment. Spread the chicken out in one layer and roast for 12 to 15 minutes, turning once, until cooked through and charred at the edges. For a more shawarma-like char, finish it for 2 minutes under the broiler.
Whisk the tahini with the rest of the garlic (crushed), the rest of the lemon and enough cold water to make a pourable sauce. It should look like thin cream. Season with a pinch of salt.
Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and let it sit for a few minutes to soften.
Build the bowls: romaine first, then the cucumber, tomato, pickles and parsley, then the chicken, sumac onions and sliced avocado. Spoon the sauce over.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the sauce, the avocado and the tomato in separate containers. Reheat the chicken in a hot pan for 2 minutes and add the sauce cold.
tip: Slice the breasts thin and don't overcook them. Boneless thighs stay juicier overnight.
ingredients: half for the marinade, half for the sauce

name: Lemon and paprika chicken şiş on cauliflower and kale tabbouleh with lemon-tahini
inspiredBy: Turkish tavuk şiş, the grilled chicken skewers, over a Lebanese-style tabbouleh with finely chopped raw cauliflower and kale in place of the bulgur
about: Juicy chicken marinated in lemon, garlic and paprika, grilled until charred at the edges and set over a bright, mostly-parsley tabbouleh with finely chopped cauliflower and kale for body and a generous ribbon of lemon-tahini. It is a fresh, sharp lunch, and the parsley, kale and cauliflower bring **vitamin C, vitamin K and calcium**.
steps: Mix the chicken with the garlic, half the lemon juice, a third of the olive oil, the paprika, Aleppo pepper, cumin and half the salt. Leave it for 1 hour, or up to a day in the fridge.

Mix the cauliflower, parsley, kale, mint, cucumber and red onion in a bowl. Dress with most of the remaining lemon juice, half the remaining olive oil and the rest of the salt. Leave it for 10 minutes so the cauliflower and kale soften a little.

Thread the chicken onto skewers. Heat a grill or a heavy pan over medium-high heat with the last of the olive oil and cook the skewers for 10 to 12 minutes, turning. Pull them off the heat the moment the juices run clear.
Whisk the tahini with the last of the lemon juice and enough cold water, about 1 tablespoon, to make a pourable sauce.
Spoon the tabbouleh onto a plate, set the chicken on top and drizzle with the tahini sauce.
tip: Cut the cauliflower by pulsing it in a food processor, a few short bursts, so it doesn't turn to mush. For a packed lunch, grill the skewers the night before and keep the tahini sauce separate.
ingredients: boneless, skinless breasts, cut in chunks
half for the marinade, the rest for the tabbouleh and sauce
stems removed, leaves very finely sliced

name: Beef-stuffed eggplant with tomato, peppers and lemony kale
inspiredBy: Turkish karnıyarık, the "split belly" eggplant stuffed with spiced beef, tomato and pepper, with walnuts in the filling as in a Turkish içli köfte, and garlicky greens in place of the pilaf
about: Silky roasted eggplant halves split open and filled with a savoury beef, onion, tomato and pepper mixture with toasted walnuts, baked in a little tomato sauce and served with a pile of garlicky sautéed kale. It is a classic Turkish family dish, and it makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is ready. The eggplant and kale bring **fibre, calcium and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Score the cut side of each eggplant half in a crisscross, brush with about a third of the olive oil and season with salt. Roast cut side up on a lined tray for 25 minutes, until soft and golden.
Meanwhile, toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, and set them aside.
Warm half the remaining olive oil in a large pan and cook the onion and red pepper until soft, about 6 minutes. Add half the garlic, then the beef, and break it up. Brown it well, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste, paprika, Aleppo pepper, diced tomato, pepper and a splash of water. Simmer for 5 to 6 minutes, until thick. Stir in the parsley, walnuts and half the lemon juice.

Press the middle of each roasted eggplant half down with a spoon to make a boat. Mound in as much filling as the boats will hold and spoon the rest around them, top each with a slice of tomato and pour about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of water into the tray around them.
Bake for 20 minutes, until the eggplant is meltingly soft and the tops are lightly browned.

While it bakes, warm the last of the olive oil in a wide pan, add the rest of the garlic, sliced, and stir for 30 seconds. Add the kale with a splash of water and a pinch of salt, cover and cook for 5 minutes, until tender. Finish with the rest of the lemon juice.
Serve two eggplant halves and their filling per person with the kale. Keep the second for tomorrow's lunch; it reheats well and keeps for 3 days.
tip: Salting the eggplant isn't necessary. Roasting it face up gives it the soft, sweet texture without extra oil. Roast the eggplant halves on Sunday and the filling comes together in 25 minutes.
ingredients: lean round steak, minced by the butcher or ground in a food processor
1 small, slim eggplant per person (Japanese or Italian), halved lengthwise
diced, with a thin slice kept back for each eggplant half

name: Gulf-style grilled sea bass with spiced cauliflower rice and dakkous
inspiredBy: Gulf grilled fish with baharat, machboos-style spiced rice made from cauliflower, and the tomato-garlic chili sauce called dakkous, finished with toasted nuts the way machboos is
about: Sea bass fillets rubbed with baharat and lemon, grilled until the skin crisps, over cauliflower cooked with cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric and loomi in the style of a machboos, with wilted spinach, toasted hazelnuts and a hot, garlicky tomato dakkous. The fish, cauliflower and spinach bring **selenium, vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until golden, and chop them roughly. Mix a third of the olive oil with half the lemon juice, half the garlic (crushed), the baharat, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Rub it over the fish and leave it for 15 minutes.

Make the dakkous. Chop the tomato, serrano, the rest of the garlic and the cilantro very finely together on a board, or pound them in a mortar, then stir in the cumin, the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. It should be a coarse, juicy sauce.
Warm half the remaining olive oil in a wide pan and cook the onion until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric and loomi and stir for 20 seconds.
Add the cauliflower and a pinch of salt. Cook, stirring, for 5 to 6 minutes, until just tender but with a little bite. Add the spinach and cook for 1 minute more, until it wilts.
Heat a grill pan, a heavy frying pan or the grill to high. Cook the fish skin side down for 4 to 5 minutes without moving it, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes more.
Serve the fish over the cauliflower rice, scattered with the hazelnuts, with the dakkous, and a small salad of arugula and cucumber dressed with the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
tip: Any firm white fish works: sea bream, snapper or haddock fillets cook the same way.
ingredients: half for the fish, half for the dakkous
ground, or a pinch of crushed dried lime

name: Pan-seared fresh anchovies with sumac onions and a parsley, radish and kale salad
inspiredBy: Turkish hamsi tava, the fresh Black Sea anchovies cooked in a hot pan, with a Levantine sumac onion salad and no cornmeal coating, and the walnut and hazelnut tarator Turkish fish restaurants serve with fried fish
about: Whole fresh anchovies seared in a hot pan until the skins crackle, over a sharp salad of parsley, radish, kale and arugula with thin sumac onions, lemon and a spoonful of rough walnut and hazelnut tarator. Anchovies are the little oily fish people fry all along the Turkish coast. A serving carries **omega-3, calcium and selenium**.
steps: Toast the walnuts and hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Pound them in a mortar, or blitz them in a mini chopper, with a little of the garlic, a squeeze of the lemon, a pinch of salt and a splash of water, into a rough, creamy tarator.
Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes to soften.
Rub the kale with a pinch of salt and half the garlic for a minute to soften it. Toss it with the parsley, radish, cucumber and arugula, the onions, half the lemon juice and a third of the olive oil.
Pat the anchovies very dry and season them with salt, pepper and the rest of the garlic. Heat the rest of the olive oil in a large non-stick pan over high heat.

Lay the anchovies in the pan in a single layer, in two batches if you need to, and cook for 2 minutes without moving them, until the skins are crisp. Flip and cook for 1 minute more, until just opaque.
Pile the salad on a plate and set the anchovies on top. Spoon the tarator alongside, squeeze over the rest of the lemon and finish with the Aleppo pepper.
tip: Fresh sardines are easier to find in North America and work the same way: scale and gut them, or ask the fishmonger, and cook 2 to 3 minutes a side. Smelt and small mackerel fillets also work.
ingredients: half for the salad, the rest to squeeze over the fish
stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

name: Sardine, tomato and parsley salad with avocado and lemon-tahini
inspiredBy: Lebanese-style canned sardines with tomato, parsley and lemon, with avocado and a tahini dressing added
about: Canned sardines, soft bones and all, flaked over a bright salad of ripe tomato, cucumber, a big handful of parsley and creamy avocado, with lemon-tahini poured over. It takes 10 minutes and nothing gets cooked. The sardines bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin B12**.
steps: Toss the red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes.
Whisk the tahini with the crushed garlic, half the lemon juice and cold water, a teaspoon at a time until pourable.
Toss the romaine, tomato, cucumber, parsley and mint with the olive oil, the rest of the lemon juice, the onions and a pinch of salt and pepper.
Pile the salad onto a plate. Flake the sardines over it in big pieces and add the avocado.
Drizzle the tahini dressing over everything and eat right away.
tip: Buy sardines packed in water or brine, not oil, for a fresher taste. Drain them but keep the soft bones: that is where the calcium is.
ingredients: canned in water or brine, drained, bones in
half for the salad, half for the dressing

name: Lamb and beef kofta platter with baba ghanoush, charred pepper and a sumac arugula salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese kafta mashwiyye, the grilled lamb and beef skewers with parsley, served mezze-style with smoky baba ghanoush
about: Juicy lamb and beef skewers with parsley, scented with baharat and cinnamon, grilled and served on a platter with smoky baba ghanoush, a charred red pepper, a sharp arugula salad with parsley and sumac, and a walnut and tahini tarator. It is the weekend project, and it makes two portions. The meat brings **zinc and iron**, and the eggplant adds potassium and fibre.
steps: Prick the eggplant and char it directly over a gas flame, under a very hot broiler or on the grill for 15 to 20 minutes, turning, until the skin is blackened and the flesh is collapsing. Set it in a bowl and cover it for 10 minutes.

Scoop the soft flesh out, drain off any bitter liquid, and mash it with a third of the tahini, a third of the lemon juice, a little garlic, a drizzle of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. It should be smoky and slightly rough.

Make the kofta mixture. Knead the lamb and beef with the onion, two thirds of the parsley, a spoonful of the olive oil, the baharat, the cinnamon, the salt and the pepper for a full minute, until sticky and well combined. Shape it into long, flat fingers around skewers, or into short ovals if you are using a pan.

Brush the kofta and the pepper strip with some of the olive oil. Grill, broil or pan-sear the kofta for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until browned and just cooked through. Char the pepper skin side down until blistered, then slice it.

Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Whisk the rest of the tahini with the rest of the garlic, half the remaining lemon juice, the walnuts and about 2 tablespoons of cold water into a pourable tarator.
Toss the arugula with the rest of the parsley, the sumac, the last of the lemon juice and a drizzle of the remaining olive oil.
Serve the kofta on a platter with the baba ghanoush, pepper, tomato slices and salad, with the tarator spooned over. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Lean lamb can go dry, so don't skip the grated onion, and take the kofta off as soon as they are just cooked through. Reheat leftover kofta in a hot pan for 2 minutes.
ingredients: lean leg, ground twice or minced by the butcher
lean round, ground or minced by the butcher
finely chopped, two thirds for the kofta
a third for the baba ghanoush, the rest for the sauce
toasted and finely chopped, for the sauce
for the baba ghanoush, the sauce and the salad
one wide strip, about a quarter of a pepper, for charring

name: Baked whole trout with a cilantro, walnut and chili sauce, and garlicky kale
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra, the baked fish with a spicy cilantro and nut sauce, made with a whole trout and served with Black Sea style sautéed kale
about: A whole trout stuffed with parsley and baked until the skin crisps, under a hot, green sauce of cilantro, garlic, chili, walnuts and lemon, with a pile of garlicky sautéed kale. It is simple enough for a weekend dinner and good enough to be a feast. The trout and walnuts bring **omega-3, B12 and copper**, and the kale adds calcium and vitamin A.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the trout dry and make 3 shallow slashes on each side. Rub the skin and the inside with a little of the olive oil, salt and pepper, and tuck the parsley sprigs into the cavity.
Lay the trout on a lined tray and roast it for 18 to 22 minutes, until the flesh flakes at the thickest part and the skin is crisp.

While it bakes, make the sauce. Blitz the walnuts with the cilantro, most of the garlic, the serrano, half the lemon juice, half the remaining olive oil and a pinch of salt, adding a few tablespoons of water, until you have a thick, spoonable sauce.

Warm the rest of the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and add the last of the garlic, sliced. Stir for 30 seconds, then add the kale with a splash of water and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until tender.

Lift the trout onto a platter, spoon the sauce over and around it, and squeeze over a little of the remaining lemon juice. Dress the kale with the rest of the lemon and the sumac and serve it alongside.
tip: A whole trout gives about two thirds of its weight as fish. Ask the fishmonger to gut and scale it; fillets work too, roasted for 10 to 12 minutes.
ingredients: 1 whole trout, cleaned; buy a fish about half as heavy again as the weight shown
about half for the sauce, the rest for the fish and kale
a few sprigs for the fish

name: Toasted hazelnuts with Aleppo pepper and lemon
inspiredBy: the warm, salted hazelnuts sold in Turkish nut shops (çerez), from the Black Sea hazelnut groves
about: A warm handful of hazelnuts toasted in a dry pan with a little Aleppo pepper, a squeeze of lemon and salt, the way a Turkish nut shop sells them. They are sweet, crunchy and a little hot, and bring **vitamin E, magnesium and healthy fat** with almost no carbs.
steps: Heat a small dry pan over medium heat. Add the hazelnuts and toast, shaking the pan, until they smell nutty and the skins crackle, about 4 minutes.
Tip them into a bowl, rub off any loose skins with a towel if you like, and toss with the Aleppo pepper, lemon juice and salt while they are warm.
tip: Toast a big batch on Sunday and keep it in a jar for the week.

name: Muhammara with cucumber and radish
inspiredBy: Syrian muhammara from Aleppo, the roasted red pepper and walnut dip, made without the breadcrumbs and pomegranate molasses
about: A rich, smoky, slightly hot dip of roasted red pepper and walnuts with a squeeze of lemon, scooped up with cucumber and radish. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3**, and the pepper brings vitamin C.
steps: Use a jarred roasted red pepper, drained and rinsed, or roast a whole pepper under a hot broiler or over a flame until blackened all over, about 15 minutes. Let it steam in a covered bowl, then peel off the skin and remove the seeds.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Blitz the pepper, walnuts, olive oil, lemon juice, garlic, Aleppo pepper, cumin and salt to a thick, slightly coarse paste.
Spoon into a bowl and serve with the cucumber and radish.
tip: It keeps for 5 days in the fridge, so make a double batch.

name: Warm za'atar olives
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian olives warmed with za'atar and olive oil
about: Rinsed black olives warmed in olive oil with a little za'atar and lemon. It is salty, herby and very satisfying, and the olives bring **vitamin E and healthy fat** with almost no carbs.
steps: Rinse the olives under cold water and pat them dry.
Warm the olive oil in a small pan over low heat. Add the olives and the za'atar and stir for 2 minutes, until warm and fragrant.
Squeeze the lemon over everything and eat warm.
tip: Rinsing cuts the salt on olives noticeably. Leave the pits in for the best flavour, and watch your teeth.

name: Avocado with lemon, za'atar and olive oil
inspiredBy: the way labneh is dressed on a Levantine breakfast table, with olive oil, lemon and za'atar, here on avocado
about: A whole ripe avocado, halved, with a squeeze of lemon, a drizzle of olive oil and a good shake of za'atar. It takes a minute, and the avocado brings **potassium, folate and fibre**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the stone.
Squeeze the lemon over the cut face, drizzle with the olive oil and sprinkle with the za'atar and a tiny pinch of salt.
Eat it with a spoon, straight from the skin.
tip: Pick the avocado a couple of days ahead. It should give slightly when pressed.

name: Spiced hazelnuts and walnuts with sumac and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: the mixed roasted nuts sold across the Gulf and the Levant, with the Black Sea hazelnuts and the walnuts of the Syrian and Turkish kitchen
about: Hazelnuts and walnuts toasted in a dry pan with sumac, Aleppo pepper and a little salt. It is a crunchy, tangy little handful that brings **vitamin E, plant omega-3 and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking now and then, until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes.
Toss with the olive oil, sumac, Aleppo pepper and salt while they are warm.
tip: Make extra and keep it in a jar for up to a week.

name: Olive oil artichoke hearts with dill, lemon and toasted hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Turkish zeytinyağlı enginar, the cold artichoke hearts dressed with olive oil, lemon and dill
about: Tender artichoke hearts dressed with olive oil, lemon and fresh dill, with toasted hazelnuts for crunch. It is a classic Turkish cold meze that takes five minutes from a jar, and the artichokes bring **fibre and folate** for very few carbs.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes. Tip them out to cool, then chop them roughly.
Drain the artichoke hearts, rinse them well and pat them dry. Halve them if they are large.
Toss them with the olive oil, lemon juice, dill, Aleppo pepper and a tiny pinch of salt.
Pile onto a plate and scatter the hazelnuts over the top.
tip: Choose artichoke hearts packed in brine or water rather than oil, and rinse them.
ingredients: hearts in brine, drained and rinsed

name: Avocado with lemon-tahini, sumac and radish
inspiredBy: the lemon-tahini and sumac that dress hummus on a Levantine table, here spooned over avocado
about: A small ripe avocado, halved, with a ribbon of lemon-tahini, a dusting of sumac, thin radish and a little cilantro. It is creamy and tangy, and the avocado and tahini bring **fibre, potassium and calcium**.
steps: Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, a pinch of the salt and enough cold water, about 1 tablespoon, to make a pourable sauce.
Set the avocado halves on a plate and spoon the sauce into and over them.
Top with the radish and cilantro and finish with the sumac.
tip: Pick the avocado a couple of days ahead. It should give slightly when pressed.
ingredients: about 1 small avocado, halved and pitted

name: Roasted pumpkin seeds with sumac and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: the salted roasted seeds sold at every nut shop in Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, eaten by the handful
about: Pumpkin seeds toasted in a dry pan with sumac, Aleppo pepper and a pinch of salt until they pop and turn golden. They are crunchy, tangy and a little hot, and bring **zinc, magnesium and iron**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff and turn golden, about 4 minutes.
Toss with the olive oil, sumac, Aleppo pepper and salt while they are warm.
tip: They keep for 2 weeks in a jar, so toast a bigger batch if you like them.

name: Olive and walnut dip with crisp romaine
inspiredBy: the olive and walnut pastes of Hatay and Gaziantep, served as a meze with raw vegetables
about: A coarse, garlicky paste of rinsed olives, toasted walnuts, parsley and lemon, scooped up with crisp romaine leaves. It is salty, nutty and bright, and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and copper**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until fragrant.
Pulse the olives, walnuts, garlic, lemon juice, olive oil and parsley in a small processor to a coarse paste, adding a spoonful of water if it is stiff.
Spoon into a bowl, sprinkle with the Aleppo pepper and serve with the romaine leaves for scooping.
tip: It keeps for 4 days in a jar in the fridge.

name: Greek yogurt bowl with mango, lime, mint and toasted seeds
inspiredBy: Inspired by Thai and Vietnamese fruit with lime and mint
about: Thick Greek yogurt under juicy mango, with a squeeze of lime, torn mint and warm toasted sesame and sunflower seeds. It is a cool, bright start with **plenty of protein**, vitamin C from the mango and vitamin E from the seeds.
steps: Toast the sesame and sunflower seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking often, until they smell nutty and turn pale gold. Tip them onto a plate.
Spoon the yogurt into a wide bowl and top with the mango.
Squeeze over the lime, scatter on the warm seeds and finish with the torn mint.
tip: Toast a small jar of mixed seeds on Sunday and this is a two-minute breakfast. Pineapple or papaya work in place of the mango.

name: Egg and tofu scramble with shiitake, spinach and sweet potato
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese tofu and egg stir-fries and Korean sweet potato breakfasts
about: Soft-set eggs folded with silken tofu, browned shiitake, spinach and ginger, next to chunks of tender steamed sweet potato. It gives you **protein, fibre and a slow carb** to carry you well past mid-morning.
steps: Press the tofu between paper towels while you start. Put the sweet potato in a covered microwave dish with a splash of water and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until a knife slides in easily. Or steam it on the stove for 12 minutes.
Warm the canola oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the shiitake in a single layer and leave them for 3 minutes, then stir and cook for 2 minutes more, until browned.
Add the ginger, then the spinach by the handful, and stir until just wilted, about 1 minute.
Crumble the pressed tofu into the pan and cook for 2 minutes to steam off the water.
Beat the eggs with the soy sauce, pour them over and turn the heat to low. Fold gently for 2 minutes, until softly set and still glossy.
Serve with the sweet potato. Scatter on the scallion and chili flakes and finish with a drizzle of perilla oil, as Korean cooks do with greens.
tip: Microwave the sweet potato the night before and the pan part takes 8 minutes.

name: Warm silken tofu bowl with edamame, ginger-soy and bonito
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese hiyayakko and Chinese savoury tofu pudding
about: Silky tofu warmed through with sweet edamame, a spoon of ginger and soy, curls of bonito, nori and toasted seeds, with crisp Asian pear on the side. It is a light, savoury Japanese-style start with **plenty of plant protein** and lots of fibre.
steps: Boil the edamame for 3 minutes, or as the bag says, then drain. Toast the sesame and sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Slide the tofu into a shallow bowl and microwave for 1 minute, or until warm. Tip off any liquid.
Pile the edamame around the tofu. Spoon the grated ginger, soy sauce and perilla oil over the top.
Scatter on the bonito, scallion, nori and the warm seeds. Eat with the pear slices on the side.
tip: Chilled tofu works just as well on a hot morning: skip the microwave.

name: Salmon and edamame rice bowl with spinach and carrot-daikon pickle
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese salmon-flake rice bowls and namasu
about: Flaked canned salmon over a small bed of brown rice, with edamame, wilted spinach, cucumber and a quick carrot and daikon pickle, finished with sesame and nori. The salmon brings **omega-3 and calcium** (the soft bones are edible), and the crunchy pickles make the bowl big and bright.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain and let it cool a little.
Toss the carrot, daikon and cucumber with the rice vinegar and ginger and leave for 10 minutes while the rice cooks, until lightly pickled and crisp.
Boil the edamame for 3 minutes, adding the spinach for the last 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze the spinach dry.
Stir the soy sauce, sesame oil and a spoonful of the pickling liquid together. Pile the rice into a bowl and top with the salmon, edamame, spinach and the pickled vegetables.
Spoon the soy dressing over the top and finish with the sesame seeds, nori and scallion.
tip: Cook a pot of brown rice on Sunday for the first four rice meals and again on Wednesday for the other eight: roughly 1 to 1⅓ cups dry on Sunday and 1⅓ to 2¼ cups on Wednesday, the smaller amounts for Light. It keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge, so this bowl takes 10 minutes.

name: Vietnamese chicken pho with a big plate of herbs
inspiredBy: Inspired by phở gà, served southern-style with a plate of sprouts and herbs
about: A fragrant broth built on charred shallot and ginger, star anise and cinnamon, with poached chicken, a small nest of rice noodles, a mound of crunchy sprouts and a heap of cilantro, mint and scallion. The chicken makes this **a big serving of lean protein**, and the herbs, lime and chili season it so you need very little salt. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Set a dry pot over high heat and char the shallot halves and ginger coins for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until blackened in spots and sweet-smelling. Add the star anise, coriander seed and clove for the last minute, until fragrant.

Pour in the broth, the cinnamon and about ¼ cup of water for each portion. Simmer gently, half covered, for 15 minutes to draw out the spices. Add the chicken, cover and cook very gently for 5 minutes, then turn off the heat and leave it in the hot broth for 10 minutes, until cooked through.
Lift out the chicken and shred it. Strain the broth, stir in the fish sauce and the salt and taste: it should be savoury, warm and a little sweet.
Cook the rice noodles as the packet says, usually 4 to 6 minutes, then rinse under cold water and drain.
Divide the noodles and shredded chicken between bowls and ladle on the hot broth. Pile the sprouts, cilantro, mint, scallion and lime wedges on a plate with the chili flakes for everyone to add.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch with the broth, noodles and herbs in separate containers. Reheat the broth until steaming and pour it over.
tip: Thai basil, if you can find it, is a lovely extra at the table.
ingredients: from a lime, cut into wedges to squeeze

name: Korean soft tofu stew with shrimp, napa cabbage and an egg
inspiredBy: Inspired by Korean sundubu-jjigae
about: A bubbling, brick-red stew of silky tofu, shrimp, napa cabbage and kimchi, with an egg cooked firm in the centre at the end. The tofu, shrimp and egg together bring **a big helping of protein and B12**, and the chili warms you without much salt. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.

Warm the canola oil in a wide pot over medium-low heat. Add the scallion whites, garlic and kimchi and cook for 3 minutes until soft. Stir in the gochugaru for 20 seconds, until it smells toasty and turns the oil red. Do not let it scorch.

Add the bonito, shiitake, napa and about ¾ cup of water for each portion (the napa and tofu add their own juices, and sundubu should be thick and spoonable). Bring to a simmer and cook for 8 minutes, until the cabbage is soft.
Add the soy sauce and the salt, then spoon in the tofu in big chunks and let it warm for 2 minutes. Add the shrimp and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes, until they turn pink.

Ladle the second portion into a container to cool. Make a small well in the stew left in the pot and crack in an egg. Cover and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until the white and yolk are both firm. Scatter on the scallion greens and drizzle with the perilla oil.
Serve with the rice. Pack the second portion with its rice for tomorrow's lunch. When you reheat it, set a fresh egg in the same way.
tip: Cook the rice on Sunday and this is 20 minutes. Mash the yolk into the broth for a richer stew. Bonito stands in for the anchovy stock Korean cooks use. Look for shrimp with no added salt or phosphates.
ingredients: whites and greens kept apart, sliced

name: Japanese grilled mackerel set with miso soup, spinach and daikon
inspiredBy: Inspired by a Japanese teishoku of saba shioyaki
about: Crisp-skinned broiled mackerel with a pile of grated daikon and lime, sesame spinach, a small bowl of tofu and shiitake miso soup, and brown rice, all on one tray. The mackerel carries **a big dose of omega-3**, and the miso is used by the teaspoon so the sodium stays sensible.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain. Make a batch ahead if you can.

Heat the broiler to high. Salt the skin side of the mackerel, leave it for 10 minutes, then pat it dry and broil it flesh side up, about 10 cm from the heat, for 3 minutes. Flip it and broil skin side up for 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin is blistered and crisp and the fish flakes. Serve it skin side up.
Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 1 minute, plunge it into cold water, squeeze it dry and cut it into lengths. Toss with the soy sauce and the crushed sesame seeds.

Simmer about ¾ cup of water with the bonito and shiitake for 4 minutes. Add the tofu and warm for 2 minutes. Take the pot off the heat, whisk the miso in with a little hot broth and stir it back in. Never boil it after the miso goes in. Add the scallion.
Mound the grated daikon beside the mackerel and squeeze the lime over both. Serve with the rice, the spinach and the soup.
tip: Salmon or trout fillets broil the same way if mackerel is hard to find. Buy Atlantic or chub mackerel, never king mackerel.

name: Ginger shrimp with gai lan, edamame and brown rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Cantonese stir-fried shrimp with Chinese broccoli
about: Plump shrimp tossed over high heat with garlic, ginger, shiitake, edamame and big green stalks of gai lan, in a light, savoury soy, stock and rice vinegar sauce. The shrimp are **lean protein for very few calories**, the edamame add fibre and iron, and the gai lan brings calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain.
Pat the shrimp dry and toss with half the stock and the white pepper. Stir the soy sauce, rice vinegar and the rest of the stock with 1 tablespoon of water.
Boil the gai lan and the edamame together for 2 minutes, then drain well.
Heat a wok or large skillet until very hot. Add half the canola oil and the shrimp in one layer and sear for about 90 seconds a side, until just pink. Tip them out.

Add the rest of the oil, the shiitake, garlic and ginger and stir-fry for 2 minutes. Add the gai lan and edamame, return the shrimp, pour in the sauce and toss for 1 minute, until the sauce bubbles and coats everything lightly. Finish with the sesame oil.
Serve over the rice.
tip: Broccoli stems or broccolini work if you cannot find gai lan. Look for a bag of shrimp with no added salt or phosphates. Cook the rice on Sunday.
ingredients: gai lan, stalks cut in 5 cm lengths, thick ones halved

name: Thai chicken larb in lettuce cups with cucumber and raw cabbage
inspiredBy: Inspired by Thai larb gai from Isan
about: Minced chicken tossed warm with lime, fish sauce, chili, shallot, mint, cilantro and nutty toasted rice powder, spooned into crisp lettuce cups with cucumber, carrot and raw cabbage. It is lean, loud and bright, with **plenty of lean protein** and a small scoop of rice to round it out. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Toast a tablespoon of the dry brown rice in a dry pan over medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until deep golden and fragrant. Grind it to a coarse powder in a mortar or spice grinder.
Rinse the rest of the rice and cook it in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.

Put the chicken in a pan with a splash of water over medium heat and cook, breaking it up with a spoon, for 5 to 6 minutes, until cooked through and no longer pink. Take it off the heat and let it cool for a minute.
Stir the lime juice, fish sauce, salt and chili flakes together, then toss with the warm chicken, the shallot and the rice powder.
Fold in the mint, cilantro and scallion. Taste: it should be sour first, then salty, then hot.
Spoon into the lettuce cups and serve with the cucumber, carrot, cabbage and rice. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch with the lettuce and herbs kept apart.
tip: Sticky rice makes the classic powder; brown rice gives a nuttier, coarser one. Use fewer chili flakes for a milder larb, or add a sliced fresh chili for more fire.
ingredients: finely minced by hand or pulsed in a food processor
some toasted dry for the powder, the rest rinsed

name: Japanese salmon, napa cabbage and tofu miso nabe with rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Hokkaido ishikari-nabe, a salmon and miso hot pot
about: A shallow pot of gently simmered napa cabbage, spinach and tender salmon with shiitake, tofu and ginger in a light miso dashi, with a lime-soy dip and a scoop of rice to finish. It is **a huge, warming bowl for few calories**, with omega-3 from the salmon and plenty of fibre. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.
Simmer about 1½ cups of water for each portion with the bonito and the ginger for 5 minutes, then strain. Return the broth to a wide pot.
Whisk the miso with a little hot broth and stir it back in. Keep the pot at a gentle simmer and never boil it after the miso goes in.
Layer the napa in the pot with the carrot and shiitake. Cover and simmer gently for 6 minutes, until the cabbage is soft.

Tuck in the tofu and lay the salmon on top. Cover and keep the pot barely simmering for 4 minutes, until the salmon is just opaque, pushing the spinach under the broth for the last minute. Scatter on the scallion.

Stir the lime juice, soy sauce and perilla oil into a small dipping dish. Ladle the nabe into bowls, add a scoop of rice and dip as you go. Pack the second portion and the rice separately for tomorrow's lunch, and reheat it gently, just until the salmon is warm.
tip: Chicken thigh or shrimp work in place of the salmon.

name: Chinese braised beef shank and daikon with gai lan
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese red-braised beef and daikon
about: Lean beef shank braised slowly with star anise, cinnamon, ginger and a splash of soy until it falls apart, with sweet daikon and carrot that drink up the sauce, over a little brown rice with garlicky gai lan on the side. It is the weekend project: mostly hands-off, with **a lot of iron, zinc and B12**. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.
Blanch the beef in boiling water for 2 minutes to clean it, then drain and rinse.

Warm the canola oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef for 4 to 5 minutes, then add the ginger, half the garlic, the scallion, star anise and cinnamon and stir for 1 minute, until fragrant.

Add the stock, soy sauce and enough water to just cover the beef. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for 1 hour 30 minutes, until the beef is nearly tender. In a pressure cooker, 40 minutes is enough.

Add the daikon and carrot and simmer, uncovered, for 25 to 30 minutes, until the vegetables are soft and the sauce has thickened and turned glossy. Stir in the rice vinegar. If the sauce is still thin, boil it hard for the last 5 minutes.

Stir-fry the gai lan with the rest of the garlic in a hot pan with a splash of water for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and tender, then drizzle with the sesame oil. Serve everything over the rice.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The braise is better the next day.
tip: A pressure cooker brings the braise down to about 40 minutes. Freeze extra portions for up to 3 months.
ingredients: gai lan, stalks cut in lengths

name: Chinese steamed sea bass and tofu with ginger, scallion and gai lan
inspiredBy: Inspired by Cantonese steamed whole fish
about: Sweet, tender sea bass steamed over silky tofu and shiitake with ginger and scallion, finished with a spoon of hot oil, soy and cilantro, with steamed gai lan and a little brown rice. It is quick, clean and light, with **over 35 g of lean protein** and very little fat.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain. Make a batch ahead if you can.
Set a rack or heatproof plate over simmering water in a wide pot or wok. Put the tofu, shiitake and the sliced ginger on a plate, lay the fish on top, sprinkle with the stock and white pepper.
Cover and steam over high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes at the thickest part. Steam the gai lan on a second plate or tier for 4 minutes.
Pour off the liquid on the plate. Scatter the ginger matchsticks, scallion and cilantro over the fish.

Heat the canola oil in a small pan or a metal ladle until it shimmers, then pour it over the scallion and ginger so it sizzles. Drizzle on the soy sauce and sesame oil. Serve with the gai lan and rice.
tip: Branzino, black or striped bass work; skip Chilean sea bass. Cod or haddock fillets steam the same way. Batch-cook the rice on Sunday and this is a 20-minute dinner.
ingredients: half sliced, half cut into fine matchsticks

name: Warm edamame with lime and chili
about: A bowl of warm, bright green edamame tossed with lime and a pinch of chili. It is **a filling bowl of protein and fibre** in about five minutes.
steps: Boil the edamame for 3 minutes, or as the bag says, then drain.
Toss with the lime juice, chili flakes and salt, and eat warm.

name: Carrot and daikon sticks with a sesame-miso dip
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese miso-dipped raw vegetables
about: Crunchy carrot and daikon sticks with a sharp little dip of miso, rice vinegar, ginger and sesame. The carrot gives you **a day's worth of vitamin A**, and the dip is just a teaspoon of miso, so it stays light on salt.
steps: Stir the miso, rice vinegar, ginger and 1 tablespoon of water into a smooth dip, then stir in the sesame seeds.
Serve the carrot and daikon sticks with the dip.

name: Smashed cucumber with garlic, rice vinegar and sesame
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese pai huang gua
about: Cucumber smacked into craggy pieces so it soaks up a sharp garlic, vinegar and soy dressing, with toasted sesame on top. It is **a big, crunchy, very low-calorie bowl** that fills a gap between meals.
steps: Lay the cucumber on a board and smash it with the flat of a knife, then cut it into bite-sized chunks.
Toss with the salt and leave for 5 minutes, then drain off the liquid. Toss with the garlic, rice vinegar, soy sauce, sesame oil and chili flakes, and scatter on the sesame seeds.
ingredients: smashed with the flat of a knife and cut into chunks

name: Greek yogurt with Asian pear, ginger and toasted sesame
about: Thick Greek yogurt with crisp Asian pear, a little grated ginger and warm toasted sesame seeds, built from flavours common in Chinese and Japanese cooking. It brings **a good hit of protein and calcium** with a gentle crunch.
steps: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking often, until they smell nutty.
Stir the grated ginger into the yogurt and spoon it into a bowl. Fan the pear slices on top and scatter with the warm seeds.

name: Mango with lime, chili and toasted sunflower seeds
about: Juicy mango with a squeeze of lime, a pinch of chili and warm toasted sunflower seeds, a nod to the chili-salt dip on Thai fruit carts. The seeds add **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the mango is rich in vitamin C.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Toss the mango with the lime juice and chili flakes and scatter on the warm seeds.

name: Soy-marinated hard-boiled eggs with scallion
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese ajitsuke tamago
about: Firm hard-boiled eggs marinated in a light soy and ginger bath. They give you **protein and choline** in a pocket-sized snack.
steps: Lower the eggs into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes, until the white and yolk are firm. Move them to ice water for 5 minutes, then peel.
Stir the soy sauce, rice vinegar and ginger with 1 tablespoon of water. Put the eggs and the marinade in a small zip bag, press out the air and marinate for at least 2 hours, turning once.
Halve and top with the scallion.
tip: Make them the night before. They keep 3 days in the fridge, so make a fresh pair for Sunday.
ingredients: in the shell, at room temperature

name: Chilled silken tofu with ginger, scallion and soy
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese hiyayakko
about: A cool block of silken tofu with fresh ginger, scallion, soy, bonito and a pinch of chili and sesame. It is **a quick, light protein snack** that fills you up for very few calories.
steps: Slide the tofu onto a small plate and pat the top dry with a paper towel.
Pile the ginger and scallion on top, drizzle with the soy sauce and perilla oil, and scatter on the bonito, sesame seeds and chili flakes.

name: Greek yogurt bowl with blueberries and toasted almonds
inspiredBy: Inspired by the North American yogurt parfait
about: Thick nonfat Greek yogurt with juicy blueberries, a scatter of warm toasted almonds and a dusting of cinnamon. It gives you **over 30 g of protein** and a little crunch, so it keeps you going well past mid-morning.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until they smell nutty. Tip them onto a plate.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the blueberries.
Scatter on the warm almonds and dust with cinnamon.
tip: Toast a jar of almonds on Sunday and breakfast takes two minutes. Frozen blueberries work well: they thaw into a purple syrup while you make coffee.

name: Mushroom and spinach scramble on whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Inspired by the American diner scramble
about: A diner-style scramble of well-browned mushrooms, wilted spinach and scallion, soft-set and piled on hot toast. It is a filling plate with **plenty of protein and greens** before 9 a.m.
steps: Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and leave them alone for 3 minutes, then stir and cook for another 3 minutes until browned and their juices have cooked off.
Add the onion and cook for 2 minutes until soft, then add the spinach by the handful and stir until it just wilts.
Beat the eggs with the salt and pepper. Pour them over the vegetables, turn the heat to low and fold gently for 2 to 3 minutes, until completely set with no runny egg left.
Scatter on the scallion and serve on the hot toast.
tip: Brown a double batch of mushrooms on Wednesday and keep half in the fridge for Friday, and that breakfast takes 8 minutes. A splash of hot sauce at the table is very good here.

name: Cottage cheese with pineapple, lime and toasted almonds
about: Creamy cottage cheese under juicy pineapple chunks, with warm toasted almonds and a squeeze of lime. It brings **a big helping of protein** and plenty of vitamin C, and takes ten minutes, or five with almonds toasted ahead.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until they smell nutty. Tip them onto a plate.
Spoon the cottage cheese into a bowl and top with the pineapple.
Squeeze over the lime and scatter on the warm almonds.
tip: Peaches, mango or a handful of berries work in place of pineapple.

name: Salmon, chickpea and tomato salad with lemon and oregano
inspiredBy: Inspired by Tuscan tonno e fagioli, with canned salmon and chickpeas
about: Flaked canned salmon over baby spinach with chickpeas, sweet cherry tomatoes and paper-thin onion, tossed in a bright olive oil and lemon dressing, with a slice of garlic toast. It is a quick cousin of Tuscan tuna and beans, and the salmon and chickpeas give you **omega-3, protein and fibre** on one big plate.
steps: Soak the onion slices in half the lemon juice for 5 minutes while you prep. It softens the bite.
Whisk the rest of the lemon juice with the minced garlic, oregano, Aleppo pepper, olive oil, salt and pepper.
Toss the chickpeas and tomatoes with most of the dressing and the onion with its juices.
Pile the spinach on a plate, spoon over the chickpea salad and flake the salmon on top. Drizzle with the last of the dressing.
Toast the bread, rub it with the garlic you kept back while it is hot, and serve alongside.
tip: Choose canned salmon with the bones in. They mash into the fish and are a good source of calcium.
ingredients: minced, with a little kept back to rub on the toast

name: Sesame-ginger chicken and cabbage crunch salad
inspiredBy: Inspired by the Chinese-American chicken salad
about: Poached chicken shredded over a mountain of crunchy cabbage, spinach, carrot and edamame, in a gingery rice vinegar, soy and lime dressing with a little toasted sesame oil. It is the **big crunchy bowl** of a Californian Chinese chicken salad, with a spoonful of mashed pineapple in place of the usual sugar.
steps: Cover the chicken with cold water in a small pot, add a slice of the ginger and the scallion tops, bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until it is white all the way through. Lift it out, let it cool a few minutes, then shred it with two forks.
Whisk the rice vinegar, soy sauce, both oils, ginger, lime juice and the mashed pineapple into a dressing.
Toss the cabbage, spinach, carrot, edamame, scallion and cilantro with most of the dressing.
Pile onto a plate, top with the chicken, spoon over the rest of the dressing and finish with a few more cilantro leaves.
tip: Poach the chicken the night before and the salad takes five minutes at lunch. Keep the dressing separate until you eat.

name: Turkey chili with black beans, mushrooms and avocado
inspiredBy: Inspired by American weeknight chili, with lean turkey and black beans
about: A thick, smoky chili made with very lean ground turkey, black beans and tomatoes, with finely chopped mushrooms stirred in for extra volume and a meaty bite. Topped with avocado and cilantro, with lime stirred through. The **beans, turkey and vegetables together** make a bowl high in protein and fibre, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and mushrooms for 8 to 9 minutes, until soft and the mushroom juices have cooked off.
Add the turkey and break it up with a spoon. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until no pink is left.
Stir in the garlic, chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, cayenne and oregano and cook for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Add the crushed tomatoes, the beans, the salt and a splash of water. Simmer, partly covered, for 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick and the flavours have come together.
Stir in the spinach and let it wilt for a minute, then the lime juice. Divide into two portions. Top one with the avocado and cilantro and eat it now.
Cool the second portion, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow's lunch. Add its toppings fresh when you reheat it.
tip: This freezes well for up to 3 months, so doubling it is an easy way to bank two more lunches.

name: Miso soup with tofu, shrimp, edamame and soba
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese miso shiru, with shrimp and soba added to make it a meal
about: A big, comforting bowl of mushroom-ginger miso soup with soft tofu, shrimp, edamame, cabbage, carrot and a little soba, so it eats like a noodle-shop dinner. The tofu and shrimp give you **plenty of lean protein**, and it comes together in about 40 minutes. It makes two portions, so lunch tomorrow is ready.
steps: Warm the oil in a big pot over medium-high heat. Brown the mushrooms for 4 to 5 minutes until golden, then add the ginger, garlic and carrot for a minute.

Pour in about 400 ml of water per portion (800 ml for both), or 300 ml per portion if your list shows less than a tablespoon of miso, so the broth stays full-flavoured. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until the mushrooms have flavoured the broth.
Meanwhile, cook the soba in a separate pot of boiling water for the time on the packet, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Drain and rinse under cold water so the noodles do not turn gummy.
Add the cabbage and edamame to the broth and simmer for 2 minutes, then slide in the tofu and shrimp and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, until the shrimp are pink and curled. Turn the heat to low.
Ladle a little hot broth into a small bowl, stir the miso into it until smooth, then stir it back into the pot. Do not boil the soup after the miso goes in, or it loses its flavour.

Divide the soba into two bowls and ladle the soup over. Finish with the scallion and sesame seeds, and eat one now. Cool the second portion of soup separately from its noodles, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow.
tip: Keep the soba separate from the soup in the fridge and combine them when you reheat, so the noodles stay springy. Do not boil the soup again, or the miso goes dull.

name: Smoky lime chicken burrito bowl on crisp greens
inspiredBy: Inspired by the Tex-Mex burrito bowl, with greens in place of most of the rice
about: Smoky lime chicken, black beans and a small scoop of brown rice on a big bed of romaine, with crunchy cabbage, fresh pico de gallo and avocado. It has **all the burrito-bowl flavour** with the greens doing most of the filling. Makes two portions, so the second is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Mix half the lime juice with the garlic, chili powder, smoked paprika, cumin and a pinch of the salt, and coat the chicken in it. Leave for 15 minutes or up to 8 hours in the fridge.
Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.
Stir the tomato, onion and cilantro with the rest of the lime juice, a pinch of cayenne and the rest of the salt to make a quick pico de gallo.

Warm the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat and cook the chicken for 5 to 6 minutes a side, until browned and cooked through. Rest it for 5 minutes, then slice. Warm the beans in the same pan for a minute.
Build the bowls on a bed of romaine and cabbage with the rice, beans, chicken, pico and avocado.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow, keeping the greens and pico in a separate container from the warm parts so nothing goes soggy.
tip: Marinate the chicken in the morning and dinner takes 20 minutes.

name: Shrimp and vegetable stir-fry with ginger, garlic and brown rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Cantonese-style shrimp and vegetable stir-fry
about: Plump shrimp tossed in a hot pan with broccoli, spinach and mushrooms in a savoury ginger-garlic sauce, over a modest scoop of brown rice. The shrimp bring **lean protein for very few calories**, and the heap of vegetables keeps the plate big. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.
Stir the soy sauce and rice vinegar with a tablespoon of cold water in a small bowl. Pat the shrimp dry.

Heat a large wok or skillet over high heat until it is properly hot. Add half the oil and the shrimp, in two batches if your pan is small, and cook for about 90 seconds a side until just pink. Tip them out.

Add the remaining oil and the broccoli and mushrooms. Stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes, until the broccoli is bright green and still has bite. Add the garlic, ginger, scallion and spinach for the last minute, stirring until the spinach just wilts.

Return the shrimp, pour in the sauce and toss over high heat for 30 seconds, until it bubbles. The spinach adds its juices, so you get a light, savoury pan sauce that soaks into the rice. Finish with the sesame oil and scatter with the sesame seeds.
Serve one portion over the rice. Cool the second portion with its rice, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow.
tip: Reheat the leftovers in a hot pan for 2 minutes rather than the microwave, so the shrimp stay tender. Many frozen shrimp are brined, so look for a bag with no added salt or phosphates.

name: Sicilian-style sardine, chickpea and tomato stew with garlic toast
inspiredBy: Inspired by Sicilian pasta con le sarde and Tuscan chickpea stews
about: Canned sardines folded into a garlicky tomato and chickpea stew with carrot, fennel seed and spinach, finished with lemon and served with garlic toast. Sardines and fennel are the classic Sicilian pair, and because you eat the soft bones it carries **omega-3 and calcium**, with some vitamin D.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and carrot for 7 to 8 minutes, until soft and starting to turn golden. Add most of the garlic, the fennel seed and the Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the oregano, crushed tomatoes, chickpeas, salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, until thick and glossy.
Stir in the spinach by the handful until it wilts, then break the sardines into big pieces and fold them in gently. Warm through for 2 minutes and finish with the lemon juice and pepper.
Toast the bread and rub it with the reserved garlic while it is hot. Serve the stew in a wide bowl with the toast.
tip: Choose sardines packed in olive oil, and keep the bones in: they melt in the stew and carry the calcium.
ingredients: sliced, with a little kept back to rub on the toast

name: Chicken pozole rojo with cabbage, lime and avocado
inspiredBy: Inspired by Jalisco-style pozole rojo, with chicken breast, which is also a classic way to make it
about: A deep red guajillo chile broth with tender chicken and white hominy, finished with a big pile of crunchy cabbage, cilantro, lime and a little avocado. It is **lean, filling and high in protein**, and the toppings make it feel like a feast. It is the weekend project, and the second portion is Sunday's lunch.
steps: Put half the onion, half the garlic and a pinch of the cumin in a large pot with about 1 litre of water. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes to make a quick broth.
Meanwhile, toast the guajillo chiles in a dry pan over medium heat for about 30 seconds a side, until fragrant. Do not let them blacken. Soak them in hot water for 15 minutes.
Blend the soaked chiles with the rest of the onion and garlic, the rest of the cumin, the oregano, half the salt and a cup or so of their soaking water until smooth.
Lift the onion out of the broth. Strain the chile sauce into the pot, add the hominy and simmer for 20 minutes, until the broth is deep red and tastes rich.

Add the chicken and the rest of the salt and keep the pot at a gentle simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece. Stir in half the lime juice. Wash your hands and the board with hot soapy water after handling the raw chicken.

Ladle into big bowls and pile on the cabbage, cilantro and avocado, with the rest of the lime. Put the second portion, without its toppings, in a shallow container and into the fridge within 2 hours. Reheat it once until steaming hot (74 °C) tomorrow.
tip: Breast stays juicy only if it never boils, so keep the pot gently trembling once the chicken goes in, and warm the leftover gently. Make the chile sauce a day ahead and the project is half done.

name: Blackened salmon with garlicky greens, lemon and brown rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Louisiana blackened fish
about: Sockeye salmon with a smoky, peppery Cajun crust, seared in a hot pan and served with garlicky broccoli and spinach, a squeeze of lemon and a small scoop of brown rice. The salmon gives you **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the crust makes a lean fillet taste rich.
steps: Start the rice first: simmer the brown rice in plenty of water for about 30 minutes until tender, then drain.
Pat the salmon dry, rub it all over with most of the oil and press the Cajun seasoning firmly onto the flesh side.

Heat a heavy skillet, cast iron if you have one, over medium-high heat for about 3 minutes until very hot, and turn the fan on, because blackening smokes a little. Lay the salmon in flesh side down and cook for about 3 minutes, until a dark crust forms. Flip it and cook the skin side for 2 to 4 minutes more, until the centre is just opaque. A little translucent in the middle is fine. Move the salmon to a plate.

Turn the heat to medium. Add the rest of the oil and the garlic to the same skillet for 20 seconds, then the broccoli and a splash of water, cover and steam for 3 minutes. Add the spinach by the handful and stir until just wilted, about 2 minutes.
Season the greens with half the lemon juice and the pepper. Serve the salmon over the rice with the greens alongside and the rest of the lemon squeezed over the fish.
tip: Oiling the fish rather than the pan is the classic blackening trick: the crust sets without sticking. If the blend is very salty, use a little less.

name: Warm edamame with lemon and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese izakaya edamame
about: A bowl of warm shelled edamame with a little salt, a good squeeze of lemon and a pinch of Aleppo pepper. It is **plant protein and fibre** in a snack that takes five minutes.
steps: Simmer the edamame in a small pot of water with a pinch of the salt for 3 to 4 minutes, until bright green and tender. Drain well.
Toss with the lemon juice, the rest of the salt and the Aleppo pepper and eat warm.

name: Apple slices with almonds
about: Crisp apple slices with some almonds, toasted if you have a minute. The apple brings **fibre and crunch**, and the almonds make it last.
steps: Slice the apple into wedges and fan them on a plate.
Serve with the almonds alongside, warm from a dry pan if you have a minute.

name: Smoky roasted chickpeas
inspiredBy: Inspired by Spanish garbanzos fritos
about: Canned chickpeas roasted until crisp with smoked paprika, cumin and a little salt. They give you **fibre and plant protein** in something that crunches like chips.
