Season with salt and pepper, and finish with the Parmesan, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil.
tip: To make it a quick lunch, cook the soup base (steps 1 and 2) on Sunday and keep it in the fridge. On the day, add the pasta and broccoli, and it is ready in about 20 minutes. It thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water.
ingredients: whole-wheat, broken spaghetti or any small shape
small florets, plus the peeled stalk, chopped (about half a head)

name: Cretan dakos-style salad with chickpeas, tomato and feta
inspiredBy: Cretan dakos, where a barley rusk is topped with grated tomato and soft cheese, here with rye toast and chickpeas
about: Crisp rye toast pieces topped with juicy grated tomato, cucumber, chickpeas, feta and olives, finished with a few walnuts, oregano and olive oil. It is inspired by the dakos of Crete, with chickpeas for protein and just a thin slice of bread. The **chickpeas and feta** make it a full lunch, and the tomato juice softens the toast just enough.
steps: Toast the rye until it is dry and crisp, then break it into rough pieces and put them in a shallow bowl.
Grate the tomato on a box grater, leaving the skin behind, and stir in the salt. Spoon it over the toast pieces and let them soak for a minute.
Toss the chickpeas with the cucumber and onion and spoon them over the top.
Crumble on the feta, scatter on the olives, walnuts and oregano, and finish with the olive oil.
tip: Toast the bread until it is really dry, like a rusk. If your toast is soft, leave it in a 160°C (325°F) oven for 10 minutes first.
ingredients: a small, thin slice, toasted hard

name: Barley risotto with chicken, mushrooms, broccoli and cannellini
inspiredBy: Italian orzotto from Friuli and Veneto, where pearl barley is cooked the way risotto is
about: Pearl barley simmered slowly with onion and garlic until creamy, with broccoli cooked right in the pot, then stirred together with browned chicken and mushrooms, cannellini beans and spinach. Parmesan goes in at the end and toasted hazelnuts on top. A small portion of barley goes a long way when the **chicken, beans and vegetables** do most of the work, and a lemony arugula salad sits beside it.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes and chop them roughly. Warm a third of the olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat and cook the onion for about 5 minutes, until soft. Stir in the garlic and thyme for 1 minute.

Stir in the barley for a minute, then add hot water a ladleful at a time, keeping the barley just covered. Simmer, stirring now and then, for 25 minutes, then drop the broccoli florets on top and keep simmering for 8 to 10 minutes, until the barley is tender with a little bite, the broccoli is soft and the pot is creamy.

While the barley simmers, warm another third of the olive oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and brown the chicken for 4 to 5 minutes. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and cook for 7 to 8 minutes more, stirring only now and then, until they are golden and the liquid has cooked off.

Stir the chicken and mushrooms into the barley with the beans and spinach, and cook for 2 minutes, until the spinach has wilted and the chicken is cooked through. Stir in the Parmesan, half the lemon juice, salt, pepper and the parsley, and scatter the toasted hazelnuts on top.
Toss the arugula with the rest of the lemon juice, the last of the olive oil and a pinch of salt, and serve it beside the orzotto. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: It thickens as it sits, so loosen the leftover portion with a splash of water or stock when you reheat it.
ingredients: boneless skinless thighs, in small pieces

name: Grilled sardines on a white bean, tomato and arugula salad
inspiredBy: Italian sarde alla griglia, served the Tuscan way on a lemony white bean salad
about: Fresh sardines grilled until the skin blisters, laid over cannellini beans tossed with tomato, grated carrot, onion, parsley and red wine vinegar, on a bed of arugula. It is simple, bright and ready in about 25 minutes. The sardines are the **omega-3 and calcium** hero of the week, and the soft bones are edible.
steps: Toss the beans with the tomato, carrot, onion, parsley, garlic, vinegar, half the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Let them sit for 10 minutes so the flavours settle.
Heat the broiler on high and line a tray with foil. Pat the sardines dry and rub them with a little olive oil, salt, pepper and oregano.
Broil the sardines on the tray for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Spread the arugula on a plate, spoon the beans over it and lay the sardines on top. Squeeze over the lemon juice and drizzle with the rest of the olive oil.
tip: A grill pan works too but it smokes, so open a window. Ask the fishmonger to scale and gut the sardines and you save 10 minutes. Frozen sardines work well: thaw them in the fridge overnight, and cook them the same day.

name: Chicken souvlaki with horiatiki salad and tzatziki
inspiredBy: Greek souvlaki with the village salad, the plate a taverna brings without asking
about: Lemony, oregano-scented chicken skewers with a chunky village salad of tomato, cucumber, pepper, olives and feta, a spoonful of garlicky tzatziki and a few bites of warm pita. The salad is half the plate and goes first. The **chicken and yogurt carry the protein**, so the pita can stay small.
steps: Mix the chicken with the lemon juice, half the garlic, a little of the olive oil, half the oregano, salt and pepper. Marinate for at least 20 minutes, or a few hours in the fridge.
Make the tzatziki: grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the garlic, the dried dill and a pinch of salt.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or leave it loose for a pan. Cook in a hot grill pan or skillet for 10 to 12 minutes, turning, until browned at the edges and cooked through.
Toss the tomato, the rest of the cucumber, the pepper, onion and olives with a little salt. Set the feta on top and drizzle with the rest of the olive oil and the remaining oregano.

Warm the pita in the pan for a minute. Eat the salad first, then the chicken with the tzatziki and a few bites of pita. Pack the second portion, with the salad and tzatziki in separate containers, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: For the leftover lunch, eat the chicken cold on the salad, or warm it for a minute and tuck it into the pita.
ingredients: boneless skinless thighs, cut in 3 cm cubes

name: Spanish lentil stew with beef, smoked paprika, carrot and spinach
inspiredBy: Spanish lentejas estofadas, the lentil pot that turns up in homes across Spain
about: A thick lentil stew with plenty of smoky paprika, a little lean ground beef, carrot and a whole bag of spinach wilted in, brightened with a splash of vinegar at the end. The paprika and browned beef flavour the whole pot. The **lentils bring iron, folate and fibre**, so it is a full bowl on its own.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the ground beef for 4 minutes, breaking it up, until no pink is left and it reaches 71 °C (160 °F). Add the onion and carrot and cook for 7 minutes, until soft.
Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika for 30 seconds, then add the crushed tomatoes, lentils, bay leaf and enough water to cover everything by about 3 cm.

Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 30 to 35 minutes, until the lentils are tender and the stew is thick. Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw beef. Add a splash of water if it gets dry.
Stir in the spinach a few handfuls at a time, letting each lot wilt before adding the next, then add half the vinegar, and season with salt and pepper. Take out the bay leaf.
Serve the stew in bowls with the parsley and a splash of the rest of the vinegar. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Lentejas are even better the next day. Leave out the beef and add a spoonful of extra smoked paprika for a vegetarian pot.

name: Baked salmon with tomatoes, broccoli, zucchini and olives over a little farro
inspiredBy: Greek psari plaki, fish baked with tomato, onion and garlic, here as a tray bake with a spoonful of farro
about: Salmon baked on a tray with juicy tomatoes, broccoli, zucchini, onion and olives, then spooned over a small portion of nutty farro. It is a Greek-style tray bake in the spirit of psari plaki: one tray, no fuss. The **salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the vegetables take up most of the plate.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the tomato, broccoli, onion, olives and zucchini on a baking tray with half the olive oil, the oregano and a pinch of salt. Roast for 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, simmer the farro in plenty of salted water for 15 to 20 minutes, until tender but chewy. Drain.

Nestle the salmon among the vegetables, scatter the garlic over the tray, and drizzle with the rest of the olive oil and the lemon juice, and season with salt and pepper. Roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the salmon flakes easily.
Spoon the farro onto a plate, top with the vegetables and salmon, and finish with the parsley and a lemon wedge.
tip: Cook a little extra farro on Sunday and use it here to skip step two. Fresh salmon is best on the day, so buy it that morning or thaw it overnight. On the Light size the farro is a couple of spoonfuls, enough to catch the juices.

name: Fasolada, the Greek white bean soup
inspiredBy: Greek fasolada, often called the national dish of Greece
about: A slow-simmered white bean soup with carrot, tomato, a warm pinch of Aleppo pepper and a finish of good olive oil, served with olives and a lemony arugula salad. It is the everyday soup of Greek homes, and the weekend project dish of the week. The **beans are the fibre and protein**, and the soup tastes even better on day two.
steps: The night before, cover the beans with plenty of cold water and soak them overnight.
Drain the beans, put them in a large pot, cover with fresh water and bring to a boil. Boil for 10 minutes, then drain. This takes away the foam and makes them easier to digest.
Return the beans to the pot with fresh water to cover by 3 cm. Add the onion, carrot, garlic and bay leaf, and simmer gently for about 45 minutes, until the beans are almost tender.

Stir in the crushed tomatoes, most of the olive oil and the Aleppo pepper. Simmer for 20 to 25 minutes more, until the beans are very soft and the soup is thick and creamy, adding a splash of hot water if it gets too thick. Season with salt near the end.
Finish with the parsley and half the lemon juice. Toss the arugula with the rest of the lemon, a little olive oil and salt.
Serve the soup in a deep bowl with the olives and the salad on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: In a pressure cooker the soaked beans take about 12 minutes, which turns this into a weeknight soup. It keeps 4 days in the fridge and freezes for 3 months. Greek cooks use boukovo flakes here, if you can find them.

name: Seared mackerel on pisto with chickpeas
inspiredBy: Spanish caballa a la plancha served on pisto manchego, the La Mancha vegetable stew
about: Crisp-skinned mackerel served on a soft stew of zucchini, red pepper and tomato with a few chickpeas, finished with lemon and parsley and a piece of rye toast to mop up the juices. It is a Spanish fish-and-vegetables plate that is mostly vegetables. The **mackerel brings plenty of omega-3**.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the onion and pepper for 6 minutes, until soft. Add the zucchini and cook for 5 minutes more.

Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika for 30 seconds, then add the crushed tomatoes and a pinch of salt. Simmer for 12 minutes, until thick, then stir in the chickpeas and the sherry vinegar for the last 3 minutes.

Pat the mackerel dry and season the skin with salt. Heat the rest of the oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat and press the fillets down, skin side down. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until the skin is crisp.
Flip and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more. Spoon the pisto onto a plate, lay the mackerel on top, squeeze over the lemon and scatter on the parsley. Serve with the toast.
tip: Ask for the pin bones to be removed, and the fillets cook in minutes. Make a double batch of pisto if you like: it is excellent cold the next day.

name: Strawberries with walnuts
about: Sweet strawberries with a small handful of walnuts. The **walnuts add omega-3 and protein**, so the fruit does not stand alone.
steps: Halve the strawberries and eat them with the walnuts.

name: Strawberries with almonds
about: A bowl of sweet strawberries with a small handful of almonds. The **almonds add protein and fibre**, so the fruit does not stand alone.
steps: Halve the strawberries and eat them with the almonds, which can be toasted in a dry pan for 3 minutes if you like.

name: Lupini beans with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish and Italian bar snacks, where lupini come in a little dish with a drink
about: Tender lupini beans tossed with lemon, olive oil and parsley, the little tapas dish you find in bars across southern Italy and Spain. They are a surprisingly **high-protein, high-fibre** snack with very little starch.
steps: Rinse the lupini well. The skin is edible, so eat them skin and all, or pop each bean out of its skin as you go, the way bars serve them.
Toss with the lemon juice, olive oil, parsley and oregano, with salt to taste.
tip: Buy jarred lupini in brine at an Italian or Portuguese shop, or in the international aisle, and rinse them well.

name: Roasted chickpeas with smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Spanish garbanzos fritos, baked instead of fried
about: Crisp roasted chickpeas with smoked paprika and a pinch of salt, the baked version of Spain's fried garbanzos. They are crunchy, savoury and full of **fibre and plant protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Drain the chickpeas and pat them very dry with a clean towel.
Toss them with the olive oil, smoked paprika and salt, and spread them on a baking tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway through, until crisp. Eat them the same day while they are crunchy.
tip: They soften as they sit, so make them fresh. For a quick fix, toss them in a hot pan with the paprika for 5 minutes.
ingredients: no salt added, drained and patted very dry

name: Sardines on rye toast with lemon and onion
inspiredBy: Spanish tosta de sardinas, the bar snack of canned sardines on good bread
about: A slice of toasted rye piled with canned sardines, thin red onion, lemon and parsley, the way Spanish bars serve it. The little soft bones in canned sardines bring **calcium and omega-3**, and the whole snack takes 5 minutes.
steps: Toast the rye until crisp.
Drain the sardines and mash them roughly with the lemon juice and pepper.
Pile them on the toast and top with the onion and parsley.
tip: Look for sardines packed in olive oil, and keep a tin or two in the pantry for the days you need a fast, filling snack.

name: Greek yogurt with hazelnuts and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Greek yiaourti with a handful of nuts, the simplest dessert in a Greek home
about: A bowl of thick Greek yogurt with chopped toasted hazelnuts and a dusting of cinnamon, without the honey. It is the kind of thing you might be served after a meal in a Greek home. The **yogurt brings protein and calcium**, and the hazelnuts add crunch and vitamin E.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes and chop them roughly.
Spoon the yogurt into a small bowl, scatter on the hazelnuts and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Mussels on rye with onion, sherry vinegar and lemon
inspiredBy: Spanish tapas of mejillones en escabeche, served on a slice of good bread
about: A thin slice of rye toast topped with canned mussels dressed in sherry vinegar and olive oil, with thin onion, lemon and parsley. It is the kind of tin-on-toast snack Spanish bars serve with a drink, and a quiet **powerhouse of protein, iron and vitamin B12**.
steps: Toast the rye until crisp.
Toss the onion with the sherry vinegar, olive oil and paprika, and leave it for a few minutes to soften.
Pile the mussels on the toast, spoon the onion and its dressing over them, and finish with the lemon and parsley.
tip: Look for mussels in escabeche or natural at a Spanish or Portuguese shop. Smoked mussels also work: drain them well. Mussels in escabeche are already dressed, so use just a few drops of vinegar on the onion.
ingredients: a large tin, or a tin and a half, in escabeche or natural, drained

name: Olives with lemon, oregano and almonds
inspiredBy: a Spanish bar plate of olives and almonds
about: A small dish of olives with a few almonds and a squeeze of lemon, the way Spanish bars set it down with a drink. The **almonds add protein and vitamin E**, and the olives bring the salty, savoury bite.
steps: Rinse the olives to wash off some of the brine and pat them dry.
Toss with the lemon juice and oregano and serve with the almonds.

name: Cannellini crostini with lemon and olive oil
inspiredBy: Tuscan fettunta, bread with beans, minus the garlic rub
about: A thin slice of toasted rye topped with warm, lemony cannellini beans, parsley and a drizzle of olive oil, a simple Tuscan snack. The **beans carry the protein and fibre**, and the bread is just the base.
steps: Warm the beans in a small pan with a splash of water for 2 minutes, then crush about half of them with a fork.
Toast the rye and spoon the beans on top.
Finish with the lemon juice, olive oil, parsley, salt and pepper.

name: Orange with walnuts
about: Juicy orange segments with a small handful of walnuts. The **walnuts add omega-3 and protein**, and the orange adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the orange and break it into segments, and eat them with the walnuts.

name: Cannellini and lemon dip with vegetable sticks
inspiredBy: a Tuscan white bean puree, the cousin of hummus
about: A creamy puree of cannellini beans, garlic, lemon and olive oil with crunchy cucumber and carrot sticks. It is the Tuscan answer to hummus. The beans give you **fibre and protein**, and the raw vegetables add crunch.
steps: Mash or blend the beans with the garlic, lemon juice, half the olive oil, the rosemary and salt, adding a splash of water until it is soft and creamy.
Spoon the dip into a small bowl, drizzle with the rest of the olive oil, and serve with the cucumber and carrot sticks.
tip: Make a double batch midweek: it keeps for 4 days in a jar in the fridge, so the second one is ready for Saturday.

name: Turkish-style breakfast plate with boiled eggs, white cheese, olives and walnuts
inspiredBy: Turkish kahvaltı, the everyday village-style breakfast plate
about: Two boiled eggs, salty white cheese, olives and walnuts with tomato, cucumber and a handful of rocket, and a wedge of warm whole-wheat pita to finish. It is how a lot of Turkish homes start the day, and the vegetables and eggs come first. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the walnuts add omega-3.
steps: Lower the eggs into boiling water and cook them for 8 to 9 minutes, until the yolks are just set. Cool them under cold water, then peel and halve them.
Slice the tomato and cucumber and arrange them on a plate with the rocket, the olives and the cheese.
Drizzle the olive oil over the tomatoes and scatter on the parsley, pul biber and black pepper. Put the walnuts on the side.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster and cut it into wedges. Eat the vegetables and eggs first and the bread last.
tip: Boil the eggs on Sunday and keep them in their shells in the fridge, and the plate takes about 5 minutes. On another morning, swap the walnuts for a spoonful of za'atar on the cheese and add a few slices of green pepper.
ingredients: Turkish beyaz peynir, or any firm white cheese

name: Ful medames with chickpeas, lemon, cumin and tomato
inspiredBy: Egyptian, Levantine and Gulf ful, the classic breakfast of mashed fava beans
about: Warm, soft fava beans and chickpeas mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, then topped with chopped tomato, onion and parsley, a drizzle of olive oil, a swirl of tahini and a sprinkle of toasted sesame. This is the breakfast of the whole region, and the beans carry **plenty of fibre and plant protein** that keep you full until lunch. The bread is just a small piece of pita for scooping.
steps: Tip the fava beans, chickpeas and a splash of water into a small pot with the cumin and half the garlic. Warm them over medium heat for about 5 minutes, mashing about a third with a fork so the beans turn thick and creamy.
Stir the tahini with the rest of the garlic, half the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of water until it is smooth and pourable.
Spoon the ful into a shallow bowl. Squeeze over the rest of the lemon juice and top with the tomato, onion and parsley.
Drizzle with the olive oil and the tahini, and finish with the toasted sesame seeds and a pinch of pul biber. Warm the pita and tear it up for scooping.
tip: On a weekend morning, slice a boiled egg on top, the way many Egyptian and Lebanese homes do. Mash the beans a little more or less to taste. On the lighter sizes the pita is a few bites for scooping.
ingredients: cooked from dried, or a tin with no salt added, drained

name: Shakshuka with chickpeas, feta and a small pita
inspiredBy: shakshuka, North African by origin and now a favourite breakfast across the Levant and the Gulf, with chickpeas in the sauce
about: Two eggs poached in a thick, cumin-scented sauce of tomato, sweet pepper, spinach and a few chickpeas, mopped up with a small warm pita. It is still mostly vegetables, and the eggs and chickpeas give you **protein and choline** to start the day.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the onion and pepper until soft, about 6 minutes. Add the garlic, cumin, paprika and pul biber and stir for 1 minute until it smells toasty.
Pour in the passata and add the chickpeas, spinach and salt. Simmer for about 12 minutes, until the spinach has wilted and the sauce coats a spoon.
Make two wells in the sauce with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Cover the pan and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until the whites and yolks are both firm.
Crumble the feta over the top and scatter on the parsley. Bring the pan to the table, warm the pita and use it to scoop.
tip: Make the sauce the evening before, while the mujaddara simmers, and keep it in the fridge. In the morning, reheat it and add the eggs, and it takes about 10 minutes.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added
more if you like it hot

name: Hummus with shawarma-spiced chicken and sesame, with a carrot and parsley salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese hummus bil lahme and chicken shawarma, with a bigger salad
about: Creamy home-made hummus topped with chicken breast seared with garlic, lemon, allspice and cinnamon and toasted sesame seeds, with a crunchy carrot, parsley and sumac onion salad and a small warm pita. The chickpeas, tahini and parsley bring **fibre and iron**, and the carrot adds vitamin A. The salad is a real part of the plate, not a garnish.
steps: Toss the chicken strips with half the garlic, a squeeze of lemon, a little of the olive oil, the allspice, cinnamon, paprika, pepper and a pinch of salt. Let it marinate for 30 minutes while you make the hummus.

Make the hummus. Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of their liquid for 5 minutes. Blitz them while still warm with the tahini, the rest of the garlic, a good squeeze of lemon, the cumin, a pinch of salt and a couple of spoonfuls of ice-cold water for a good 2 minutes, until it is smooth and fluffy.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden, about 2 minutes, and tip them out.
Warm some of the olive oil in the same pan over medium-high heat and sear the chicken for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until browned at the edges and cooked through. Rest it for 2 minutes.
Toss the carrot, onion and parsley with the sumac, the rest of the lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.

Spread the hummus in a shallow bowl, make a well in the middle and pile in the chicken, sliced across the grain if the strips are thick. Scatter on the sesame seeds and serve with the salad and the warm pita. Eat the salad first.
tip: Make the hummus on Sunday (it keeps 4 days in the fridge) and leave the chicken in its marinade overnight, and lunch takes about 10 minutes.
ingredients: for the hummus, the chicken and the salad
boneless, skinless chicken breast, sliced in thin strips
a little in the marinade, some for searing, the rest for the salad

name: Mujaddara with lentils and a little bulgur, with a lemony cabbage salad and garlicky yogurt
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian mujaddara, with more lentils than grain
about: Brown lentils and a little bulgur cooked with cumin and sweet browned onions, with a crunchy lemon and mint cabbage salad and garlicky yogurt on the side. The lentils do most of the work, so it is **high in fibre, iron and folate** and the starch comes in a modest portion. It makes two servings for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Simmer the lentils with the cumin in plenty of water for about 15 minutes, until they are almost tender but still have some bite. Drain, keeping some of the cooking water.

While they cook, fry the onions in two-thirds of the olive oil with a pinch of salt over medium-low heat, stirring often, until deep golden brown, 25 to 30 minutes. Lift out about a third for the top.

Add the lentils, bulgur, cinnamon and the rest of the salt to the pan with the remaining onions. Pour in enough of the lentil water to cover by about a centimetre, then cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes so the bulgur finishes steaming, then fluff with a fork.

Stir the yogurt with the mashed garlic, half the mint and a pinch of salt. Toss the cabbage and parsley with the lemon juice, the rest of the mint and the rest of the olive oil, rubbing the cabbage a little to soften it.
Top the mujaddara with the browned onions and serve with the salad and the yogurt. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salad and yogurt kept separate and dressed fresh.
tip: The onions are the secret. If they start to catch, add a splash of water and keep going. Brown them on Sunday and keep them in the fridge, and Monday's dinner takes about 40 minutes. The salad is part of the meal, so eat it first. On the lighter sizes the bulgur is just a spoonful or two.

name: Grilled sardines with fattoush
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush, with grilled sardines and just a little toasted pita
about: Fresh sardines grilled until the skin blisters, on a big bowl of fattoush with peppery arugula, cucumber, tomato, onion and herbs in a sumac and pomegranate molasses dressing. The sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D** in the week, and the toasted pita is a handful of crunch, not the base of the meal.
steps: Tear the pita into bite-size pieces and toast them in a dry pan or the toaster for 3 to 4 minutes, until crisp and golden.
Whisk the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses, mashed garlic, most of the olive oil, half the sumac and a pinch of salt for the dressing.

Rub the sardines with the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Grill them under a very hot broiler, or in a hot cast-iron pan, for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until the skin blisters and the flesh is opaque.
Toss the arugula, cucumber, tomato, onion, parsley and mint with the dressing. Add the toasted pita and the rest of the sumac right before serving so the bread stays crisp.
Lay the sardines on top of the salad and serve at once.
tip: No fresh sardines? Check Middle Eastern, Portuguese or Asian fishmongers for frozen ones, which are fine thawed, and so are fresh mackerel fillets, grilled the same way. Sardines from a can are a good weeknight shortcut: skip the grilling and use them straight from the tin.
ingredients: fresh or thawed sardines, cleaned and gutted

name: Chickpea fatteh with garlicky yogurt, toasted pita and sesame
inspiredBy: Syrian and Lebanese fatteh, with the chickpeas as the main event and only a little pita
about: Warm, cumin-scented chickpeas under a cool garlicky yogurt and tahini sauce, with a scatter of crisp toasted pita and sesame seeds, and a tomato and parsley salad on the side. It is a proper Levantine lunch that is **mostly chickpeas, with a high-protein yogurt sauce**, and the pita is just the crunch on top.
steps: Tear the pita into small pieces and toast them in a dry pan for 3 to 4 minutes, until golden and crisp, adding the sesame seeds for the last minute.
Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the cumin, a splash of their canning liquid and a pinch of salt for about 5 minutes. Keep them warm.
Stir the yogurt with the tahini, the mashed garlic, half the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and about 2 tablespoons of the warm chickpea liquid until it is smooth and pourable.
Toss the tomato, red onion and half the parsley with the rest of the lemon juice, a few drops of the oil and a pinch of salt.

Spoon the warm chickpeas and a little of their liquid into a shallow bowl. Pour over the yogurt sauce and scatter on the toasted pita, sesame seeds and the rest of the parsley. Finish with the paprika and the rest of the olive oil, and serve with the salad.
tip: Add the pita and sesame just before you eat, so they stay crisp.
ingredients: rinsed, with a splash of their canning liquid

name: Freekeh bil djej, spiced chicken and cracked freekeh with chickpeas and almonds
inspiredBy: Syrian and Palestinian freekeh with chicken, with chickpeas and extra vegetables
about: Tender chicken and smoky cracked green wheat cooked together with cinnamon and allspice, with chickpeas and sweet carrot, toasted almonds on top and a peppery arugula and mint salad with lemon. Freekeh is a **high-fibre whole grain** with a nutty, slightly smoky flavour, and the chickpeas and chicken make the portion filling. It makes two servings for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a heavy pot and brown the chicken for about 5 minutes, turning once. Lift it out onto a plate.
Add the onion and carrot to the pot and cook for 6 minutes, until soft and golden. Stir in the cinnamon, allspice, cardamom, pepper, bay leaf and salt for 30 seconds.

Add the freekeh and chickpeas to the pot with enough water to cover by about 2 centimetres. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook on low for 10 minutes. Nestle the chicken back on top, cover again and cook for 12 to 15 minutes more, until the freekeh is tender, the water is gone and the chicken is cooked through.
Rest it, covered, for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden.
Dress the arugula and mint with the lemon juice, the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Fluff the freekeh, top with the almonds and parsley and serve with the salad. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salad dressed fresh.
tip: Most of the cooking time is hands-off, so make the salad while it simmers. Shred the chicken into the freekeh before you pack the second portion, so it does not dry out when reheated. For a weeknight shortcut, brown the chicken, then pressure-cook everything for 10 minutes at high pressure and rest. Cracked freekeh cooks in about 20 minutes. Whole freekeh takes closer to 45, so soak it first.
ingredients: boneless, skinless chicken breast, cut in large pieces
or the seeds of 3 pods, crushed

name: Lamb kofta with parsley tabbouleh and walnut tarator
inspiredBy: Lebanese kafta bi tahini and tabbouleh, with walnuts pounded into the tahini sauce as in Turkish tarator, and bulgur as a small supporting grain
about: Spiced fingers of lean lamb and parsley on a big, bright tabbouleh that is mostly parsley, tomato and mint with just a little soaked bulgur, with a lemony walnut and tahini tarator to spoon over. The parsley brings **vitamin K, vitamin C and iron**, the lemon helps your body use that iron, and the walnuts add omega-3. It makes two servings for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Soak the bulgur in a little of the lemon juice and a splash of water for 20 minutes, until it is tender but still has a little chew.
Finely chop the parsley, mint, tomato and half the onion. Toss them with the soaked bulgur, the olive oil, a squeeze of lemon and half the salt to make the tabbouleh.

Knead the lamb with the grated onion, a handful of chopped parsley, the allspice, cinnamon, coriander, cumin, pepper and the rest of the salt for a couple of minutes, until it feels sticky. Shape it into small fingers.
Grill the kofta under a hot broiler or in a hot pan for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until browned outside and cooked through.

Chop the walnuts as finely as you can, or crush them in a mortar. Stir them into the tahini with the crushed garlic, a good squeeze of lemon, a pinch of salt and a splash of water until you have a thick, spoonable tarator.

Serve the kofta on the tabbouleh with the tarator sauce drizzled over. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Keep the tabbouleh and kofta in separate containers, and spoon the sauce on at lunch.
tip: Chill the kofta mixture for 20 minutes if it feels too soft to shape. Tabbouleh is best on the day it is made, but it holds up fine for lunch tomorrow. Keep tomorrow's share of the tomato whole and dice it into the tabbouleh at lunch, so it doesn't go watery.
ingredients: lean lamb, minced (ask the butcher, or mince lean shoulder)
half grated for the kofta, half finely chopped for the tabbouleh
a big bunch: a little for the kofta, the rest for the tabbouleh
for the bulgur, the tabbouleh and the tahini sauce

name: Samke harra-style salmon with cilantro and walnuts, on roasted cauliflower and an arugula salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra, spicy fish with a cilantro and walnut paste
about: A fillet of salmon baked under a garlicky cilantro and walnut paste with a little heat, on golden roasted cauliflower and a sharp arugula, parsley and sumac onion salad, with a lemony tahini drizzle. The salmon and walnuts give you **omega-3**, and the cauliflower and greens keep it a plate of vegetables first. It is fresh fish, so cook it the day you buy it or thaw it.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Toss the cauliflower with a third of the olive oil, the cumin and a pinch of salt and roast it for 20 minutes, until golden at the edges.
Blitz the cilantro, walnuts, garlic, half the lemon juice, the pul biber, half of the remaining olive oil and a pinch of salt into a thick, rough paste.

Put the salmon on a lined tray, skin side down, and spread the paste thickly over the top. Slide it in beside the cauliflower for the last 12 to 14 minutes, until the fish flakes easily but is still moist in the middle.
Toss the arugula with the parsley, the sliced onion, the sumac, most of the remaining lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.

Stir the tahini with the last of the lemon juice and a splash of water into a pourable, taratour-style drizzle. Pile the salad on a plate, add the roasted cauliflower and lay the salmon on top. Drizzle with the tahini.
tip: The paste is also good on cod or any firm white fish. Leave out the chili for a milder version. The tahini drizzle is the classic partner for samke harra.
ingredients: pul biber, or a pinch of cayenne

name: Mercimek çorbası, Turkish red lentil soup with lemon and pul biber oil
inspiredBy: Turkish mercimek çorbası, the everyday red lentil soup
about: Silky red lentil soup with onion and carrot, finished with a spoonful of sizzling olive oil and pul biber and a squeeze of lemon, served with a small warm pita and a peppery arugula and sumac onion salad. Red lentils are **rich in fibre, folate and iron**, and the lemon on top helps your body absorb that iron.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a pot and cook the onion and carrot for about 6 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic, cumin and the spoonful of passata and stir for 1 minute.
Add the lentils and about 2 cups (500 ml) of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils have collapsed.
Blend the soup with an immersion blender until mostly smooth, leaving a little texture. Season with the salt and pepper and loosen it with hot water if it is too thick.
Warm the rest of the oil in a tiny pan with the pul biber for 30 seconds, until it sizzles and turns red.
Ladle the soup into a bowl, squeeze over the lemon and spoon on the red oil. Serve with the warm pita and the arugula and onion tossed with the sumac, a few drops of lemon and a pinch of salt.
tip: The soup freezes well, so double it and freeze a portion. Add the lemon and the red oil after reheating. On the lighter sizes the pita is a few bites, just enough for dipping.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added

name: Maqluba, upside-down lamb, eggplant and cauliflower with a little brown basmati
inspiredBy: Palestinian and Syrian maqluba, with more vegetables and much less rice than usual
about: The famous upside-down pot: tender lean lamb, golden roasted eggplant and cauliflower and chickpeas, topped with a modest layer of brown basmati and flipped onto a platter, with a cool yogurt and cucumber salad. The eggplant, cauliflower and chickpeas make it **high in fibre** with only a small portion of rice. It is the weekend project, and it makes two servings for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the eggplant and cauliflower with half the olive oil and a pinch of salt, spread them on two trays and roast for 25 minutes, until golden. Rinse the rice and soak it in cold water while the lamb cooks.
In a heavy pot, brown the lamb and onion in the rest of the oil for about 8 minutes. Stir in the baharat, cinnamon, allspice, turmeric and half the salt.
Cover the lamb with water by about 3 centimetres, bring to a simmer and cook, covered, for 40 minutes, until the lamb is tender. Strain, keeping both the lamb and the broth, and wipe out the pot.

Use a small, deep pot, about 18 cm across, so the layers stack high and hold together when you flip. Layer the pot: first the lamb, then the roasted eggplant in overlapping rounds, then the cauliflower and the chickpeas, packing everything in tightly. Drain the rice and spread it evenly on top, then press the whole thing down gently with a plate.

Pour the warm broth slowly down the side of the pot until it just reaches the top of the rice, no higher, and add the rest of the salt. There is only a thin layer of rice to drink it up, so more broth turns the pot soupy. Keep the rest of the broth to warm the leftovers. Bring to a boil, lay a clean tea towel under the lid, cover tightly, turn the heat to its lowest setting and cook for 40 minutes, until the rice is tender.
Rest the pot, covered, for 15 minutes. Meanwhile, toast the almonds in a dry pan and stir the yogurt with the cucumber, mint and a pinch of salt.

Run a knife around the edge of the pot, put a large platter on top and flip it firmly. Wait 5 minutes, then lift the pot away. Scatter the almonds and parsley over the top and serve with the yogurt salad. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Roast the vegetables and simmer the lamb the day before, and the Saturday assembly takes about an hour of mostly hands-off time. If the flip frightens you, serve it from the pot like a layered stew, because it tastes the same. On the lighter sizes the rice layer is a thin one, about 3 tablespoons cooked each, and the lamb and vegetables carry the pot.
ingredients: lean lamb shoulder, cut in small cubes

name: Gulf-style mackerel in loomi and tomato sauce with spinach and a little bulgur
inspiredBy: Gulf fish stews with dried lime (samak bil loomi), made with Atlantic mackerel in place of kanaad and a little bulgur in place of the usual rice
about: Mackerel fillets poached in a tangy tomato sauce with onion, garlic, dried black lime and warm spices, with spinach stirred in and a little coarse bulgur cooked in the same pot, standing in for the rice a Gulf kitchen would serve. Mackerel is one of the best sources of **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the loomi gives the sauce a sour, earthy depth. A crunchy cabbage and mint salad comes alongside.
steps: Pierce the dried lime a few times with a knife. Warm the olive oil in a wide, deep pan and cook the onion for 5 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic, cumin, ground coriander, turmeric and cinnamon and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the passata, the dried lime, the salt and about half a cup of water. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes.
Stir in the bulgur with a splash more water, cover and cook on low for 12 minutes, until the bulgur is nearly tender and the sauce has thickened.

Fold in the spinach and lay the mackerel fillets on top, skin side down, so they rest on the bulgur and steam gently instead of boiling in the sauce. Cover and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily.
Toss the cabbage with the mint, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Fish out the dried lime from the sauce.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon juice over the fish, scatter on the cilantro and serve in a wide bowl with the salad alongside.
tip: No dried black lime? Use the zest and juice of a lemon, added at the end. The dish will be brighter but not quite as earthy. Fresh sardines or trout also work here. On the lighter sizes the bulgur is just a spoonful or two.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added
about half a dried black lime, pierced with a knife

name: Hummus with carrot, red pepper and cauliflower
inspiredBy: Lebanese hummus bi tahini, with plenty of crunchy vegetables for scooping
about: Smooth, lemony hummus with crunchy carrot sticks, red pepper and raw cauliflower. A classic mezze snack that is **protein and fibre together**, so it holds you well between meals.
steps: Blitz the chickpeas with the tahini, lemon, garlic, cumin, salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until completely smooth, about 2 minutes.
Spoon it into a bowl, drizzle with the olive oil and serve with the vegetable sticks.
tip: It keeps for 4 days in the fridge, so a double batch gives you a second snack or a spoonful with tomorrow's lunch.

name: Oven-roasted chickpeas with sumac and lemon
inspiredBy: the roasted chickpeas (leblebi) sold at Turkish and Levantine nut shops
about: Crunchy chickpeas roasted with cumin and sumac and finished with a squeeze of lemon. A **protein and fibre snack** that is best eaten the day you roast it.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a towel and leave them to air-dry for 10 minutes, since dry chickpeas get crunchy.
Toss them with the oil, sumac, cumin, pul biber and salt, spread them on a tray and roast for 30 to 35 minutes, shaking the tray twice, until crisp.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and eat warm.
tip: They are crunchy for a few hours and chewy after, so eat them the same day.

name: Labneh with cucumber, olives and za'atar
inspiredBy: the Levantine labneh plate, eaten at breakfast and as a snack
about: Thick, tangy labneh swirled with olive oil and za'atar, with cucumber sticks for scooping and a few olives. It is **high in protein and calcium** and nearly carb-free, so it keeps the plate steady.
steps: Spread the labneh on a small plate, make a swirl in the middle with the back of a spoon and drizzle with the olive oil. Sprinkle on the za'atar.
Eat it with the cucumber sticks and the olives.

name: Lupini beans with lemon, mint and chili
inspiredBy: termis (lupini beans), the street snack of Lebanon, Syria and Egypt
about: Plump lupini beans tossed with lemon, mint and a little pul biber. Lupini are a **high-protein bean** with plenty of fibre too, so this one will hold you for hours.
steps: Rinse the lupini well under cold water and toss them with the lemon juice, mint, olive oil and pul biber.
tip: Look for lupini beans in jars in the Italian or Middle Eastern aisle. Rinse them well, because they are packed in brine. Eat the whole bean, or pinch it to pop the bean out of its skin.
ingredients: jarred lupini, drained and rinsed well

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the Levantine pairing of fruit and nuts
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a small handful of walnuts for crunch. The walnuts bring **omega-3 and protein**, and the pomegranate adds fibre and vitamin C.
steps: Spoon the pomegranate seeds into a bowl and eat them with the walnuts.
tip: To get the seeds out, cut the pomegranate in half and whack the back of each half with a wooden spoon over a bowl. Out of season? Frozen pomegranate arils work.

name: Apple with walnuts and cinnamon
about: Crisp apple slices dusted with cinnamon and a small handful of walnuts. The walnuts bring **omega-3, protein and healthy fat**, so the fruit never comes on its own.
steps: Slice the apple, dust it with the cinnamon and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Muhammara with red pepper and carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Syrian muhammara from Aleppo, with extra vegetables and less bread
about: A roasted red pepper and walnut dip, thickened with a little pita the Aleppo way and sharpened with pomegranate molasses and pul biber, with red pepper and carrot sticks for scooping. The walnuts bring **omega-3**, and the red pepper adds vitamin C.
steps: Drain the jarred roasted red pepper well and pat it dry. Cut the fresh pepper into sticks.
Blitz the roasted pepper with the walnuts, the torn piece of pita, the pomegranate molasses, olive oil, pul biber, cumin and salt until it is a thick, rough dip.
Serve with the pepper and carrot sticks.
tip: A single portion is too small for most blenders, so use a mini chopper or the cup of a stick blender, or make a bigger batch to share. It keeps 4 days in the fridge. To roast your own pepper, broil it for 10 minutes until blackened, cover to cool, then peel.
ingredients: about a third as drained jarred roasted red pepper for the dip, the rest fresh in sticks
a small piece of whole-wheat pita

name: Apple with almonds and cinnamon
about: Crisp apple slices dusted with cinnamon and a small handful of almonds. The almonds bring **protein, vitamin E and healthy fat**, so the fruit never comes on its own.
steps: Slice the apple, dust it with the cinnamon and eat it with the almonds.

name: Sardines on whole-wheat pita with red onion, parsley and lemon
inspiredBy: the canned sardine sandwiches eaten across Lebanon, Egypt and the Gulf
about: Canned sardines mashed lightly with lemon and spread on a small piece of toasted pita, piled with thin red onion, parsley and a pinch of sumac. Sardines with their soft bones are a great source of **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the pita is just a small base.
steps: Toast the pita until crisp and break it into two or three pieces.
Mash the sardines roughly with the lemon juice, the pul biber and the pepper.
Pile the sardines onto the pita, top with the onion and parsley, sprinkle on the sumac and eat right away.
tip: Look for sardines packed in olive oil with the bones in. The bones are soft and you will not notice them, and they are where the calcium is.
ingredients: canned sardines in olive oil, with the bones, drained

name: Warm chickpeas with cumin, lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: balila, the warm chickpeas sold at street stalls in Syria and Lebanon
about: A cup of warm chickpeas with cumin, garlic, lemon and parsley, the way balila vendors serve it. A big **protein and fibre snack** that is gone in minutes.
steps: Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water, the garlic, the cumin and the salt for about 5 minutes.
Spoon them into a cup with a little of their warm liquid, then add the lemon juice, olive oil, parsley and pul biber.

name: Cacık, cold cucumber and yogurt soup with walnuts and mint
inspiredBy: Turkish cacık, served thinner as a cold soup, with walnuts on top as in Balkan tarator
about: Thick yogurt loosened with cold water and stirred with cucumber, garlic, mint and a little olive oil, with chopped walnuts on top. A cool, **high-protein, high-calcium** snack that is nearly carb-free.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with a good splash of cold water until it is pourable, then stir in the grated cucumber, the mashed garlic and most of the mint.
Pour into a bowl, drizzle with the olive oil and top with the walnuts and the rest of the mint.
tip: Chill it for 20 minutes if you have time. Squeeze the grated cucumber a little first if it is very watery.

name: Labneh and za'atar on whole-wheat pita with cucumber
inspiredBy: a Levantine breakfast classic, as an afternoon snack
about: A small toasted whole-wheat pita spread with thick labneh, olive oil and za'atar, with cucumber slices on the side. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**, and the za'atar brings sesame and thyme.
steps: Toast the pita until warm and a little crisp at the edges.
Spread it with the labneh, drizzle with the olive oil and sprinkle on the za'atar. Eat it with the cucumber slices.

name: Hummus with whole-wheat pita and vegetables
inspiredBy: Lebanese hummus bi tahini with warm pita
about: Smooth hummus with a small warm whole-wheat pita and carrot and cucumber sticks. The chickpeas and tahini bring **fibre, protein and iron**, and the vegetables make it a proper plate.
steps: Blitz the chickpeas with the tahini, lemon, garlic, cumin, salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until completely smooth.
Spoon the hummus onto a plate, drizzle with the olive oil and serve with the warm pita and the vegetable sticks.
tip: Use leftover hummus from the week and the snack takes two minutes.

name: Moong dal chilla with fenugreek and mint chutney
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Gujarati moong dal cheela (puda), with fresh fenugreek leaves
about: Thin, savoury pancakes of ground yellow moong dal with onion, grated carrot, spinach and fresh fenugreek leaves, hot off the pan with a sharp mint and cilantro chutney. Moong dal is the classic steady-energy breakfast: **plenty of protein and fibre**, and it digests slowly.
steps: Drain the soaked dal and blend it with the ginger, half the green chili, the hing, the turmeric, half the salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until completely smooth. The batter should pour like thin pancake batter, so add a splash more water if it is thick.
Stir in the onion, carrot, spinach, fenugreek leaves, cumin and half the cilantro.
Make the chutney: blitz the mint, the rest of the cilantro and green chili, the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of water until it is a bright, loose green sauce.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little of the oil. Pour in a ladle of batter and spread it gently with the back of the ladle into a round a little thicker than a crêpe. Cook until the top looks set and the underside is golden with brown spots, about 3 minutes.
Drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge, flip and cook for 1 minute more. Repeat with the rest of the batter and eat the chillas hot with the chutney.
tip: Soak the dal the night before, and mornings take about 15 minutes. Frozen methi works if fresh is hard to find. If a chilla sticks or tears, the pan is too cool or the batter too thick.
ingredients: split yellow moong dal, soaked for 4 hours or overnight
half for the batter, half for the chutney
half in the batter, half in the chutney

name: Foxtail millet vegetable upma
inspiredBy: South Indian rava upma, made with foxtail millet (thinai) and lots of vegetables
about: A soft, peppery upma with mustard seeds, curry leaves and tender, nutty chana dal, loaded with carrot and cabbage. Foxtail millet is an intact grain, so it digests more slowly than semolina, and the chana dal adds **protein and fibre**.
steps: The night before, soak the millet and the chana dal together in plenty of water. In the morning, drain them well.
Warm the oil in a pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the drained chana dal, and stir for about 2 minutes until the dal turns golden. Add the curry leaves and hing.
Add the onion, ginger and green chili and cook until the onion is soft, about 4 minutes. Add the carrot and cabbage with a splash of water and cook for 4 minutes.

Stir in the turmeric, the salt and the drained millet and stir for a minute. Pour in boiling water, about twice the volume of the millet and dal together, cover and cook over low heat until the millet and dal are tender and the water is gone, about 15 minutes. Rest it, covered, for 5 minutes.
Fluff with a fork, squeeze over the lemon, scatter with cilantro and serve hot.
tip: Soak both the night before, and it is about 20 minutes in all. Unsoaked chana dal stays hard, so do not skip it.
ingredients: split chana dal, soaked with the millet

name: Methi besan thepla with curd
inspiredBy: Gujarati methi thepla, with extra chickpea flour for a slower, more filling bite, and sunflower seeds where many cooks use sesame
about: Soft, speckled Gujarati flatbreads with fresh fenugreek leaves, ajwain and a sprinkle of sunflower seeds, made with chickpea flour next to the whole wheat. Served with cold curd and tomato, they are a breakfast with **protein, calcium and fibre**, and they travel well too.
steps: Mix the two flours in a bowl with the ajwain (rub it between your palms first), the turmeric, Kashmiri chili, hing and sunflower seeds. Rub in about a teaspoon of the oil with your fingertips.

Add the squeezed-dry fenugreek leaves, the grated garlic, the minced green chili and a spoonful of the curd, then the salt last so the leaves do not go wet. Knead into a soft dough. The leaves let out water as you knead, so add a little more curd only if it is still dry. Then rest it, covered, for 10 minutes.
Divide the dough into balls and roll each one into a thin round, dusting with a little flour. Besan makes the dough delicate, so go gently. If it sticks, roll it between two sheets of parchment.

Heat a flat pan or tawa over medium-high heat. Cook each thepla for about a minute, flip, brush with a little oil and cook until golden with brown spots, about 1 minute more. Press the edges so it puffs a little.
Serve the theplas warm with the rest of the curd and the sliced tomato.
tip: Cook the theplas the night before and reheat them in a dry pan. Do not knead the dough ahead, as the leaves turn it soggy. Frozen methi from a South Asian grocery works when fresh is hard to find.
ingredients: fresh fenugreek leaves, picked, chopped and squeezed dry
a spoonful in the dough, the rest on the side

name: Chana chaat with sprouted moong
inspiredBy: Delhi and Lahore street chana chaat
about: A tangy, crunchy bowl of chickpeas and sprouted moong with cucumber, tomato, raw onion, cold yogurt and a squeeze of tamarind, finished with chaat masala and roasted peanuts. It is a no-cook lunch with **fibre and plant protein in every spoonful**, and the sourness is the point.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with the tamarind paste, the lemon juice and a splash of water until smooth, then stir in the chaat masala, black salt, crushed cumin and Kashmiri chili.
Tip the chickpeas into a big bowl. Mash a handful of them with the back of a spoon so the dressing clings.
Add the sprouts, cucumber, tomato, onion, green chili and cilantro. Pour over the dahi dressing and toss well.
Taste and add more lemon or chaat masala if you like it sharper. Top with the crushed peanuts just before you eat, so they stay crunchy.
tip: Dress it just before eating. Blanch store-bought sprouts for a minute, or sprout your own: soak the moong 8 hours, drain, and wait 24 to 36 hours. For a packed lunch, keep the dressing and the peanuts in a small jar.

name: Chicken do pyaza with a roti and cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Pakistani chicken do pyaza, "two onions"
about: Tender chicken thighs in a thick black pepper and ginger gravy, with the onions added twice, once cooked soft and once left with a little bite, served with one fresh roti and a crisp cucumber and onion salad. It is mostly **protein and vegetables**, which keeps the plate steady, and it is just as good cold.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds for 15 seconds, then the chopped onion for the gravy and cook, stirring, until deep golden, about 9 minutes.

Add the ginger, garlic and green chili and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the turmeric, the crushed coriander, the Kashmiri chili and the black pepper, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a thick paste, about 5 minutes.

Add the chicken and the salt and stir over medium-high heat for 5 minutes until it turns opaque. Add a splash of water, cover and cook for 10 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the gravy clings to it.
Stir in the onion wedges and the garam masala and cook uncovered for 3 minutes, so the onions soften but keep a little bite. Finish with half the cilantro.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides.
Toss the cucumber and the sliced onion with the lemon juice, the rest of the cilantro and a pinch of salt, and eat the salad first, then the chicken with the roti.
tip: Cook it the night before and reheat it for lunch. It keeps 3 days, so a double batch on Sunday covers two lunches. If you want it milder, use half the black pepper. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: skinless thighs, cut in bite-size pieces
90 g chopped for the gravy, 35 g in wedges added at the end, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Lauki chana dal with a roti and onion salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Gujarati dudhi chana dal
about: Split chickpeas cooked soft with tender bottle gourd in a garlicky cumin tadka, with one fresh whole-wheat roti and an onion and lemon salad. Chana dal is one of the **lowest glycaemic dals** there is, and the lauki makes it light and sweet.
steps: Soak the dal in plenty of water for 1 hour, then drain. Put it in a pot with the tomato, chopped onion, ginger, turmeric, salt and plenty of water, about three times the volume of dal. Simmer partly covered until the dal is nearly soft, about 25 minutes, then add the lauki and cook for 15 minutes more, until both are completely soft.

While the dal cooks, knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough and rest it for 15 minutes. Roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate.
Mash the dal lightly with a spoon so it turns creamy, and add hot water if it is too thick. Stir in the garam masala and amchur.

Warm the ghee in a small pan. Add the cumin seeds, then the hing and the sliced garlic, and cook until the garlic is golden, about 1 minute. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chili and pour the tadka over the dal.

Cook the roti on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides. Toss the sliced onion with the lemon juice, the green chili, the cilantro and a pinch of salt, and serve with the dal and roti.
tip: The dal freezes well, so cook a double batch and keep half for another night. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: split chana dal, soaked for 1 hour
peeled and cut in small cubes
30 g chopped, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Rajma masala with brown basmati and onion-tomato salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi rajma chawal, with the beans taking the lead and a small rice portion
about: Red kidney beans in a thick, gingery onion and tomato gravy, spooned beside a little brown basmati and a sharp onion and tomato salad. The beans carry **iron, folate and slow carbohydrate**, and the salad comes first so you start with the crunch.
steps: Use the Sunday brown basmati: boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, cool and keep it up to 4 days in the fridge, freezing a portion for later in the week. Warm your portion with a splash of water. On the lighter sizes it is just a spoonful or two, and that is the idea.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the bay leaf and cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 15 seconds, then add the chopped onion and cook until deep golden, about 8 minutes.

Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the crushed coriander, turmeric and Kashmiri chili, then the tomato for the gravy, and cook, pressing with the spoon, until it becomes a thick jammy paste that leaves oil at the edges, about 6 minutes.

Add the kidney beans, the salt and about a cup of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few beans against the side of the pan so the gravy thickens. Stir in the garam masala and the kasuri methi (crush it between your fingers).
Toss the sliced onion and the rest of the tomato, diced, with the lemon juice, cilantro and a pinch of salt for the salad.
Serve the rajma with the rice, with the salad to eat first. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and keep the salad separate so it stays crisp.
tip: The rajma freezes well. Warm the Sunday rice while the beans simmer and both are ready together.
ingredients: 60 g chopped for the gravy, the rest sliced for the salad
100 g for the gravy, the rest for the salad

name: Kerala-style mackerel curry with cabbage and carrot thoran and brown basmati
inspiredBy: Kerala ayala (mackerel) curry, soured with tamarind in place of kudampuli, and cabbage and carrot thoran
about: Mackerel simmered in a tangy red tamarind gravy with ginger, green chili and curry leaves, with a quick cabbage and carrot thoran dressed in fresh coconut and a spoonful or two of brown basmati. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, and the thoran is your fresh, crunchy vegetable.
steps: Use the Sunday brown basmati: boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, cool and keep it up to 4 days in the fridge, freezing a portion for later in the week. Warm your portion with a splash of water. On the lighter sizes it is just a spoonful or two, and that is the idea.

Warm half the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the fenugreek seeds for 10 seconds, then the onion, ginger, most of the garlic, half the green chili and half the curry leaves. Cook until the onion is soft and just golden, about 6 minutes.

Stir in most of the turmeric and the Kashmiri chili for 30 seconds, then the tomato, and cook until it breaks down, about 4 minutes. Add the tamarind, the salt and about half a cup of water and simmer for 5 minutes.

Slide the fish into the gravy, spoon some of it over the top and simmer gently, partly covered, until the fish is just cooked through, about 8 minutes. Swirl the pan rather than stirring so the fish stays whole.

Make the thoran while the fish simmers. Warm the rest of the oil in a second pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the rest of the curry leaves, the cabbage and carrot, a pinch of salt and the pepper. Cook, stirring, until the vegetables are tender but still have a bite, about 5 minutes. Crush the coconut with the rest of the green chili and garlic and the last pinch of turmeric, and stir it in at the end.
Serve the fish curry with the rice and the thoran, starting with the thoran. Eat this one fresh rather than saving it for tomorrow.
tip: Coconut oil is the traditional Kerala cooking fat, but canola keeps the saturated fat lower here. Sardines or kingfish work too.
ingredients: cleaned, cut into steaks or fillets
for the thoran; fresh grated, or unsweetened desiccated

name: Gujarati-style tuvar dal with spinach, bhindi and a roti
inspiredBy: the Gujarati dal, rotli and shaak plate, with tamarind for the sweet-sour and no sugar or jaggery
about: A thin, sweet-sour Gujarati tuvar dal with cloves, cinnamon and a sizzling ghee tadka, a dry okra sabzi, and one fresh roti. The dal is the big part of the plate, so it brings **plenty of protein and fibre** along with its slow carbohydrate.
steps: Rinse the dal and cook it with the tomato, most of the turmeric and plenty of water, about three times the volume of dal, until completely soft, about 40 minutes, or 12 minutes in a pressure cooker. Whisk it smooth.

Add the tamarind, the ginger, half the green chili, the clove, cinnamon, salt and the spinach, with enough hot water to make it pourable like thin soup. Simmer for 10 minutes, until the spinach has melted in.

Make the bhindi: warm the canola in a wide pan over medium-high heat, add the okra in two batches so it browns instead of steaming, and cook, stirring only now and then, until it is browned and no longer sticky, about 8 minutes in all. Add the crushed coriander, the last pinch of turmeric, a pinch of the cumin and a pinch of salt.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough and rest it for 15 minutes. Roll a thin round for each portion (a small, palm-sized one on the lighter sizes) and cook on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots.

Warm the ghee in a small pan. Add the cumin and mustard seeds and let them pop, then the garlic, hing, curry leaves and the rest of the green chili. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chili and pour the tadka over the dal. Stir in the cilantro.
Serve the dal with the bhindi and a roti each. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and warm the roti in a dry pan or wrapped in foil.
tip: An Instant Pot or pressure cooker gets the dal done in about 12 minutes. Soak the dal for 30 minutes and it takes about 25 in an open pot. Kokum is the traditional souring agent if you have it. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: washed, dried well and cut in rounds

name: Tandoori chicken tray with roasted chickpeas, kachumber and mint raita
inspiredBy: Punjabi tandoori chicken, baked on a tray at home
about: Chicken thighs marinated in yogurt and Kashmiri chili, roasted on one tray with cauliflower, carrot, onion and chickpeas until the edges char, with a cooling mint raita and a tomato and onion kachumber. The chickpeas and vegetables give **protein, fibre and crunch** next to the chicken, with one roti for the starch.
steps: Make the marinade: stir the marinating yogurt with the grated ginger and garlic, half the lemon juice, the Kashmiri chili, garam masala, cumin, coriander, turmeric, kasuri methi (crushed between your fingers), about half a teaspoon of the oil and the salt. Coat the chicken and leave it for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) and line a big tray. Toss the chickpeas with a little of the oil and a pinch of salt and roast them alone for 10 minutes while the oven finishes heating and the chicken sits.

Toss the cauliflower, carrot and onion wedges with the rest of the oil and a pinch of salt, add them to the tray with the chickpeas and nestle the chicken on top. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning the chicken once, until it is charred at the edges and cooked through, and the chickpeas are crisp.

Make the raita: stir the chopped mint and a pinch of salt into the remaining yogurt. Toss the tomato and the rest of the onion, finely chopped, with the remaining lemon juice and the chaat masala for the kachumber.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots.

Toast the almonds in a dry pan and scatter them over the tray. Serve the chicken tray with the kachumber first, then the raita and the roti. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the raita and kachumber in separate containers.
tip: Marinate it in the morning if you can; even 15 minutes helps. Reheat the leftover tray for 8 minutes at 200°C so the edges crisp again. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: skinless thighs, cut in big chunks
about 3 tablespoons for the marinade, the rest for the raita
55 g in wedges for the tray, the rest for the kachumber
toasted and chopped, for the top

name: Pepper and tamarind salmon with parippu and spinach mallung
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan ambul thiyal (sour fish curry, usually tuna), with parippu and a mallung
about: Salmon rubbed with black pepper and tamarind and cooked until sticky, with a creamy red lentil parippu, a spinach mallung and a spoonful or two of brown basmati. It is a Sri Lankan rice-and-curry plate where the lentils and greens take up most of the room, and the salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Use the brown basmati you froze on Sunday, thawed overnight in the fridge, and warm your portion with a splash of water. Cooking this on its own? Boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, and keep the rest up to 4 days

Make the parippu: put the lentils in a pot with half the turmeric, the cinnamon, the cardamom, half the garlic, half the onion and plenty of water. Simmer until the lentils collapse into a creamy dal, about 18 minutes. Stir in half the coconut and half the salt. Finish the parippu with a quick tempering: pop a few of the mustard seeds and a few curry leaves in about half a teaspoon of the oil and stir it in.
Mix the black pepper, half the turmeric, the tamarind, the ginger, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt into a paste and rub it over the salmon.
Warm half of the remaining oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook the salmon for 3 to 4 minutes per side, spooning over any paste left in the bowl, until it is sticky and just cooked through.

Make the mallung: in a second pan, warm the last of the oil, pop the rest of the mustard seeds, then add the rest of the curry leaves, the Kashmiri chili, the rest of the garlic and onion and the green chili. Add the spinach and a splash of water, cook for 2 to 3 minutes until wilted, then stir in the rest of the coconut and a pinch of salt.
Serve the salmon with the parippu, the mallung and the rice, starting with the greens. Eat this one fresh rather than saving it for tomorrow.
tip: Ambul thiyal cooks dry in a clay pot with tuna and goraka (a sour fruit), so this is a quicker pan version with tamarind. Mackerel works as well as salmon.
ingredients: skinless fillet, in two or three pieces
half for the parippu, half for the mallung; fresh grated, or unsweetened desiccated
30 g for the parippu, 30 g for the mallung

name: Barley haleem with goat and dals
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Hyderabadi haleem, with barley doing most of the wheat's job
about: The slow, rich Pakistani stew of tender goat, barley and lentils beaten smooth and finished with fried onions, ginger, lemon and fresh herbs, with a crisp cucumber and onion salad. Barley digests slowly, and together with the dals it makes a pot **full of fibre and protein**.
steps: Soak the barley and the dals in plenty of water for at least 4 hours or overnight, then drain.

Warm the canola in a heavy pot over medium heat. Fry the thinly sliced onion, stirring often, until it is deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, about 12 minutes. Lift out about two thirds and keep it for the top.

Add the chopped onion to the pot with the bay leaf, cumin, clove and cinnamon and cook for 4 minutes. Add the grated ginger, the garlic and the goat, and brown the meat for about 5 minutes. Stir in the turmeric, Kashmiri chili, coriander, black pepper and salt.
Add plenty of water to cover and simmer the goat, partly covered, until it is very tender, about 1 hour 15 minutes, or 30 minutes in a pressure cooker.
Add the drained barley and dals and more hot water, and cook gently, stirring now and then, until everything is falling apart, about 45 minutes, or 25 minutes in a pressure cooker.

Pick out any bones and the bay leaf. Beat the haleem hard with a wooden spoon, or give it a few pulses with a hand blender, until the meat shreds and it turns thick and stretchy. Stir in the garam masala and the ghee.

Toss the cucumber with the onion you kept for the salad, thinly sliced, a squeeze of the lemon and a pinch of salt. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Serve the haleem topped with the fried onions, the almonds, the ginger strips, the rest of the lemon juice, the green chili and the cilantro, with the salad to eat first.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Haleem keeps for 4 days in the fridge and freezes well.
tip: Make a double batch in a pressure cooker, which cuts the cooking to about an hour, and freeze two portions. Boneless lamb or beef works in place of goat.
ingredients: bone-in or boneless goat stewing meat, cut in chunks
35 g sliced thinly for frying, 20 g for the salad, the rest chopped
half grated, half cut in thin strips to serve

name: Palak paneer with a roti and cucumber-onion salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi palak paneer
about: Soft cubes of paneer in a smooth, garlicky spinach gravy with ginger and garam masala, with one fresh whole-wheat roti and a cucumber and onion salad. The spinach brings **folate and vitamin A**, and the paneer and yogurt are the protein.
steps: Boil a pot of water, drop in the spinach and push it under for 1 minute, then drain and rinse under cold water so it stays bright green. Squeeze it lightly and blend with the green chili to a smooth purée.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, then the onion for the gravy and cook until golden, about 7 minutes. Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the turmeric, the crushed coriander and the Kashmiri chili, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a thick paste, about 5 minutes.

Pour in the spinach purée with a splash of water and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the paneer, the salt and the garam masala, crush the kasuri methi in over the top and simmer for 3 minutes more. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the yogurt.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides.
Toss the cucumber and the sliced onion with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and serve with the palak paneer and the roti, eating the salad first.
tip: Firm tofu cubes are a good swap for the paneer, and they take on the gravy just as well. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: 55 g for the gravy, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Guava chaat with almonds
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Punjabi roadside fruit chaat
about: Ripe guava chunks tossed with lemon and chaat masala, with a small handful of almonds for crunch. Guava is one of the **highest-fibre fruits**, and the almonds bring protein and healthy fat, so the fruit never comes on its own.
steps: Toss the guava with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt, and eat it with the almonds.
ingredients: cut in chunks, seeds and all

name: Oven-roasted masala chickpeas
inspiredBy: Indian roasted chana, made from canned chickpeas
about: Crunchy chickpeas roasted with chaat masala, amchur and a little Kashmiri chili. A **protein and fibre snack** you can keep in a jar for a day or two.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a towel, since dry chickpeas get crunchy.
Toss them with the oil, chaat masala, amchur, Kashmiri chili and salt, spread them on a tray and roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and eat warm.
tip: Roast a double batch and keep half in a jar for another day. Once cooled, they stay crunchy for a day or two.

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil sundal
about: Tamil temple-style chickpeas with mustard seeds, curry leaves and a bit of raw onion. Warm, savoury and full of **plant protein and fibre**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan. Pop the mustard seeds, then add the Kashmiri chili, curry leaves, hing and chopped green chili for 20 seconds.
Add the chickpeas and the salt and toss for 3 minutes until hot. Stir in the onion and finish with the lemon juice.

name: Cucumber and mint raita
inspiredBy: North Indian and Pakistani raita
about: Cold yogurt with grated cucumber, mint and roasted cumin, with a pinch of black salt. **High in protein and calcium**, it is a snack you eat with a spoon.
steps: Loosen the yogurt with a splash of water, then stir in the grated cucumber, mint, crushed cumin and black salt.
ingredients: thinned with a splash of water

name: Sprouted moong kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka kosambari
about: A Karnataka salad of sprouted moong with carrot, tomato, a little coconut and lemon, tempered with mustard seeds. Crunchy, light and a good **hit of protein and fibre** for very few calories.
steps: Toss the sprouts, carrot, tomato, coconut, cilantro and green chili in a bowl.
Warm the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, and pour it over the salad with the lemon juice and the salt. Toss and eat right away.

name: Masala peanuts
inspiredBy: Indian and Pakistani masala peanuts
about: Warm roasted peanuts tossed with chopped onion, tomato, green chili, lemon and chaat masala, as sold at every Pakistani and Indian street corner. A small bowl gives you **protein and healthy fats** with some freshness on top.
steps: Toss the peanuts with the onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, then add the lemon juice, chaat masala and salt. Eat it right away so the peanuts stay crunchy.

name: Masala boiled egg with carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Indian masala egg
about: A hard-boiled egg with chaat masala, black pepper and lemon, with crunchy carrot sticks on the side. Small, quick and **a good source of choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it in cold water, peel and halve.
Sprinkle the egg with the chaat masala, pepper, salt and lemon juice and eat it with the carrot sticks.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday and keep them in their shells in the fridge for the week.

name: Egg chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Delhi anda chaat
about: A boiled egg chopped with raw onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, with lemon and chaat masala, the way it is sold from street carts in Pakistan and Delhi. Small, sharp and a good source of **choline and protein**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it in cold water, peel and chop it roughly.
Toss the egg with the onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, then add the lemon juice, chaat masala, pepper and salt and eat it right away.
tip: Use one of the Sunday eggs and it is ready in 5 minutes, or boil one while you chop.

name: Toor dal rasam in a mug
inspiredBy: Tamil milagu rasam
about: A thin, peppery South Indian rasam with a spoon of toor dal, tomato, garlic and curry leaves, sipped warm. It gives you **a little protein and fibre** and a lot of flavour.
steps: Simmer the dal with plenty of water until very soft, about 30 minutes (12 in a pressure cooker), and whisk it smooth.
Add the tomato, garlic, tamarind, rasam powder, pepper, salt and a cup of water and simmer for 10 minutes.
Warm the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds and curry leaves, pour it in and finish with cilantro. Sip it hot.
tip: Make a double batch on Sunday and keep it in the fridge for 3 days; reheat a mug at a time.

name: Haldi doodh with cardamom and almonds
inspiredBy: Indian haldi doodh (turmeric milk)
