about: Two eggs set in a thick, garlicky tomato sauce with soft sweet red pepper and a pinch of chili, finished with a spoonful of nutty dukkah and served with warm bread for scooping. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the dukkah brings vitamin E.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small, wide pan. Cook the onion and red pepper over medium heat until the onion is soft and just golden, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic, cumin, paprika and chili and stir for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Pour in the passata with the salt and a splash of water. Simmer, stirring now and then, until it turns thick and jammy, about 8 minutes.
Make two little wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook on low for 6 to 8 minutes, until the whites and the yolks are firm.
Scatter with the parsley and finish with a spoonful of dukkah, the way Egyptians do with eggs. Warm the bread in a dry pan, tear it up and scoop.
tip: Make the tomato sauce the night before and keep it in the fridge. In the morning, heat it, crack in the eggs and breakfast is ready in 10 minutes.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added

name: Ful medames with tinned sardines, tahini, lemon and cucumber
inspiredBy: Cairo and Alexandria ful, with the tinned sardines many Egyptians keep in the cupboard for a quick plate
about: Warm, creamy fava beans mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with tinned sardines broken over the top, a drizzle of tahini and a pile of cucumber, onion and parsley. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the sardines add omega-3, B12 and calcium from their soft bones.
steps: Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the beans with a splash of water in a small pot with the garlic and cumin, stirring now and then, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole beans. Stir in the lemon juice and most of the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it pours like thin cream.
Spoon the ful into a shallow bowl. Break the sardines over the top, drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the oil, and pile on the cucumber, onion and parsley. Add the shatta on the side.
Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and scoop.
tip: Cook a big batch of dried fava, or open a tin with no salt added and drain it, and keep the rest for the next ful morning. Dried fava turns creamy in a slow cooker or a pressure cooker.
ingredients: cooked from dried, or a tin with no salt added, drained
tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Ful medames with tahini, lemon and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: the Cairo breakfast ful, the way a home cook finishes it with tahini, lemon and an egg
about: Warm, creamy fava beans mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with a boiled egg, a drizzle of tahini and a pile of tomato, onion and parsley. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the egg adds choline.
steps: Use an egg boiled the night before, or lower one into boiling water for 10 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the beans with a splash of water in a small pot with the garlic and cumin, stirring now and then, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole beans. Stir in the lemon juice and most of the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it pours like thin cream.
Spoon the ful into a shallow bowl. Drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the oil, pile on the tomato, onion and parsley, and set the halved egg on top. Add the shatta on the side.
Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and scoop.
tip: Boil Thursday's and Friday's eggs together on Wednesday night. They keep 4 days in the fridge.
ingredients: cooked from dried, or a tin with no salt added, drained

name: Eggs with basterma-style pastrami and tomato, with olives and baladi bread
inspiredBy: the Cairo breakfast of eggs fried with basterma, made here with beef pastrami as the nearest widely sold cured beef
about: Peppery, smoky cured beef crisped in the pan, then softened tomato and red pepper with two eggs cooked right on top and a spoonful of dukkah to finish. Salty and rich, so a little goes a long way. The eggs and beef bring **protein, choline and B12**.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan. Add the pastrami strips and fry for about 2 minutes, until the edges are crisp and it smells peppery and smoky.
Add the tomato and red pepper and cook until they soften, about 4 minutes.
Crack the eggs over the top, sprinkle with the cumin and pepper, cover and cook for 6 to 8 minutes until the whites and the yolks are firm. The pastrami is salty, so you should not need extra salt.
Scatter with parsley and finish with a spoonful of dukkah. Serve with the olives and warm bread.
tip: Real basterma has a fenugreek and garlic crust. If you find it at a Middle Eastern shop or an Armenian deli, use it the same way.
ingredients: sliced thin, then cut in strips
black olives, rinsed, on the side

name: Sudanese-style ful with egg, white cheese, tomato, sesame and rocket
inspiredBy: the Sudanese breakfast ful, finished with white cheese, sesame and plenty of raw rocket
about: Fava beans mashed with garlic, lemon and chili, with a boiled egg, crumbled white cheese, tomato, onion, toasted sesame and a big handful of peppery rocket. It is a different mood from Egyptian ful. The beans and rocket bring **iron, folate and vitamin K**, and the egg and cheese add choline and calcium.
steps: Use an egg boiled the night before, or lower one into boiling water for 10 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden and nutty, about 2 minutes.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the beans with a splash of water, the garlic, cumin and the shatta, stirring, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash with a fork until mostly creamy. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Spoon into a shallow bowl. Pour the rest of the olive oil over the middle and scatter on the white cheese, tomato, onion, sesame and rocket. Halve the egg and set it on top.
Warm the bread and tear it up to scoop.
tip: In Sudan the oil is often toasted sesame oil. A teaspoon in place of half the olive oil is lovely. Gebna beida is salty, so a little goes a long way.
ingredients: cooked from dried, or a tin with no salt added, drained

name: Baked green ta'meya with cucumber and rocket salad, tahini and olives
inspiredBy: Egyptian ta'meya, the fava falafel of Cairo and Alexandria, baked instead of deep-fried
about: Green fava patties packed with parsley and dill, crusted in sesame and baked until crisp, with a peppery cucumber and rocket salad, a lemony tahini sauce and a few black olives. The fava and herbs bring **protein, folate, iron and vitamin K**. This makes two portions, so Sunday's breakfast is done.
steps: The night before, cover the fava with plenty of cold water and soak for at least 12 hours. Drain well. Do not cook them first, they should be raw and just soft.
Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Line a tray with parchment and brush it with a little of the oil.
Pulse the fava, parsley, dill, onion, garlic, half the sesame, cumin and salt in a food processor until it looks like coarse green crumbs. It should hold together when you squeeze a handful.
Shape into small flattened patties, about 6 per portion. Press the edges into the rest of the sesame seeds, set them on the tray and brush with the remaining oil.
Bake for 12 minutes, flip, and bake another 10 to 12 minutes until deep golden and crisp outside, still green inside.
While they bake, stir the tahini with half the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and enough water to make a pourable sauce. Toss the cucumber and rocket with the rest of the lemon.

Serve the ta'meya with the salad, the tahini sauce, the olives and warm bread, with a little dukkah for dipping. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's breakfast and re-crisp it in a hot oven or toaster oven for 8 minutes.
tip: Peeled split dried fava from a Middle Eastern grocer gives the greenest, lightest ta'meya. Whole dried fava from the supermarket works too, but peel the skins after soaking. Canned fava will not work, the raw soaked fava is what holds the patties together.
ingredients: dried, soaked overnight, peeled and split if you can find them
half in the mix, half to coat
black olives, rinsed, on the side

name: Sardine, tomato and rocket in baladi bread with tahini and lemon
inspiredBy: the Egyptian tinned sardine sandwich, a lunch-hour classic in Cairo
about: Mashed tinned sardines with onion, cumin and lemon, stuffed into a toasted pocket with tomato, rocket and a tahini and lemon sauce with a pinch of dried mint. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium and omega-3**, and it comes together in ten minutes.
steps: Mash the sardines roughly with a fork with half the lemon juice, the cumin, the chili and the onion.
Stir the tahini with the olive oil, the dried mint, the salt and a spoonful of water to make a thick sauce.
Split the pita and toast it for a minute in a dry pan or toaster.
Spread the sauce inside, then fill with the sardines, tomato, rocket and parsley. Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the top and eat it right away.
tip: Pack the pita, filling and salad separately if you are taking it to work and assemble at lunch so the bread stays crisp.
ingredients: tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Tinned mackerel in garlicky tomato with salata baladi and baladi bread
inspiredBy: a cheap, quick Cairo supper of tinned fish warmed in tomato and scooped up with bread, with the everyday salad on the side
about: Tinned mackerel warmed through in a garlicky, cumin-scented tomato sauce, scooped up with warm bread, with a crunchy salata baladi of cucumber, tomato, onion and parsley on the side. The mackerel brings **omega-3, B12 and vitamin D**, and the cooked tomato brings lycopene and vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil with the crushed garlic in a small pan over low heat for 1 minute, without letting it brown.
Add the passata, cumin, chili, half the lemon juice and half the salt. Simmer for about 4 minutes, until it thickens.
Flake in the mackerel and warm it through for 2 minutes. Do not stir too hard, you want big flakes.
Toss the cucumber, fresh tomato, onion and parsley with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Warm the bread in a dry pan. Scoop the mackerel and sauce up with the bread and eat the salad alongside.
tip: Tinned sardines work the same way. Mash the soft bones in with a fork for extra calcium.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added

name: Molokhia with chicken and brown rice, with garlic and coriander taqliya
inspiredBy: Cairo molokhia, the green jute leaf soup, served over brown rice rather than white
about: Silky, deep green jute leaves in chicken broth, finished with a sizzle of garlic and coriander, spooned over brown rice and tender chicken, with sharp onion in vinegar on the side. The jute brings **vitamins A and K, folate and calcium**, and the chicken and rice make it a full meal.
steps: Start the brown rice first, in a pot with twice its volume of water. It needs about 40 minutes.

Put the chicken, the quartered onion, bay leaf, cardamom, pepper and half the salt in another pot with enough water to cover, about 700 ml for two portions. Simmer, covered, until the chicken is just tender, 18 to 20 minutes.
Lift out the chicken and keep it warm. Strain the broth back into the pot and bring it to a gentle simmer.
Stir in the molokhia, still frozen is fine, and the rest of the salt. Bring back to a gentle simmer, not a hard boil, and cook for 5 minutes. It should be glossy and fall off the spoon in ribbons.

Make the taqliya. Warm the olive oil in a small pan and fry the garlic with the ground coriander for 1 to 2 minutes, until the garlic is just golden. Do not let it brown. Tip it sizzling into the pot and stir once.
Toss a few thin slices of raw onion with the vinegar and a pinch of salt.

Serve the rice with the molokhia ladled over and the chicken on top, with the onions and lemon wedges on the side. Squeeze the lemon over at the table, since it dulls the green if it cooks. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the rice in a separate container.
tip: Ghee is the traditional fat for the taqliya, and a teaspoon of it is delicious here if you have some. Molokhia freezes well, so a double batch makes a quick dinner later.
ingredients: frozen minced molokhia, or fresh, or dried
quartered, plus a little thinly sliced

name: Koshari with lentils, chickpeas and a little pasta
inspiredBy: Cairo koshari, reimagined with brown rice and lentils doing most of the work, and a small handful of whole-wheat pasta
about: The Cairo street classic: lentils, rice, pasta and chickpeas under a spiced tomato sauce, crisp onions and a sharp garlic and vinegar splash. Here it leans on lentils and chickpeas for **fibre, iron and slow carbs**, with less rice and pasta than the street version.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sliced onions with most of the oil and a pinch of salt and spread them in a single layer over two trays. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, flipping once, until deep golden. They crisp up as they cool.
Simmer the brown rice alone in plenty of water for 10 minutes. Add the lentils and half the cumin and simmer for about 22 minutes more, until both are tender. Drain and season with a pinch of salt.
Cook the pasta in boiling salted water until just al dente, then drain.

For the sauce, warm the rest of the oil and half the garlic (finely chopped) over low heat for 1 minute. Stir in the tomato paste, the passata, the rest of the cumin, the coriander, cinnamon and salt. Simmer for 12 minutes until thick, then stir in the chickpeas to warm through.
Crush the remaining garlic and stir it into the vinegar with a splash of water. This is the daqqa.

Pile the lentils and rice into bowls, top with the pasta, the saucy chickpeas and the crispy onions. Spoon over the garlic vinegar, scatter with parsley and add a spoonful of shatta at the table. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the onions in a separate container.
tip: Cook the lentil and rice base on Sunday and keep it in the fridge, then koshari is a 25-minute job. Re-crisp the leftover onions in a dry pan before you eat them.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added

name: Alexandrian grilled sardines with cumin and lemon, tahini sauce and baladi salad
inspiredBy: the grilled sardines of Alexandria's fish markets, rubbed with cumin and garlic
about: Fresh sardines rubbed with garlic, cumin and lemon, grilled until the skin blisters, with a lemony tahini sauce, a crunchy tomato, cucumber, carrot and parsley salad and warm bread. The sardines bring **omega-3, vitamin D, B12 and calcium**.
steps: Mash half the garlic with the salt, then stir in the cumin, paprika, chili, half the oil and half the lemon juice. Rub this all over the sardines, inside and out, and leave them for 15 minutes.
Heat the broiler (or a grill pan or barbecue) as hot as it goes. Cook the sardines for 3 to 4 minutes on each side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes off the bone.
Make the tahini sauce. Mash the rest of the garlic, stir in the tahini and half the remaining lemon juice, and thin with water until it pours like cream.
Toss the tomato, cucumber, carrot, onion and parsley with the rest of the lemon juice and oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the sardines hot with the salad, the tahini sauce and warm bread.
tip: Ask the fishmonger to gut and scale the sardines. If you cannot find fresh ones, mackerel fillets work the same way.

name: Bamia bil lahma, okra and beef in garlicky tomato, with brown rice
inspiredBy: Egyptian bamia, the okra and meat stew every Cairo family makes, with a garlic and coriander taqliya
about: Tender okra and small chunks of beef simmered in a thick tomato sauce, finished with a sizzle of garlic and coriander, over brown rice. Okra is **rich in fibre, folate and vitamin K**, and the garlic and tomato make it taste like Friday lunch.
steps: Brown the beef in half the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and cook until golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the tomato paste, the passata, the bay leaf, the pepper, half the salt and 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for about 55 minutes, until the beef is nearly tender.
Start the rice in a separate pot with twice its volume of water about 35 minutes before the end, and cook until fluffy.
Add the okra whole, trimming only the stems, and simmer for another 15 minutes, until tender. Do not stir too much, it will turn slimy. Shake the pot instead.
Fry the sliced garlic with the ground coriander in the rest of the oil until golden, about 1 minute, then tip the sizzling taqliya into the pot with the lemon juice.
Serve over the rice, scattered with parsley. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: A pressure cooker cuts the beef to about 20 minutes, which makes this a weeknight dish. Cut the okra without piercing the pods and do not soak it, so it stays firm.
ingredients: small whole pods, frozen is fine
passata or tomato sauce, no salt added

name: Sudanese chicken and peanut mullah with spinach, sorghum asida and rocket
inspiredBy: Sudanese mullah dakwa, the peanut and tomato stew, with asida made from sorghum
about: Chicken simmered with onion, tomato, ginger and ground roasted peanuts into a thick, rich stew with spinach folded in, mounded around a soft sorghum asida with a peppery rocket salad. The chicken, peanuts and spinach bring **protein, vitamin E, magnesium and folate**.
steps: Grind the peanuts with a splash of water in a mortar or small blender until they make a coarse paste. This is the dakwa.

Brown the chicken in the olive oil for 4 to 5 minutes. Lift it out. In the same pot, cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, baharat, cumin, ginger and chili and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the tomato paste, then the passata and salt. Simmer for 5 minutes, then return the chicken with 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer for 20 minutes.

Stir a ladle of the sauce into the peanut paste to loosen it, then stir it all into the pot. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes more, until thick and the oil shines at the edges. Fold in the spinach for the last 2 minutes and add the lemon juice.

Meanwhile, make the asida for tonight only. Whisk all the sorghum flour with twice its weight of cold water until smooth. Bring another twice its weight of salted water to a boil, pour in the paste while whisking, then switch to a wooden spoon and beat hard over low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until stiff, smooth and glossy. Shape into a mound in a bowl and make a well.

Spoon the mullah into the well and serve the rocket dressed with a squeeze of lemon alongside. Asida is best fresh, so pack the second portion of mullah, with its rocket in a separate box, for tomorrow's lunch with warm pita or rice.
tip: A tablespoon of natural peanut butter stands in for the ground peanuts. Ghee is the traditional fat in Sudan and is delicious here.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added
baladi bread or whole-wheat pita, for tomorrow's portion

name: Alexandrian sayadeya, spiced mackerel over caramelized onion and cumin brown rice
inspiredBy: Alexandria's sayadeya, the fisherman's rice, made with brown rice and baked mackerel instead of fried fish
about: Deeply caramelized onions and cumin cooked into brown rice, topped with spice-rubbed mackerel, sweet browned onions and a few toasted almonds, with a bright tomato and parsley relish. It is Alexandria's weekend dish. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Cook the onions in half the oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-low heat, stirring often, for 25 to 30 minutes, until deep brown and sweet. Add a splash of water if they start to catch. Set a third of them aside for the top.

Add half the garlic and most of the cumin to the pot, then the rice. Stir for 1 minute, then add about 2.2 times the rice's volume of boiling water and half the salt. Cover and cook on low for 35 to 40 minutes, until the rice is tender. Rest, covered, for 5 minutes.
Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F). Mash the rest of the garlic with the remaining cumin, the chili, a little of the lemon juice and the rest of the oil, and rub it all over the mackerel.
Roast the mackerel skin-side up for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin crackles and the flesh flakes.
Toss the tomato with the parsley, the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.

Spoon the rice onto plates, top with the mackerel, the reserved onions and the almonds, and serve the relish beside it. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the fish, rice and relish in separate containers. Reheat the rice with a splash of water. The fish is good cold or warm.
tip: Make the onions the day before, they are the slow part, and the whole dinner comes together in 45 minutes. Mullet or sea bass is what Alexandrians use, and either works here too.

name: Kebda Iskandarani, chicken liver with garlic, cumin and sweet pepper in baladi bread
inspiredBy: Alexandria's street-corner liver, a favourite sandwich in Egypt's port city, made with chicken liver
about: Quick-seared chicken liver with plenty of garlic, cumin and red pepper, finished with lemon, stuffed in warm bread with tomato and a garlicky yogurt sauce, with roasted sweet potato wedges and crisp chickpeas on the side. Liver is one of the richest foods for **iron, B12 and vitamin A**, and a small portion once a week is plenty. Skip it if you are pregnant or planning to be.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges and the chickpeas with a third of the oil, half the cumin and half the salt on a tray and roast for 30 minutes, turning once, until the wedges are golden and soft and the chickpeas are a little crisp.
Stir a little crushed garlic and a pinch of salt into the yogurt and set aside. Crush the rest of the garlic with the remaining salt and cumin.

Pat the liver dry. Heat the rest of the oil in a wide pan until very hot. Add the liver in one layer, then the red pepper and the garlic mix, and cook, tossing, for about 4 minutes in all, until the liver is browned and no pink remains. Overcooked liver goes dry, so do not go much past that.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and stir in the parsley.

Split the warm bread, spread a spoonful of the garlic yogurt inside and tuck in the tomato and liver. Serve the rest of the yogurt as a dip for the wedges and chickpeas, with the shatta for those who want it.
tip: Soaking the liver in milk or lemon water for 15 minutes mellows the flavour if you are new to liver. In Alexandria it is often served with tahini too.
ingredients: no salt added, drained, roasted with the wedges

name: Hummus el-sham, warm cumin chickpeas with lemon
inspiredBy: hummus el-sham, the warm chickpeas sold in paper cups on Cairo street corners
about: Chickpeas warmed with cumin, olive oil and a squeeze of lemon, like the cups sold at Cairo street corners. A bowl brings **plant protein and fibre**.
steps: Warm the chickpeas with the olive oil, cumin and a splash of the tin's liquid in a small pan or the microwave for 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the lemon juice, salt and pepper, and eat warm.

name: Termis (lupini beans) with lemon and cumin
inspiredBy: termis, the lupini beans sold from Egyptian street carts
about: Firm, salty lupini beans tossed with lemon and cumin, a famous Egyptian street snack. They bring **plant protein and fibre** for very few calories.
steps: Rinse the lupini and toss with the lemon, cumin and salt.
Squeeze each bean out of its skin with your fingers and eat the soft inside, or eat them whole.

name: Sardines with tomato and shatta on baladi bread
inspiredBy: sardin ala el-eish, tinned sardines mashed onto warm bread with a kick of shatta, a quick Cairo bite
about: Tinned sardines mashed with lemon and a spoonful of shatta, piled onto warm bread and topped with sliced tomato. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium and omega-3**.
steps: Warm the bread in a dry pan or the toaster.
Mash the sardines with the lemon, shatta and pepper, pile onto the bread and lay the tomato on top.
ingredients: tinned in water or brine, drained

name: Carrot, orange and almond smoothie
inspiredBy: carrot and orange juice from Cairo juice bars, thickened with almonds as in a koktail
about: Carrots and an orange blended into a sweet, golden drink with a few almonds for body, like the corner juice stands in Cairo. The carrots bring **a full day of vitamin A**, and the almonds and orange bring vitamin E and vitamin C. Keep the pulp in for fibre.
steps: Soak the almonds in warm water for 10 minutes, then drain. Grate the carrots.
Blend the carrots, orange, almonds and about 100 ml of cold water for 2 minutes, until as smooth as it will go.
Add the lemon juice, taste, and serve over ice. Add a little more water if it is too thick.

name: Roasted sweet potato with cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon
inspiredBy: batata, the roasted sweet potato sold from carts on winter streets in Cairo
about: A hot roasted sweet potato with a pinch of cinnamon and a squeeze of lemon, like the carts on Cairo corners in winter. It brings **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Prick the sweet potato and microwave it for 8 minutes, or roast at 200°C (400°F) for about 45 minutes for the best flavour, until it is soft and collapses when squeezed.
Split it open and sprinkle with the cinnamon, lemon juice and salt.
tip: Roast it on Tuesday next to the koshari onions, since the oven is already hot, and rewarm it on Wednesday.

name: Zabadi with chopped dates and cinnamon
inspiredBy: plain yogurt with dates, the way a Nile Valley kitchen would sweeten it
about: Plain yogurt with chopped dates and cinnamon, sweetened by the fruit. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Stir the chopped date into the yogurt, then sprinkle with the cinnamon.
ingredients: ½ medjool or 2 small dates, chopped

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
inspiredBy: the almond-stuffed dates of Egyptian and Sudanese tea tables
about: Soft dates stuffed with whole almonds, served with tea in many Nile Valley homes. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Slit the dates and remove the pits. Tuck an almond into each date, and eat the rest of the almonds alongside.

name: Dates with tahini
inspiredBy: dates and tahini, a sweet, nutty pairing from the Egyptian breakfast table
about: Soft dates filled with a little tahini and a pinch of cinnamon, rich and sweet. The tahini brings **calcium, copper and vitamin E**, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Slit the dates and remove the pits. Spoon a little tahini into each and eat.
ingredients: 1½ medjool or 3 small Egyptian dates, pitted

name: Gebna beida, olives and mint in baladi bread
inspiredBy: the Egyptian white cheese sandwich, with olives and dried mint
about: A simple Egyptian sandwich of salty white cheese, black olives, sliced tomato and dried mint in a small pita. The cheese is salty, so a little is enough to season the whole pocket.
steps: Split the pita and fill with the white cheese, olives and tomato. Rub the dried mint between your fingers over the top. Eat right away.

name: Zabadi bil khiar, yogurt with cucumber, garlic and mint
inspiredBy: the cool yogurt and cucumber salad on Egyptian tables, eaten with bread
about: Cool plain yogurt with grated cucumber, a little garlic and dried mint, scooped up with a few bites of bread. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Squeeze the grated cucumber lightly in your hand. Stir it into the yogurt with the crushed garlic, dried mint and salt.
Eat with torn pieces of bread.
ingredients: baladi bread or whole-wheat pita, torn for scooping

name: Baladi bread with olive oil and dukkah
inspiredBy: the Egyptian snack of bread dipped in olive oil, then in dukkah
about: Warm bread, a little olive oil and a spoon of dukkah, the Egyptian mix of toasted hazelnut, sesame, coriander and cumin. It brings **vitamin E and healthy fats**.
steps: Warm the bread in a dry pan. Tear it up, dip each piece in the oil and then in the dukkah.

name: Orange with dates
inspiredBy: a Nile Valley fruit plate of oranges and dates
about: A juicy orange with a soft date alongside. The orange brings **vitamin C**, and the date adds sweetness and potassium.
steps: Peel the orange and break it into segments. Eat it with the date.

name: Ginger-pear oatmeal with walnuts
about: Creamy oats simmered with a little milk, fresh ginger and cinnamon, topped with chopped pear and toasted walnuts. The oats bring **slow-digesting fibre** and the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fat and crunch.
steps: Wash the pear and chop it into small pieces. Grate the ginger finely.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes, then chop them.

Stir the oats, milk, a splash of water, the ginger, cinnamon and iodized salt together in a small pot. Bring it to a gentle bubble and cook, stirring, until creamy, about 5 minutes. Add a splash more water if it gets too thick.
Stir half of the pear into the oatmeal for the last minute so it softens. Spoon into a bowl and top with the rest of the pear and the walnuts.
tip: Make it the night before: soak the oats in the milk in the fridge, eat within 2 days, and warm it in the morning.

name: Raspberry yogurt bowl with toasted oats and almonds
about: Thick Greek yogurt with tart raspberries, toasted oats and almonds for crunch. It is a quick breakfast with **protein, calcium and vitamin E** to carry you to lunch.
steps: Toast the oats and the almonds together in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until golden and nutty, about 3 minutes. Tip them out to cool.
Wash the raspberries. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl.
Top with the raspberries, the toasted oats and almonds, and a pinch of cinnamon.
tip: Toast a few days of oats and almonds at once and keep them in a jar for up to a week.

name: Spinach and mushroom omelette with whole-grain toast and tomatoes
about: A fluffy, fully set omelette folded around garlicky mushrooms and spinach, with whole-grain toast and cherry tomatoes. The eggs bring **protein and choline** and the spinach and tomatoes bring vitamins A and C.
steps: Wash the spinach and tomatoes. Wipe the mushrooms clean and slice them. Mince the garlic. Beat the eggs with a pinch of the iodized salt and the pepper.

Warm half of the canola oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Cook the mushrooms until golden and dry, about 4 minutes, adding the garlic for the last 30 seconds. Stir in the spinach until just wilted, then tip it onto a plate.

Wipe the pan, warm the rest of the oil over medium heat and pour in the eggs. Cook, lifting the edges, until the underside is set, about 2 minutes. Spoon the filling on one half, fold the other over and cook for another 2 minutes, until the egg is completely firm all the way through.
Toast the bread and serve it with the omelette and the tomatoes, sprinkled with the rest of the salt.

name: Ginger chicken noodle soup with egg ribbons, edamame and greens
inspiredBy: Inspired by classic chicken noodle soup and Chinese ginger-scallion chicken soups, with whole-wheat spaghetti
about: A clear, fragrant chicken soup with lots of ginger, carrot, napa cabbage and spinach, plus edamame, firm egg ribbons and whole-wheat noodles to make it a meal. It is made with low-sodium broth, so it is **comforting without being very salty**, and the chicken and egg bring protein and choline. It makes two portions.
steps: Wash the carrot, napa cabbage, spinach and scallions. Slice the carrot into thin coins, the cabbage into ribbons, the ginger into matchsticks and mince the garlic. Keep the scallion whites and greens apart.
Warm the sesame oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the ginger, garlic, scallion whites and carrot for 4 minutes, until fragrant and starting to soften.

Add the chicken, the broth, the soy sauce and enough water to cover everything. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook until the chicken is cooked through and reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece, about 12 minutes. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw chicken.
Meanwhile, boil the noodles in a separate pot of water until tender, about 8 minutes, then drain. Cooking them apart keeps the broth clear and the noodles from going soft in the leftovers.

Stir the frozen edamame into the soup and simmer until steaming hot all the way through, about 3 minutes. Stir in the cabbage and spinach for 1 to 2 minutes, until wilted. Slowly pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream while stirring the soup gently, and simmer for 2 more minutes, until the egg is completely set in firm ribbons. Season with the lime juice and the iodized salt.
Divide the noodles between two bowls, ladle the soup over, and top with the scallion greens.

Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: cool the soup, which has the egg in it, and the noodles separately in shallow containers within 1 hour, then refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat the soup until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and pour it over the noodles.
tip: Add a squeeze of fresh lime and a few chili flakes at the table for heat.
ingredients: washed and sliced into thin coins

name: Seared salmon soba with mushrooms, spinach and ginger-soy sauce
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese soba with grilled fish, made with a simple soy-ginger-lime sauce
about: Nutty buckwheat soba tossed with browned mushrooms, wilted spinach and edamame, topped with a seared salmon fillet and a bright ginger-soy sauce. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and some vitamin D**, and the edamame and spinach bring folate and iron.
steps: Buy the salmon the day you cook it, or thaw frozen salmon overnight in the fridge. Wash the spinach, mushrooms and scallion. Whisk the soy sauce, vinegar, lime juice, ginger and half of the sesame oil with a spoonful of water for the sauce.
Boil the soba in plenty of water until just tender, 4 to 5 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water so it does not clump.

Pat the salmon dry. Warm the canola oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat and sear the salmon skin side down for 4 minutes, then flip and cook for 3 to 4 minutes more, until it reaches 70 °C (158 °F) in the thickest part and flakes easily. Move it to a clean plate, and wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw fish.
In the same pan, cook the mushrooms and garlic for 4 minutes, until golden. Add the spinach and cook until wilted, about 1 minute.
Pour hot water over the frozen edamame in a bowl until steaming hot all the way through, then drain.

Toss the soba with the mushrooms, spinach, edamame, the rest of the sesame oil and half of the sauce. Pile it into a bowl, set the salmon on top, and finish with the rest of the sauce, and the scallion.
tip: Check the soba label: 100% buckwheat is wheat-free, but many packs are part wheat.
ingredients: skin-on or skinless fillet, pin bones removed

name: Dan dan-style turkey noodles with green beans, napa cabbage and cucumber
inspiredBy: Inspired by Sichuan dan dan noodles, with peanut butter standing in for sesame paste, a pinch of Sichuan pepper, lean ground turkey, whole-wheat spaghetti and far less oil and chili
about: Chewy whole-wheat noodles and green beans in a savoury, nutty peanut-soy sauce, topped with garlicky ground turkey, napa cabbage and cool cucumber. The turkey brings **protein, iron and zinc**, and the sauce is built on peanut butter rather than oil. It makes two portions.
steps: Wash the green beans, cabbage, cucumber and scallions. Toast the Sichuan peppercorn in a dry pan for 30 seconds and crush it. Whisk it with the peanut butter, soy sauce, vinegar, chili flakes, pepper, half of the garlic and half of the ginger and 2 tablespoons of warm water until smooth, for the sauce.
Boil the noodles in plenty of water for about 8 minutes, adding the green beans for the last 3 minutes. Scoop out a mug of the cooking water, then drain.

While they cook, warm the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Cook the turkey, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned and cooked through to 74 °C (165 °F), about 6 minutes. Add the rest of the garlic and ginger for the last minute, then stir in the napa cabbage for 1 to 2 minutes, until just wilted. Wash your hands, board and spoon after handling the raw turkey.
Toss the hot noodles and green beans with the sauce, loosening it with a splash of the cooking water.
Divide between two bowls and top with the turkey, cabbage and scallions. Put half of the cucumber on the bowl you are eating now and keep the rest in the fridge for the second portion.

Pack the second portion, without the cucumber, into a shallow container within 1 hour, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat it until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and add the saved cucumber on top.
tip: Use less chili for a mild bowl, or add a spoonful of chili crisp at the table.
ingredients: washed and trimmed, cut in thirds
washed and sliced into thin matchsticks

name: Japchae-style tofu noodles with spinach, carrot and mushrooms
inspiredBy: Inspired by Korean japchae, made with whole-wheat noodles in place of sweet potato starch noodles, with tofu for protein
about: Silky-chewy noodles tossed with golden tofu, firm egg ribbons, mushrooms, carrot, red pepper and garlicky spinach in a sesame-soy glaze. The calcium-set tofu and egg bring **protein, choline and some calcium** and the vegetables bring vitamin A, and it eats well warm or cold, so it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Wash the spinach, carrot and red pepper. Wrap the tofu in a clean towel and press it for 10 minutes, then cut it into cubes. Slice the vegetables into thin, even strips.

Boil the noodles until tender, about 8 minutes, dropping the spinach into the pot for the last 30 seconds. Scoop the spinach out with tongs, squeeze it dry and toss it with a third of the garlic, a little of the sesame oil and a pinch of pepper.
Drain the noodles, rinse them and snip them a few times with scissors so they are easy to toss.

Beat the eggs and cook them as a thin flat omelette in a little of the canola oil in the nonstick pan, until completely firm all the way through, about 3 minutes a side, then slice it into ribbons. Wipe the pan, warm the rest of the canola oil over medium-high heat and brown the tofu on all sides, about 6 minutes, and move it to a plate. Cook the onion, carrot, pepper and mushrooms in the same pan for 4 to 5 minutes, until just tender, adding the rest of the garlic at the end.
Add the noodles, the soy sauce and the rest of the sesame oil to the pan and toss for 2 minutes, until glossy and hot. Fold in the tofu, the spinach and the egg ribbons.
Serve in bowls sprinkled with the chopped walnuts.
Pack the second portion into a shallow container within 1 hour, refrigerate and eat within 3 days, cold or reheated until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F).
tip: Short on time? Skip pressing the tofu and use a bag of mixed stir-fry vegetables.

name: Turmeric salmon with whole-wheat noodles and a lime-chili herb salad
inspiredBy: Inspired by Vietnamese turmeric fish (chả cá) and cold herb noodle bowls (bún), with whole-wheat spaghetti
about: Turmeric-rubbed salmon seared until crisp at the edges on cool noodles with cucumber, carrot and napa cabbage and handfuls of mint and cilantro, dressed with lime, soy and chili. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the herbs bring vitamin K and plenty of flavour.
steps: Buy the salmon the day you cook it, or thaw it overnight in the fridge. Wash the cucumber, carrot, cabbage and herbs.
Boil the noodles for about 8 minutes, until tender, then drain and rinse them under cold water until cool.
Whisk the lime juice, soy sauce, garlic and chili flakes with 2 tablespoons of water for the dressing. Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes.

Pat the salmon dry and rub it with the turmeric. Warm the oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat and cook it skin side down for 4 minutes, then flip and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, until it reaches 70 °C (158 °F) and flakes easily. Move it to a clean plate and flake it into large pieces. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw fish.
Pile the noodles, cabbage, cucumber and carrot in a bowl, top with the salmon and the herbs, spoon over the dressing and finish with the pumpkin seeds.
tip: A squeeze more lime keeps it fresh. Add a few drops of fish sauce if you have it.

name: Pho-style beef noodle soup with napa cabbage and a plate of herbs
inspiredBy: Inspired by Vietnamese pho, with a quick chicken-stock broth and whole-wheat spaghetti instead of rice noodles
about: A fragrant quick chicken-stock broth spiced with star anise and cinnamon and built on charred onion and ginger, with tender slices of lean beef and napa cabbage, and mint, cilantro, scallion and lime to pile on. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the broth is made with low-sodium stock so you can season it to taste. It makes two portions and is the one slow dish of the week.
steps: Wash the cabbage, scallion and herbs. Put the beef in the freezer for 20 minutes so it is firm, then slice it as thinly as you can across the grain. Keep it covered in the fridge until you need it.

Char the onion and the ginger: set them cut side down in a dry pot over high heat until blackened in spots, about 6 minutes. Add the star anise, cinnamon, clove and coriander seed and toast for 30 seconds.

Pour in the broth and about the same amount of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered, for 30 minutes. Strain out the solids, return the broth to the pot and season it with the soy sauce.
Meanwhile, boil the noodles in a separate pot for about 8 minutes until tender, then drain.

Bring the broth to a rolling simmer. Add the cabbage and cook for 2 minutes, then add the beef and cook until no pink remains and it reaches 71 °C (160 °F), about 2 minutes. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw beef.
Divide the noodles between two bowls, ladle the soup over, and pass the scallion, mint, cilantro, lime juice and chili flakes at the table.

Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: cool the soup and the noodles separately in shallow containers within 1 hour, then refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat the soup until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), pour it over the noodles and add the fresh herbs.
tip: Use thin spaghetti or capellini for a lighter bowl; brown rice vermicelli works the same way if you find it. In a rush? Simmer the broth for 15 minutes with ground ginger and cinnamon and skip straining.
ingredients: sirloin, sliced very thinly across the grain
washed and cut in wide strips

name: Herb, chickpea and spinach noodle soup with yogurt and mint
inspiredBy: Inspired by Persian ash reshteh, with whole-wheat spaghetti for the noodles, chickpeas for the beans and yogurt in place of kashk
about: A thick green soup of cilantro and spinach with chickpeas and noodles, finished with a firm-boiled egg, a spoonful of yogurt, golden mint and chopped walnuts. The chickpeas and egg bring **plant protein, iron, folate and choline**, and the lime brightens the herbs and helps your body absorb that iron.
steps: Wash the carrot, spinach, scallions and cilantro. Chop the onion, grate the carrot, slice the scallions, mince the garlic and chop the herbs.

Put the egg in a small pot of cold water, bring it to a boil and simmer for 10 minutes, until the yolk is completely firm, then cool it under cold water, peel it and slice it. Cool and keep it in the fridge if you make it ahead.
Warm half of the canola oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and carrot until soft and golden, about 8 minutes, adding the garlic and turmeric for the last minute.
Pour in the broth and enough water to cover by a finger. Add the chickpeas, bring to a simmer and cook for 8 minutes.

Add the noodles and simmer until tender, about 8 minutes, stirring so they do not stick. Stir in the spinach, scallions and cilantro and cook for 3 more minutes, until the soup is thick and deep green. Season with the lime juice, iodized salt and pepper.
Warm the rest of the oil in a small pan, stir in the dried mint for 15 seconds until fragrant, and take it off the heat straight away.
Ladle the soup into a bowl, swirl in the yogurt, drizzle over the mint oil and top with the sliced egg and the walnuts.
tip: Short on time? Use a bag of pre-washed herbs and spinach.

name: Peanut-lime noodle bowl with edamame, cabbage and carrot
inspiredBy: Inspired by Thai-style peanut noodles, with whole-wheat spaghetti, a lime-forward sauce and lots of crunchy raw vegetables
about: Cool whole-wheat noodles tossed with a lime-peanut sauce, edamame, napa cabbage, carrot and red pepper. The edamame and peanut butter bring **plant protein and vitamin E**, and the raw vegetables give it crunch and vitamin C.
steps: Wash the cabbage, carrot, red pepper, scallion and cilantro. Shred, grate and slice them.
Boil the noodles until tender, about 8 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water until cool.
Pour hot water over the frozen edamame in a bowl until steaming hot all the way through, then drain and cool under cold water.
Whisk the peanut butter, lime juice, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, ginger and chili flakes with 2 tablespoons of warm water until smooth and pourable.
Toss the noodles, edamame and vegetables with the sauce. Top with the scallion and cilantro.
tip: Packing it? Keep the sauce in a small jar and toss just before you eat. Cool the noodles within 1 hour, keep it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.

name: Chickpea soba salad with cucumber, spinach, mint and lime-ginger dressing
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese cold soba (zaru soba) with a bright lime-ginger dressing and chickpeas for protein
about: Nutty buckwheat soba with chickpeas, cucumber and carrot, baby spinach, fresh mint and cilantro, and a sharp lime-ginger dressing with walnuts on top. The chickpeas, edamame and soba bring **plant protein, fibre and magnesium** in a lunch that packs well.
steps: Wash the cucumber, carrot, spinach, mint and cilantro. Slice and grate the vegetables, and tear the herbs.
Boil the soba in plenty of water until just tender, 4 to 5 minutes, then drain and rinse well under cold water.
Pour hot water over the frozen edamame in a bowl until steaming hot all the way through, then drain and cool under cold water.
Whisk the lime juice, vinegar, soy sauce, sesame oil and ginger with a spoonful of water for the dressing.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes. Toss the soba, chickpeas, edamame, vegetables and spinach with the dressing in a big bowl. Top with the herbs and the walnuts.
tip: Packing it? Keep the dressing apart and toss it in just before you eat. Cool the soba within 1 hour, keep it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.

name: Sardine and spinach noodles with ginger, garlic and lime
inspiredBy: Inspired by Filipino sardine guisado (canned sardines sautéed with garlic, ginger and tomato), served over whole-wheat spaghetti with spinach and chickpeas
about: Whole-wheat noodles tossed in a hot skillet with garlic, ginger, tomatoes, chickpeas and spinach, with flaked canned sardines warmed through, a splash of soy sauce and plenty of lime. Sardines eaten with their soft bones bring **omega-3 fats, calcium and vitamin D**, and the spinach and chickpeas bring iron and folate.
steps: Wash the spinach, tomatoes and cilantro. Halve the tomatoes, slice the garlic and cut the ginger into matchsticks.
Boil the noodles in plenty of water until tender, about 8 minutes. Scoop out a mug of the cooking water, then drain.

While they cook, warm the oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the garlic, ginger and chili flakes for 30 seconds, until fragrant, then add the tomatoes and chickpeas. Cook until the tomatoes are soft and jammy, about 4 minutes, then add the spinach until wilted, about 1 minute.
Flake in the sardines and add the soy sauce, then warm everything for 1 to 2 minutes, until the sardines are hot.

Add the noodles with a splash of the cooking water and toss until glossy, 2 minutes. Finish with the lime juice, pepper and cilantro. Cover and refrigerate any leftover sardines in the opened tin and use them within 2 days.
tip: Taking it to work? Cool the noodles within 1 hour, pack it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day. Fish is not a leftover to keep.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, drained, with bones

name: Pear with almonds
about: A juicy pear with a handful of almonds. It is easy to pack and filling. **Fibre and vitamin E** in one snack.
steps: Wash the pear and slice it.
Eat with the almonds.

name: Apple with almonds
about: Crisp apple with a handful of almonds. Sweet, crunchy and filling. **Vitamin E and fibre** together.
steps: Wash the apple and slice it.
Eat with the almonds.

name: Carrot and cucumber sticks with lime-yogurt dip
about: Crunchy sticks for dipping into a cool yogurt dip with lime and cilantro. A light snack with **calcium and vitamin A**.
steps: Wash the carrot, cucumber and cilantro and cut the vegetables into sticks.
Stir the yogurt with the lime juice, cilantro and iodized salt.
Serve the sticks with the dip.

name: Apple slices with pumpkin seeds
about: Crisp apple with a spoonful of toasted pumpkin seeds. The seeds bring **magnesium and zinc**, and the toasting makes them nutty.
steps: Wash and slice the apple.
Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they pop and smell nutty, then eat them with the apple.

name: Crunchy chili-lime chickpeas
about: Oven-roasted chickpeas with chili and lime: a crunchy, salty-sour snack. They bring **fibre and plant protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Pat the chickpeas very dry on a towel.
Toss them with the oil, chili powder and iodized salt on a tray and roast, shaking once, until crisp, about 25 minutes.
Squeeze over the lime juice and let them cool for a few minutes to crisp up.
tip: Roast a double batch and keep them in an open jar for 3 days; they soften in a sealed one.
ingredients: rinsed, drained and patted very dry

name: Pear and walnuts
about: A ripe pear with a handful of walnuts. Sweet, juicy and crunchy. **Fibre, plus plant omega-3 fat** from the walnuts.
steps: Wash the pear and slice it.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Banana with peanut butter
about: A ripe banana with a spoonful of peanut butter. Sweet, creamy and filling. **Potassium and vitamin E** in one snack.
steps: Peel and slice the banana.
Serve with the peanut butter for dipping.

name: Warm edamame with lime and chili
about: Warm edamame with lime and a pinch of chili. A salty, tangy snack that brings **plant protein, folate and iron**.
steps: Pour hot water over the frozen edamame and leave until steaming hot all the way through, about 3 minutes, then drain.
Toss with the lime juice, chili flakes and iodized salt.

name: Greek yogurt with raspberries
about: Thick Greek yogurt with a handful of raspberries and a pinch of cinnamon. It is cool and tangy and brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Wash the raspberries.
Spoon the yogurt into a cup and top with the raspberries and a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Banana with walnuts and cinnamon
about: A ripe banana with chopped walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. Sweet and warm-spiced. **Potassium and fibre**, with plant omega-3 fat.
steps: Peel and slice the banana.
Top with the chopped walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Apple with peanut butter
about: Crisp apple slices with a spoonful of peanut butter. Crunchy and creamy together. **Fibre, protein and vitamin E**.
steps: Wash and slice the apple.
Serve with the peanut butter for dipping.

name: Apple with walnuts
about: Crisp apple with a handful of walnuts. Crunchy and sweet, with **fibre and plant omega-3 fat** from the walnuts.
steps: Wash the apple and slice it.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Greek yogurt with pear and walnuts
about: Thick Greek yogurt with diced pear, chopped walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. It is creamy and crunchy, with **protein, calcium and plant omega-3 fat**.
steps: Wash the pear and dice it. Chop the walnuts.
Spoon the yogurt into a cup and top with the pear.
Sprinkle over the walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Dan dan-style turkey noodles with green beans, napa cabbage and cucumber
inspiredBy: Inspired by Sichuan dan dan noodles, with peanut butter standing in for sesame paste, a pinch of Sichuan pepper, lean ground turkey, whole-wheat spaghetti and far less oil and chili
about: Chewy whole-wheat noodles and green beans in a savoury, nutty peanut-soy sauce, topped with garlicky ground turkey, napa cabbage and cool cucumber. The turkey brings **protein, iron and zinc**, and the sauce is built on peanut butter rather than oil. It makes two portions.
steps: Wash the green beans, cabbage, cucumber and scallions. Toast the Sichuan peppercorn in a dry pan for 30 seconds and crush it. Whisk it with the peanut butter, soy sauce, vinegar, chili flakes, pepper, half of the garlic and half of the ginger and 2 tablespoons of warm water until smooth, for the sauce.
Boil the noodles in plenty of water for about 8 minutes, adding the green beans for the last 3 minutes. Scoop out a mug of the cooking water, then drain.

While they cook, warm the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Cook the turkey, breaking it up with a spoon, until browned and cooked through to 74 °C (165 °F), about 6 minutes. Add the rest of the garlic and ginger for the last minute, then stir in the napa cabbage for 1 to 2 minutes, until just wilted. Wash your hands, board and spoon after handling the raw turkey.
Toss the hot noodles and green beans with the sauce, loosening it with a splash of the cooking water.
Divide between two bowls and top with the turkey, cabbage and scallions. Put half of the cucumber on the bowl you are eating now and keep the rest in the fridge for the second portion.

Pack the second portion, without the cucumber, into a shallow container within 1 hour, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat it until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and add the saved cucumber on top.
tip: Use less chili for a mild bowl, or add a spoonful of chili crisp at the table.
ingredients: washed and trimmed, cut in thirds
washed and sliced into thin matchsticks

name: Pho-style beef noodle soup with napa cabbage and a plate of herbs
inspiredBy: Inspired by Vietnamese pho, with a quick chicken-stock broth and whole-wheat spaghetti instead of rice noodles
about: A fragrant quick chicken-stock broth spiced with star anise and cinnamon and built on charred onion and ginger, with tender slices of lean beef and napa cabbage, and mint, cilantro, scallion and lime to pile on. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the broth is made with low-sodium stock so you can season it to taste. It makes two portions and is the one slow dish of the week.
steps: Wash the cabbage, scallion and herbs. Put the beef in the freezer for 20 minutes so it is firm, then slice it as thinly as you can across the grain. Keep it covered in the fridge until you need it.

Char the onion and the ginger: set them cut side down in a dry pot over high heat until blackened in spots, about 6 minutes. Add the star anise, cinnamon, clove and coriander seed and toast for 30 seconds.

Pour in the broth and about the same amount of water. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered, for 30 minutes. Strain out the solids, return the broth to the pot and season it with the soy sauce.
Meanwhile, boil the noodles in a separate pot for about 8 minutes until tender, then drain.

Bring the broth to a rolling simmer. Add the cabbage and cook for 2 minutes, then add the beef and cook until no pink remains and it reaches 71 °C (160 °F), about 2 minutes. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw beef.
Divide the noodles between two bowls, ladle the soup over, and pass the scallion, mint, cilantro, lime juice and chili flakes at the table.

Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: cool the soup and the noodles separately in shallow containers within 1 hour, then refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat the soup until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), pour it over the noodles and add the fresh herbs.
tip: Use thin spaghetti or capellini for a lighter bowl; brown rice vermicelli works the same way if you find it. In a rush? Simmer the broth for 15 minutes with ground ginger and cinnamon and skip straining.
ingredients: sirloin, sliced very thinly across the grain
washed and cut in wide strips

name: Ginger chicken noodle soup with egg ribbons, edamame and greens
inspiredBy: Inspired by classic chicken noodle soup and Chinese ginger-scallion chicken soups, with whole-wheat spaghetti
about: A clear, fragrant chicken soup with lots of ginger, carrot, napa cabbage and spinach, plus edamame, firm egg ribbons and whole-wheat noodles to make it a meal. It is made with low-sodium broth, so it is **comforting without being very salty**, and the chicken and egg bring protein and choline. It makes two portions.
steps: Wash the carrot, napa cabbage, spinach and scallions. Slice the carrot into thin coins, the cabbage into ribbons, the ginger into matchsticks and mince the garlic. Keep the scallion whites and greens apart.
Warm the sesame oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the ginger, garlic, scallion whites and carrot for 4 minutes, until fragrant and starting to soften.

Add the chicken, the broth, the soy sauce and enough water to cover everything. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook until the chicken is cooked through and reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece, about 12 minutes. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw chicken.
Meanwhile, boil the noodles in a separate pot of water until tender, about 8 minutes, then drain. Cooking them apart keeps the broth clear and the noodles from going soft in the leftovers.

Stir the frozen edamame into the soup and simmer until steaming hot all the way through, about 3 minutes. Stir in the cabbage and spinach for 1 to 2 minutes, until wilted. Slowly pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream while stirring the soup gently, and simmer for 2 more minutes, until the egg is completely set in firm ribbons. Season with the lime juice and the iodized salt.
Divide the noodles between two bowls, ladle the soup over, and top with the scallion greens.

Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: cool the soup, which has the egg in it, and the noodles separately in shallow containers within 1 hour, then refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat the soup until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and pour it over the noodles.
tip: Add a squeeze of fresh lime and a few chili flakes at the table for heat.
ingredients: washed and sliced into thin coins

name: Chickpea soba salad with cucumber, spinach, mint and lime-ginger dressing
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese cold soba (zaru soba) with a bright lime-ginger dressing and chickpeas for protein
about: Nutty buckwheat soba with chickpeas, cucumber and carrot, baby spinach, fresh mint and cilantro, and a sharp lime-ginger dressing with walnuts on top. The chickpeas, edamame and soba bring **plant protein, fibre and magnesium** in a lunch that packs well.

Boil the soba in plenty of water until just tender, 4 to 5 minutes, then drain and rinse well under cold water.
Pour hot water over the frozen edamame in a bowl until steaming hot all the way through, then drain and cool under cold water.
Whisk the lime juice, vinegar, soy sauce, sesame oil and ginger with a spoonful of water for the dressing.

tip: Packing it? Keep the dressing apart and toss it in just before you eat. Cool the soba within 1 hour, keep it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.

name: Ginger-pear oatmeal with walnuts
about: Creamy oats simmered with a little milk, fresh ginger and cinnamon, topped with chopped pear and toasted walnuts. The oats bring **slow-digesting fibre** and the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fat and crunch.
steps: Wash the pear and chop it into small pieces. Grate the ginger finely.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes, then chop them.

Stir the oats, milk, a splash of water, the ginger, cinnamon and iodized salt together in a small pot. Bring it to a gentle bubble and cook, stirring, until creamy, about 5 minutes. Add a splash more water if it gets too thick.
Stir half of the pear into the oatmeal for the last minute so it softens. Spoon into a bowl and top with the rest of the pear and the walnuts.
tip: Make it the night before: soak the oats in the milk in the fridge, eat within 2 days, and warm it in the morning.

name: Greek yogurt with pear and walnuts
about: Thick Greek yogurt with diced pear, chopped walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. It is creamy and crunchy, with **protein, calcium and plant omega-3 fat**.
steps: Wash the pear and dice it. Chop the walnuts.
Spoon the yogurt into a cup and top with the pear.
Sprinkle over the walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Seared salmon soba with mushrooms, spinach and ginger-soy sauce
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese soba with grilled fish, made with a simple soy-ginger-lime sauce
about: Nutty buckwheat soba tossed with browned mushrooms, wilted spinach and edamame, topped with a seared salmon fillet and a bright ginger-soy sauce. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and some vitamin D**, and the edamame and spinach bring folate and iron.
steps: Buy the salmon the day you cook it, or thaw frozen salmon overnight in the fridge. Wash the spinach, mushrooms and scallion. Whisk the soy sauce, vinegar, lime juice, ginger and half of the sesame oil with a spoonful of water for the sauce.
Boil the soba in plenty of water until just tender, 4 to 5 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water so it does not clump.

Pat the salmon dry. Warm the canola oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat and sear the salmon skin side down for 4 minutes, then flip and cook for 3 to 4 minutes more, until it reaches 70 °C (158 °F) in the thickest part and flakes easily. Move it to a clean plate, and wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw fish.
In the same pan, cook the mushrooms and garlic for 4 minutes, until golden. Add the spinach and cook until wilted, about 1 minute.
Pour hot water over the frozen edamame in a bowl until steaming hot all the way through, then drain.

Toss the soba with the mushrooms, spinach, edamame, the rest of the sesame oil and half of the sauce. Pile it into a bowl, set the salmon on top, and finish with the rest of the sauce, and the scallion.
tip: Check the soba label: 100% buckwheat is wheat-free, but many packs are part wheat.
ingredients: skin-on or skinless fillet, pin bones removed

name: Raspberry yogurt bowl with toasted oats and almonds
about: Thick Greek yogurt with tart raspberries, toasted oats and almonds for crunch. It is a quick breakfast with **protein, calcium and vitamin E** to carry you to lunch.
steps: Toast the oats and the almonds together in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until golden and nutty, about 3 minutes. Tip them out to cool.
Wash the raspberries. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl.
Top with the raspberries, the toasted oats and almonds, and a pinch of cinnamon.
tip: Toast a few days of oats and almonds at once and keep them in a jar for up to a week.

name: Ginger chicken soba soup with egg ribbons, edamame and greens
inspiredBy: Inspired by classic chicken noodle soup and Chinese ginger-scallion chicken soups, with soba
about: A clear, fragrant chicken soup with lots of ginger, carrot, napa cabbage and spinach, plus edamame, firm egg ribbons and soba noodles to make it a meal. It is made with low-sodium broth, so it is **comforting without being very salty**, and the chicken and egg bring protein and choline. It makes two portions.

Stir the frozen edamame into the soup and simmer until steaming hot all the way through, about 3 minutes. Stir in the cabbage and spinach for 1 to 2 minutes, until wilted. Slowly pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream while stirring the soup gently, and simmer for 2 more minutes, until the egg is completely set in firm ribbons. Season with the lime juice and the iodized salt.
Divide the soba between two bowls, ladle the soup over, and top with the scallion greens.

Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: cool the soup, which has the egg in it, and the noodles separately in shallow containers within 1 hour, then refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat the soup until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and pour it over the noodles.
tip: Add a squeeze of fresh lime and a few chili flakes at the table for heat.
ingredients: washed and sliced into thin coins

name: Japchae-style tofu and soba noodles with spinach, carrot and mushrooms
inspiredBy: Inspired by Korean japchae, made with soba noodles in place of sweet potato starch noodles, with tofu for protein
about: Silky-chewy noodles tossed with golden tofu, firm egg ribbons, mushrooms, carrot, red pepper and garlicky spinach in a sesame-soy glaze. The calcium-set tofu and egg bring **protein, choline and some calcium** and the vegetables bring vitamin A, and it eats well warm or cold, so it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Wash the spinach, carrot and red pepper. Wrap the tofu in a clean towel and press it for 10 minutes, then cut it into cubes. Slice the vegetables into thin, even strips.

Boil the soba until tender, 4 to 5 minutes, dropping the spinach into the pot for the last 30 seconds. Scoop the spinach out with tongs, squeeze it dry and toss it with a third of the garlic, a little of the sesame oil and a pinch of pepper.
Drain the soba and rinse it under cold water.

Beat the eggs and cook them as a thin flat omelette in a little of the canola oil in the nonstick pan, until completely firm all the way through, about 3 minutes a side, then slice it into ribbons. Wipe the pan, warm the rest of the canola oil over medium-high heat and brown the tofu on all sides, about 6 minutes, and move it to a plate. Cook the onion, carrot, pepper and mushrooms in the same pan for 4 to 5 minutes, until just tender, adding the rest of the garlic at the end.
Add the noodles, the soy sauce and the rest of the sesame oil to the pan and toss for 2 minutes, until glossy and hot. Fold in the tofu, the spinach and the egg ribbons.
Serve in bowls sprinkled with the chopped walnuts.
Pack the second portion into a shallow container within 1 hour, refrigerate and eat within 3 days, cold or reheated until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F).
tip: Short on time? Skip pressing the tofu and use a bag of mixed stir-fry vegetables.

name: Peanut-lime soba bowl with edamame, cabbage and carrot
inspiredBy: Inspired by Thai-style peanut noodles, with soba, a lime-forward sauce and lots of crunchy raw vegetables
about: Cool soba noodles tossed with a lime-peanut sauce, edamame, napa cabbage, carrot and red pepper. The edamame and peanut butter bring **plant protein and vitamin E**, and the raw vegetables give it crunch and vitamin C.
steps: Wash the cabbage, carrot, red pepper, scallion and cilantro. Shred, grate and slice them.
Boil the soba until tender, 4 to 5 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water until cool.
Pour hot water over the frozen edamame in a bowl until steaming hot all the way through, then drain and cool under cold water.
Whisk the peanut butter, lime juice, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, ginger and chili flakes with 2 tablespoons of warm water until smooth and pourable.
Toss the noodles, edamame and vegetables with the sauce. Top with the scallion and cilantro.
tip: Packing it? Keep the sauce in a small jar and toss just before you eat. Cool the noodles within 1 hour, keep it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.

name: Oat and rye porridge with lingonberry jam and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Swedish havregrynsgröt and Finnish ruisputro, with rye flakes half and half with oats and lingonberries on top
about: Creamy porridge of oats and rye flakes cooked in milk, with a cool spoonful of skyr, tart lingonberry jam and chopped hazelnuts on top. The oats, rye and hazelnuts bring **steady-release fibre, magnesium and vitamin E**, and the skyr adds protein.
steps: Put the oats, the rye flakes, the milk and the salt in a small pot over medium heat. Stir often until it bubbles gently and turns thick and creamy, about 8 minutes. Add a splash of water only if it thickens too fast.
While it cooks, toast the hazelnuts in a small dry pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, then chop them roughly.
Spoon the porridge into a bowl and top with the skyr, the lingonberry jam and a pinch of cinnamon. Scatter with the hazelnuts.
tip: Lingonberry jam is tart on purpose, a bit like cranberry sauce with more perfume. If you can't find it, a spoon of cranberry sauce or frozen blueberries works. No rye flakes? Use all oats.
ingredients: the kind that is mostly berries

name: Skyr with blueberries, toasted oats and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Icelandic skyr with berries, with toasted oats and hazelnuts for crunch
about: Thick, cool skyr with juicy blueberries and a crunchy mix of toasted oats and hazelnuts. It is an Icelandic way of eating skyr, and it is **ready in under ten minutes**. The skyr brings plenty of protein and calcium, and the hazelnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the oats in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they smell nutty and look a shade darker, about 4 minutes. Add the hazelnuts for the last minute so they warm through.
Tip both onto a plate to cool for a minute, then roughly chop the hazelnuts.
Spoon the skyr into a bowl and tumble the blueberries over it. Scatter on the oats and hazelnuts. The berries are usually sweet enough.
tip: Toast a whole jar of oats and hazelnuts on Sunday and it keeps all week. Loosen the skyr with a splash of milk, as Icelanders do, which matters most in a big bowl. Frozen blueberries work well too, just thaw them first.

name: Open-faced rye with egg, shrimp and dill
inspiredBy: Danish smørrebrød with egg and shrimp, with skyr standing in for the mayonnaise
about: Dark rye bread with butter, radishes, sliced egg and a pile of little shrimp, with a lemony skyr and dill spoonful on top. It is a Danish smørrebrød, and a breakfast to eat slowly. The shrimp and egg bring **protein, choline and iodine**, and the rye brings fibre.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes, until the white and yolk are both firm. Cool it under cold water, then peel and slice it.
Stir the skyr with the lemon juice, half the dill, finely chopped, and a pinch of white pepper until it is smooth and loose enough to spoon.
Butter the rye all the way to the edges. Layer on thin slices of radish, then the egg.
Spoon over the skyr, pile on the shrimp and finish with the rest of the dill. Eat it with a knife and fork, like they do in Denmark.
tip: Boil the egg the night before and this takes five minutes on a weekday morning. Dense rye is closest to Danish rugbrød, so look for German-style whole rye or pumpernickel in the bakery or packaged aisle.

name: Pickled herring on rye with egg, beets and dill
inspiredBy: Swedish sillmacka and Danish sild på rugbrød
about: Buttered dark rye topped with sweet-sour pickled herring, ruby beets, sliced egg, thin onion and a generous spoon of skyr and dill. It is a classic Nordic lunch plate that needs **almost no cooking**. The herring brings omega-3 and vitamin D, the egg adds choline, and the beets and rye bring fibre.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water and cook for 10 minutes, until the white and yolk are both firm. Cool it under cold water, then peel and slice it.
Drain the herring and pat it dry. If the pieces are large, cut them into bite-size strips.
Slice the onion as thin as you can and let it sit in cold water for 5 minutes to take the edge off, then drain. Stir the skyr with half the dill, finely chopped, and a pinch of white pepper.
Butter the rye all the way to the edges. Lay on the beets and the egg, then the herring.
Spoon the skyr over, top with the onion and the rest of the dill, and eat it with a knife and fork.
tip: Boil an egg or two on Sunday night and this is a five-minute lunch. Pickled herring is salty, so a quick rinse before you pat it dry takes the edge off. Look for the plain or mustard kinds in the fridge section. Dense rye is closest to Danish rugbrød, so look for German-style whole rye or pumpernickel in the bakery or packaged aisle.

name: Pytt i panna with roast beef, a fried egg and pickled beets
about: Crisp little cubes of potato and mushroom fried with onion and tender roast beef, with a fried egg on top, pickled beets on the side and a spoon of mustard. It is the Swedish "bits in a pan" supper, and a fine use of a Saturday lunch hour. The egg and beef bring protein, iron and choline, and UV-exposed mushrooms add **a good dose of vitamin D**.
steps: Boil the potato cubes in a pot of water for 5 minutes, until they are just tender at the edges. Drain well and let them steam dry for a couple of minutes, which is what makes them crisp.
Warm most of the oil in a big non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the potatoes and fry, turning only now and then, until golden and crisp at the edges, about 12 minutes.

Add the mushrooms, the onion and the roast beef and cook until the water from the mushrooms has cooked off, the onion is soft and the beef has a few browned edges, about 6 minutes. Season with the pepper and a tiny pinch of salt, since deli beef is already salty.
Push everything to one side, add the rest of the oil and fry the egg until the white is set, then flip it and cook another minute so the yolk is firm.
Slide the hash onto a plate with the egg on top. Serve with the pickled beets, a spoonful of mustard and a scatter of parsley.
tip: This is a great way to use up leftover boiled potatoes. Skip the boiling step and go straight to the pan.
ingredients: vitamin D mushrooms if you can find them, cut in small cubes
leftover roast or deli roast beef, cut in small cubes

name: Swedish-style meatballs with potatoes, creamed spinach and lingonberries
inspiredBy: Swedish köttbullar with stuvad spenat, made lean with oats soaked in milk and a light gravy
about: Small, tender meatballs with allspice and onion, a light creamy gravy, boiled potatoes, soft creamed spinach, a spoon of lingonberry jam and crisp cucumber. It makes two portions, so **tomorrow's lunch is done**. The beef brings iron, zinc and B12, and the spinach brings folate and vitamin K.
steps: Stir the oats into a little of the milk, about a third of it, and leave them for 10 minutes to swell. Meanwhile, put the potatoes on to boil in lightly salted water, about 20 minutes.
Grate the onion into a bowl. Add the beef, the soaked oats, the allspice, white pepper, a little nutmeg and most of the salt. Mix with a fork until just combined, since overworking makes them tough.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into small balls, about the size of a walnut. Chill them for 10 minutes if you have time, so they hold their shape.
Warm the oil in a large non-stick skillet over medium heat. Brown the meatballs in batches, shaking the pan to roll them, until golden all over and cooked through, about 8 minutes. Lift them out.

Mash one hot boiled potato chunk into most of the remaining milk with a splash of the potato water until smooth. Leave the empty pan on the heat for a moment so the bits on the bottom turn a shade darker, then pour in the milk slowly, scraping them up so the gravy takes their colour. Simmer for 2 or 3 minutes until it coats a spoon. Season with a pinch of salt and pepper, then slide the meatballs back in.

Wilt the spinach in a dry pot over medium heat, a big handful at a time, until soft. Squeeze out the extra water, chop it, then stir in a spoon of that gravy, a pinch of nutmeg and a pinch of salt and warm through. Dress the sliced cucumber with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt.

Toss the potatoes with the chopped parsley. Serve the meatballs and gravy with the potatoes, spinach, a spoon of lingonberry jam and the cucumber. Pack the second portion, with its gravy, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The meatballs freeze beautifully. Cook a double batch of just the meatballs and pull a few out on a busy night. Reheat them gently in the gravy with a splash of water.
ingredients: a third for soaking the oats, the rest for the gravy and the spinach

name: Norwegian-style lapskaus with beef, rutabaga, barley and kale
inspiredBy: Norwegian lapskaus and Swedish kalops, with pearl barley and kale added
about: A thick, comforting stew of lean beef, rutabaga, carrot and potato with allspice and bay, pearl barley for chew and kale stirred in at the end. Pickled beets and a little mustard bring the acid. It makes two portions, and the **kale and carrot bring vitamins A and K** while the beef brings iron and zinc.
steps: Pat the beef dry. Warm half the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef in two batches until deeply golden, about 5 minutes per batch. Lift it out.
Lower the heat, add the rest of the oil and the chopped onion and cook until soft and sweet, about 5 minutes. Stir in the allspice and thyme for a minute.

Return the beef to the pot with the barley, the bay leaves and the salt. Add enough water to cover everything by about 2 cm, bring to a boil, then turn the heat down and simmer gently, partly covered, for 40 minutes.

Add the rutabaga, carrot and potato in 2 cm cubes. Simmer for another 20 to 25 minutes, until everything is tender and the stew has thickened, since the edges of the potato melt into it. Top up with water if the barley has drunk it all.
Stir in the kale and cook for 5 minutes, until bright green and soft. Take out the bay leaves, stir in the mustard and most of the parsley, and taste for salt.

Serve with the pickled beets alongside and the rest of the parsley scattered over. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The barley drinks up liquid overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A pressure cooker makes this a 40-minute dinner: brown the beef, then cook everything but the kale for 25 minutes. It also holds well in a slow cooker while you're out.

name: Lohikeitto, Finnish salmon and potato soup, with rye bread
inspiredBy: Finnish lohikeitto, made with milk in place of the cream
about: Chunks of salmon poached in a creamy, dill-flecked soup of potato and leek, with allspice and a squeeze of lemon, and buttered dark rye on the side. It is the soup Finns make on a cold night, and it makes two portions. The salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the potato and leek bring potassium.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the leek, stirring, until it is glossy and soft but not browned, about 5 minutes.
Add the potato in 2 cm cubes, the allspice, the bay leaves and the salt, with enough water to just cover. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 12 to 15 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Cut the salmon into 3 cm chunks. Turn the heat to low, slip them in and poach gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until just opaque. Don't stir hard, or they'll break up.
Stir in the milk and warm it through without letting it boil. Add the dill, the lemon juice and the white pepper, and fish out the bay leaves.
Serve in wide bowls with the rye and a little butter. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and reheat it gently so the salmon stays tender.
tip: A spoonful of crème fraîche on top is lovely if you have some. If you like it thicker, mash a few potato cubes against the side of the pot.
