about: Garlicky, spiced chicken köfte shaped on skewers and cooked until browned, with a nutty bulgur pilav and a crunchy shepherd's salad of tomato, cucumber and pepper. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is already cooked. The chicken and bulgur bring **protein, niacin and fibre**, and the salad brings vitamin C.
steps: Cut the chicken into small cubes and pulse in a food processor in short bursts until finely ground and sticky, or ask the butcher to grind it. Squeeze the grated onion lightly, leaving it moist.

Mix the chicken with the onion, garlic, parsley, pepper paste, Aleppo pepper, cumin, sumac, black pepper and half the salt. Knead for 2 minutes, until sticky. Chill for at least 20 minutes, or up to a day.

For the pilav, warm a third of the oil in a small pot and toast the bulgur for 1 minute. Add the rest of the salt and 1.5 times its volume in hot water. Cover and simmer gently for 12 minutes, then leave it off the heat, covered, for 10 minutes. Make enough for both portions.
With wet hands, mould the chicken around skewers or into long fingers about 2 cm thick. Heat half the remaining oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat, or heat the broiler.
Cook the köfte, turning now and then, until browned all over and cooked through with no pink in the middle, 8 to 10 minutes.
For the çoban salatası, chop the tomato, cucumber, green pepper and red onion into small, even pieces. Toss with the rest of the oil, the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a little chopped parsley.
Serve the köfte on the pilav with the salad. Pack the second portion of köfte and pilav for tomorrow, and chop the salad fresh then.
tip: Warm the leftover köfte and pilav in a pan with a splash of water. A spoonful of yogurt on the side is lovely if you have it.
ingredients: finely chopped, some for the salad

name: Cornmeal and hazelnut sardines with Black Sea kale and lemon potatoes
inspiredBy: Black Sea hamsi tava, fried fresh anchovies in cornmeal, made with sardines or fresh anchovies, a little of the region's hazelnut and karalahana (Black Sea kale)
about: Fresh sardines rolled in cornmeal and a little ground hazelnut, then pan-fried until golden and crisp, the way people on the Black Sea coast fry their anchovies, with garlicky kale and parsley-lemon potatoes. It is quick and punchy. The sardines bring **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the kale and hazelnuts bring calcium and vitamin E.
steps: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water, bring to a boil and cook until just tender, about 12 to 15 minutes. Drain, then toss with half the lemon juice and the parsley.

While they cook, warm a third of the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and soften the onion for 5 minutes. Add the garlic and Aleppo pepper for 30 seconds, then the kale with a splash of water. Cover and cook until the kale is tender and bright, 8 to 10 minutes. Season with salt.
Pat the sardines very dry with paper towels and season with salt and pepper. Mix the cornmeal with the ground hazelnuts on a plate, roll the sardines in it and pat off the excess.

Warm the rest of the oil in a large non-stick pan over medium heat. Fry the sardines for 3 minutes a side, keeping the heat at medium because the ground hazelnut scorches, until the coating is golden and crisp and the flesh flakes.
Serve the sardines on the kale with the potatoes beside them and the rest of the lemon squeezed over everything.
tip: Fresh sardines are scarce. Whole frozen ones, thawed and patted dry, work. Ask the fishmonger to scale and gut them. They are small, so you will want 5 or 6.
ingredients: fresh, cleaned and gutted, heads off. Fresh anchovies work too
leaves stripped from the stems, sliced

name: Etli kuru fasulye, Turkish white bean stew with beef, kale and bulgur pilav
inspiredBy: Turkish etli kuru fasulye, with some Black Sea karalahana kale stirred in
about: Turkey's favourite home stew: tender white beans in a thick, savoury red pepper sauce with Aleppo pepper, a little beef and a handful of kale, served with bulgur pilav and a sumac onion salad on the side. It makes two portions, and it is even better the next day. The beans and kale bring **fibre, folate, iron and calcium**.
steps: Soak the beans in plenty of water overnight, or cover them with boiling water for 1 hour if you forgot. Drain them.

Warm half the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and brown the beef for 5 minutes. Add the onion and carrot and cook until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, pepper paste and Aleppo pepper and stir for 2 minutes, until it darkens.

Add the beans with enough hot water to cover them by 3 cm, about 3 cups for two portions. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for about 1 hour, until the beans are creamy and the beef is tender. Add the salt and pepper when the beans are nearly done.
Stir in the kale for the last 10 minutes and let the sauce reduce until thick.

For the pilav, warm the rest of the oil in a small pot, toast the bulgur for 1 minute, then add 1.5 times its volume in hot water and a pinch of salt. Cover and cook gently for 12 minutes, then leave it covered for 10 minutes. Make enough for both portions.
Toss the red onion with the sumac, the lemon juice and half the parsley and squeeze it with your fingers to soften. Serve the beans over the pilav with the onion salad and the rest of the parsley.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: Short on time? In a pressure cooker, the soaked beans take about 25 minutes. Two 400 g tins of white beans work too, simmered for just 25 minutes. For a vegetarian version, leave out the beef.
ingredients: leaves stripped from the stems, sliced

name: Saffron salmon with sabzi polo style herb rice and grilled tomatoes
inspiredBy: Persian sabzi polo ba mahi, the Nowruz herb rice with fish, made with brown basmati and a baked salmon fillet
about: A saffron and lemon salmon fillet, baked until just flaky, on a bed of brown basmati rice steamed through with a mountain of parsley, dill, cilantro and scallion. Grilled tomatoes alongside, as in a Persian kebab house. The salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the herb rice is a big hit of vitamin K.
steps: Rinse the rice and simmer it in plenty of salted boiling water for 25 minutes, like pasta. Drain it, return it to the pot, cover with a tea towel under the lid and leave it for 10 minutes to steam. If you have time, soak the rinsed rice for 30 minutes first.

Mash the garlic with a little of the salt. Mix it with the steeped saffron and its water, half the lemon juice, the turmeric, pepper and a teaspoon of the oil. Coat the salmon and leave it for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 220 C. Put the salmon skin-side down on a tray with the halved tomatoes, cut-sides up. Drizzle the tomatoes with a little oil and a pinch of salt. Roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the salmon flakes and the tomato edges are charred.

Warm the rest of the oil in a small pan, stir in the fenugreek for 20 seconds, and fold it through the hot rice with the parsley, dill, cilantro and scallion and a pinch of salt. Return the rice to the pot, cover with the towel lid and steam on the lowest heat for 5 minutes, so the herbs wilt into the rice and it turns bright green.
Serve the salmon on the herb rice with the tomatoes and the rest of the lemon.
tip: Cook extra brown basmati the tea-towel way and keep it for 4 to 5 days in the fridge, or freeze it in portions.
ingredients: ground and steeped in 1 tbsp hot water

name: Fesenjan-inspired chicken with walnut and pomegranate, with brown basmati
inspiredBy: Persian fesenjan from Gilan, with a lighter hand with the walnuts and a brown basmati base
about: Chicken thighs slowly simmered in a rich, dark sauce of ground toasted walnuts and sweet-sour pomegranate molasses, with turmeric and cinnamon, and finished with fresh pomegranate seeds. It is the Persian celebration stew, and it is even better the next day. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3, magnesium and copper**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 4 minutes, until they smell nutty. Cool them, then grind to a coarse, damp-sand texture in a food processor, in short pulses so they do not turn to paste.
Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the turmeric, add the chicken and turn it for 3 minutes, until it just loses its pink.

Stir in the ground walnuts, the cinnamon, salt, pepper and just enough water to cover the chicken. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover with the lid slightly ajar, and cook for 40 minutes, stirring often so it does not catch. The sauce will darken and thicken.

Stir in the pomegranate molasses and the saffron water, and simmer for 20 minutes more, until the oil from the walnuts rises to the top and the chicken is very tender. Taste: it should be sour first, then sweet. Add a little more water if it has thickened too far.

For the rice, rinse the brown basmati and simmer it in plenty of salted boiling water for 25 minutes, then drain. Return it to the pot, wrap the lid in a tea towel and let it steam for 10 minutes. Make enough for both portions.
Serve the chicken over the rice, scattered with the pomegranate seeds. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Warm it gently with a splash of water, because the sauce thickens overnight.
tip: Like most Persian stews it is even better made a day ahead. Pomegranate molasses varies by brand, so taste first. If it is too sharp, a small spoon of pekmez rounds it out.
ingredients: boneless, skinless thighs, cut in 4 cm pieces
ground and steeped in 1 tbsp hot water

name: Grilled mackerel (uskumru) with tahini sauce, sumac onions and arugula
inspiredBy: Turkish grilled mackerel, with a Hatay-style tahini tarator
about: A fat, oily mackerel fillet seared until the skin is crisp, then served the Turkish coastal way, with sumac onions, peppery arugula, tomato and warm lavash to tuck it into, plus a lemony tahini sauce borrowed from Hatay and the Levant. It takes 20 minutes. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the tahini and arugula add calcium.
steps: Toss the sliced red onion with the sumac, half the parsley, a pinch of salt and a third of the lemon juice. Squeeze it with your fingers until it softens and turns pink. Leave it while you cook.
Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and whisk it with the tahini, half the remaining lemon juice and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water, until pale and pourable like thin cream.
Pat the mackerel dry and season both sides with salt, pepper and the Aleppo pepper. Rub the skin with a little of the oil.
Heat a heavy pan or the broiler on high. Cook the fillets skin-side down for 4 minutes without moving them, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes, until just cooked through.
Dress the arugula and sliced tomato with the rest of the lemon juice, the rest of the oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the mackerel on the sumac onions with the salad, a spoonful of the tahini sauce and the rest of the parsley, and the warm lavash alongside. Tuck some into a piece of bread if you like.
tip: Mackerel is strongly flavoured, so do not skip the lemon and the sumac onions. If you cannot find fresh mackerel, use sardines or trout.

name: Medjool dates stuffed with walnuts and hazelnuts
about: Soft dates stuffed with walnut halves and a hazelnut, the sweet nibble Persian and Turkish families serve with tea. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and magnesium**, the hazelnuts bring vitamin E, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Slit the dates open, take out the pits and press a walnut half and a hazelnut or two into each date. Serve with a cup of tea.

name: Ayran with cucumber sticks
about: The salty, frothy Turkish yogurt drink, with dried mint and cucumber sticks on the side. It is **calcium and protein** in a glass.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with 130 ml of cold water, the salt and the dried mint until frothy, and serve over ice if you like.
Eat the cucumber sticks alongside.

name: A Medjool date stuffed with walnut and hazelnut
about: One soft date stuffed with a walnut half and a hazelnut, the small sweet bite that goes with a cup of tea. The walnut brings **plant omega-3**, the hazelnut brings vitamin E, and the date brings potassium.
steps: Slit the date open, take out the pit and press a walnut half and a hazelnut or two into it. Serve with a cup of tea.

name: Mast-o-khiar, cucumber yogurt with dill and mint
inspiredBy: Persian mast-o-khiar, with a little lavash to scoop
about: Cool, thick yogurt with grated cucumber, fresh dill and mint, with torn lavash for scooping. It is the Iranian answer to a hot afternoon. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the cucumber keeps it light.
steps: Squeeze the grated cucumber lightly. Stir it into the yogurt with the dill, mint and salt, and loosen with a spoonful of cold water.
Serve in a bowl with the torn lavash for scooping.

name: Yogurt with pekmez and dried figs
inspiredBy: Pekmezli yoğurt, the Turkish afternoon bowl, with Aegean dried figs
about: Thick yogurt with a drizzle of dark grape molasses (pekmez) and chopped dried figs, a simple Turkish afternoon treat. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the figs add fibre.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, drizzle with the pekmez and scatter over the chopped figs.

name: Roasted chickpeas, leblebi style
inspiredBy: Turkish leblebi, the roasted chickpeas sold at every market, made from tinned chickpeas in the oven
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas with cumin, Aleppo pepper and lemon, in the style of the leblebi sold at Turkish nut shops. They bring **plant protein, fibre and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Pat the chickpeas very dry and toss with the oil, cumin, Aleppo pepper and salt on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crunchy. Squeeze over the lemon while they are hot. They crisp further as they cool.
tip: Roast a fresh tray on the day. They lose their crunch after 3 days in a jar.

name: Dried figs with hazelnuts
about: Aegean dried figs with hazelnuts from the Black Sea coast, a sweet and nutty Turkish tea-time plate. The hazelnuts bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the figs bring fibre and a little calcium.
steps: Serve the figs and hazelnuts together on a small plate. Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes first if you like.

name: Orange slices with cinnamon
about: Sliced orange with a pinch of cinnamon, a Persian-style fruit plate. The orange brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the orange and slice it into rounds. Sprinkle with the cinnamon and chill for 10 minutes if you have time.

name: Tahini and pekmez on warm lavash
inspiredBy: Turkish tahin-pekmez, tahini swirled with grape molasses
about: A thick swirl of tahini and pekmez (grape molasses) on warm whole-wheat lavash, a very Turkish sweet snack. The tahini brings **calcium, copper and healthy fats**.
steps: Warm the lavash. Spread the tahini over it, then drizzle with the pekmez and swirl them together with a knife. Fold and eat.

name: Dried figs with walnuts and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Turkish incir ve ceviz, the classic pairing, with a few Black Sea hazelnuts
about: Chewy dried figs with walnut halves and a few hazelnuts, a classic Turkish and Persian pairing. The figs bring **fibre and a little calcium**, the walnuts bring plant omega-3, and the hazelnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Tuck a walnut half into each fig, or serve them side by side on a plate with the hazelnuts.

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the pomegranate and walnut pairing of fesenjan, as a snack
about: Ruby pomegranate seeds with a handful of walnut halves, the sweet-tart and rich pairing that Persian cooks love. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and magnesium**, and the pomegranate brings vitamin C.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a bowl and eat them with the walnut halves, a spoonful of each at a time.

name: Orange with toasted hazelnuts
about: Mediterranean oranges with toasted Black Sea hazelnuts, a simple Turkish pairing. The hazelnuts bring **vitamin E and magnesium** and the orange brings vitamin C.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until fragrant. Peel and slice the orange and eat it with the nuts.

name: Overnight oats with Greek yogurt, figs and almonds
inspiredBy: Greek yogurt with dried fruit and nuts, turned into make-ahead oats
about:
Rolled oats soaked overnight in thick Greek yogurt with chopped dried figs and a pinch of cinnamon, finished with chopped almonds. It is **ready when you wake up**, creamy and a little sweet, with a crunch on top.

The oats bring fibre, the yogurt brings calcium and protein, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: The night before, stir the oats, yogurt, chopped figs and cinnamon together in a jar with a splash of milk or water. It should look a little too loose, since the oats will drink it up.
Cover and chill overnight, and eat within 2 days. The figs soften and sweeten the oats as they sit.
In the morning, give it a good stir. It should be thick and spoonable. A splash more milk or water loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Scatter the chopped almonds on top just before eating, so they stay crunchy.
tip: Mix two jars at a time to save effort; they keep up to 2 days in the fridge. A chopped orange works in place of the figs in season.

name: Baked eggs in tomato and pepper with toast
inspiredBy: Spanish huevos a la flamenca, with a smoky paprika base
about: Eggs set in a bubbling sofrito of sweet pepper, onion, tomato and a handful of spinach, and a good dose of smoky paprika. Eat it with toast to mop up the sauce. It is a **proper hot breakfast**, rich in eggs for choline, with vitamin C from the pepper and tomato.
steps: Rinse the pepper, then dice it. Warm the olive oil in a small non-stick frying pan over medium heat and cook the onion and pepper with a pinch of the salt until soft, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and smoked paprika and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant. The paprika blooms in the hot oil, so don't let it scorch.
Tip in the tomatoes, breaking them up with a spoon. Simmer until the sauce is thick and jammy, about 8 minutes, then stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Make two wells in the sauce and crack in the eggs. Cover and cook over low heat until the whites are set and the yolks are firm, about 7 minutes.
Scatter with parsley and serve with the toast. Wash your hands after cracking the eggs.
tip: A pinch of chili flakes with the paprika gives it a gentle kick.

name: Ricotta toast with apple, walnuts and honey
inspiredBy: Italian ricotta and honey on toast
about: Thick whole-wheat toast spread with creamy ricotta, topped with sliced crisp apple, toasted walnuts and a drizzle of honey. It takes **five minutes** and feels like a treat. Ricotta brings calcium and protein, and the walnuts bring omega-3 and vitamin E.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, then chop them roughly.
Toast the bread until golden and crisp. Spread the ricotta over it right away.
Lay the apple slices on top, scatter with the walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon, and finish with a drizzle of honey.
tip: A ripe pear or a few fresh figs in season work just as well as the apple. Little ones under 4 do better with the walnuts finely chopped. Do not give honey to a child under 1 year.

name: Shrimp saganaki with feta, tomato and crusty bread
inspiredBy: Greek shrimp saganaki, with a little less feta and a cucumber salad on the side
about: Plump shrimp in a quick tomato sauce with garlic, oregano and a hint of chili, topped with a crumble of salty feta and served with whole-wheat bread and a crisp cucumber salad. It's a **quick lunch**, on the table in about 25 minutes. The shrimp bring selenium and iodine and the tomato brings vitamin C.
steps: If the shrimp are frozen, thaw them overnight in the fridge and cook them within 2 days. Rinse them and pat them dry. Keep them in the fridge until the sauce is ready, and wash your hands and the board after handling them.
Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and glossy, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic, oregano and chili for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes, breaking them up with a spoon, with the salt. Simmer until the sauce is thick, about 8 minutes.
Nestle the shrimp into the sauce and cook, turning once, until they are pink, curled and opaque all the way through (74 °C), about 3 to 4 minutes. Don't overcook them, or they turn rubbery.
Take the pan off the heat, crumble the feta over the top and let it soften for a minute. Finish with the parsley and lemon juice.
Serve with the bread for mopping and the cucumber dressed with lemon, a pinch of oregano and a few drops of the olive oil.
tip: If you like it hot, add more chili at the table, not in the pot.

name: Pasta e fagioli with kale and a little anchovy
inspiredBy: Italian pasta e fagioli, with whole-wheat pasta and a melted anchovy in the soffritto
about: A thick, comforting Italian bean and pasta soup built on a soffritto of onion and carrot, with white beans, tomato, rosemary and kale. A single anchovy melts into the oil and adds **deep savoury flavour** without tasting fishy. Beans and kale bring iron and folate, and the tomato and lemon help you absorb it.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and carrot with a pinch of the salt until soft and sweet, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, anchovy, rosemary and bay and stir until the anchovy melts away, about 2 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, until it darkens a shade. Add the tomatoes and break them up with a spoon.
Add the white beans and enough water to cover everything by about 3 cm. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes. Mash a few spoonfuls of the beans against the side of the pot to thicken the broth.

Add the pasta (short tubes like ditalini, or broken spaghetti) and the kale with a little more water if it looks dry. Cook until the pasta is tender, about 10 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't catch. It should be thick enough to hold a spoon upright.
Season with the remaining salt, a squeeze of lemon and plenty of black pepper. Serve in wide bowls with a thread of olive oil.

Pasta is a cooked grain, so cool the second portion in a shallow container and refrigerate within 1 hour. Tomorrow, loosen it with a splash of water, since the pasta drinks the broth, and reheat it to 74 °C.
tip: Leave the anchovy out and add an extra squeeze of lemon for a fish-free version. New to this many beans? Build up over the week and drink plenty of water.

name: Grilled sardines with lemon potatoes and wild greens
inspiredBy: Greek and Portuguese grilled sardines, with horta-style greens
about: Whole sardines grilled until the skin blisters, served with tender lemony potatoes and a pile of olive-oil-dressed spinach, the way you'd eat horta by the sea. Sardines are one of the **best fish sources of omega-3 and vitamin D**, and their soft bones add calcium.
steps: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold water with a pinch of the salt. Bring to a boil and cook until just tender, about 15 minutes. Drain and let the steam escape.
Rinse the sardines and pat them dry. Brush with a little of the olive oil and sprinkle with salt and pepper. Wash your hands, the board and the plate after handling raw fish.
Heat a grill or a cast-iron pan until very hot. Grill the sardines about 3 to 4 minutes a side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh is opaque and flakes at the spine (70 °C inside).
While the fish cooks, boil the spinach in salted water for 2 minutes, until tender. Drain well and dress with olive oil, the garlic and a squeeze of lemon.
Toss the warm potatoes with the oregano, remaining olive oil and most of the lemon juice. Slice the tomato and onion into a quick salad with the parsley.
Serve the sardines with a squeeze of lemon over the top, alongside the potatoes, greens and salad.
tip: No grill? Roast the sardines on a very hot tray, 8 minutes, until opaque. Ask the fishmonger to clean them, or use a pan and open the window.
ingredients: cleaned and gutted, heads on or off

name: Smoky lentils with Swiss chard and a spoon of yogurt
inspiredBy: Spanish lentejas, with a smoky paprika base
about: A cosy Spanish-style pot of green lentils with potato, carrot and plenty of smoked paprika, which gives it a deep, smoky flavour. Swiss chard goes in at the end and a spoon of cool yogurt balances the smoke. **Lentils bring a big share of your iron**, and the vinegar at the end helps you absorb it.
steps: Rinse the lentils and pick through for any stones. Warm the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and soften the onion and carrot for 8 minutes.
Add the garlic and tomato paste and stir for a minute. Add the smoked paprika and stir for 20 seconds, until it smells deeply smoky. It scorches fast, so keep the heat gentle.

Add the lentils, potato, bay leaf and enough water to cover by about 3 cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently until the lentils and potato are tender, about 30 minutes. Top up with water if it gets dry.
Stir in the salt and the chard and cook until tender, 4 minutes. Remove the bay leaf and finish with the vinegar. Taste, since it should be smoky, savoury and a little sharp.
Serve in bowls with a spoon of yogurt and the parsley. Cool the second portion within 1 hour in a shallow container, refrigerate within 2 hours and reheat to 74 °C tomorrow.
tip: Stir a spoon of the pot into a little yogurt for the kids. It freezes well in single portions.

name: Portuguese chickpea and tuna salad with tomato and parsley
inspiredBy: Portuguese salada de grao com atum
about: A bright Portuguese-style salad of chickpeas, flaked light tuna, ripe tomato, onion and lots of parsley, dressed with olive oil and red wine vinegar. It's a **quick lunch** that tastes better after the chickpeas soak up the dressing. Chickpeas bring iron and zinc, the tuna brings protein, niacin and B12, and the tomato helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Rinse the tomato, cucumber and parsley, then dice the tomato and cucumber. Soak the sliced onion in cold water for 5 minutes to soften its bite, then drain well.
Whisk the olive oil, vinegar, garlic and salt in a bowl. Add the chickpeas, tuna, onion, tomato, cucumber and olives and toss.
Let the salad sit for 5 minutes so the chickpeas drink in the dressing. Stir in most of the parsley.
Scatter with the remaining parsley and serve.
tip: Make the salad without the tomato the night before and add it fresh. Keep it cold and eat it within 1 day. Keep the rest of the opened tin in a lidded container in the fridge and use it within 2 days, flaked into a sandwich or on toast.

name: Baked cod with chickpeas, spinach and tomato
inspiredBy: Portuguese and Spanish baked cod and chickpeas, with fresh cod in place of salt cod
about: Fresh cod baked on a bed of chickpeas, spinach and tomato, scented with smoked paprika, lemon and olives. The chickpeas soak up the juices and the cod stays tender on top. It's a **one-dish dinner that makes tomorrow's lunch**. Cod is a lean protein with iodine, and the chickpeas add fibre, iron and zinc.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Warm half of the olive oil in an ovenproof skillet or wide pan and cook the onion with a pinch of salt until softened, about 6 minutes. Add the garlic and smoked paprika and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes, breaking them up, then the chickpeas and olives. Simmer for 5 minutes, then stir in the spinach until it wilts.

Rinse the cod, pat it dry, and season with salt and a little pepper. Wash your hands and the board after handling raw fish. Nestle the fillets into the chickpeas and drizzle with the remaining olive oil.
Bake until the cod is opaque and flakes easily, about 12 to 15 minutes, with an internal temperature of 70 °C (158 °F).
Finish with the lemon juice and parsley and serve in wide bowls. Cool the second portion quickly, refrigerate within 2 hours, and reheat it tomorrow until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Hake or pollock work the same way. If your fillets are thin, add them for the last 8 minutes. Frozen fillets are fine: thaw them in the fridge overnight and cook them within 2 days.

name: Greek briam with white beans and feta
inspiredBy: Greek briam, the roasted summer vegetable tray, with white beans for a full dinner
about: A tray of potatoes, zucchini, eggplant, red pepper and tomatoes roasted slowly in olive oil and oregano, with white beans tucked in and a little feta on top. It's **meat-free comfort food** that tastes even better the next day. Beans bring iron and fibre, and the feta brings calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Wash all the vegetables before cutting them.
Toss the potatoes, zucchini, eggplant, red pepper, onion and garlic in a roasting dish with the olive oil, oregano and salt. Pour the tomatoes and their juice over the top and add a splash of water.
Roast, stirring once, for 35 minutes, until the potatoes are nearly tender and the juices have thickened.
Tuck the white beans into the vegetables, crumble the feta over the top and roast for 10 minutes more, until the edges are caramelized and the potatoes are completely soft.
Finish with the parsley and a squeeze of lemon, and add a spoonful of yogurt to each bowl. Refrigerate the second portion within 2 hours and reheat it to 74 °C tomorrow.
tip: It roasts hands-off while you do other things, and takes closer to 45 minutes if you slice the potatoes thin. Cut the vegetables in similar sizes so everything is tender together. Add a handful of olives if you like.

name: Portuguese fish and shellfish stew with potatoes and peppers
inspiredBy: Portuguese caldeirada, lightened with more vegetables and less oil
about: A big, fragrant Portuguese-style fish stew of cod, salmon, mussels, clams and shrimp on a base of potatoes, red pepper, tomato and onion, with paprika, saffron and a bay leaf. It's the **weekend project**: layer the pot, simmer gently and eat it from deep bowls. The seafood brings iron, zinc and B12, and the salmon brings omega-3.
steps: Soak the clams in a bowl of cold water with about 2 tbsp of salt per litre for 20 minutes, then lift them out and rinse. Scrub the mussels and clams under cold running water, and pull the beards off the mussels just before cooking. Throw out any with cracked shells, and tap any that are open: if they stay open, throw them out.

Until you cook them, keep the shellfish in the fridge in an open bowl under a damp cloth, never in a sealed bag or fresh water, and cook them the day you buy them. If the shrimp are frozen, thaw them overnight in the fridge. Wash your hands, boards and knives well after handling raw fish and shellfish.

Warm the olive oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrot and red pepper with a pinch of salt for 8 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic, paprika and saffron and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes, bay leaf and the potatoes with enough water to nearly cover them. Bring to a simmer and cook until the potatoes are just tender, about 15 minutes.
Lay the cod and salmon on top of the potatoes and season with the remaining salt. Cover and simmer gently for 5 minutes.

Scatter the mussels and clams over the fish, cover tightly and cook until the shells open, about 5 minutes. Add the shrimp for the last 3 minutes, until pink and opaque. The fish should flake easily and be 70 °C (158 °F) inside, and the shellfish steaming hot right through (74 °C).
Throw away any mussels or clams that haven't opened after cooking. Stir in the parsley and lemon juice and serve in deep bowls.
For tomorrow's lunch, take the shellfish out of their shells, cool the second portion in a shallow container, refrigerate within 2 hours, eat it tomorrow and reheat it once to 74 °C.
tip: A splash of fish stock in place of some of the water gives a deeper broth. Hake, pollock or haddock work in place of the cod. Mussels and clams are weighed without their shells, so shop for roughly four times that weight of mussels and five times that of clams in the shell.
ingredients: weighed without shells, so buy about four times as much in the shell
weighed without shells, so buy about five times as much in the shell

name: Zucchini, potato and ricotta frittata with a tomato salad
inspiredBy: Italian frittata, with potato and zucchini and a little ricotta for softness
about: A thick, golden Italian frittata of sweet onion, tender potato, zucchini and ricotta, set gently and finished under the grill, served with a juicy tomato and oregano salad. It's an **easy, satisfying meat-free dinner** that's also lovely cold. Eggs bring protein and choline, and the potato brings potassium.
steps: Wash the zucchini and potato. Warm half of the olive oil in an ovenproof non-stick pan over medium-low heat. Cook the potato and onion with a pinch of salt, covered, stirring now and then, until the potato is tender, about 15 minutes.
Stir in the grated zucchini for the last 3 minutes. Tip the vegetables into a bowl and let them cool for a few minutes.
Beat the eggs with the ricotta, parsley and the remaining salt, then fold in the vegetables.
Heat the remaining oil in the pan, pour in the mixture and cook over low heat until the edges are set, about 8 minutes. Meanwhile, heat the grill.
Finish under the grill until the top is set and lightly golden and the centre is firm, about 3 minutes (the centre reads 74 °C, or 165 °F).
Toss the tomatoes with the oregano, vinegar and a pinch of salt. Serve the frittata in wedges with the tomato salad.
tip: It's lovely cold too: make it in a bigger pan, refrigerate the extra wedges within 2 hours and pack one in tomorrow's sandwich. Wash your hands after cracking eggs.

name: Greek yogurt with dried figs and walnuts
about: Thick Greek yogurt with chopped dried figs and toasted walnuts. It's a **calcium and omega-3 snack** that feels like dessert.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, then chop them.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the figs and walnuts.

name: Orange and almonds
about: A juicy orange with a small handful of almonds. The orange brings **vitamin C** and the almonds bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Wash the orange before peeling it. Peel and segment it, and eat with the almonds.
tip: Chop the almonds for children under 4.

name: Smoky roasted chickpeas
inspiredBy: Spanish-style smoked paprika chickpeas
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas tossed with smoked paprika. A **crisp, high-fibre snack** that also brings plant protein and iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Dry the chickpeas very well with a towel, since dry means crisp.
Toss with the olive oil, smoked paprika and salt on a tray. Roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crunchy.
Toss with a squeeze of lemon. Eat the same day, since they soften as they sit.

name: Sardines on toast with tomato and lemon
inspiredBy: Portuguese tosta de sardinhas
about: Canned sardines mashed onto crisp whole-wheat toast with sliced tomato and lemon. A **small fish snack** with omega-3, vitamin D and calcium from the soft bones.
steps: Toast the bread until crisp.
Lay the tomato slices on the toast and top with the sardines, mashing them gently with a fork.
Finish with lemon juice, parsley and a grind of pepper.
tip: Keep the rest of the opened tin in a lidded container in the fridge and use it within 2 days.

name: Tuscan white bean dip with carrot and cucumber
inspiredBy: Tuscan cannellini bean dip with rosemary
about: A quick garlicky white bean dip with rosemary and lemon, served with crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks. A **fibre-rich snack** with plant protein and iron.
steps: Wash the carrot and cucumber, then cut into sticks.
Blitz the beans, olive oil, garlic, lemon, rosemary and salt with a splash of water until smooth.
Serve the dip with the sticks. Keep leftover dip in the fridge up to 3 days.

name: Apple with walnuts and cinnamon
about: Crisp apple slices with toasted walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. A **crunchy snack** with fibre and a little omega-3.
steps: Wash and slice the apple.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes.
Serve together with a dusting of cinnamon.
tip: Chop the walnuts for children under 4.

name: Medjool dates stuffed with almonds
about: Soft dates stuffed with whole almonds. A **sweet, quick snack** with potassium and vitamin E.
steps: Slit the dates open, pull out the pits, and tuck an almond into each.
tip: Chop the almonds for young children.

name: Tzatziki with cucumber and toasted bread
inspiredBy: Greek tzatziki
about: Cool garlicky Greek yogurt with grated cucumber, lemon and a little olive oil, scooped up with cucumber slices and a piece of toasted whole-wheat bread. A **cooling, high-protein snack**.
steps: Wash the cucumber. Grate half of it and squeeze it dry in a clean towel, then slice the rest.
Stir the grated cucumber into the yogurt with the garlic, lemon, olive oil and salt.
Serve with the cucumber slices and toast. It keeps in the fridge up to 3 days.
ingredients: half grated and squeezed dry, half sliced

name: Boiled egg with tomato and oregano
about: A boiled egg with sliced tomato, olive oil and a dusting of oregano. A **simple protein snack** with choline and vitamin C.
steps: Put the egg in a small pot of cold water, bring to a boil, then simmer 10 minutes, until the yolk is firm. Cool under cold water and peel.
Slice the egg and tomato, drizzle with olive oil and dust with oregano, black pepper and salt.

name: Tuscan white bean toast with tomato
inspiredBy: Tuscan fettunta with beans
about: Crisp whole-wheat toast piled with mashed white beans, sliced tomato, a little garlic and olive oil. A **filling snack** with plant protein, fibre and iron.
steps: Toast the bread and rub it with the cut side of the garlic.
Mash the beans with a fork, olive oil and salt, and spread over the toast.
Top with the tomato and parsley.

name: Chickpea, tomato and cucumber cup
inspiredBy: Greek and Portuguese chickpea salads
about: A small cup of chickpeas with chopped tomato, cucumber, oregano, lemon and olive oil. A **fresh, filling snack** with plant protein, fibre and iron.
steps: Wash the tomato and cucumber, then dice them.
Toss everything together in a small bowl.
Let it sit for 5 minutes so the chickpeas soak up the dressing.

name: Overnight rye and oat muesli with skyr, blueberries and lingonberry
inspiredBy: Nordic overnight muesli, with rye flakes and skyr
about: Rolled oats and rye flakes soaked overnight in milk and skyr, with blueberries, a spoonful of lingonberry jam and toasted sunflower seeds on top. It is ready when you wake, creamy and a little tart, with a crunch from the seeds. The oats and rye bring **slow-release fibre**, and the milk and skyr bring calcium and protein.
steps: The night before, stir the oats, rye flakes, cinnamon, milk and skyr together in a jar. It should look a little too loose, because the flakes will drink it up. Cover and chill overnight, and eat within 2 days.
Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 2 minutes, and let them cool.
In the morning, give the muesli a good stir. It should be thick and spoonable. A splash of milk loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Top with the blueberries (rinse fresh ones first), the lingonberry jam and the toasted seeds, and eat straight away so the seeds stay crisp.
tip: Mix it the night before. A jar keeps up to 2 days in the fridge, and the seeds go on fresh each morning. If anyone eating is pregnant, over 65 or immunocompromised, bring frozen berries to a boil for 1 minute and cool them first.

name: Warm oat and rye porridge with apple, cinnamon and hazelnuts
inspiredBy: Swedish havregrynsgröt and Finnish kaurapuuro, with rye flakes for chew
about: A creamy milk porridge of rolled oats and rye flakes, with grated apple stirred in at the end and toasted hazelnuts on top. It is the **bowl of every Nordic morning**, plain and filling, and it keeps you full well past mid-morning. The milk brings calcium and iodine, and the hazelnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Let them cool, then chop roughly.
Put the oats, rye flakes, milk, a splash of water and the salt in a small pot. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring often so it doesn't catch.
Cook until thick and creamy, about 6 to 8 minutes. Wash the apple, grate it and stir it in for the last minute.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the cinnamon and hazelnuts.
tip: Make it with water for a lighter bowl, or stir in a spoon of skyr at the end for extra protein.
ingredients: washed and grated with the skin on

name: Egg and cucumber smørrebrød on buttered rye with scallion tops and dill
inspiredBy: Danish smørrebrød, a Copenhagen lunch turned into a breakfast
about: Buttered dark rye topped with a skyr and mustard spread, sliced boiled egg, cool cucumber and a shower of scallion tops and dill. It is the **Danish open-faced classic**, savoury and fresh in equal measure. Rye brings fibre, and the egg brings protein and choline.
steps: Lower the eggs into a pan of boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, until the yolks are fully set. Cool them in cold water, peel and slice.
Stir the skyr with the mustard and a grind of pepper until smooth.
Wash the cucumber, scallion and dill before slicing and chopping. Slice the cucumber thinly.
Butter the rye, spread it with the skyr mixture, then layer on the cucumber and the egg. Finish with the scallion tops, dill and a little more pepper.
tip: Boil the eggs on Sunday night and keep them, unpeeled, in the fridge. Use them within 5 days.
ingredients: boiled until the yolk is set

name: Tofu and mushroom miso soup with barley rice and quick daikon pickle
inspiredBy: Japanese asa-gohan, the breakfast set, kept to one soup and one pickle
about: A Japanese-style breakfast: miso soup with firm tofu, spinach, mushrooms and scallion, a small bowl of chewy barley rice, a snap of vinegared daikon and a little torn nori. It is **gentle, warming and quick to eat**. Tofu brings protein, and the mushrooms bring vitamin D.
steps: Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes, then drain. Start it first, or cook it the night before. Cook only what you will eat. If any is left, spread it in a shallow dish so it cools within 1 hour, and refrigerate it.
While the barley cooks, toss the daikon with the rice vinegar and salt. Leave it for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the extra liquid.

Simmer the ginger and mushrooms in about 350 ml water for 6 minutes. Add the bonito flakes for the last 2 minutes, then lift them out with a small sieve. This is a quick dashi, and it is what makes the soup taste like miso soup should.
Add the tofu to the pot and warm it for 2 minutes. Add the spinach and scallion for the last 30 seconds, until the spinach just wilts.
Take the pot off the heat. Stir the miso with a ladle of hot broth until smooth, then stir it back in. Don't let it boil after the miso goes in, or it loses its flavour.
Serve the soup with the barley, the pickle and the torn nori on top.
tip: Seaweed is kept to a small piece of nori because it is very rich in iodine. Cook the barley the night before and cool it within 1 hour for a quick weekday version, reheating it until steaming hot (74 °C). On a weekday, make just the soup and eat it with the leftover barley.
ingredients: any kind, cut into small cubes
peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

name: Pickled herring and egg on rye with dill skyr, beets and new potatoes
inspiredBy: Danish sildemad and Swedish sillbricka, with skyr in place of the usual sour cream
about: Dark rye with pickled herring, a sliced boiled egg, thin onion and sweet pickled beet under a cool dill and lemon skyr sauce, with a small plate of dill potatoes on the side. It is the **sharp, sweet and creamy** balance of a Danish lunch table. Herring is rich in omega-3 and vitamin D, but it is cured and salty, so it is a once-a-week fish. Not for anyone pregnant, over 65 or with a weakened immune system unless heated to 74 °C (165 °F).
steps: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold water, bring to a boil and cook until a knife slides in easily, about 15 minutes. Drain and let the steam escape. Toss with half of the dill. Boil the eggs alongside for 9 minutes, until the yolks are set, then cool, peel and slice them.
Stir the skyr with the lemon juice and the rest of the dill until smooth.

Take the herring straight from the fridge and drain it. Cured fish should be kept cold, so don't leave it out for more than 2 hours. Choose Atlantic herring, not Baltic, and use it by the date on the jar. If anyone eating is pregnant, over 65 or has a weakened immune system, skip the herring, or warm it in a small covered pan over low heat until steaming hot (74 °C).
Butter the rye, lay on the herring, egg, beet and onion, and spoon the skyr sauce on top. If the slice looks small for the toppings, cut it in half and stack them on both halves.
Serve with the warm potatoes on the side.
tip: Buy the smallest jar and keep it in the coldest part of the fridge, at 4 °C or colder. Finish it within 3 days of opening or by its date, whichever comes first. Rinse the herring first for a milder taste.
ingredients: boiled until the yolk is set

name: Yellow pea soup with kale, mustard and rye bread
inspiredBy: Swedish ärtsoppa, the Thursday pea soup
about: A thick, smoky yellow pea soup in the Swedish ärtsoppa style, simmered with onion, carrot and marjoram and finished with kale and a splash of vinegar. The smoked paprika gives it a **deep, smoky flavour**. The peas bring plenty of fibre, folate and plant protein, the kale adds vitamin C and vitamin K, and a dab of mustard on top is how Swedes eat it.
steps: Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and carrot until soft, about 6 minutes. Stir in the marjoram and paprika for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the split peas and enough water to cover them by about 5 cm. Bring to a boil and skim off any foam.
Simmer gently with the lid slightly ajar, stirring now and then, until the peas have collapsed into a thick soup, about 45 minutes. Add water if it gets too thick.
Wash the kale, remove the stems, shred it and stir it in for the last 5 minutes, until tender and bright green. Season with the salt and finish with the vinegar.
Stir a spoonful of mustard into each bowl and serve with the rye bread.
Pack the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. It keeps up to 3 days; reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Short on time? A pressure cooker has the peas ready in about 15 minutes. The soup freezes well in single portions.

name: Lohikeitto, Finnish salmon soup with leeks, dill and rye
inspiredBy: Finnish lohikeitto, made with milk and a little butter in place of cream
about: Finland's creamy salmon soup: leek, potato and carrot simmered in milk with allspice, then big pieces of salmon poached at the very end and a handful of dill. Served with a slice of dark rye, it is a **whole meal in a bowl**. The salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D, and the milk brings calcium and iodine.
steps: If the salmon is frozen, thaw it overnight in the fridge and cook it within 2 days. Cut it into big cubes, and wash your hands, the knife and the board afterwards.

Melt the butter in a pot over medium heat and cook the leek until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the potato, carrot, allspice and enough water to just cover. Simmer until the potato is tender, about 15 minutes.
Pour in the milk and warm it to a gentle simmer. Don't let it boil hard, or it can split.
Slide in the salmon and poach gently, off a boil, until it is opaque and flakes easily (70 °C), about 5 minutes.
Season with the salt, white pepper and a squeeze of lemon. Stir in most of the dill and serve with the rye bread and the rest of the dill on top.

Pack the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. It keeps up to 3 days; reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C). Reheat gently so the fish doesn't toughen.
tip: A splash of cold milk loosens the soup when you reheat it. Don't boil it hard, or the fish turns dry.
ingredients: skin and pin bones removed, cut into large cubes

name: Tofu and egg simmered with mushrooms and spinach over barley rice
inspiredBy: Japanese tamago-toji donburi, made with tofu and mushrooms
about: Firm tofu and mushrooms simmered in a light soy and ginger broth, with beaten egg swirled in until just set and spinach wilted through, all spooned over chewy barley rice. It is **Japanese home comfort**, in the style of a tamago-toji donburi. The egg and tofu bring protein and choline, and the mushrooms bring vitamin D.
steps: Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes, then drain.

While the barley cooks, simmer the onion, mushrooms and ginger in about 150 ml water for each portion you are cooking, with the soy sauce and sugar, for 8 minutes, until the onion is soft and the broth smells savoury.
Add the tofu and simmer for 3 minutes. Add the spinach and let it wilt.

Pour the beaten egg in a slow circle over the top, cover and cook over low heat until it is completely set, with no runny egg left (74 °C), about 2 minutes. Hold back a little broth if the bowl looks wet.
Spoon over the barley and finish with the scallion and sesame seeds.

Pack the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. It keeps up to 3 days; reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C). Cool leftover barley within 1 hour, too.
tip: Slide the pot off the heat just as the egg sets, because it keeps cooking in the hot broth. The egg is firmer on the second day, which is normal.
ingredients: any kind, drained and cut into cubes

name: Miso-simmered mackerel with sesame spinach, pickled daikon and barley rice
inspiredBy: Japanese saba no misoni, with a pickle and spinach on the side
about: Atlantic mackerel simmered in a ginger and miso broth until the sauce turns glossy, with a quick sesame spinach, a sharp daikon pickle and a bowl of chewy barley rice. This is **Japanese home cooking at its best**. Mackerel is a top source of omega-3, selenium and vitamin B12, and the ginger and miso tame its richness.
steps: If the mackerel is frozen, thaw it overnight in the fridge and cook it within 2 days. Never refreeze it.
Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes, then drain. Cool leftover barley within 1 hour.
Toss the daikon with the vinegar, half of the sugar and the salt. Leave it for 15 minutes while the fish cooks.

Simmer the bonito flakes in about 200 ml water for 2 minutes in a wide pan, then lift them out with a small sieve. Add the ginger, soy sauce and the rest of the sugar and bring to a boil. Add the mackerel skin side up and cover with a piece of parchment or a lid that sits just above the fish. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw fish.

Simmer gently for 8 minutes. Stir the miso with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then stir it into the pan. Simmer for 4 more minutes, spooning the sauce over, until the fish is opaque all the way through (70 °C) and the sauce is glossy.
Wash the spinach, boil it for 1 minute, drain, rinse in cold water and squeeze dry. Toss with the ground sesame and a spoonful of the mackerel's simmering liquid.

Serve the fish and its sauce over the barley with the scallion on top, with the spinach and the drained daikon on the side. Pack the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. It keeps up to 3 days; reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Ask the fishmonger to remove the pin bones. Use Atlantic or Pacific (chub) mackerel, never king mackerel, which is high in mercury. Keep it on ice or in the coldest part of the fridge and cook it the day you buy it.
ingredients: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

name: Warm dill potato salad with eggs, pickled beets and rye
inspiredBy: Danish kartoffelsalat, with skyr in place of the mayonnaise
about: Warm sliced potatoes tossed in a skyr, mustard and lemon dressing with dill, grated carrot and onion, topped with boiled eggs and served with sweet pickled beets. It is a **Danish-style potato supper** that tastes just as good cold the next day. Egg and skyr bring the protein, and the potatoes bring potassium and vitamin C.
steps: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold water with a pinch of the salt. Bring to a boil and cook until a knife slides in easily, about 20 minutes. Drain.
Add the eggs to boiling water in a separate pan and cook for 9 minutes, until the yolks are completely set. Cool them in cold water, peel and quarter.
Stir the skyr with the mustard, lemon juice, oil and the rest of the salt to make the dressing. Wash the carrot and grate it coarsely.
Slice the potatoes while still warm and fold them gently into the dressing with the onion, carrot and most of the dill. Warm potatoes soak up the dressing best.
Top with the eggs and the remaining dill, and serve with the beets on the side.
Pack the second portion into a shallow container and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. Eat it cold the next day, within 2 days of cooking. There is no need to reheat it.
tip: Add a spoon of capers or a few slices of pickled cucumber if you like more bite.
ingredients: boiled until the yolk is set

name: Ishikari-style salmon and tofu hot pot with miso, cabbage and barley rice
inspiredBy: Hokkaido ishikari nabe, with a light miso broth
about: A Hokkaido hot pot of salmon, tofu, napa cabbage, potato and mushrooms in a light miso broth with a small knob of butter, the way northern Japan shares a cold evening. It is a **weekend project** that is easy to cook at the table, with a bowl of chewy barley alongside. The salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D, and the mushrooms add more vitamin D.
steps: If the salmon is frozen, thaw it overnight in the fridge and cook it within 2 days. Wash your hands, the knife and the board after handling the raw fish.
Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes, then drain. Cool any leftover barley within 1 hour.
Bring about 600 ml water, the ginger and the bonito flakes to a simmer in a wide pot and simmer for 3 minutes. Lift out the flakes with a small sieve. Add the potato slices and simmer for 8 minutes.
Add the carrot to the pot. Lay the cabbage stems and tofu on top and simmer for 4 minutes. Stir the miso and soy sauce with a ladle of hot broth until smooth, then stir them in.
Add the salmon, the cabbage leaves and the mushrooms, cover and simmer very gently until the salmon is opaque and flakes (70 °C), about 5 minutes.
Add the butter and the scallion and finish with pepper. Eat from the pot, with the barley on the side. This makes one generous portion, so double it for two and eat it all the same evening.
tip: Pour the last of the broth over the barley. For two people, use a bigger pot and double everything.
ingredients: skin and pin bones removed, cut into thick pieces
any kind, cut into large cubes
washed and cut into wide pieces
peeled and sliced about 1 cm thick

name: Cold-smoked salmon and soft scrambled eggs on rye with dill and cucumber
inspiredBy: Danish røget laks med røræg
about: Buttery scrambled eggs on dark rye with folds of cold-smoked salmon, a dill and lemon skyr cream and cool cucumber. It is a **Danish favourite**, rich and fresh in one bite, and the smoked salmon is only a small part of the plate. Smoked salmon is salty and not for anyone pregnant, over 65 or with a weakened immune system unless heated to 74 °C (165 °F), for example folded into the hot scrambled eggs at the end. It is one of only two cured fish meals this week.
steps: Take the smoked salmon out of the fridge only when you are ready to eat. Keep it at 4 °C or colder, never leave it out for more than 2 hours, and finish an opened pack within 3 days or by its date, or sooner if the pack says so.
Stir the skyr with half of the lemon juice and the dill until smooth.
Wash the cucumber and scallion before cutting. Peel the cucumber into thin ribbons with a vegetable peeler.
Melt the butter in a non-stick pan over low heat. Add the beaten eggs and stir slowly with a spatula until they are creamy and fully set, with no runny egg left (74 °C), about 3 minutes.

Spoon the eggs onto the rye and add the skyr cream. Fold the salmon on top. If anyone eating is pregnant, over 65 or has a weakened immune system, fold the salmon into the hot eggs for the last minute instead, until steaming hot (74 °C).
Top with the cucumber, scallion and a grind of pepper, and finish with the rest of the lemon.
tip: Buy the smallest pack (about 100 g) and freeze the rest unopened, or share it. Cold-smoked salmon is not cooked, so anyone pregnant, over 65 or immunocompromised should heat it as above, or pan-fry a small piece of fresh salmon until it flakes (70 °C) instead. Refrigerated hot-smoked salmon needs the same care.
ingredients: washed and cut into thin ribbons

name: Pan-seared tofu with miso butter, potatoes, mushrooms and spinach
inspiredBy: Hokkaido-style jaga-bata (potato and butter), with miso-glazed tofu
about: Crisp-edged tofu glazed with a little miso and soy sauce, served over potatoes with butter-fried mushrooms, carrot and wilted spinach, and topped with fried eggs. It is **inspired by Hokkaido's potato and butter cooking**, savoury and slightly sweet, with sesame for crunch. Tofu brings protein, the spinach and carrot bring vitamin A, and the mushrooms bring vitamin D.
steps: Boil the potatoes in a pot of water until a knife slides in easily, about 15 minutes. Drain well.
Press the tofu between clean towels under something heavy for 10 minutes, then pat it dry.
Heat the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Fry the tofu until golden and crisp at the edges, about 4 minutes a side. Lift it onto a plate.

Mix the miso, soy sauce, sugar and rice vinegar with 2 tablespoons of water. Melt half of the butter in the same pan and cook the mushrooms and carrot until golden and just tender, about 5 minutes. Add the washed spinach and stir until it wilts, about 1 minute.
Pour in the miso mixture, let it bubble for 1 minute, then return the tofu to the pan and turn it in the sauce. Toss the potatoes with the rest of the butter.
Fry the eggs in a little oil in a clean pan until the white is set and the yolk is firm (74 °C).
Serve the tofu and vegetables over the potatoes, topped with the eggs, the sesame and the scallion.
tip: A squeeze of lemon at the table brightens it. Spoon any pan sauce over the potatoes.
ingredients: any kind, pressed dry and cut into thick slabs
washed and cut into thin matchsticks

name: Apple wedges with toasted hazelnuts
about: Crisp apple wedges with a handful of toasted hazelnuts, a classic Nordic pair. It is **crunchy and sweet**, and it carries vitamin E from the hazelnuts and fibre from the apple.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Let them cool.
Wash the apple, cut it into wedges and serve with the hazelnuts.
tip: Toast a bigger batch of nuts on Sunday and keep them in a jar for the week.

name: Skyr with blueberries and toasted rye flakes
about: Thick skyr with sweet blueberries and a crunch of toasted rye flakes. It is **creamy, tart and crisp** at once, with a lot of protein for a snack.
steps: Toast the rye flakes in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Cool them.
Spoon the skyr into a bowl, top with the blueberries (rinse fresh ones first) and scatter over the rye flakes just before eating.
tip: Thawed frozen blueberries make a purple swirl through the skyr. If anyone eating is pregnant, over 65 or immunocompromised, bring frozen berries to a boil for 1 minute and cool them first.

name: Apple and gjetost on toasted rye
inspiredBy: Norwegian brunost on bread, with apple
about: Slices of crisp apple and a few thin shavings of gjetost, Norway's caramel-sweet brown cheese, on toasted dark rye. It is a **sweet and savoury** snack, with calcium from the cheese and fibre from the apple and rye.
steps: Toast the rye until crisp. Wash and slice the apple, and shave the cheese into paper-thin curls with a cheese slicer or vegetable peeler.
Lay the apple and cheese on the toast and eat right away so it stays crisp.
tip: Gjetost is rich and sweet, so a little goes a long way.

name: Daikon and carrot sticks with miso skyr dip
inspiredBy: a Japanese miso dip, with a Nordic skyr base
about: Crunchy daikon and carrot sticks with a quick dip of skyr, a little miso and rice vinegar. It is **cool, savoury and fresh**, with a scatter of toasted sesame on top, and the carrots bring plenty of vitamin A.
steps: Peel the daikon and wash the carrot, then cut both into sticks.
Stir the skyr, miso and rice vinegar until smooth. Spoon it into a small bowl and scatter over the sesame seeds.
Serve with the sticks for dipping.
tip: The dip keeps 2 days in the fridge. Cut the sticks fresh.

name: Toasted rye with skyr, quick-pickled cucumber and dill
about: Toasted dark rye spread with thick skyr and topped with cucumber pickled in rice vinegar for ten minutes, plus a little dill. It is **crunchy and bright**, with protein from the skyr and fibre from the rye.
steps: Wash the cucumber, slice it very thinly and toss it with the rice vinegar and sugar. Leave it for 10 minutes so it softens, then drain.
Toast the rye until crisp, spread it with the skyr, top with the drained cucumber and dill, and eat straight away.
tip: Pickle a bigger batch in a jar. It keeps up to 5 days in the fridge.

name: Buttery mushrooms on toasted rye with dill and lemon
inspiredBy: Swedish and Danish svampmacka
about: Sliced mushrooms fried in butter until golden and piled on toasted rye with dill and a squeeze of lemon, like a Nordic svampmacka. It is **savoury and a little earthy**. UV-exposed mushrooms bring vitamin D.
steps: Heat the butter in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and cook without stirring for 2 minutes, then stir until golden and any liquid has cooked off, about 5 minutes more.
Season with pepper and the lemon juice.
Toast the rye, pile the mushrooms onto it, scatter over the dill and eat while warm.
tip: Any mushroom works, but the UV-exposed ones bring vitamin D.

name: Warm blueberries with skyr
inspiredBy: Finnish mustikkakeitto, with skyr
about: Blueberries warmed with a little sugar and lemon until they burst and turn into a jammy sauce, spooned over cold skyr. It is **warm and cold at once**, like a Finnish blueberry soup. Blueberries bring vitamin C and skyr brings protein and calcium.
steps: Put the blueberries, sugar, lemon juice and a spoonful of water in a small pot. Warm over medium heat until the berries burst and the juices turn syrupy, about 4 minutes.
Spoon the skyr into a bowl and pour the warm berries over the top.

name: Mushroom miso soup in a mug with ginger and scallion
inspiredBy: Japanese miso soup, in a mug
about: A quick mug of miso soup with sliced mushrooms, ginger and scallion. It is **warming and light**, a Japanese afternoon pick-me-up, with vitamin D from the mushrooms.
steps: Simmer the ginger and mushrooms in about 250 ml water for 8 minutes, until the broth smells earthy.
Take the pot off the heat. Stir the miso with a ladle of hot broth until smooth, then stir it back in. Pour into a mug and top with the scallion.
tip: Miso is salty, so it is kept to a spoonful. Add a few cubes of tofu if you want more protein.

name: Grated carrot and pear salad with sunflower seeds
inspiredBy: Danish gulerodssalat
about: Sweet grated carrot and juicy pear with lemon, a little oil and toasted sunflower seeds. It is **bright and crunchy**, like a Danish gulerodssalat, and the carrots bring vitamin A and the seeds vitamin E.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Cool them.
Wash the carrot and pear, grate them and toss with the lemon juice and oil.
Scatter over the seeds just before eating so they stay crisp.

name: Blueberry and oat smoothie with milk
about: Milk blended with blueberries, rolled oats and a pinch of cinnamon into a thick purple smoothie. It is **cool and filling**, and the milk brings calcium and iodine.
steps: Put the milk, blueberries, oats and cinnamon in a blender.
Blend until smooth and thick, about 1 minute, and drink right away.
tip: Soak the oats in the milk for 10 minutes first for a smoother texture. If anyone eating is pregnant, over 65 or immunocompromised, bring frozen berries to a boil for 1 minute and cool them first.

name: Skyr with lingonberry jam and toasted hazelnuts
about: Thick skyr swirled with a spoonful of tart lingonberry jam and topped with toasted hazelnuts. It is **tangy, creamy and crunchy**, with a lot of protein for a snack and vitamin E from the hazelnuts.
steps: Toast the hazelnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes. Cool and chop them roughly.
Spoon the skyr into a bowl, swirl in the lingonberry jam and scatter over the hazelnuts.

name: Black sesame and almond oat porridge with banana
inspiredBy: Chinese black sesame porridge (zhi ma hu), made with oats for a quicker morning
about: Creamy oats cooked in milk with a little fresh ginger, then topped with toasted black sesame, almonds, walnuts and banana. It is a warm, nutty bowl that comes together in ten minutes. The **almonds and milk bring vitamin E and calcium**, alongside the oats' fibre.
steps: Toast the black sesame seeds and almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for about 2 minutes, until they smell nutty. Tip them onto a board and crush the sesame lightly.
Put the oats, milk, ginger, cinnamon and salt in a small pot. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring often so the milk doesn't catch.
Cook for about 5 minutes, until the porridge is thick and creamy, then stir in the mashed banana.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the sliced banana, the toasted sesame and almonds, and the walnuts.
tip: Toast and crush a jar of black sesame and almonds ahead of time and spoon it on straight from the jar.
ingredients: ripe, half mashed and half sliced

name: Korean steamed egg custard with rice, shiitake and spinach
inspiredBy: Korean gyeran-jjim, eaten the way it is at a family table, next to a bowl of rice
about: A silky, savoury egg custard steamed gently until completely set, served with warm rice and a quick sauté of shiitake and spinach. It is soft, easy food for a slow morning. The **eggs bring choline and B12**, and the spinach brings folate.
steps: Wash the spinach and mushrooms. Beat the eggs well with the salt and about the same volume of water, until no streaks of white remain. Pour the mixture into a heatproof bowl through a small sieve, then stir in half of the scallion.
Set a rack or a small upturned bowl in a pot with about 2 cm of water and bring it to a gentle simmer. Cover the custard bowl loosely with foil and set it on the rack. Put the lid on the pot.

Steam on low heat for 12 to 15 minutes, until the custard is completely set: the centre should not wobble, a knife should come out clean, and the centre should reach 74 °C (165 °F). Never serve it soft or runny.

While it steams, reheat the rice (thawed in the fridge overnight if it was frozen) with a splash of water and a lid, in the microwave or a pot, until it is steaming hot (74 °C). Warm the canola oil in a pan and cook the shiitake for 3 minutes, until browned. Add the spinach and cook for 1 minute, until just wilted.

Toss the spinach with the perilla oil. Drizzle the custard with the soy sauce and sesame oil, and scatter over the rest of the scallion and the sesame seeds. Serve with the rice, shiitake and spinach.
tip: On Sunday, cook enough brown basmati for the three custard mornings (a generous ½ cup raw, or about ¾ cup at Big), chill it within 1 hour, keep Monday's portion in the fridge and freeze the other two. Thaw one in the fridge the night before, use within 2 days and reheat until steaming. A pouch of cooked brown rice works too. Keep perilla oil in the fridge, use it within 2 months and never heat it. No perilla? Use sesame oil.
ingredients: brown basmati from your Sunday batch

name: Ginger congee with tofu, spinach and egg
inspiredBy: Chinese rice porridge (zhou), the everyday food of zuo yuezi, with no herbs
about: Rice simmered until it falls apart into a soft, steaming porridge with fresh ginger, tofu, shiitake and spinach, with egg stirred in and crushed walnuts on top. Congee is the classic first food of a Chinese confinement month, and this pot makes two bowls so the next morning is ready. The **egg and tofu make it a protein breakfast**.
steps: Wash the spinach and mushrooms. Put the rinsed rice and the ginger in a large pot with about 8 parts water to 1 part rice by volume. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down to a steady, gentle simmer.

Simmer partly covered for about 50 minutes, stirring every so often and scraping the bottom, until the grains have burst and the congee is thick and creamy. Add a splash of hot water if it gets too thick.
Stir in the shiitake and tofu and cook for 5 minutes, until the mushrooms are soft and the tofu is hot through.
Stir in the soy sauce, salt and spinach. Pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream, stirring gently, and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until the egg has set into soft ribbons with no runny bits.
Ladle into bowls and finish with the sesame oil, scallion, white pepper and walnuts.
Divide into shallow containers, chill within 2 hours, eat tomorrow or freeze, and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Use a cooker's keep-warm setting only if it holds above 60 °C. Otherwise cook the base the evening before, chill it in shallow containers and bring it to a boil in the morning before adding the tofu, mushrooms, spinach and egg.

name: Sesame-ginger greens with seared tofu and rice
inspiredBy: Cantonese ginger greens and Korean sigeumchi namul, on a rice bowl
about: Tender water spinach dressed in a warm ginger, garlic and toasted sesame dressing, with golden tofu and steamed brown rice. It is a quick, bright plate. The **greens and tofu bring calcium** and folate, and the sesame adds its nutty flavour.
steps: Cook the rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain well and keep it covered.

Wash the water spinach well, since grit hides between the stems. Cut the tofu into thick slabs. Warm the canola oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and sear the tofu for 3 to 4 minutes per side, until golden and crisp at the edges.
Boil the water spinach in a pot of water for 1 minute, until the stems are just tender and the leaves are bright green. Drain well.

Warm the sesame oil in a small pan over low heat. Add the ginger and garlic and stir for about 30 seconds, until fragrant but not browned. Take off the heat and stir in the soy sauce, lemon juice and salt.
Toss the greens with the warm dressing. Serve on top of the rice with the tofu, scattered with the scallion and sesame seeds.
tip: Swap in bok choy, spinach or broccoli. Whatever is crisp and green works with this dressing.
ingredients: cut into short lengths and washed

name: Ginger and sesame chicken soup
inspiredBy: Chinese sesame oil chicken (ma you ji), made as a soup
about: A warm, fragrant pot of chicken simmered with plenty of fresh ginger, toasted sesame oil, shiitake, carrot and bok choy. The **ginger and sesame oil carry the aroma**, so it tastes rich without anything fancy. It makes two bowls and freezes well.
steps: Wash all the vegetables. Warm the sesame oil and canola oil in a soup pot over medium-low heat. Add the ginger and stir for 2 to 3 minutes, until it is fragrant and just starting to turn golden at the edges. Don't let it scorch.
Add the chicken and stir for about 3 minutes, until the outside is pale. Add the shiitake, carrot and soy sauce, then enough water to cover everything by about 3 cm.

Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then turn down to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook for 25 minutes, until the carrot is tender and the chicken reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece, with no pink inside.
Cook the rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain well and keep it covered.
Add the bok choy and the salt to the soup and simmer for 3 minutes, until the greens are soft. Ladle the soup over or beside the rice and finish with the white pepper and scallion.
Divide into shallow containers, chill within 2 hours, eat tomorrow or freeze, and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C). The soup freezes on its own for up to 3 months.
tip: Add more ginger if you love it. For the freezer, freeze the soup without the rice and cook fresh rice on the day.

name: Salmon and ginger congee with water spinach
inspiredBy: Cantonese fish congee (yu pin zhou), with salmon for its omega-3 fat
about: Soft, savoury congee topped with tender flakes of salmon, fresh ginger, water spinach (ong choy) and scallion. Fish congee is a home favourite in southern China, and the salmon gives it **omega-3 fat (DHA) and vitamin D**. It makes two bowls, so tomorrow's lunch is ready.
steps: Wash the water spinach well. Put the rinsed rice and the sliced ginger in a large pot with about 8 parts water to 1 part rice by volume. Bring to a boil, then turn down to a steady simmer.
Simmer partly covered for about 50 minutes, stirring now and then, until the grains have burst and the congee is thick and creamy. Add a splash of hot water if it tightens.
Toss the salmon with the soy sauce, the ginger matchsticks and the white pepper.
Stir the salt and water spinach into the congee and cook for 2 minutes. Lay the salmon on top, cover and simmer for 4 to 5 minutes, until the fish is opaque, flakes easily and reaches 70 °C (158 °F).
Break the salmon into large flakes, ladle into bowls and finish with the sesame oil, scallion and sesame seeds.
Divide into shallow containers, chill within 2 hours, eat tomorrow or freeze, and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Chill the base within 2 hours and bring it to a boil before adding the fish. No water spinach? Use bok choy or spinach.
ingredients: skin removed, cut into thick slices
half thinly sliced and half cut into fine matchsticks

name: Miyeok-guk, Korean seaweed soup with beef and tofu
inspiredBy: Korean miyeok-guk, the seaweed soup eaten after a birth and on birthdays
about: A clear, savoury soup of tender beef, tofu, garlic and a small amount of wakame, deepened with toasted sesame oil, with sesame spinach and rice alongside. Seaweed is very rich in iodine, so it's kept to a few grams: enough for flavour and some **iodine**, without overdoing it. It makes two bowls and freezes well.
steps: Wash the spinach well. Soak the wakame in cold water for 10 minutes, until soft and swollen to many times its size. Drain, squeeze out the water and cut it into short lengths.
Cook the rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain well and keep it covered.
Warm the sesame oil and canola oil in a soup pot over medium heat. Add the beef and half of the garlic and stir for 3 to 4 minutes, until the beef is browned and no pink remains.

Add the wakame and stir for 1 minute. Add the soy sauce and about 1½ cups of water for each serving. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until the beef is very tender and the broth tastes rich.

Add the tofu for the last 5 minutes. Season with the salt and stir in the rest of the garlic. Meanwhile, blanch the spinach in boiling water for 1 minute, drain, squeeze and toss with the perilla oil and sesame seeds, the way Korean namul is dressed.

Serve the soup with the rice and the spinach. Divide into shallow containers, chill within 2 hours, eat tomorrow or freeze, and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C). Freeze the soup without the rice and spinach.
tip: Weigh 3 g dry per serving, not a pinch. It swells a lot in the pot. Use wakame (miyeok) only: kelp, kombu and dashima carry far more iodine. Lovely as it is, keep this soup to a couple of bowls a week. Keep perilla oil in the fridge, use it within 2 months and never heat it. No perilla? Use sesame oil.
ingredients: very thinly sliced against the grain
weighed dry, soaked and drained, soaking water discarded

name: Red lentil, spinach and carrot dal with ginger-cumin tadka and brown rice
inspiredBy: North Indian masoor dal with a ghee tadka
about: Soft red lentils simmered with turmeric, tomato, carrot and spinach, then finished with a sizzling ghee, cumin, garlic and ginger tadka and a squeeze of lemon. Served with brown basmati rice and a spoonful of yogurt, it is comforting food that freezes beautifully. The **lentils bring iron, folate and protein**, and the lemon helps with iron.
steps: Cook the rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain well and keep it covered.

Wash the vegetables. Put the lentils, carrot, onion, tomato, turmeric and about 3 times the lentils' volume of water in a pot. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then simmer for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the lentils have collapsed into a soft, thick dal.
Stir in the spinach and the salt and cook for 3 minutes, until the spinach has wilted. Add a splash of hot water if the dal is too thick.

For the tadka, heat the ghee and canola oil in a small pan until shimmering. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for about 20 seconds, then add the garlic and ginger and cook for 30 seconds, until golden but not brown.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal and stir in the garam masala and lemon juice.
Serve with the rice and the yogurt. Divide into shallow containers, chill within 2 hours, eat tomorrow or freeze, and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C). The dal freezes for up to 3 months.
tip: Make the tadka fresh each time. It is what makes leftover dal taste new.
ingredients: rinsed until the water runs clear

name: Braised mackerel with daikon and bok choy
inspiredBy: Korean godeungeo-jorim, braised mackerel with radish, with less salt and heat
about: Meaty mackerel simmered with sweet daikon, onion, ginger and a little soy and chili until the sauce clings, with bok choy laid over to steam at the end. The sauce is sweetened with grated apple instead of sugar. **Mackerel is a low-mercury oily fish**, a good source of omega-3 fat (DHA), B12 and vitamin D.
steps: Cook the rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes, until tender, then drain well and keep it covered.

Wash the vegetables. Spread the daikon, carrot and onion in a wide pot. Add the ginger, garlic, soy sauce, gochugaru, grated apple and about half a cup of water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer for 12 minutes, until the daikon and carrot are nearly tender.
Nestle the mackerel pieces on top and spoon the sauce over them. Cover and simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, until the fish is opaque, flakes easily with a fork and reaches 70 °C (158 °F).
Lay the bok choy over the fish for the last 3 minutes, just until it turns bright green and tender.

Drizzle with the sesame oil and scatter with the scallion. Serve with the rice. If there are any leftovers, refrigerate them within 2 hours, eat them the next day and reheat until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Buy Atlantic mackerel or saba, never king mackerel (high mercury). Thaw frozen fillets in the fridge and cook them within 2 days.
