tip: Make a double batch on a quiet day. Before you sit down, pour half into a shallow container, cool it and freeze it within 2 hours. Thaw it in the fridge, use it within 2 days and reheat until steaming hot (74 °C).

name: Lighter chicken kabsa with brown basmati and cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Saudi and Gulf chicken kabsa and machboos, with more vegetables and less rice and fat
about: Chicken simmered with tomato, loomi and warm spices, with brown basmati rice cooked in the same pot and topped with toasted almonds. A cool cucumber and parsley salad with lemon sits beside it. It is the full, fragrant Gulf iftar plate with the rice portion trimmed and the carrot and tomato doing more of the work, and the brown basmati brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Wash the carrot, tomato, cucumber and parsley. Pat the chicken dry and rub it with half the baharat, the turmeric and a splash of the lemon juice. Cover and keep it in the fridge while you make the base. Wash your hands, knife and board after handling the raw chicken, and do not reuse that rub.

Warm the oil in a wide, heavy pot and soften the onion for 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, the rest of the baharat, the cinnamon and cardamom for 30 seconds, then add the tomato paste and grated tomato and cook for 5 minutes until jammy.
Add the loomi, the carrot, the salt and enough hot water to cover the rice by about 1.5 cm once it goes in. Stir in the rinsed rice, cover and cook on low.

After about 10 minutes, lay the chicken on top of the rice, cover again and keep cooking on low for another 25 minutes, until the rice is tender and the chicken reaches 74 °C. Added late, the chicken stays juicy instead of drying out.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, scatter them over the rice and let it rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
Toss half the cucumber and parsley with half the remaining lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Keep the other half undressed in the fridge and dress it tomorrow.

Before you sit down to eat, spoon the second portion into a shallow container and get it into the fridge within 1 hour, since rice does not wait. Eat it within 3 days and reheat it once, until steaming hot at 74 °C. Then serve the kabsa with the salad.
tip: A pressure cooker makes the brown rice ready in about 20 minutes. A spoonful of chopped green chili with tomato is the traditional daqoos on the side.

name: Baked salmon with lemon tahini and fattoush
inspiredBy: Gulf and Levantine baked fish with tarator, and a classic fattoush
about: Salmon baked with cumin and garlic and finished with a lemony tahini sauce, beside a big fattoush of romaine, cucumber, tomato and herbs with toasted khubz and a dusting of sumac. The salmon is rich and the salad is sharp and crunchy. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the peppers and tomato bring vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Wash the romaine, cucumber, tomato, pepper and herbs. If the salmon was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days.
Rub the salmon with a third of the oil, the garlic, cumin, paprika and a pinch of the salt, and lay it on a lined tray. Wash your hands after touching the raw fish.
Tear the khubz into pieces, toss with a teaspoon of the oil and bake beside the salmon for 6 to 8 minutes until crisp.
Bake the salmon for 12 to 15 minutes, until it flakes easily and reaches 70 °C.
Whisk the tahini with half the lemon juice and a splash of water until it pours like cream.
Toss the romaine, cucumber, tomato, pepper, parsley and mint with the rest of the lemon juice and oil, the sumac and the remaining salt. Add the khubz chips just before serving so they stay crunchy.
Serve the salmon with the tahini spooned over and the fattoush on the side.
tip: Trout works the same way if you prefer it.

name: Grilled beef kofta with tabbouleh and lemon tahini
inspiredBy: Levantine kofta with tabbouleh, with a little bulgur and plenty of parsley and mint
about: Herby lean beef kofta shaped on skewers and grilled until browned, with a bright tabbouleh of parsley, tomato, mint and a little bulgur, and a lemony tahini sauce. It is smoky, fresh and light. The beef brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the tabbouleh brings vitamins C and K.
steps: Wash the tomato, cucumber, parsley and mint. Cover the bulgur with boiling water by 2 cm and leave it for 15 minutes, then drain well and press out the extra water.

Mix the beef with the onion, half the parsley, the baharat, cinnamon, pepper and half the salt. Mix with your hands until it holds together, then shape it into long ovals on skewers. Wash your hands, board and bowl afterwards.
Whisk the tahini with half the lemon juice, the garlic and a splash of water until smooth and pourable.
Brush a grill pan or skillet with half the oil and cook the kofta over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until browned and the centre reaches 71 °C.
Toss the bulgur with the tomato, cucumber, the rest of the parsley, the mint, the rest of the lemon juice and oil, and the remaining salt.
Serve the kofta over the tabbouleh with the tahini sauce spooned on top.
tip: Chilling the shaped kofta for 15 minutes helps it hold on the skewer. Buy halal meat if that matters at your table.

name: Baked mackerel with cumin potatoes, chickpeas and red pepper
inspiredBy: spice-rubbed baked fish from Egypt and the Gulf coast
about: Atlantic mackerel rubbed with cumin, garlic, paprika and lemon, baked over potatoes, chickpeas, tomato and red pepper until the juices turn into a sauce, with a crunchy cucumber salad and khubz. It is rich, tangy and quick to put together. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the potatoes bring potassium.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Wash the potato, tomato, red pepper, cucumber and parsley. If the fish was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days.
Toss the potatoes, chickpeas, onion, pepper and half the oil with half the cumin and paprika and half the salt, and spread them in a baking dish. Roast for 20 minutes.

Mix the garlic, half the lemon juice, the remaining oil, cumin, paprika and a pinch of salt into a paste and rub it over the mackerel. Wash your hands and the board afterwards, and do not reuse anything that touched the raw fish.
Lay the tomato slices over the potatoes and set the mackerel on top. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes, until the fish flakes and reaches 70 °C.
Toss the cucumber with the parsley, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of black pepper and a pinch of salt. Warm the khubz.
Spoon the pan juices over the fish and potatoes and serve with the salad and khubz.
tip: Sardine fillets or trout are good in the same dish.

name: Baked lamb sambousek with fattoush
inspiredBy: Levantine and Egyptian meat sambousek, baked on a tray instead of deep-fried
about: Half-moon pastries of whole-wheat dough around spiced lamb and onion, brushed with a little oil and baked until golden and crisp, with a big lemony fattoush on the side. You get the Ramadan favourite without a pan of frying oil. The lamb brings **iron and zinc**, and the vitamin C in the salad helps you absorb that iron.
steps: Mix the flour with a pinch of the salt, a third of the oil and enough warm water to make a soft, smooth dough. Knead for 5 minutes, then cover and rest for 20 minutes.

Soften the onion in a teaspoon of the oil for 4 minutes. Add the lamb, cumin, cinnamon, baharat and half the remaining salt and cook, breaking it up, until no pink remains and it reaches 71 °C. Stir in a squeeze of the lemon juice and let it cool. Wash your hands, board and spoon after handling the raw lamb.
Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Roll the dough thin, cut circles about 10 cm wide, fill each with a spoonful of lamb, fold into half-moons and press the edges closed with a fork.
Arrange on a lined tray, brush with the remaining oil and bake for 15 to 18 minutes, until golden and crisp.
Wash the romaine, cucumber, tomato and herbs. Toss them with the rest of the lemon juice, the sumac and a pinch of salt.
Serve the hot sambousek with the fattoush.
tip: A serving makes about five pastries at Standard, a few fewer at Light and more at Big. Freeze extra unbaked pastries on a tray, then bake straight from frozen, adding about 6 minutes, until golden and hot all the way through (74 °C). Keep this a once-a-week treat.

name: Baked trout over caramelized onion and cumin brown rice
inspiredBy: sayadiyah, the fisherman's rice of the Levant and Egypt, with baked trout
about: Trout fillets baked with lemon and garlic, over brown basmati cooked in a deep, sweet base of slowly browned onions and cumin, with a fresh tomato and cucumber salad. It is fragrant, savoury and complete on one plate. The trout brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the onions and cumin give the rice its colour and flavour.
steps: Wash the tomato, cucumber and parsley. If the trout was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days.
Warm most of the oil in a wide pot and cook the onions over medium-low heat for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until deep golden brown. Take out about a third for the top.

Stir the cumin and turmeric into the pot for 20 seconds, add the rinsed rice, half the salt and enough hot water to cover the rice by 1.5 cm. Cover and cook on low for about 35 minutes, until the rice is tender.

When the rice has about 15 minutes left, heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Rub the trout with the garlic, half the lemon juice and the rest of the oil, season with the pepper and a pinch of salt, and bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until it flakes and reaches 70 °C. Wash your hands after handling the raw fish.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden.
Toss the tomato and cucumber with the parsley, the rest of the lemon juice and the remaining salt.
Serve the trout over the rice, topped with the reserved onions and the almonds, with the salad alongside.
tip: If you cook extra rice, spread it in a shallow container so it cools within 1 hour, refrigerate it within 2 hours and use it within 3 days.

name: Watermelon with white cheese and mint
inspiredBy: the Egyptian summer pairing of watermelon and white cheese
about: Cold watermelon cubes with crumbled feta and fresh mint, a favourite Egyptian pairing. Sweet, salty and cooling. The watermelon is mostly water, and the cheese brings a little **calcium and protein**.
steps: Wash the outside of the watermelon before cutting. Cut it into cubes and chill them.
Scatter over the feta and mint just before serving.

name: Pomegranate yogurt with walnuts and cinnamon
about: Thick plain yogurt topped with ruby pomegranate seeds, toasted walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. Creamy, tart and crunchy. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Wash the pomegranate before cutting, then pop out the seeds.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the seeds, walnuts and cinnamon.

name: Warm saffron and cardamom milk with almonds and walnuts
inspiredBy: Gulf spiced milk, unsweetened
about: A mug of warm milk steeped with saffron and cardamom, with a handful of almonds and walnuts on the side. Soothing before bed, with no added sugar. The milk brings **calcium and B12**, and the nuts bring vitamin E and plant omega-3.
steps: Warm the milk with the cardamom and saffron in a small pot over low heat for 4 minutes, until steaming. Watch it so it does not boil over.
Pour into a mug and serve with the almonds and walnuts.

name: Cumin and lemon roasted chickpeas
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp with a little oil, cumin and paprika, then squeezed with lemon. A salty-crunchy snack with real staying power. The chickpeas bring **fibre, folate and plant protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Pat the chickpeas very dry with a towel.
Toss with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt and spread on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking once, until crisp. Squeeze over the lemon juice and eat the same day.
ingredients: no salt added, drained and patted very dry

name: Dried apricot and laban cooler, qamar al-din style
inspiredBy: qamar al-din, the apricot drink of Ramadan, with no added sugar
about: Dried apricots soaked and blended with yogurt and cardamom into a thick, tangy, fruity cooler, with no sugar added. A treat for the evening that still carries some protein. The apricots bring **fibre and vitamin A**, and the yogurt brings calcium.
steps: Soak the apricots in warm water for 20 minutes, then drain.
Blend the apricots with the yogurt, cardamom and a splash of cold water until smooth. Chill and serve cold.
tip: A treat, not a daily habit, because dried fruit is concentrated sugar.
ingredients: unsulphured if you can find them

name: Yogurt with fresh figs, walnuts and almonds
about: Thick plain yogurt topped with split fresh figs, chopped walnuts and almonds and a pinch of cinnamon. Creamy, sweet and nutty. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the nuts bring vitamin E and plant omega-3.
steps: Wash the figs and cut them in half.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the figs, walnuts, almonds and cinnamon.
tip: Fresh figs, watermelon and pomegranate are seasonal: use dried figs or whatever fruit is good where you live.

name: Hummus with red pepper and carrot sticks
about: Creamy homemade hummus with lemon, garlic and a little tahini, scooped up with crunchy red pepper and carrot sticks. Fresh and filling. The chickpeas bring **fibre, folate and plant protein**.
steps: Wash the pepper and carrot and cut them into sticks.
Blend the chickpeas with the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, cumin, salt and a splash of cold water until very smooth.
Spoon into a bowl, drizzle with the oil and serve with the sticks. The hummus keeps up to 3 days in the fridge.

name: Minted laban
inspiredBy: Gulf and Levantine laban, a cool thinned yogurt drink
about: Plain yogurt whisked with cold water, dried and fresh mint and a pinch of salt until it pours like a thick drink, served over ice. It is cooling, tangy and the classic way to end a fast. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Wash and chop the mint.
Whisk the yogurt with cold water, the mint and the salt until smooth and pourable. Serve over ice.
tip: Drink a glass of water with every snack to spread your fluids between iftar and suhoor.

name: Orange segments with roasted almonds and mint
about: Juicy orange segments with a handful of almonds and a little torn mint. Fresh and light, with a crunch. The orange brings **vitamin C**, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Wash the orange, then peel it and cut it into segments over a bowl to keep the juice.
Scatter over the almonds and mint and serve.

name: Date-sweetened mahalabia with cardamom and almonds
inspiredBy: mahalabia, the Arab milk pudding of the Ramadan table, lightened and sweetened with a date
about: A soft, silky milk pudding scented with cardamom, set with a little cornstarch and sweetened with mashed date instead of sugar syrup, topped with chopped almonds. It is the gentle sweet to end the evening. The milk brings **calcium and B12**, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Whisk the cornstarch into a few spoonfuls of the cold milk until smooth.
Heat the rest of the milk with the mashed date and cardamom in a small pot over medium heat, stirring, until it steams. Watch it so it does not boil over.
Stir in the cornstarch mixture and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon; it sets a little more as it cools.
Pour into a bowl, top with the almonds and eat warm, or chill it in the fridge for up to 2 days.
tip: Tea and coffee are fine after iftar; keep them light at suhoor, since they make you pass more water.

name: Whole-wheat khubz with labneh, tomato and mint
about: Warm whole-wheat khubz spread with thick labneh and topped with sliced tomato and fresh mint. Cool, tangy and filling. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Wash the tomato and mint. Warm the khubz in a dry pan until soft.
Spread with the labneh, then top with the tomato and mint. Fold and eat.

name: Dates stuffed with walnuts
about: Soft medjool dates filled with walnut, with the rest of the walnuts alongside. A classic Ramadan sweet bite with a little crunch. The dates bring **potassium and fibre**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Split the dates and take out the pits.
Tuck a walnut half inside each date, press closed, and eat the rest of the walnuts alongside.

name: Apple, walnut and almond overnight oats with milk and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Canadian overnight oats, set up after iftar so suhoor takes no cooking
about: Rolled oats soaked overnight in milk and yogurt with grated apple, walnuts, almonds and cinnamon. It is thick, cold and creamy, and it is waiting in the fridge when the alarm goes. The oats and milk digest slowly, so they carry you through the day, and the milk and yogurt bring **protein and calcium**.
steps: After iftar, stir the oats, milk, yogurt, cinnamon and the pinch of salt together in a jar or bowl. Cover and put it in the fridge to soak overnight, at least 4 hours.
At suhoor, wash the apple and grate it, skin and all. Stir half of it into the oats, loosening them with a splash of cold milk or water if they have thickened too much.
Top with the rest of the apple, the walnuts and the almonds.
Soaked oats keep in the fridge for up to 3 days, so you can mix two nights at once.
tip: Leave the apple out and use a few spoonfuls of mashed pear if you prefer.

name: Turkish-style spinach and eggs with tomato and warm pita
inspiredBy: Turkish ıspanaklı yumurta, spinach with eggs
about: Spinach wilted with onion and garlic and a few chickpeas, with eggs set right in the pan and cooked until the yolks are firm. It comes with sliced tomato and warm pita, and only a pinch of salt. The eggs and spinach bring **protein, choline and iron**, and the tomato helps you absorb that iron.
steps: Wash the spinach and tomato, and slice the tomato.
Warm the oil in a lidded skillet over medium heat. Soften the onion and garlic for about 4 minutes, until the onion is soft and just starting to colour.
Add the spinach a handful at a time and stir until wilted, about 2 minutes. Stir in the chickpeas and season with the Aleppo pepper, black pepper and salt.
Make small wells in the spinach and crack the eggs into them. Cover and cook on low for 8 to 10 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are firm, not runny.
Warm the pita while the eggs cook, then serve everything with the tomato.
tip: Short on time before dawn? Wilt the spinach after iftar, chill it within 2 hours, then reheat it until steaming hot (74 °C) before you crack the eggs in. Use it within 2 days. Have a glass of water, or a small glass of milk or ayran, with it.

name: Turkish-style suhoor plate with labneh, boiled egg, tomato, cucumber and almonds
inspiredBy: Turkish kahvaltı, the breakfast table
about: The kind of plate you would find on a Turkish breakfast table, built for suhoor: creamy labneh, a boiled egg, juicy tomato and cucumber, almonds and pita, with a pear to finish. There is hardly any salt on it. The egg and labneh bring **protein, choline and calcium**, and the vegetables and pear bring water and fibre.
steps: Put the egg in a small pot of cold water, bring it to a boil, then simmer for 10 minutes, until the yolk is firm. Cool it under cold water. If you boil it ahead, chill it within 2 hours in its shell and peel it just before eating. It keeps up to a week.
Wash the tomato, cucumber and pear. Slice them and fan them on a plate.
Spread the labneh on the plate, drizzle it with the olive oil and sprinkle with the dried mint and pepper.
Add the egg, halved, and the almonds. Serve with the warm pita.
tip: Put a few slices of tomato and cucumber on the table at iftar too. They help you start rehydrating.

name: Dates, water and mercimek çorbası (Turkish red lentil soup)
inspiredBy: Turkish mercimek çorbası, the lentil soup of iftar tables
about: Break the fast with dates and water, then a bowl of velvety red lentil soup with carrot and a little tomato paste, finished with Aleppo pepper, dried mint and lemon. It is warm, gentle on an empty stomach and quick to make. The lentils bring **iron, folate and protein**, and the lemon helps your body use that iron.
steps: Rinse the lentils until the water runs clear. Wash and dice the carrot and onion.
Warm the oil in a pot and soften the onion and carrot for about 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, cumin, paprika and tomato paste and cook for a minute, until the paste darkens.
Add the lentils and enough water to cover by about 4 cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until everything is very soft.
Blend the soup smooth with an immersion blender. Season with the salt, black pepper and half the lemon juice, adding water if it is too thick.
Before you sit down, ladle the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. Reheat it once tomorrow until steaming hot, 74 °C. It keeps up to 3 days.

To open the fast, eat the dates with a glass of water, then ladle out the soup. Take a short pause before the main plate. Finish each bowl with the rest of the lemon, the Aleppo pepper and the dried mint.
tip: A warm pita alongside is the classic way to eat it.

name: Dates, water and Moroccan harira (tomato, lentil and chickpea soup with egg)
inspiredBy: Moroccan harira, the soup that opens the fast across the Maghreb
about: Dates and water first, then the soup Moroccan families break the fast with all month: tomatoes, lentils and chickpeas simmered with celery, spinach, cilantro and parsley, with ginger and cinnamon, brightened with lemon and finished with a beaten egg stirred through. It is hearty and tangy. The lentils and chickpeas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the tomatoes and lemon bring vitamin C.
steps: Rinse the lentils. Wash and dice the celery, dice the onion, and wash and chop the spinach, cilantro and parsley.
Warm the oil in a pot and soften the onion and celery for about 6 minutes. Stir in the ginger, turmeric, cinnamon and pepper for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes with their juice, the lentils, the chickpeas and about 600 ml water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 25 minutes, until the lentils are tender.

Stir in the spinach, cilantro, parsley, salt and lemon juice. Bring it back to a gentle boil and pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream, stirring, until it sets in ribbons, 1 to 2 minutes. Make sure the egg is fully cooked, with nothing runny.
Before you sit down, ladle the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. Reheat it once tomorrow until steaming hot, 74 °C. It keeps up to 3 days.
To open the fast, eat the dates with a glass of water, then ladle out the soup. Take a short pause before the main plate.
tip: Many cooks also stir in a few broken vermicelli noodles or a spoon of cooked rice at the end.

name: Dates, water and Canadian lentil and vegetable soup
inspiredBy: a Canadian lentil and vegetable soup
about: Dates and water, then a thick, hearty lentil soup with carrot, celery, onion and tomato, wilted spinach and a bay leaf, finished with lemon. It is the kind of pot a Canadian kitchen makes all winter, and it is even better the next day. The lentils bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the spinach and tomato bring vitamins A and C.
steps: Rinse the lentils. Wash and dice the carrot and celery, dice the onion, and wash the spinach.
Warm the oil in a pot and soften the onion, carrot and celery for about 7 minutes. Add the garlic and thyme and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the lentils, the tomatoes, the bay leaf and about 700 ml water. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 25 minutes, until the lentils are tender.
Stir in the spinach for the last 3 minutes. Remove the bay leaf and season with the salt, pepper and lemon juice.
Before you sit down, ladle the second portion into a shallow container, cool it, and get it into the fridge within 2 hours. Reheat it once tomorrow until steaming hot, 74 °C. It keeps up to 3 days.
To open the fast, eat the dates with a glass of water, then ladle out the soup. Take a short pause before the main plate.
tip: Mash a few spoonfuls of the lentils against the side of the pot to thicken it.

name: Dates, water and roasted butternut and red lentil soup
inspiredBy: Canadian roasted squash soup, with red lentils for body
about: Dates and water first, then a silky soup of roasted butternut squash and red lentils with ginger, cumin and a squeeze of lemon, topped with toasted pumpkin seeds. It is warm, sweet from the squash and surprisingly filling. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**, and the lentils bring protein and iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 210 °C (410 °F). Peel, seed and cube the squash, toss it with half the oil and a pinch of the salt and roast on a tray for 25 to 30 minutes, until soft and browned at the edges. If you like, roast the eggplant for the stew on a second tray alongside.

Meanwhile, warm the rest of the oil in a pot and soften the onion for 5 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger and cumin and stir for 30 seconds. Add the rinsed lentils and 600 ml water and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the roasted squash and blend smooth with an immersion blender. Season with the rest of the salt, the pepper, cinnamon and lemon juice.
Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they start to pop.
To open the fast, eat the dates with a glass of water, then ladle out the soup and top with the pumpkin seeds. Take a short pause before the main plate.
tip: Make a double batch. Before you sit down, pour the extra into shallow containers, cool it and freeze it within 2 hours. Thaw it in the fridge, use it within 2 days and reheat until steaming hot (74 °C).

name: Sheet-pan lemon-oregano chicken thighs with sweet potato, broccoli and garlic yogurt
inspiredBy: a Canadian sheet-pan dinner with Turkish and Mediterranean flavours
about: Boneless chicken thighs, sweet potato and broccoli roasted together on one tray with lemon, garlic and oregano, with a cool garlicky yogurt sauce and a warm pita. It is easy weeknight iftar food, and the second portion reheats well. The chicken brings **protein, zinc and B vitamins**, and the sweet potato and broccoli bring vitamins A and C.
steps: Wash the sweet potatoes, broccoli and parsley. Whisk half the oil with the lemon juice, half the garlic, the oregano, paprika, pepper and half the salt. Coat the chicken in it in a covered bowl in the fridge for at least 20 minutes, and never reuse the leftover marinade.

Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Toss the sweet potato wedges with the rest of the oil and a pinch of salt and roast on a large tray for 15 minutes. If the tray looks crowded, use two trays and swap them halfway.

Add the chicken to the tray and roast 10 minutes. Add the broccoli and roast another 10 to 12 minutes, until the chicken reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest part and the vegetables are browned at the edges. Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw chicken.
Stir the rest of the garlic and salt into the yogurt with the parsley and a splash of water.

Before you sit down, put the second portion of chicken and vegetables in a shallow container and into the fridge within 2 hours, and keep the yogurt sauce in its own covered container. Then serve the first portion with the yogurt and the warm pita.
Eat the second portion within 3 days, reheated once to 74 °C (165 °F) all the way through, and serve the garlic yogurt cold.
tip: Buy halal chicken at a halal butcher or the halal counter of your supermarket. Swap the sweet potato for squash or potato if you like.

name: Lemon-herb roasted salmon with potatoes, carrots and broccoli
inspiredBy: Canadian roasted salmon and vegetables
about: A salmon fillet rubbed with lemon, garlic and parsley and roasted on one tray beside crisp-edged potatoes, carrots and broccoli, with the pan juices spooned over. It is a classic Canadian fish supper, simple and tasty. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the broccoli and lemon bring vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Wash the potatoes, carrots, broccoli and parsley. If the salmon was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days.
Toss the potatoes and carrots with two thirds of the oil and half the salt and roast on a large tray for 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, rub the salmon with half the lemon juice, the garlic, the paprika and half the parsley. Wash your hands after touching the raw fish. Toss the broccoli with the rest of the oil.
Make room on the tray and add the broccoli and the salmon together. Roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the salmon flakes easily and reaches 70 °C (158 °F).
Squeeze the rest of the lemon juice over everything and scatter with the rest of the parsley and a pinch of pepper.
Serve the salmon on the vegetables with the pan juices spooned over.
tip: Frozen salmon fillets work well. Thaw them in the fridge overnight.

name: Turkish köfte with bulgur pilav and shepherd salad (çoban salatası)
inspiredBy: Turkish köfte with pilav and çoban salatası
about: Juicy beef and parsley köfte seasoned with cumin and Aleppo pepper, with a tomato bulgur pilav and a crisp, lemony shepherd salad of tomato, cucumber and red pepper. A spoon of yogurt cools it all. The beef brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the tomato, pepper and lemon bring vitamin C to help you absorb that iron.
steps: Wash the parsley, tomato, cucumber and pepper. Grate half the onion into a bowl, squeeze out some of the liquid, and mix in the beef, half the parsley, the cumin, Aleppo pepper, pepper and a third of the salt. Knead for a minute, shape into small oval patties and chill for 15 minutes. Wash your hands afterwards.

For the pilav, soften the rest of the onion, diced, in a third of the oil for 4 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste, then the bulgur, and add enough water to cover it by about 1 cm. Cover and simmer for 12 minutes, then rest it off the heat for 5 minutes and fluff.
Cook the köfte in a hot, lightly oiled pan or under a hot broiler for 4 to 5 minutes a side, until browned and cooked through to 71 °C (160 °F).
Toss the tomato, cucumber, red pepper and the rest of the parsley with the lemon juice, the rest of the oil, the sumac and a pinch of salt.
Serve the köfte with the pilav, the salad and the yogurt.
Put any leftover pilav into a shallow container and into the fridge within 1 hour.
tip: Buy halal ground beef. Köfte freeze well raw: freeze a tray of them, thaw in the fridge and use within 2 days.
ingredients: grated for the köfte and diced for the pilav

name: Moroccan-style chicken and chickpea skillet with apricots and warm pita
inspiredBy: Moroccan chicken tagine with chickpeas and dried fruit, cooked in a skillet
about: Chicken thighs braised with onion, tomato, chickpeas, a little dried apricot and warm spices (ras el hanout, ginger, cinnamon), with fresh cilantro and lemon, and warm pita to scoop it up the way a tagine is eaten. It is fragrant, sweet and savoury and cooks in one pan. The chicken and chickpeas bring **protein, iron and zinc**, and the tomato and lemon bring vitamin C.
steps: Wash the cilantro. Toss the chicken with the ras el hanout, ginger, cinnamon, pepper and a pinch of the salt.
Warm half the oil in a wide, lidded skillet over medium-high heat and brown the chicken for 4 minutes, turning. Take it out, and wash your hands and the board.
In the same pan, soften the onion in the rest of the oil for 6 minutes. Add the garlic for 30 seconds, then the tomatoes, apricots, chickpeas and 150 ml water.
Return the chicken, cover and simmer for 20 minutes, until the chicken reaches 74 °C (165 °F) and the sauce is thick. Stir in the rest of the salt and the lemon juice.
Scatter with the cilantro and serve with the warm pita. Chill any leftovers in a shallow container within 2 hours and reheat once to 74 °C.
tip: Buy halal chicken. Add a few green olives, rinsed, if you like the classic taste.

name: Chermoula-baked trout with roasted broccoli, red pepper and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Moroccan chermoula fish
about: Rainbow trout baked under a green chermoula of cilantro, parsley, garlic, cumin and lemon, with broccoli, red pepper and chickpeas roasted until golden, and warm pita to scoop up the juices. It is bright, herby and flaky. The trout brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the chickpeas bring iron and fibre.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Wash the broccoli, red pepper and herbs. If the trout was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days.
Toss the red pepper and chickpeas with a third of the oil, the paprika, half the cumin and half the salt and roast on a large tray for 12 minutes. Add the broccoli and roast 10 more minutes.
Stir the cilantro, parsley, garlic, the rest of the cumin, the lemon juice, the rest of the oil, a pinch of salt and the pepper into a loose chermoula.
Spread two thirds of the chermoula over the trout and leave it in the fridge for 10 minutes. Never reuse the marinade. Wash your hands after touching the raw fish.
Push the vegetables aside, lay the trout on the tray and bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until it flakes easily and reaches 70 °C (158 °F).
Serve with the rest of the chermoula spooned over and the warm pita.
tip: Any fatty fish works with chermoula. Salmon is a good stand-in.

name: Turkish-style beef, eggplant and lentil stew with bulgur and yogurt
inspiredBy: Turkish and Moroccan lentil and eggplant pots, with a little beef
about: A thick stew of lean beef, eggplant and green lentils simmered in tomato and red pepper with cumin, paprika and a little Aleppo pepper, with spinach stirred in, piled over bulgur with yogurt and parsley. It is smoky, hearty and the best kind of Sunday pot. The lentils and beef bring **iron, zinc and protein**, and the tomato, pepper and lemon bring vitamin C.
steps: Rinse the lentils. Wash the eggplant, red pepper, spinach and parsley. Toss the eggplant cubes with a third of the oil and roast them at 220 °C (425 °F) for 20 minutes, or alongside the squash at 210 °C (410 °F) for about 25 minutes, until golden and soft.

Warm the rest of the oil in a pot and brown the beef for 5 minutes, breaking it up. Add the onion and red pepper and cook for 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, cumin, paprika, Aleppo pepper and tomato paste for a minute. Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw beef.

Add the lentils, the tomatoes and 400 ml water. Simmer for 25 minutes, until the lentils are tender and the beef is cooked through to 71 °C (160 °F). Stir in the roasted eggplant, spinach, salt, pepper and the lemon juice and cook 3 minutes more.
Cook the bulgur: cover it with water by 1 cm, simmer for 12 minutes, then rest 5 minutes and fluff. Cool any leftover bulgur in a shallow container within 1 hour.
Spoon the stew over the bulgur and top with the yogurt and parsley.
tip: Buy halal ground beef. Roast the eggplant and the squash for the soup together, so the oven is used once. The stew keeps up to 3 days in the fridge, or freeze single portions, thaw in the fridge, use within 2 days and reheat to 74 °C (165 °F).

name: Ayran with mint
inspiredBy: Turkish ayran
about: Plain yogurt whisked with cold water, a pinch of salt and dried mint until it pours like a thick drink. It is cooling, tangy and the everyday drink of Turkish tables. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Whisk the yogurt with the salt and dried mint, then whisk in cold water, about 150 ml for every 200 g of yogurt, until smooth and pourable.
Serve over ice, or chill it for up to 2 days.
tip: A glass of water with every snack helps spread your fluids between iftar and suhoor.

name: Orange slices with cinnamon and orange blossom
inspiredBy: Moroccan orange with cinnamon, a light finish on the iftar table
about: Cold orange rounds with a dusting of cinnamon and a few drops of orange blossom water, the simple Moroccan fruit plate that ends many iftars. It is juicy, fragrant and refreshing. The orange brings **vitamin C** and a little extra fluid for the evening.
steps: Wash the orange, cut away the peel and white pith with a sharp knife, and slice it into thin rounds.
Fan the slices on a plate, sprinkle with the orange blossom water and dust with the cinnamon. Chill for 15 minutes if you have time.

name: Lighter sütlaç (Turkish rice pudding with less sugar)
inspiredBy: Turkish sütlaç with much less sugar
about: A small bowl of creamy Turkish rice pudding, made with milk, a little rice and a mashed date for a gentle sweetness, scented with cinnamon and topped with a few walnuts. It is lighter than the usual one, and it is the week's first small sweet. The milk brings **calcium and B12**.
steps: Rinse the rice, put it in a small pot with 100 ml water and simmer for 10 minutes, until the water is mostly absorbed.
Add the milk and the mashed date. Simmer on low for 15 minutes, stirring often so it does not catch, until it is thick and creamy.
Pour into a bowl and top with the walnuts and cinnamon. Eat it warm, or cool it within 1 hour, chill it and eat it within 2 days.
tip: Use a small heavy-bottomed pot and keep the heat low, because the milk catches easily. For fırın sütlaç, the baked kind, slide the bowl under a hot broiler for a minute, until golden on top.

name: Cumin and paprika roasted chickpeas
about: No-salt-added chickpeas roasted until crisp with oil, cumin and paprika. They are crunchy, savoury and easy to make ahead. The chickpeas bring **fibre, iron and protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Pat the chickpeas very dry.
Toss them with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt and spread them on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray twice, until crisp. Squeeze the lemon over them.
tip: Eat them the same evening for the best crunch. They soften as they sit.

name: Carrot and cucumber sticks with parsley labneh
about: Crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks with a bowl of labneh stirred with garlic, lemon and parsley. It is cool and fresh and easy on the stomach in the evening. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**, and the carrots bring vitamin A.
steps: Wash the carrot, cucumber and parsley, and cut the vegetables into sticks.
Stir the labneh with the parsley, lemon juice, garlic and salt.
Serve the sticks with the dip.

name: Pear with walnuts
about: A ripe pear, sliced, with a small handful of walnuts. It is soft and crunchy together. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fat**, and the pear brings fibre.
steps: Wash and slice the pear.
Serve with the walnuts.

name: Yogurt with apple, cinnamon and toasted pumpkin seeds
about: Plain yogurt with diced apple, a dusting of cinnamon and toasted pumpkin seeds. It is creamy, tart and crunchy. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the pumpkin seeds bring magnesium and zinc.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they start to pop.
Wash and dice the apple, spoon the yogurt into a bowl, and top with the apple, seeds and cinnamon.

name: Warm cardamom milk with almonds
about: A mug of warm milk with a pinch of cardamom and cinnamon, with a small handful of almonds on the side. It is gentle and comforting before bed. The milk brings **calcium, B12 and protein**, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Heat the milk with the cardamom and cinnamon in a small pot, until it steams. Do not let it boil over.
Pour into a mug and serve with the almonds.

name: Baked apple with dates, walnuts and cinnamon
inspiredBy: a Canadian baked apple with a Turkish date filling
about: A whole apple cored and stuffed with chopped date, walnuts and cinnamon, baked until soft. It is warm, sweet from the fruit and a little crunchy, and it is the week's second small sweet. The apple brings **fibre**, and the walnuts bring omega-3 fat.
steps: Heat the oven to 180 °C (350 °F). Wash the apple and core it, leaving the bottom closed.
Mix the date, walnuts and cinnamon and pack it into the apple. Stand it in a small dish with 3 tablespoons of water.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the apple is soft when pierced with a knife.
Serve warm, with the pan juices spooned over.
tip: Bake two and keep the second one covered in the fridge for up to 3 days. Eat it cold, or reheat it until steaming hot (74 °C).

name: Whole-wheat pita with labneh, cucumber and mint
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with labneh, with sliced cucumber and dried mint folded inside. It is light, cooling and filling. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Wash the cucumber and warm the pita.
Spread it with the labneh, add the cucumber and mint, drizzle with the oil and fold.

name: Orange wedges with walnuts and cinnamon
about: A juicy orange cut into wedges, with a small handful of walnuts and a pinch of cinnamon. It is fresh and a little crunchy. The orange brings **vitamin C**, and the walnuts bring omega-3 fat.
steps: Wash the orange and cut it into wedges.
Serve with the walnuts and dust the orange with the cinnamon.

name: Dried apricots with walnuts
inspiredBy: a Turkish-style fruit and nut plate
about: A small plate of soft dried apricots with walnut halves. It is chewy and crunchy and sweet from the fruit alone. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fat**, and the apricots bring fibre and potassium.
steps: Serve the apricots with the walnuts.

name: Palak anda bhurji with a lighter whole-wheat paratha, dahi and apple
inspiredBy: Pakistani and North Indian anda bhurji, with a paratha roasted in a spoonful of oil instead of fried
about: Soft, fully set scrambled eggs with spinach, onion, tomato, green chili and cilantro, a whole-wheat paratha roasted on a dry pan with only a brush of oil, cool dahi and a crisp apple. It is slow and filling before the fast, and the salt is held low on purpose. The eggs and whole wheat bring **protein, choline and fibre**, the spinach adds vitamin K and folate, and the dahi adds calcium.
steps: Wash the tomato, spinach, cilantro and apple. Knead the flour with a splash of warm water into a soft dough, cover it and rest it for 15 minutes.

Roll the dough into a round about 18 cm across, brush the top with a little of the oil, fold it in half and in half again, then roll it out again into a small triangle or round, so it has soft layers.
Roast the paratha on a hot dry pan for about 1 minute a side, brushing a few drops of oil on each side, until it has golden spots and puffs a little. Keep it warm under a clean cloth.

Warm the rest of the oil in a small non-stick pan and soften the onion with the turmeric and cumin for 3 minutes. Add the tomato, chili and spinach and cook until the tomato breaks down and the spinach wilts, about 3 minutes.
Pour in the beaten eggs with the salt and stir gently over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until there is no runny egg left and the eggs are firm and reach 74 °C. Fold in the cilantro.
Serve the bhurji with the paratha, a bowl of dahi and the sliced apple, and a big glass of water.
tip: Knead the dough after iftar and keep it covered in the fridge overnight, so suhoor is only the rolling and the pan. Dough keeps for 2 days in the fridge. Plain Greek-style yogurt or hung curd gives the thick dahi these dishes want.

name: Palak daliya with moong, peanuts, dahi and an orange
inspiredBy: North Indian and Pakistani daliya khichdi, broken wheat cooked with moong dal and vegetables
about: Cracked wheat simmered with moong dal, carrot, peas, spinach, onion and ginger until soft and porridge-like, tempered with cumin and topped with roasted peanuts like an upma, with a bowl of dahi and an orange on the side. It digests slowly and stays gentle on a dry mouth, with almost no added salt. The wheat and moong bring **fibre, folate and plant protein**, and the dahi adds calcium.
steps: Wash the carrot, spinach, cilantro and orange. Drain the moong you soaked in the fridge, and rinse the daliya.
Warm the oil in a small pressure cooker or heavy pot, add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 10 seconds. Add the onion and ginger and cook for 3 minutes until soft.
Stir in the turmeric, moong, daliya, carrot and peas, then add about four times their volume in water and the salt.

Pressure cook for 3 whistles, about 12 minutes, or cover and simmer on low for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring now and then, until the moong and wheat are soft and the porridge is thick. Add a splash of hot water if it gets stiff.
Stir in the spinach and cilantro for the last 2 minutes. Serve warm topped with the peanuts, with the dahi, the peeled orange and a big glass of water.
tip: Soak the moong in the fridge after iftar and make the whole pot before dawn in a pressure cooker, or cook it the evening before, chill it in a shallow container within 1 hour and reheat it until steaming hot (74 °C) for suhoor. Keeps up to 3 days.
ingredients: whole green moong, soaked in the fridge overnight or for at least 4 hours and drained

name: Masala oats with a firm boiled egg and apple
inspiredBy: Indian masala oats, cooked like a savoury upma with tomato, peas and spinach
about: Rolled oats cooked with onion, tomato, peas, spinach, ginger and cumin into a warm, savoury porridge, finished with roasted peanuts, with a firm boiled egg, a bowl of dahi and a crisp apple on the side. Oats are slow to digest, so this is a steady start to the fast with very little salt. The oats, egg and dahi bring **fibre, protein and choline**, and the oats and egg bring iron, which the tomato helps you absorb.
steps: Wash the tomato, spinach and apple. Lower the egg into a small pot of boiling water, cook it for 10 minutes so the yolk is firm, then cool it under cold water and peel it.
Warm the oil in a pan, add the cumin seeds for 10 seconds, then the onion, ginger and chili and cook for 3 minutes until the onion is soft.
Add the tomato, turmeric and peas and cook for 3 minutes, until the tomato breaks down.

Stir in the oats, salt and about 300 ml hot water. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until the oats are soft and the mixture is a thick upma, not a wet porridge. Fold in the spinach for the last minute until it wilts, then rest it for 1 minute under a lid.
Top with the peanuts. Serve with the halved egg, the dahi, the sliced apple and a big glass of water.
tip: This is a modern, home-style take on masala oats. The egg can be boiled after iftar and kept in its shell in the fridge for up to 3 days. Short on time? Skip the cooking: soak the oats overnight in a little water in the fridge, then warm them through with the cooked tomato mixture until steaming.
ingredients: boiled until the yolk is firm
unsalted if you can, roughly chopped

name: Dates, water and a dahi fruit chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani iftar fruit chaat, with thick dahi and no sugar syrup
about: The traditional opening, a date, or about three small dates (30 g), and a glass of water, then a bowl of orange, ripe pear and pomegranate folded through thick dahi with lemon, chaat masala and black pepper, and roasted peanuts for crunch. It is the sweet-and-sour fruit chaat of every Pakistani iftar table without the added sugar. The dahi and peanuts bring **protein**, the fruit brings vitamin C and potassium, and the dates bring quick energy.
steps: Wash the orange, pear and pomegranate well before cutting.
Dice the pear, segment the orange, and take the seeds from the pomegranate.
Fold the fruit through the dahi with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black pepper, and chill it for 10 minutes so the flavours come together. Keep cut fruit and chaat chilled until you eat.
Break your fast with a date, or about three small dates, and a glass of water. Then eat the chaat, topped with the crushed peanuts just before serving so they stay crisp.
tip: Plain Greek-style yogurt or hung curd gives the thick dahi these dishes want. Cut the fruit just before iftar and keep it chilled.
ingredients: one large, or a few small ones

name: Dates, water and a chana chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani and North Indian chana chaat, with no fried papri or sweet chutney
about: A date, or about three small dates (30 g), and a glass of water to open the fast, then a big bowl of chickpeas tossed with onion, tomato, cucumber, mint, pomegranate, roasted peanuts and chaat masala. It is the zesty chickpea chaat of the Lahore iftar table without the fried papri or sweet chutney. The chickpeas bring **fibre, folate and plant protein**.
steps: Wash the tomato, cucumber, herbs and pomegranate. Drain and rinse the chickpeas.
Chop the onion, tomato, cucumber, chili, cilantro and mint small, and take the seeds from the pomegranate.
Toss everything except the peanuts in a bowl with the lemon juice, chaat masala, cumin and salt. Taste, and add lemon if it is not sharp enough.
Let it stand for 5 minutes. Break your fast with a date, or about three small dates, and a glass of water, then eat the chaat topped with the peanuts.
tip: Cook dried chickpeas if you prefer. Soak about 250 g overnight in the fridge, then boil until tender (about 1 hour, or 15 minutes in a pressure cooker). That makes about three portions. Cool them in a shallow container within 1 hour and keep them in the fridge for up to 3 days.
ingredients: one large, or a few small ones
no salt added, drained and rinsed

name: Dates, water and baked onion pakora with mint dahi
inspiredBy: Pakistani and North Indian iftar pakora, baked on a tray in a little oil instead of deep fried
about: Crisp besan fritters of thinly sliced onion, green chili, cilantro and ajwain, baked on a tray with only a brush of oil, with a thick mint and dahi chutney. You still get the crunch of the iftar piyaz pakora, and a date, or about three small dates (30 g), and a glass of water start the meal. The chickpea flour and dahi bring **protein and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F) and line a baking tray with parchment. Wash the chili, cilantro and mint.

Toss the onion with the salt and leave it for 5 minutes, so it softens and lets out a little juice. Whisk the besan with the ajwain, cumin, kashmiri chili and turmeric, then stir in the onion and its juice, the chili and cilantro. Add water a spoonful at a time, about 2 to 3 tablespoons, until every slice is coated in a thick batter.
Brush the parchment with half the oil. Drop spoonfuls of the mixture onto the tray, flatten them slightly, and brush the tops with the rest of the oil.
Bake for 12 minutes, turn them over and bake for 8 to 10 minutes more, until golden and crisp at the edges.
Blend or finely chop the mint with the dahi and lemon juice for the chutney.
Break your fast with a date, or about three small dates, and a glass of water. Serve the pakora hot with the chutney.
tip: No oven? Shallow-fry the spoonfuls in a non-stick pan with a spoonful of oil, 3 minutes a side, and drain them well on paper towel. Pakora are best eaten the same day.
ingredients: one large, or a few small ones

name: Dates, water and a sprouted moong and egg chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Bengali sprouted moong chaat, boiled, with chickpeas and egg
about: A date, or about three small dates (30 g), and a glass of water, then a bowl of boiled moong sprouts and chickpeas with a firm chopped egg, cucumber, tomato, onion and pomegranate, folded through thick dahi, finished with lemon, chaat masala and a few roasted peanuts. The sprouts are boiled for a full 4 minutes, so they are cooked through but keep a little bite. The egg, chickpeas and dahi bring **protein, choline and calcium**, and the sprouts add folate.
steps: Wash the tomato, cucumber, cilantro and pomegranate, and rinse the sprouts. Raw sprouts can carry bacteria, so boil them in a pot of water for a full 4 minutes until steaming and tender with a little bite, drain and cool them under cold water.
Lower the egg into boiling water, cook it for 10 minutes so the yolk is firm, then cool it under cold water, peel it and chop it.
Chop the cucumber, tomato, onion, chili and cilantro, and take the seeds from the pomegranate.
Toss the sprouts, chickpeas, egg and vegetables with the dahi, lemon juice, chaat masala and salt. Eat within 1 hour, or keep it chilled and eat the same day.
Break your fast with a date, or about three small dates, and a glass of water. Eat the chaat topped with the crushed peanuts.
tip: Buy ready-to-use sprouts from the fridge section, fresh and cold, and keep them in the fridge; don't sprout them at home for this. Never eat them raw, and do not keep the finished chaat for tomorrow.
ingredients: one large, or a few small ones
no salt added, drained and rinsed
boiled until the yolk is firm

name: Lighter goat haleem with barley, cracked wheat and lentils
inspiredBy: Hyderabadi and Pakistani haleem, with more grain and dal and less meat, and a little ghee
about: Lean goat slow-cooked until it shreds, with cracked wheat, barley, moong and red lentils into a thick, savoury porridge, finished with browned onion, ginger, cilantro and a squeeze of lemon, and served with a warm whole-wheat roti and a quick carrot salad. It is the Ramadan classic, a project that makes two portions and feeds tomorrow. The goat brings **iron and zinc**, the moong and lentils bring folate and fibre, the carrot brings vitamin A, and the lemon helps your body absorb the iron.
steps: Rinse the cracked wheat, barley, moong and lentils together and soak them in plenty of cold water in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or overnight. Wash your hands and the board after you handle the raw goat, and wash the carrot.
Warm the oil in a heavy pot and cook the onion over medium heat for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring, until it is a deep golden brown. Scoop out a spoonful and keep it for the topping.

Add the grated ginger, garlic, garam masala, coriander, cumin, turmeric and kashmiri chili for 30 seconds, then add the goat and brown it for 5 minutes. Pour in about 1 litre of hot water, cover and simmer for 60 minutes, or pressure cook for 30 minutes, until the goat is very tender.

Drain the soaked grains and lentils and stir them into the pot with the salt and about 500 ml more hot water. Simmer, stirring from the bottom every few minutes, for 40 to 45 minutes, until everything has broken down (or pressure cook for 15 minutes). Add hot water if it sticks.

Stir in the ghee. Shred the goat with two forks and beat the haleem with a wooden spoon, or give it a few pulses with a stick blender, until thick and stretchy but not smooth. The goat should read at least 71 °C and be falling apart.
Knead the flour with warm water into a soft dough, rest it for 15 minutes, roll it thin and roast it on a hot dry pan for about 1 minute a side until it puffs.
Grate the carrot, then toss it with a little of the lemon juice and half the cilantro for a quick salad.

Before you sit down to eat, spoon the second portion into a shallow container, stir it once to let the heat out and get it into the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days and reheat it once, with a splash of water, until steaming hot (74 °C).
Ladle the haleem into bowls and top with the browned onion, ginger matchsticks, the rest of the cilantro and a squeeze of lemon. Serve with the roti and the carrot salad.
tip: Buy halal meat from a halal butcher or a store that carries certified halal. Start by mid-afternoon (a pressure cooker cuts the whole pot to about 75 minutes). Serve the first portion hot and chill the second within the hour; do not hold it warm for hours. Haleem freezes well in single portions: cool it within 1 hour, freeze it flat in a shallow container, thaw it in the fridge, use within 2 days and never refreeze.
ingredients: half grated, half in thin matchsticks

name: Lighter chicken karahi with whole-wheat roti and kachumber
inspiredBy: Peshawari and Lahori chicken karahi, built on tomato, ginger and green chili with less oil
about: Chicken thigh cooked in a wok-style pan with ripe tomatoes, garlic, ginger, green chili and crushed coriander until the sauce clings and glistens, finished with ginger matchsticks, cilantro and lemon, with a warm whole-wheat roti and a fresh kachumber. It is the quick, sharp karahi of the roadside dhaba with about a third of the oil. The chicken brings **protein, niacin and B12**, and the tomatoes bring vitamin C and potassium.
steps: Wash the tomato, cucumber and cilantro. Wash your hands, knife and board after handling the raw chicken.
Warm the oil in a wide pan or karahi over high heat, add the cumin seeds and garlic for 15 seconds, then add the chicken and fry for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until it is lightly browned all over.

Add the tomato, crushed ginger, chili, salt, kashmiri chili, crushed coriander and pepper. Cover and cook on medium for 10 minutes, then uncover and cook for 10 to 12 minutes more, stirring, until the tomato has broken down, the sauce clings to the chicken and darkens, and the chicken reaches 74 °C.
Knead the flour with warm water into a soft dough, rest it for 15 minutes, roll it thin and roast it on a hot dry pan for about 1 minute a side until it puffs. Keep it covered.
Toss the cucumber and onion with a few drops of lemon and a pinch of salt for the kachumber.
Stir the garam masala, cilantro, ginger matchsticks and the rest of the lemon juice through the karahi just before serving. Serve with the roti and kachumber.
tip: Buy halal chicken from a halal butcher or a store that carries certified halal. Use a small seeded green chili for a milder karahi. Chicken thigh stays juicier than breast in a hot pan. Knead the roti dough for the day in one batch and keep it covered in the fridge.

name: Salmon in a Bengali-style mustard jhol with brown basmati and garlic spinach
inspiredBy: Inspired by Bangladeshi shorshe maach, with salmon in place of hilsa and canola in place of mustard oil
about: Salmon simmered in a sharp, pungent sauce of ground yellow mustard, green chili and turmeric, with a small bowl of brown basmati, garlicky wilted spinach and a carrot and tomato kachumber. It is the Bengali iftar fish curry, sharp with mustard: start the rice first, and the fish itself takes about 10 minutes. The salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the spinach and lemon bring folate and vitamin C.
steps: Wash the spinach, carrot and tomato. If the salmon was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days. Rinse the brown basmati, put it in a pot with about twice its volume of water and a pinch of the salt, bring to a boil, cover and simmer on low for 30 to 35 minutes until tender.

Grind the mustard seeds with the green chili, a splash of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and 2 tablespoons of water in a spice grinder or small blender until smooth. Use it right away, because mustard paste turns bitter if it stands.
Rub the salmon with the turmeric and a pinch of salt and keep it in the fridge. Wash your hands and the board afterwards, and do not reuse anything that touched the raw fish.

Warm two thirds of the oil in a pan and stir in the mustard paste for 20 seconds. Add about 200 ml of water, bring to a simmer, then lay in the salmon, cover and cook for 7 to 8 minutes, until the fish flakes and reaches 70 °C. Do not boil hard.
In another pan, warm the rest of the oil, soften the garlic for 30 seconds, then wilt the spinach with a pinch of salt for 2 to 3 minutes.
Toss the carrot, tomato and onion with the rest of the lemon juice for the kachumber.
Serve the salmon and its sauce over or beside the brown basmati, with the spinach and kachumber.
tip: Shorshe is usually eaten with plain white rice, and brown basmati is the lighter swap. Canola stands in for mustard oil, and the yellow mustard gives the sharpness, but the dish is milder than the real thing. Cool any extra rice in a shallow container within 1 hour. Mackerel works here too. No spice grinder? Soak the mustard seeds in warm water for 15 minutes first, then blend.

name: Masoor palak dal with vegetable pulao and cucumber raita
inspiredBy: Pakistani and North Indian dal tarka with a light vegetable pulao and a cooling raita
about: Red lentils cooked soft with spinach and tomato and finished with a hot ghee tarka of cumin, garlic and chili, with a small plate of vegetable pulao and a cucumber and mint raita. It is the everyday Ramadan dal plate at a lighter weight, with brown basmati for the pulao and plenty of vegetables. The lentils bring **folate, iron and fibre**, and the raita brings calcium.
steps: Wash the spinach, tomato, carrot and mint. Rinse the lentils and brown basmati in separate bowls.

Put the lentils, half the onion, the tomato, turmeric and about 600 ml of water in a pot and simmer for 20 minutes, until the lentils fall apart. Add the spinach and half the salt for the last 3 minutes.

For the pulao, warm the oil in a second pot, add half the cumin seeds, the bay and cinnamon, then the rest of the onion for 3 minutes. Add the carrot, peas, brown basmati, the rest of the salt and about twice the rice's volume in water. Cover and cook on low for 30 to 35 minutes until the rice is tender.
For the tarka, warm the ghee in a small pan, add the rest of the cumin seeds, garlic and kashmiri chili, and sizzle for 30 to 40 seconds until the garlic is golden. Pour it over the dal.
Stir the grated cucumber, mint and ground cumin into the yogurt for the raita. Keep it in the fridge until you eat.
Spoon the dal and pulao onto a plate with the raita beside them.

Before you sit down, spoon the second portion of dal and pulao into shallow containers and refrigerate them within 1 hour (the rice cools quickly this way). Keep the raita fixings apart and mix them fresh tomorrow. Eat within 3 days and reheat once, until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: The dal freezes well without the raita. Thaw it in the fridge, use within 2 days and never refreeze. A pressure cooker finishes the lentils in 8 minutes.

name: Mackerel jhol with potato, peas and whole-wheat roti
inspiredBy: Bangladeshi and Bengali macher jhol, a thin, spiced fish curry with potato and peas
about: Atlantic mackerel simmered in a thin, golden gravy of tomato, ginger, garlic, cumin and coriander with potato and green peas, finished with lemon and cilantro, with a warm whole-wheat roti to mop it up. It is a Bangladeshi weeknight curry, homely and tangy. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the potato and peas bring potassium, folate and fibre.
steps: Wash the potato, tomato and cilantro. If the fish was frozen, thaw it in the fridge and cook it within 2 days. Rub the mackerel with a pinch of the turmeric and salt and keep it in the fridge. Wash your hands and the board afterwards, and do not reuse the rub.

Warm the oil in a pan and cook the onion for 5 minutes until soft. Add the ginger, garlic, cumin, coriander, kashmiri chili and the rest of the turmeric for 30 seconds, then the tomato and cook for 5 minutes until it breaks down.
Add the potato, the salt and about 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer for 10 minutes, add the peas and chili and simmer for 5 minutes more, until the potato is nearly tender.
Lay the mackerel in the gravy, cover and simmer gently for 8 to 10 minutes, until the fish flakes and reaches 70 °C.
Meanwhile, knead the flour with warm water into a soft dough, rest it for 15 minutes, roll it thin and roast it on a hot dry pan for about 1 minute a side until it puffs.
Finish the jhol with the cilantro and lemon juice. Serve with the roti.
tip: Sardines, trout or salmon are good in the same curry. Mackerel is oily and a little bony, so ask the fishmonger to steak or fillet it. Use Atlantic mackerel; king mackerel is high in mercury.

name: Roasted masala chickpeas
inspiredBy: Pakistani and North Indian bhuna chana, oven-roasted with chaat masala and lemon
about: Chickpeas patted dry and roasted until crisp with chaat masala, cumin and chili, finished with a squeeze of lemon. It is a crunchy, savoury snack for the evening, baked rather than fried. The chickpeas bring **fibre, folate and plant protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Dry the chickpeas very well in a clean towel, because dry chickpeas turn crisp.
Toss them with the oil, cumin, kashmiri chili and salt on a baking tray and spread them in a single layer.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray every 10 minutes, until they are golden and crisp.
Toss with the chaat masala and lemon juice while warm. Let them cool, and they will crisp a little more.
tip: They are best the day they are made. Keep any extra in a covered container in the fridge for up to 3 days, and crisp them again in a hot oven for 5 minutes.
ingredients: no salt added, drained, rinsed and patted very dry

name: Guava with almonds, lemon and chaat masala
inspiredBy: Pakistani guava chaat, a seasonal evening fruit
about: Chunks of ripe guava tossed with lemon, a pinch of chaat masala and black pepper, with toasted almonds for crunch. It is the sweet, tangy, peppery fruit the street sellers pile on a plate at dusk. The guava brings **vitamin C and fibre**, and the almonds bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Wash the guava well, then cut it in chunks.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes until fragrant, then chop them.
Toss the guava with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black pepper, top with the almonds, and eat right away.
tip: No guava? Ripe papaya takes the same seasoning.

name: Daliya kheer with less sugar, cardamom and almonds
inspiredBy: North Indian daliya kheer and Pakistani kheer, a slow-cooked pudding, here with cracked wheat and the sugar cut right back
about: Cracked wheat simmered slowly in milk with cardamom until thick and creamy, sweetened with only a little sugar and topped with sliced almonds. It is one small bowl of the traditional Ramadan sweet, served warm or chilled. The milk brings **calcium and protein**, and the cracked wheat keeps it a whole-grain pudding.
steps: Rinse the daliya and drain it. Toast it in a dry pot over medium heat for 2 minutes until it smells nutty.
Pour in the milk and cardamom and bring it to a gentle boil, then turn the heat low.
Simmer, stirring often and scraping the bottom so it does not catch, for 25 to 30 minutes, until the wheat is soft and the milk has thickened into a creamy pudding.

Stir in the sugar and half the almonds, cook for 2 minutes, and top with the rest. Serve warm or chilled; either way, refrigerate leftovers in a shallow container within 1 hour and eat them within 3 days, reheated to steaming (74 °C) if you want it warm.
tip: A pressure cooker makes it in about 12 minutes. Chill it and stir in a splash of milk when serving cold.

name: Masala peanuts with mooli sticks
inspiredBy: Pakistani masala peanuts and street-style mooli with lemon and chaat masala
about: A handful of roasted peanuts tossed with onion, cilantro, lemon and chaat masala, with crisp mooli (white radish) sticks on the side. It is the salty-sour crunch of masala peanuts with the cool, peppery bite of mooli. The peanuts bring **protein, niacin and vitamin E**, and the juicy mooli is mostly water.
steps: Wash and peel the mooli and cut it into sticks. Wash the cilantro.
Toss the peanuts with the onion, cilantro and most of the lemon juice and chaat masala.
Serve the masala peanuts with the mooli sticks on the side, with the rest of the lemon and chaat masala over them.
tip: No mooli? Carrot sticks work the same way.

name: Warm haldi doodh with almonds
inspiredBy: North Indian haldi doodh, warm milk with turmeric, pepper and cardamom
about: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, a pinch of black pepper and cardamom, sweetened with a little date and served with a few almonds. It is a soft, comforting drink for after taraweeh. The milk brings **calcium, protein and vitamin B12**.
steps: Warm the milk with the turmeric, pepper, cardamom and chopped date in a small pot, whisking, until it just begins to steam, then hold it at a gentle simmer, watching it so it does not boil over.
Keep it at a gentle simmer for 3 minutes, then pour into a mug and serve with the almonds on the side.
tip: Drink a glass of water with every snack to spread your fluids between iftar and suhoor.
ingredients: chopped; a small date or half a medjool

name: Ripe papaya with almonds and lemon
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Bangladeshi fruit plate, with lemon and black pepper
about: Chilled ripe papaya with lemon juice and black pepper and a small handful of toasted almonds. It is a soft, juicy plate that is easy to eat late in the evening. The papaya brings **vitamin C**, and the almonds bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Wash the papaya well before you peel it, and scoop out the seeds.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes until lightly golden, then chop them.
Toss the papaya with the lemon juice and black pepper, and top with the almonds.
tip: Use ripe papaya only. Unripe green papaya is not for this. Skip the almonds and add roasted peanuts if you like it more street-style.

name: Mango and cardamom lassi
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Punjabi sweet lassi, thinned yogurt with a little fruit and no added sugar
about: Thick plain yogurt whisked with cold water, ripe mango and a pinch of cardamom until it pours like a thick drink, with chopped almonds on top. It is cooling and lightly sweet from the fruit alone. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Wash the mango well before you peel it. If you use frozen mango, thaw it in the fridge.
Blend the yogurt, mango, cardamom and about 150 ml cold water until smooth. Pour over ice and scatter over the almonds.
tip: Prefer it salty? Skip the mango and blend the yogurt with water, roasted cumin and a pinch of salt for a zeera lassi.

name: Masala eggs with tomato and onion
inspiredBy: Pakistani anda chaat, firm boiled eggs with onion, tomato and lemon
about: Firm boiled eggs chopped with tomato, onion, cilantro and green chili, tossed with lemon and chaat masala. It is a savoury, cooling little bowl for a hungry evening, with the yolks cooked firm. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the tomato adds vitamin C.
steps: Wash the tomato and cilantro. Lower the eggs into a small pot of boiling water, cook them for 10 minutes so the yolks are firm, then cool them under cold water and peel them.
Chop the eggs, tomato, onion, chili and cilantro.
Toss everything with the lemon juice, chaat masala and salt, and eat it right away.
tip: Boil a few eggs ahead and keep them in their shells in the fridge for up to 3 days.
ingredients: boiled until the yolk is firm

name: Roasted sweet potato chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani shakarkandi chaat, a winter street classic, roasted instead of fried
about: Sweet potato roasted until soft and caramelized at the edges, tossed with lemon, chaat masala and a little chili. It is the sweet, tangy, spiced chaat of Pakistani street stalls in the cooler months, baked here with only a drizzle of oil. The sweet potato brings **vitamin A, fibre and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Scrub the sweet potato well and cut it into chunks.
Toss with the oil on a baking tray and roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges.
Toss with the lemon juice, chaat masala, kashmiri chili and cilantro while still warm.
tip: Roast a double batch and keep half in a shallow container in the fridge for up to 3 days, then reheat until steaming hot (74 °C).

name: Savoury ginger-soy oats with mushrooms, spinach and edamame
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese savoury rice porridge, made with oats
about: Creamy oats cooked in water with ginger and soy, topped with golden mushrooms, wilted spinach and warm edamame and a drizzle of sesame oil, with a glass of milk on the side. The edamame and oats bring **protein and fibre**, and the spinach brings iron and folate.
steps: Wash the mushrooms and spinach and slice the mushrooms. Pour hot water over the frozen edamame until steaming hot all the way through, then drain.
Bring the oats, grated ginger and 250 ml of water to a gentle simmer in a small pot, stirring, until thick and creamy, about 6 minutes.
Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a nonstick pan and cook the mushrooms until golden, about 4 minutes. Add the spinach and soy sauce and stir until the spinach wilts.
Spoon the oats into a bowl, top with the mushrooms, spinach and edamame, drizzle with the sesame oil and serve with a glass of milk.
tip: Add a splash of water if the oats thicken as they stand.

name: Warm cinnamon pear over Greek yogurt with oat and almond crunch
about: Cold Greek yogurt under soft pear simmered with cinnamon and a little ginger, topped with a crunchy toasted oat and almond mix. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the pear and oats bring fibre.
steps: Toast the oats and almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Tip them out to cool.
Wash the pear and dice it. Simmer it in the same pan with the cinnamon, ginger and a splash of water until soft, about 5 minutes.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the warm pear and scatter over the crunch.
tip: Toast a few days' worth of crunch at once and keep it in a jar.

name: Savoury brown rice breakfast bowl with kale, mushrooms and firm egg
inspiredBy: Inspired by Korean and Chinese savoury rice breakfasts
about: Warm brown rice stir-fried with mushrooms and kale, topped with firm scrambled egg and a drizzle of sesame oil, with a glass of milk on the side. **Eggs and mushrooms** bring choline and B vitamins, and the kale brings calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Wash the kale and mushrooms, slice the mushrooms and thinly slice the kale. Beat the eggs with a splash of water.
Warm the olive oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Cook the mushrooms until golden, about 4 minutes, then add the kale and a splash of water and stir until it is tender, about 3 minutes.
Add the rice and soy sauce and stir until it is steaming hot all the way through. Push everything to one side.
Pour the eggs into the empty side and stir until completely set and firm, about 2 minutes, then mix them through.
Spoon into a bowl, drizzle with the sesame oil and serve with a glass of milk.
tip: Microwave a pouch of rice for 2 minutes. Rice from a previous night must have been cooled within 1 hour in a shallow container and used within 3 days; reheat it until steaming hot.
ingredients: ready-cooked pouch or frozen, or rice cooked and chilled earlier

name: Cumin chicken, lentil and roasted vegetable brown rice bowl with lemon yogurt
inspiredBy: Inspired by Middle Eastern roasted chicken and lentil rice bowls
about: Chicken breast, carrot, zucchini and cherry tomatoes roasted with cumin and paprika, piled on brown rice with warm lentils, wilted spinach, a cool lemon-yogurt sauce and parsley. The lentils and spinach bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body absorb that iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Wash the carrot, zucchini, tomatoes, spinach and parsley. Slice the carrot thinly so it cooks quickly.

Toss the chicken, carrot, zucchini, onion and tomatoes on a tray with the oil, cumin, paprika and most of the salt. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw chicken. Roast until the carrot is tender and the chicken reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece, about 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, stir the yogurt, half of the lemon juice, the rest of the salt and a spoonful of water together. Heat the rice and the lentils separately, until steaming hot.
Stir the spinach into the hot tray for a minute, until it wilts.
Spoon the rice into a bowl, top with the lentils and the roasted chicken and vegetables, and drizzle with the yogurt sauce. Squeeze over the rest of the lemon and finish with the parsley.
tip: Packing it? Cook it the night before, cool the chicken, vegetables, rice and lentils in a shallow container in the fridge within 1 hour and keep the yogurt sauce apart. Carry it in a cold bag with an ice pack, reheat it until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), add the sauce and eat it the same day.
ingredients: ready-cooked pouch or frozen, or rice cooked and chilled earlier

name: Warm ginger-soy chickpeas with kale, red pepper and egg over brown rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese-style soy-ginger stir-fried greens and beans
about: Chickpeas, red pepper and wilted kale stir-fried with ginger, soy sauce and a drizzle of sesame oil, spooned over brown rice with a firm hard-boiled egg, lemon, cilantro and toasted walnuts. The chickpeas and kale bring **iron, folate and calcium**, and the lemon and pepper bring vitamin C to help absorb the iron.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and boil it for 10 minutes, until the yolk is completely firm, then cool it under cold water and peel it. Wash the kale, pepper and cilantro, slice the pepper and onion, grate the ginger and chop the kale, discarding the thick stems.
Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion and pepper until soft and starting to brown, about 8 minutes. Stir in the ginger and soy sauce for 30 seconds.
Add the kale and a splash of water, cover and cook until the kale is tender, about 4 minutes. Stir in the chickpeas and salt and heat until steaming hot. Heat the rice until steaming.
Season with the lemon juice. Spoon over the rice, halve the egg and set it on top, and finish with the cilantro, walnuts and a drizzle of sesame oil.
tip: Packing it? Make it the night before and cool it in a shallow container in the fridge within 1 hour. Carry it in a cold bag with an ice pack, reheat it until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and eat it the same day.
ingredients: boiled until the yolk is firm, as in the steps
ready-cooked pouch or frozen, or rice cooked and chilled earlier

name: Lemony sardine, edamame and cucumber brown rice bowl
inspiredBy: Inspired by Portuguese and Greek sardine and rice salads
about: Canned sardines flaked over brown rice with edamame, cucumber and parsley, finished with a lemon-yogurt dressing and a few almonds. The sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, and the edamame adds fibre and protein.
steps: Pour boiling water over the frozen edamame, or microwave them, until steaming hot all the way through, then drain. Heat the rice until steaming and let it cool a few minutes.
Wash the cucumber and parsley. Slice the cucumber and chop the parsley.
Stir the yogurt, lemon juice, olive oil, salt and pepper together.
Pile the rice, edamame and cucumber in a bowl, flake the sardines on top and spoon over the dressing. Finish with the parsley and almonds.
tip: Keep an opened tin covered in the fridge and use it within 2 days. Packing it? Spread the heated rice in a shallow container and chill it within 1 hour before you build the bowl, then carry it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.
ingredients: ready-cooked pouch or frozen, or rice cooked and chilled earlier

name: Cooked salmon poke-style bowl with spicy yogurt drizzle
inspiredBy: Inspired by Hawaiian poke bowls, with the salmon fully cooked
about: Cubes of soy-ginger salmon, cooked through and served warm over brown rice with cool edamame, cucumber and carrot ribbons. A spicy lemon-yogurt drizzle ties it together. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the edamame brings protein and folate.
steps: Rinse the rice and boil it in plenty of water, like pasta, until tender with a little chew, 25 to 30 minutes, then drain and fluff it.
Meanwhile, pour hot water over the frozen edamame until steaming hot all the way through, then drain. Wash the cucumber and carrot, slice the cucumber and peel the carrot into ribbons.
Stir the yogurt, chili, half of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt together for the drizzle. Stir the soy sauce, ginger and sesame oil together for the glaze.

Warm a nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Add the salmon cubes and cook, turning, until opaque and flaky and at least 70 °C (158 °F) inside, 4 to 5 minutes. Pour in the glaze for the last minute so it coats the fish. Wash your hands, board and knife after handling the raw fish.
