Brush with the oil.
Bake until golden and cooked through, with the egg set firm and the centre at 74 °C (165 °F), about 16 minutes.
Meanwhile, toss the cabbage and carrot with the rest of the yogurt, mustard, dill and lemon juice, and the salt, for a quick slaw.
Pile the spinach and plenty of slaw on a plate, set the salmon cake on top and serve with the cucumber slices.
Move any salmon left in the tin to a covered container in the fridge and use it within 2 days.
tip: Chill the shaped cake for 10 minutes if you have time, it holds together better.

name: Canned salmon on cucumber rounds
about: Flaked canned salmon with lemon and dill piled on thick cucumber rounds. It brings **omega-3 and calcium**.
steps: Wash the cucumber and dill. Cut the cucumber into thick rounds.
Mash the salmon with the lemon juice, dill and pepper and pile it onto the rounds.
Move any salmon left in the tin to a covered container in the fridge and use it within 2 days. Pack with an ice pack if it is not eaten within 2 hours.

name: Overnight oats with berries and walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by Swiss bircher muesli
about: Rolled oats soaked in milk and yogurt until creamy, with frozen berries that thaw into a jammy swirl and a crunch of walnuts. Made in five minutes the night before, it brings **fibre, protein and plant omega-3 from the walnuts** before you've touched the stove.
steps: Wash your hands, then stir the oats, milk, yogurt and cinnamon together in a jar until no dry oats are left.
Spoon the frozen berries on top, put the lid on and refrigerate overnight. They thaw and bleed into the oats, which is exactly what you want.
In the morning, stir it up and loosen it with a splash of milk if it is thick. Scatter on the walnuts so they stay crisp.
Keep it in the fridge and eat each jar within 2 days of making it.
tip: Mix each jar the night before. If you are cooking for someone who is pregnant, 60 or older, 5 or under, or has a weak immune system, boil the frozen berries for 1 minute and cool them first, or use fresh.

name: Kiwi yogurt bowl with oat crunch
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt parfait
about: Thick Greek yogurt with sliced kiwi and a warm crunch of toasted oats and walnuts. Kiwi brings **vitamin C**, the yogurt brings protein and calcium, and it takes ten minutes.
steps: Wash the kiwi. Peel and slice it.
Toast the oats and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Tip them onto a plate to cool for a minute.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, lay the kiwi on top, and scatter on the warm crunch and the cinnamon.
tip: Toast a double batch of the crunch and keep it in a jar for the week.

name: Potato, spinach and pepper hash with firm eggs
inspiredBy: Inspired by the diner skillet hash
about: Crisp-edged diced potato with red pepper and spinach, topped with eggs cooked right in the pan until the yolks are firm. A slow weekend breakfast with **protein, vitamin C and potassium** in one skillet.
steps: Wash the potatoes, pepper and spinach. Cut the potatoes into small dice, about 1 cm, so they cook through quickly.

Warm the oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium heat. Add the potatoes, salt and paprika, cover, and cook, stirring now and then, until golden at the edges and tender when poked, about 15 minutes.
Add the onion and pepper and cook until soft, about 4 minutes. Stir in the spinach until it wilts, about 1 minute.

Make a well in the hash for each egg and crack them in. Cover and cook until the whites are opaque and the yolks are firm all the way through, 6 to 8 minutes. Break the yolks gently to be sure there is nothing runny.
Finish with black pepper and serve straight from the pan. Wash your hands, the cutting board and the pan after handling raw egg.
tip: Microwave the diced potato for 3 minutes first and the pan time drops to about 8 minutes.
ingredients: scrubbed and cut into small dice, skin on

name: Spinach and pepper scramble with sweet potato
inspiredBy: Inspired by the diner scramble
about: Firm scrambled eggs with wilted spinach and red pepper, over crisp-edged cubes of sweet potato, with sliced kiwi on the side. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the kiwi's vitamin C helps your body absorb the iron in the spinach.
steps: Wash the sweet potato, spinach, pepper and kiwi. Dice the sweet potato very small, about 1 cm, so it cooks fast, and dice the pepper. Beat the eggs with the salt and pepper.

Microwave the diced sweet potato with a splash of water for 3 minutes. Warm the oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat, add the sweet potato, and cook uncovered, stirring now and then, until browned at the edges, about 5 minutes.
Add the pepper and cook for 2 minutes. Stir in the spinach until it wilts, about 30 seconds.
Pour in the eggs and keep folding gently until they are set with no runny egg left, about 2 minutes. They should be firm, not wet, and reach 71 °C (160 °F).
Serve with the sliced kiwi. Wash your hands, the pan and the board after handling raw egg.
tip: Dice and microwave tomorrow's sweet potato tonight, then cool it and keep it covered in the fridge, and the morning takes about 8 minutes.
ingredients: scrubbed and cut into small dice

name: Sardine, white bean and spinach salad
inspiredBy: Inspired by Italian tonno e fagioli, made with sardines
about: Flaky sardines, creamy white beans, baby spinach and crunchy red pepper in a sharp lemon dressing, a cool fresh plate to start a week of hot pots. The sardines bring **omega-3 fats, vitamin D and soft-bone calcium**.
steps: Wash the spinach, pepper and parsley. Slice the pepper and the onion very thinly.
In a bowl, whisk the lemon juice, olive oil and black pepper. Add the white beans, pepper and onion and toss. Let them sit for 5 minutes so the onion softens a little.
Pile the spinach on a plate, spoon the bean mixture over, and lay the sardines on top. Scatter the parsley over everything.

Eat it right away, or pack the beans and the spinach separately and put it together at lunch. If you pack it, keep the sardines and beans in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day, within 4 hours.
tip: Stir the dressed beans into the spinach only at the last minute so the leaves stay crisp.
ingredients: very thinly sliced, red if you have it

name: Red lentil and carrot soup with lemon yogurt
inspiredBy: Inspired by Middle Eastern shorbat adas
about: A silky, golden soup of red lentils and sweet carrots, warmed with cumin and turmeric and brightened with lemon. A spoonful of yogurt and toasted sunflower seeds finish it. The lentils bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body absorb that iron.
steps: Wash the carrots and parsley. Slice the carrots and dice the onion.

Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and carrots and cook, stirring, until the onion is soft and golden at the edges, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, cumin and turmeric for 1 minute, until it smells toasty.

Add the lentils, crushed tomatoes and broth, with a splash of water if you need it. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, until the lentils and carrots are completely soft, about 18 minutes.
Blend about half the soup with an immersion blender, or mash it with a potato masher, so it is creamy but still has some texture. Stir in the lemon juice, salt and pepper.

Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Ladle tonight's portion into a bowl and top it with the yogurt, sunflower seeds and parsley. Keep the toppings for the second portion apart and add them fresh tomorrow.

This pot makes two portions. Ladle the second portion into a shallow container, let the steam off for a few minutes, and have it in the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days, and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F). It thickens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it. To freeze it instead, freeze it once it is cold, thaw it in the fridge, eat it within 2 days and never refreeze it.
tip: A pinch of chili flakes in the oil wakes it up. Serve with a crunchy side salad.

name: Chicken, white bean and kale stew
inspiredBy: Inspired by Tuscan white bean soups
about: Tender chicken simmered with creamy white beans, celery, rosemary and a big handful of kale, finished with lemon. The beans and kale bring **iron, folate and calcium**, and the lemon helps your body absorb the iron.
steps: Wash the kale and celery. Cut the chicken into bite-size pieces, then wash your hands, the knife and the board after the raw chicken.

Warm the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken in a single layer for about 4 minutes, turning once, and dice the onion and celery meanwhile. Lift the chicken out onto a plate; it will finish cooking in the stew.
Lower the heat to medium and cook the onion and celery in the same pot until soft, about 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, rosemary and thyme for 1 minute.

Return the chicken to the pot with the white beans, crushed tomatoes and the broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, for 15 minutes, and tear the kale off its stems meanwhile. The chicken should reach 74 °C (165 °F) and be tender.
Stir in the kale and simmer until it is bright and tender, about 5 minutes. Mash a few spoonfuls of beans against the side of the pot to thicken the broth. Add the lemon juice, salt and pepper.

This pot makes two portions. Ladle the second portion into a shallow container, let the steam off for a few minutes, and have it in the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days, and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F). To freeze it instead, freeze it once it is cold, thaw it in the fridge, eat it within 2 days and never refreeze it.
tip: It is even better the next day. Add a splash of water when you reheat it, since the beans soak up the broth.
ingredients: trimmed and cut into bite-size pieces

name: Beef and barley soup
inspiredBy: Inspired by Eastern European beef and barley soup
about: A hearty soup of lean beef, chewy barley, carrots, celery and broccoli in a thyme-scented tomato broth. The barley thickens it as it sits, so tomorrow's bowl is even better. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, with a squeeze of lemon to lift it.
steps: Wash the carrots, celery, broccoli and parsley, and dice the onion.

Warm the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat. Add the beef and the onion and break the beef up with a spoon, then wash your hands after handling the raw beef. Cook, stirring now and then, until no pink remains, the onion is soft and the beef is browned in places, about 6 minutes. Dice the carrots and celery while it cooks.

Stir in the barley, carrots, celery, crushed tomatoes, broth, thyme and bay leaf. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, until the barley is tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes. Cut the broccoli into small florets meanwhile. The beef should reach 71 °C (160 °F).
Remove the bay leaf. Stir in the broccoli and simmer until bright green and tender, about 4 minutes. Stir in the lemon juice, salt, pepper and parsley, and add a splash of water if it is too thick.

This pot makes two portions. Cooked barley goes off quickly, so be prompt with the second portion. Ladle the second portion into a shallow container, let the steam off for a few minutes, and have it in the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days, and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F). It thickens overnight, so add water when you reheat it. To freeze it instead, freeze it once it is cold, thaw it in the fridge, eat it within 2 days and never refreeze it.
tip: Short on time? Dice the vegetables small, or use a pressure cooker: 12 minutes on high after the browning, and the barley will be ready.

name: Smoky turkey, black bean and sweet potato soup
inspiredBy: Inspired by Cuban and Tex-Mex black bean soups
about: A thick, smoky soup of lean turkey, black beans, sweet potato and kale, with a little chili heat, lemon and fresh parsley. A spoonful of yogurt and toasted sunflower seeds finish it. The turkey and beans bring **protein, fibre and folate**, and the sweet potato adds vitamin A.
steps: Wash the pepper, kale, parsley and sweet potato. Dice the onion and pepper.

Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and pepper until soft, about 6 minutes, and peel and cube the sweet potato meanwhile. Add the turkey and cook, breaking it up, until no pink remains, about 5 minutes. Wash your hands after handling the raw turkey. Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika, cumin and chili flakes for 1 minute.

Add the sweet potato, beans and broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, until the sweet potato is tender and the turkey reaches 71 °C (160 °F), about 15 minutes. Tear the kale off its stems while it simmers.

Mash about a third of the soup against the side of the pot with a spoon, or blend a ladleful, so it turns thick and creamy. Stir in the kale and simmer until tender, about 4 minutes, then add the lemon juice and salt.
Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, about 2 minutes. Ladle the soup into bowls and top with a spoonful of yogurt, the sunflower seeds and the parsley.

This pot makes two portions. Store the soup without the toppings, and add those fresh tomorrow. Ladle the second portion into a shallow container, let the steam off for a few minutes, and have it in the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days, and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F). To freeze it instead, freeze it once it is cold, thaw it in the fridge, eat it within 2 days and never refreeze it.
tip: For less heat, leave out the chili flakes. For a thicker soup, blend more of it.
ingredients: peeled and cut into small cubes

name: Salmon, potato and corn chowder
inspiredBy: Inspired by New England fish chowder
about: A creamy chowder of potatoes, corn and spinach with big flakes of salmon and a little parsley, thickened with the potatoes themselves instead of flour. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the milk brings calcium.
steps: Wash the celery, spinach, potatoes and parsley. Dice the onion and celery.
Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and celery until soft, about 6 minutes, and cube the potatoes meanwhile. Stir in the garlic and thyme for 1 minute.

Add the potatoes and broth. Bring to a boil, then simmer until the potatoes are tender, about 12 minutes. Meanwhile, cut the salmon into bite-size chunks, then wash your hands, the knife and the board after the raw salmon. Mash about a quarter of the potatoes against the side of the pot to thicken the chowder.
Stir in the milk and corn and heat gently until steaming, without boiling hard. Then add the salmon.
Simmer gently until the salmon is opaque and flakes easily, about 5 minutes. It should reach 70 °C (158 °F). Stir in the spinach until it wilts, then the lemon juice, salt, pepper and parsley.

This pot makes two portions. Ladle the second portion into a shallow container, let the steam off for a few minutes, and have it in the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days, and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F). Reheat it gently so the fish stays tender.
tip: Cod or haddock works if you prefer a milder fish, but then the omega-3 drops.
ingredients: scrubbed and cut into small cubes

name: Barley minestrone with beans and greens
inspiredBy: Inspired by Italian minestrone
about: A big pot of Italian minestrone with chewy barley instead of pasta, white beans, carrot and kale in a tomato broth with a little Parmesan. A slow Saturday project that tastes even better on Sunday. The beans and barley bring **fibre and iron**, and a squeeze of lemon at the table helps.
steps: Wash the carrot, celery, mushrooms, kale and parsley. Tear the kale off its stems, slice the mushrooms and dice the carrot, celery and onion.

Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, celery and mushrooms until the mushrooms give up their water and the onion is soft, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, oregano and basil for 1 minute.
Add the barley, crushed tomatoes and broth, with a splash of water if you need it. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, for 20 minutes, until the barley is nearly tender.
Add the white beans and carrot and simmer until the barley is tender and the carrot is soft, about 12 minutes more.
Stir in the kale and simmer until it is tender, about 5 minutes. Add the salt and a splash of water if it is too thick.
Ladle tonight's portion into a bowl and top it with Parmesan and parsley. Keep the second portion plain and top it fresh tomorrow.

This pot makes two portions. Cooked barley goes off quickly, so be prompt with the second portion. Ladle the second portion into a shallow container, let the steam off for a few minutes, and have it in the fridge within 1 hour. Eat it within 3 days, and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F). It thickens overnight, so add water when you reheat it. To freeze it instead, freeze it once it is cold, thaw it in the fridge, eat it within 2 days and never refreeze it.
tip: A squeeze of lemon or a drizzle of olive oil at the table brightens it.

name: Cod, chickpea and fennel tomato stew
inspiredBy: Inspired by Spanish and Portuguese fish stews
about: Chunks of mild cod poached in a garlicky tomato broth with chickpeas, fennel and spinach, with smoked paprika, a pinch of chili and plenty of parsley. It comes together in about forty minutes. The cod brings **lean protein and iodine**, and the chickpeas bring fibre and folate.
steps: Wash the fennel, spinach and parsley. Slice the fennel thinly and dice the onion, then cut the cod into large chunks. Wash your hands, the knife and the board after the raw fish.
Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the fennel and onion until soft and lightly golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika and chili flakes for 1 minute.
Add the crushed tomatoes, broth and chickpeas. Simmer for 10 minutes so the flavours meld and the broth thickens a little.
Nestle the fish into the stew, cover, and simmer gently until it is opaque and flakes easily, about 6 minutes. It should reach 70 °C (158 °F).
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, about 1 minute. Finish with the lemon juice, salt, pepper and parsley.
Eat it the day you make it, and put anything left in a shallow container in the fridge within 2 hours. Eat it within 2 days and reheat it once, until steaming hot (74 °C or 165 °F).
tip: Haddock, pollock or any firm white fish works instead of cod.

name: Apple slices with tahini and cinnamon
about: Crisp apple slices with a spoonful of tahini to dip in and a dusting of cinnamon. Sweet, nutty and crunchy, it brings **fibre, calcium and copper**.
steps: Wash the apple, core it and cut it into slices.
Spoon the tahini into a small bowl and dust it with the cinnamon.
Dip the apple slices as you eat.

name: Cucumber and parsley salad with sunflower seeds
about: A cold, crunchy salad of cucumber, red pepper and lots of parsley with lemon and olive oil, a bright side next to a warm bowl of soup. A few sunflower seeds add **vitamin E and crunch**.
steps: Wash the cucumber, pepper and parsley. Slice the cucumber thinly and cut the pepper into thin strips.
Toss them with the lemon juice, olive oil and salt in a bowl.
Scatter the parsley and sunflower seeds on top and eat it right away, while it is crisp.
tip: Eat it beside a bowl of soup for a cool, crisp contrast.

name: Kiwi and sunflower seeds
about: Sweet-tart kiwi with a small handful of sunflower seeds. The kiwi brings **vitamin C** and the seeds bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Wash the kiwi and cut it in half.
Eat it with a spoon, with the sunflower seeds on the side.
ingredients: washed, halved and eaten with a spoon

name: Veggie sticks with tahini lemon dip
about: Crunchy red pepper, celery and cucumber with a creamy lemony tahini dip. The tahini brings **calcium and copper**, and the pepper brings vitamin C.
steps: Wash the pepper, celery and cucumber and cut them into sticks.
Stir the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, salt and a spoonful of water together in a small bowl until it is smooth and pourable.
Serve the sticks with the dip.

name: Apple and walnuts
about: A crisp apple with a handful of walnuts. Sweet, juicy and crunchy, it brings **fibre and a little plant omega-3**.
steps: Wash the apple and slice it.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Crunchy spiced chickpeas
about: Chickpeas roasted until crisp with cumin, smoked paprika and a squeeze of lemon. A salty, crunchy snack with **fibre, protein and folate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Rinse the chickpeas, then dry them really well on a clean towel.
Toss them with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt on a baking tray. Roast, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp and deep golden, about 22 minutes.
Squeeze on the lemon juice and let them cool for a few minutes to crisp up. They are best the same day.
ingredients: drained, rinsed and patted very dry

name: Apple and fennel salad with sunflower seeds
inspiredBy: Inspired by Italian finocchio salads
about: Crisp apple and shaved raw fennel with lemon, olive oil and sunflower seeds, a bright, crunchy side for a warm bowl of soup. It brings **fibre, vitamin C and vitamin E**.
steps: Wash the apple, fennel and parsley. Cut the apple into matchsticks and shave the fennel as thinly as you can.
Toss them with the lemon juice and olive oil right away so the apple stays bright.
Scatter the sunflower seeds, parsley and black pepper over the top.
ingredients: washed, cored and cut into matchsticks

name: Greek yogurt with berries and walnuts
about: Thick Greek yogurt with berries and a few chopped walnuts. It has **protein, calcium and vitamin C** and takes a minute.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl.
Top with the berries, walnuts and cinnamon.
tip: If you are cooking for someone who is pregnant, 60 or older, 5 or under, or has a weak immune system, boil the frozen berries for 1 minute and cool them first, or use fresh.

name: Huevos pericos with arepa de choclo and hot chocolate
inspiredBy: Colombian huevos pericos, with the arepa made from frozen corn and whole-grain cornmeal instead of precooked white flour
about: Soft scrambled eggs cooked with tomato and scallion, the everyday Bogotá breakfast, served with a sweet, golden arepa de choclo, a few slices of avocado and a mug of hot chocolate made with evaporated milk. The arepa is blended from sweet corn and whole-grain cornmeal, so it has a soft middle and a toasty crust. The eggs and avocado bring **protein, choline and vitamin E**, and the milk adds calcium.
steps: Blend the corn with a splash of water, about a tablespoon, until it is mostly smooth but still a little pebbly. Stir in the cornmeal and half the salt. Let the batter sit for 10 minutes while the cornmeal drinks up the corn juice and thickens to a thick pancake batter. If it looks loose, stir in another spoon of cornmeal.
Make the chocolate caliente: warm the evaporated milk with the same amount of water in a small pot, whisk in the cocoa and cinnamon, and simmer for 2 minutes until smooth. Keep it warm.
Dice the tomato and slice the scallion, keeping the white and green parts separate.

Brush a non-stick pan with a little of the oil over medium heat. Spoon in the batter in one or two mounds and flatten each to about 1 cm thick. Cook until the bottoms are golden, about 4 minutes, then flip and cook 3 to 4 minutes more, until they feel firm and smell like toasted corn.
Wipe the pan, warm the rest of the oil and soften the scallion whites and tomato with a pinch of salt until the juices mostly cook off, about 4 minutes.
Beat the eggs, pour them in and stir gently with a spatula until they are just set and still creamy, about 1 minute. Stir through the green scallion.
Serve the eggs with the arepas, the sliced avocado and the hot chocolate.
tip: Blend the arepa batter the night before and keep it in the fridge; stir in a spoon of water in the morning and breakfast takes 10 minutes. A few cubes of cheese inside the arepa are classic if you want them.
ingredients: evaporated milk, thinned with an equal amount of water

name: Cuscuz de milho with fried egg, grilled coalho and papaya
inspiredBy: Cuscuz nordestino from northeast Brazil, steamed cornmeal with egg and grilled queijo coalho, made with coarse whole-grain cornmeal in place of flocão
about: Fluffy steamed cornmeal, the breakfast of Brazil's northeast, topped with a fried egg, golden-brown queijo coalho and juicy tomato, with sweet papaya and a mug of chocolate quente made with evaporated milk on the side. It needs no flour and no tapioca, only cornmeal, water and a steamer. The whole-grain corn and egg bring **fibre, protein and choline**, and the cheese and milk bring calcium.
steps: Stir the cornmeal with half the salt in a bowl. Sprinkle over water a spoonful at a time, tossing with a fork, until the meal looks like damp sand. Let it rest 15 minutes, so the coarse grains soften.
Make the chocolate quente: warm the evaporated milk with the same amount of water in a small pot, whisk in the cocoa, and simmer for 2 minutes until smooth. Keep it warm.

Steam the damp meal in a steamer basket or fine sieve lined with a damp cloth, set over simmering water and covered, for about 20 minutes, until tender and fluffy. Fluff it with a fork halfway through.
While it steams, slice the tomato and toss it with half the lime juice, a pinch of salt and the cilantro. Cube the papaya and squeeze the rest of the lime over it.
Brown the coalho slices in a dry non-stick pan, about 1 to 2 minutes per side, until golden and a little crusty. Lift them out.
Warm the oil in the same pan and fry the eggs until the whites are set and the yolks are firm, flipping them for the last minute if you like.
Pack the cuscuz into a bowl or plate, top with the eggs and cheese, and serve with the tomato, the papaya and the hot chocolate.
tip: Steam it the night before, then warm it covered with a spoon of water for 1 minute in the morning. Flocão (coarse flaked cornmeal) is the traditional meal and is sold at Latin and Brazilian shops. Queijo coalho grills without melting; queso panela, halloumi or paneer will do if you cannot find it.
ingredients: evaporated milk, thinned with an equal amount of water

name: Quinua con leche with banana and a little cocoa
inspiredBy: Peruvian quinua con leche, the warm quinoa and milk breakfast drink sold from street carts, thickened into a spoonable porridge
about: Quinoa simmered in evaporated milk with cinnamon, clove and a little cocoa until it turns creamy, then stirred with ripe banana. It is the warm, comforting breakfast of the Andes, with a chocolate hint. The quinoa brings **iron, magnesium and protein**, and the milk adds calcium.
steps: Rinse the quinoa in a fine sieve under cold running water for a full minute, until the water runs clear. This washes off the bitter coating.

Put the quinoa, the evaporated milk, about three times the quinoa's volume of water, the cocoa, the cinnamon and the clove in a small pot, and whisk so the cocoa dissolves. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cook on low, stirring now and then, until the grains are tender with a little white tail, about 18 minutes.
Mash half the banana into the porridge and cook 3 minutes more, until it is thick, glossy and creamy. The banana is the only sweetener, so add a little honey or sugar if you like.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the sliced banana. Add a splash of hot milk if you like it looser.
tip: Cook a double batch the night before and keep it covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; reheat with a splash of water. Ripe papaya can stand in for the banana.
ingredients: evaporated milk, thinned with an equal amount of water

name: Ceviche-style cooked cod with camote and corn
inspiredBy: Peruvian ceviche, with the cod lightly poached first, served with sweet potato and corn in the classic way
about: Tender cubes of cod in a sharp lime, ají amarillo and cilantro marinade, with sweet potato, sweet corn and crisp red onion. The cod is lightly poached so it is cooked through, and the lime marinade still makes it taste like ceviche. Cod brings **lean protein and iodine**, and the lime, cilantro and onion keep it zingy.
steps: Boil the sweet potato chunks in salted water for about 8 minutes, add the corn kernels, and boil 4 minutes more, until the sweet potato is just tender when poked with a fork. Drain and let them cool.
Soak the sliced red onion in a bowl of ice-cold water for 5 minutes to take the sting out, then drain well.

Bring a small pot of salted water to a simmer, slip in the cod cubes and poach for about 90 seconds, until just opaque. Drain well, spread on a plate and chill in the fridge for 5 minutes, so they do not keep cooking.
In a bowl, stir the lime juice with the ají amarillo paste, the grated garlic, half the cilantro and the salt. Add the cod and turn it gently. Let it sit for 10 minutes, so it soaks up the marinade.
Serve the cod with its marinade, the onion, the sweet potato and the corn, with the rest of the cilantro on top. Eat right away.
tip: Ají amarillo paste is sold at Latin grocers and online. Use any firm, mild white fish. Poach the cod and boil the camote and corn on Sunday night, then marinate for 10 minutes at lunch.

name: Quinoa solterito with black beans, corn and queijo coalho
inspiredBy: Peruvian and Bolivian solterito, the bean, corn and cheese salad, with quinoa and black beans making it a full meal, and red pepper in place of rocoto
about: Fluffy quinoa tossed with black beans, sweet corn, tomato, red pepper, red onion, avocado and diced queijo coalho in a lime, oregano and olive oil dressing. It is the kind of salad that sits happily in a lunchbox. The quinoa and beans together bring **iron, folate and protein**, and the lime helps your body use that iron.
steps: Rinse the quinoa and simmer it in twice its volume of water with a pinch of salt until the grains are tender and have popped their little white tails, about 15 minutes. Drain if needed, fluff and let cool.
Use black beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed.
Whisk the lime juice, olive oil, oregano and a pinch of salt in a large bowl.
Add the quinoa, beans, corn, tomato, red pepper and onion and toss well. Fold in the cilantro and top with the avocado and the diced coalho.
tip: Make a double batch of the salad base without the avocado and cheese; it keeps 3 days. Add them just before you eat.

name: Pollo a la parrilla with chimichurri, roasted sweet potato and ensalada criolla
inspiredBy: Argentine grilled chicken with chimichurri, cooked in a grill pan, with sweet potato (batata) and a tomato and onion salad on the side
about: Seared chicken breast, juicy inside, spooned with a sharp, garlicky parsley chimichurri, next to roasted sweet potato and a tomato and onion salad dressed with the same sauce. It tastes like a Sunday asado on a weekday. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and the big handful of parsley brings iron and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato wedges with a quarter of the olive oil and a pinch of salt, spread them on a tray and roast until soft inside and browned at the edges, about 30 minutes, turning once.

Chop the parsley very finely, with the garlic, and stir them in a small bowl with the oregano, cayenne, vinegar, most of the remaining olive oil and half the salt. Loosen it with 1 tablespoon of warm water, as Argentines do. That is your chimichurri. Let it sit while the chicken cooks, so the flavours settle together.

Slice the breast in half horizontally into two thin cutlets, so it cooks quickly and stays juicy. Season with the rest of the salt and a little oil. Cook in a hot cast-iron or grill pan, about 4 minutes a side, until browned and the juices run clear.
Rest the chicken for 5 minutes, then slice it.
Toss the tomato and onion with a spoon of the chimichurri. Serve the chicken with a generous spoonful of chimichurri on top, with the sweet potato and the salad.
tip: Chimichurri keeps 5 days in the fridge and is great on any grilled meat or fish; make a double batch. Skinless chicken thigh works too and is more forgiving, so cook it a few minutes longer. Roast the sweet potato and make the chimichurri on Tuesday night while the salmon roasts. At lunch, sear the chicken in 10 minutes.

name: Beef feijoada made light, with collards, orange and vinagrete
inspiredBy: Brazilian feijoada completa, with lean beef and a little smoked turkey sausage instead of the many cuts of salted and smoked meat, and brown rice
about: A deep, smoky black bean stew with tender beef and a little smoked turkey sausage, served over rice with garlicky collards, juicy orange slices and a sharp tomato vinagrete. Lean beef and just a little sausage keep it lighter than the Saturday classic. The black beans and collards bring **fibre, iron, folate and calcium**, and the orange and tomato help your body absorb the iron.
steps: From dry beans: drain the soaked beans and put them in a big pot with the beef, the sausage, the bay leaf, a big piece of onion and water to cover by 4 cm. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then simmer partly covered until the beans are very tender and the beef is falling apart, about 1 hour 15 minutes. Add the salt for the last 15 minutes.
From the Sunday pot: simmer the beef, sausage, bay leaf and onion piece alone in water for 1 hour, until the beef is tender. Add the cooked beans with their liquid, and simmer 20 minutes more.

Soften most of the remaining onion in half the oil for about 6 minutes, then add half the garlic and the smoked paprika and cook 1 minute. Stir it all into the pot with the pepper. Mash a few spoonfuls of beans against the side of the pot and simmer 15 more minutes, until the stew is thick and glossy.
Use a tub of Sunday rice, or start the rice first: cook 30 g of dry brown rice in twice its volume of salted water, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes.
Roll up the collard leaves and slice them into very thin ribbons. Stir-fry them in the rest of the oil with the remaining garlic for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and just wilted.
Dice the tomato with a little raw onion and stir with the vinegar, cilantro and a pinch of salt. Let it sit 10 minutes.
Serve the beans over the rice with the collards, the orange slices and the vinagrete. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: With the Sunday beans this is a 50-minute dinner, and a pressure cooker does the soaked beans and beef in about 35 minutes. Keep the vinagrete and orange fresh for the leftover lunch, and warm the stew with a splash of water.
ingredients: soaked overnight, or cooked beans from the Sunday pot
trimmed of visible fat and cut in 3 cm chunks
smoked turkey sausage, in thin rounds
half in the pot, the rest for the sofrito and the vinagrete

name: Baked salmon with pebre, potatoes and garlicky acelga
inspiredBy: Chilean salmon a lo pobre, with roasted potatoes in place of the fries, and a fresh pebre
about: Salmon baked on a tray with golden potatoes and the classic fried egg on top, with sweet caramelized onions, garlicky acelga (Swiss chard) and a spoonful of pebre, the Chilean table salsa of tomato, cilantro and chile. Chile farms much of the world's salmon, and pebre goes on everything. Salmon brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, the egg adds choline, and the chard brings vitamin A and K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potatoes with a third of the olive oil and a pinch of the salt. Spread them on a tray and roast for 15 minutes.
Slice half the onion and cook it slowly in a pan with a little oil and a pinch of salt, stirring now and then, until deeply golden and sweet, about 15 minutes.

Make the pebre: finely dice the tomato and the rest of the onion, chop the cilantro and stir them with the cayenne, a little of the garlic, the lime juice, most of the remaining oil and a pinch of salt. Let it sit.

Move the potatoes to one side of the tray. Rub the salmon with the last of the oil, the oregano, pepper and a pinch of salt and set it skin side down on the tray. Roast 10 to 12 minutes, until the fish flakes easily and the potatoes are golden.
Meanwhile, wilt the chard ribbons in a hot pan with a splash of water, the rest of the garlic and a pinch of salt until bright green and tender, about 4 minutes.
Fry the egg in a small non-stick pan over medium heat, with no extra oil, until the white is set and the yolk is firm, about 4 minutes; flip it for the last minute if you like.
Plate the salmon and potatoes with the greens, top the fish with the caramelized onions and the fried egg, and spoon the pebre alongside.
tip: Pebre keeps 3 days in the fridge and is good on everything. A fried egg on top makes it a proper a lo pobre.
ingredients: fried until the yolk is firm
half sliced for the pan, half for the pebre

name: Argentine lentil guiso with smoked turkey sausage and greens
inspiredBy: Argentine guiso de lentejas, a thick stew of lentils, sausage, potato and vegetables, with a smoked turkey sausage and less of it and a handful of greens
about: A hearty, paprika-scented lentil stew with a little smoked turkey sausage, potato and sweet pepper, finished with tender greens and a splash of vinegar. It is a classic cold-weather dish from Argentina and Uruguay, and it tastes even better the next day. The lentils and greens bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the vinegar and tomato help your body absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a heavy pot and brown the sausage for 3 minutes, until it is golden at the edges.
Add the onion and pepper and cook, stirring, until soft, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic, paprika, cumin and oregano and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the lentils, the chopped tomatoes, the bay leaf and enough water to cover everything by about 2 cm, roughly 800 ml for two portions. Bring to a boil, then simmer partly covered for 15 minutes.
Add the potatoes and keep simmering until the lentils and potatoes are both tender and the stew is thick, about 15 minutes. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Stir in the greens, the salt and the pepper and cook 4 minutes, until the greens are tender. Take off the heat and stir in the vinegar.
Ladle into bowls. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Add the salt and vinegar near the end, since they can keep lentils firm. The guiso thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat.

name: Sardines with boiled yuca, salsa criolla and avocado
inspiredBy: the Peruvian pairing of boiled yuca with salsa criolla, with canned sardines as the main
about: Soft boiled yuca and creamy avocado with whole sardines, all topped with a sharp salsa criolla of red onion, tomato, lime, ají amarillo and cilantro. It takes about 40 minutes, or 20 with frozen yuca, and tastes like the coast. Sardines with their soft bones bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, and the lime and onion bring the brightness.
steps: Cut the yuca into chunky pieces and boil in well-salted water until a fork goes in easily, about 20 to 25 minutes. Drain, and cut out any tough core thread you find.

Make the salsa criolla: toss the sliced onion with the lime juice, the ají amarillo paste, the oil, the tomato, most of the cilantro and a pinch of salt. Let it sit for 10 minutes, so the onion softens and turns pink.
Pile the warm yuca on a plate, set the sardines beside it and add the avocado.
Spoon the salsa criolla over the sardines and yuca and finish with the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Frozen peeled yuca is already prepped and cooks in about 15 minutes. A boiled potato or a sweet potato works too.
ingredients: two small tins (about 3.75 oz each), drained, with the soft bones

name: Lomo saltado with roasted potatoes and brown rice
inspiredBy: Peruvian lomo saltado, the chifa stir-fry of beef, onion and tomato, with roasted potatoes in place of fries and brown rice
about: Strips of sirloin seared hot with red onion, tomato and ají amarillo, splashed with soy and vinegar and tossed with golden potato wedges, over a little brown rice. It is a Lima favourite, born of Chinese-Peruvian cooking, and it cooks in minutes once the prep is done. The beef brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the tomato and ají bring vitamin C.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potato wedges with a third of the oil and the salt and roast on a tray until golden and tender, about 30 minutes, turning once.
Use a tub of Sunday rice, or cook 30 g of dry brown rice in twice its volume of salted water, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes.
Toss the beef strips with the soy sauce, half the vinegar, the garlic, the cumin and the pepper and let them sit for 10 minutes.
Heat a large pan or wok until it is properly hot. Sear the beef in two batches in half the remaining oil, 1 to 2 minutes each, so it browns instead of stewing. Lift it out onto a plate.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan and stir-fry the onion wedges with the ají amarillo paste for 2 minutes, until they just soften but stay crisp at the edges. Add the tomato wedges for 1 minute.
Return the beef and its juices with the rest of the vinegar and toss over the highest heat for 30 seconds, so it just coats. Then fold in the roasted potatoes and the cilantro.
Serve over the rice. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cut the beef and veg while the oven heats, and cook the stir-fry in two batches for two portions. The potatoes soften as the leftovers sit, so reheat everything in a hot pan, not the microwave.
ingredients: trimmed, sliced across the grain in thin strips

name: Moqueca de cavala with garlicky collards and brown rice
inspiredBy: moqueca capixaba from Espírito Santo, made with urucum, tomato and cilantro, without coconut or dendê
about: Mackerel simmered capixaba style, layered with tomato, onion, pepper, cilantro and scallion in urucum-red olive oil, served over brown rice with a side of garlicky couve. It is a weekend dish, but it is mostly waiting while the pot does the work. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the collards bring calcium.
steps: Put the fish in a bowl with the lime juice, a third of the garlic, a third of the salt and the pepper. Let it marinate for 15 minutes.
Use a tub of Sunday rice, or start the rice first: cook 30 g of dry brown rice in twice its volume of salted water, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes.

Warm two-thirds of the oil in a wide, shallow pot over medium-low heat. Stir in the colorau for 20 seconds, until it turns the oil orange-red. Make layers of onion rings, pepper rings, the tomato slices, the scallion and half the cilantro, sprinkling in a third of the garlic and a pinch of the salt as you go.
Pour 4 tablespoons of water over the vegetables, cover and simmer on low for 10 minutes, until the vegetables begin to soften.

Nestle the fish into the sauce, spoon some of the sauce over it, cover again and simmer gently for 8 to 10 minutes, until the fish flakes easily. Shake the pot now and then rather than stirring, so the pieces stay whole.
Meanwhile, roll the collard leaves and slice them into thin ribbons. Stir-fry in the rest of the oil with the remaining garlic and salt for 3 minutes, until bright green.
Scatter the rest of the cilantro over the stew. Serve with the rice and the collards, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Brazilians would use cavala (king mackerel) or any firm fish; Atlantic mackerel is richer in omega-3 and easier to find. Colorau (urucum powder) is sold at Brazilian and Latin shops. In Espírito Santo it is cooked in a clay pot. For a Bahian touch, swap a teaspoon of the oil for dendê (red palm oil) and add a spoonful of coconut milk.
ingredients: skin on, cut in 4 cm pieces

name: Ajiaco-inspired chicken and potato soup with corn and avocado
inspiredBy: Colombian ajiaco santafereño, with a simpler mix of potatoes, with avocado as in Bogotá, and lime in place of the cream and capers
about: A thick, golden chicken and potato soup from Bogotá, with sweet corn, plenty of cilantro and a creamy slice of avocado, brightened with a squeeze of lime at the table. It is the dish Colombians crave on cold days. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and the potatoes and corn bring potassium and fibre.
steps: Put the chicken, the scallion whites, the garlic, the guascas and the thin potato slices in a pot with water to cover by about 3 cm. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer gently for 20 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the sliced potato has begun to dissolve into the broth.
Lift out the chicken and shred it with two forks.
Add the potato chunks and the corn to the pot and simmer until the potatoes are tender, about 15 minutes. The soup should be thick and golden.
Return the chicken to the pot with the salt, the pepper and most of the cilantro, and warm through for 3 minutes.
Ladle into a deep bowl. Top with the avocado, the green scallion, the rest of the cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Make double and freeze a portion, without the avocado. Guascas are sold dried at Colombian shops; a pinch of oregano is a distant stand-in.
ingredients: half peeled and sliced thin, half in chunks
a small cob, in 3 pieces, or the same weight of frozen kernels

name: Mamão with lime
about: Cool, sweet papaya with a good squeeze of lime, the way it is served at a Brazilian breakfast table. Papaya brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into cubes or wedges.
Squeeze the lime juice over the top.

name: Açaí na tigela with banana and papaya
about: A frozen açaí bowl blended with banana and topped with sliced banana, papaya and crushed peanuts, as served at Brazilian juice bars. It is thick and cold, and since unsweetened açaí is earthy, ripe banana is the sweetener. Açaí brings **fibre and antioxidants**, and the peanuts add vitamin E.
steps: Run the frozen pulp under warm water for a few seconds to loosen it, then blend with half the banana until thick and smooth, adding a splash of water only if the blender stalls.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the sliced banana, the papaya and the crushed peanuts. Eat right away, before it melts.
ingredients: frozen unsweetened pulp, a standard pack
half in the blender, half sliced

name: Choclo con queso
about: Warm sweet corn kernels with a slab of queijo coalho and a squeeze of lime, the street snack of the Peruvian Andes. It is salty, sweet and chewy. Corn brings **fibre**, and the cheese brings calcium.
steps: Boil the corn kernels in plenty of unsalted water until tender and bright yellow, about 5 minutes. Drain.
Toss with the salt and the lime and eat warm with the queijo coalho.
ingredients: frozen kernels, or fresh off the cob

name: Maní with lime and ají
about: A small handful of roasted peanuts tossed warm with lime juice, salt and a pinch of cayenne. Peanuts bring **vitamin E, magnesium and protein**.
steps: Warm the peanuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant.
Toss with the lime juice and cayenne in a bowl.

name: Banana with peanuts and cinnamon
about: A ripe banana sliced over a spoonful of chopped roasted peanuts, with a dusting of cinnamon. It is sweet, salty and filling. The banana brings **potassium**, and the peanuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Slice the banana into a bowl.
Chop the peanuts, scatter them over and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Camote asado with toasted pepitas and lime
about: Sweet potato roasted until its edges caramelize, with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds (pepas de zapallo) and a squeeze of lime, a roasted snack that pairs well with a salty crunch. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and fibre**, and the pepitas bring iron, zinc and magnesium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato rounds with the oil and half the salt.
Roast on a tray until soft and caramelized at the edges, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat until they puff and pop, about 3 minutes.
Scatter the pepitas over the sweet potato, sprinkle with the rest of the salt and squeeze over the lime.

name: Naranja with cinnamon
about: Juicy orange segments with a dusting of cinnamon, a simple, refreshing way to finish a meal or fill a gap. Orange brings **vitamin C and folate**.
steps: Peel the oranges and cut them into rounds or segments.
Dust with the cinnamon.

name: Pepas de zapallo tostadas, with salt and ají
about: A small handful of pumpkin seeds toasted in a dry pan until they puff and pop, then tossed with salt and a pinch of cayenne. They are a common snack from Peru to Chile. Pumpkin seeds bring **iron, zinc and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff up and start to pop, about 3 minutes.
Toss with the cayenne and the salt while they are still warm.

name: Camote asado with cinnamon and lime
about: Sweet potato roasted until its edges caramelize, with a pinch of cinnamon and a squeeze of lime. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato rounds with the oil.
Roast on a tray until soft and caramelized at the edges, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Dust with the cinnamon and squeeze over the lime.

name: Arepita de choclo con queso
about: A small, sweet corn arepa with a little queijo coalho inside, cooked on a griddle until golden. It is the kind of arepa you buy hot from a Colombian street cart. Corn and cheese together bring **fibre, protein and calcium**.
steps: Blend the corn with a splash of water until mostly smooth. Stir in the cornmeal and the salt and let it sit for 10 minutes to thicken.
Fold in the cubes of queijo coalho.
Brush a non-stick pan with the oil over medium heat. Spoon in the batter and flatten to about 1 cm thick. Cook until golden, about 4 minutes a side, until the cheese is soft inside.

name: Toasted corn with lime and salt
about: Corn kernels toasted in a pan until golden and blistered, then tossed with lime and salt, in the spirit of Peruvian cancha. It is toasty, sweet and a little chewy. Corn brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Pat the corn kernels very dry with a clean towel.
Toast them in a wide pan with the oil over medium-high heat, stirring often, until golden and blistered, about 10 minutes. It spits, so keep a lid ajar.
Toss with the lime juice and the salt while still warm.
ingredients: frozen kernels, thawed and patted very dry

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil kadalai sundal
about: Warm chickpeas tossed with mustard seed, curry leaves, green chili and fresh coconut, the way they are served as a temple snack in Tamil Nadu. It is simple and savoury, with **protein and fibre** from the chickpeas.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the hing, curry leaves and finely chopped green chili for a few seconds.
Add the chickpeas and the salt and stir for 3 minutes, until hot.
Take off the heat and stir in the coconut and lemon juice. Eat warm.

name: Spiced neer mor
inspiredBy: Tamil neer mor, Kerala sambaram
about: Thin, cooling spiced buttermilk made from curd, ginger, green chili and curry leaf, the drink every South Indian household has in the afternoon. It is salty, sour and refreshing, with **calcium and protein**.
steps: Whisk the curd with about half a cup of cold water until it is smooth and pourable.
Crush the ginger, green chili and curry leaf together in a mortar or mini blender. Stir them into the buttermilk with the hing, cumin and salt.
Chill for 10 minutes if you have time, and serve over ice.

name: Guava with chili, lemon and almonds
inspiredBy: South Indian and Sri Lankan street-cart guava
about: Crisp, fragrant guava wedges with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili powder and salt, the way they are sold on the street from Chennai to Colombo, with a few soaked almonds for crunch. It is sweet, sour and spicy, and it gives you **more vitamin C than an orange** plus **vitamin E** from the almonds.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges and put them on a plate with the drained almonds.
Squeeze the lemon over, then sprinkle with the chili powder and salt.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight

name: Steamed sweet potato with chili and lime
inspiredBy: Kerala and Tamil steamed kizhangu (tubers)
about: Sweet potato steamed until tender and tossed with a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chili powder and fresh coconut, the way tubers are eaten as a snack in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It is soft, sweet and a little spicy, and it is loaded with **vitamin A**.
steps: Steam the sweet potato chunks for 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slides in easily.
Toss with the lemon juice, chili powder, salt and coconut and eat warm.

name: Kerala pepper egg fry
inspiredBy: Kerala mutta pepper fry
about: Boiled eggs tossed in a hot pan with onion, curry leaves and plenty of cracked black pepper, a tea-shop favourite in Kerala that works just as well at home. It is peppery and savoury, with **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool them in cold water and peel. Halve them.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the onion, the turmeric and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and cook until the onion is golden, about 4 minutes.
Add the pepper and salt, then the eggs, cut side down, and toss for 1 to 2 minutes, until coated and a little crisp at the edges.

name: Pesarattu with ginger chutney and curd
inspiredBy: Andhra pesarattu, the green moong dosa, with allam pachadi
about: A crisp, golden dosa made from soaked whole green moong blitzed with ginger, green chili and cumin, served the Andhra way with a sharp allam pachadi (ginger chutney) and a big bowl of curd. There is no fermenting, only an overnight soak. The moong and curd give you **plenty of protein, folate and iron** before nine in the morning.
steps: The night before, rinse the moong and soak it in plenty of cold water for at least 6 hours. Drain well in the morning.

Blend the moong with a third of the ginger, the green chili, the cumin, half the salt and about half a cup of water, until the batter is smooth and pourable, like thin pancake batter. It does not need to ferment.

Make the chutney: pound the rest of the ginger in a mortar with the tamarind, the rest of the salt and a splash of water until it is thick and spoonable. It should taste sharp and hot. Scrape it into a bowl.

Now the tempering, called thalippu or tadka. Warm a teaspoon of the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and the dried chili and let them pop for a few seconds, then add the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Pour the sizzling oil over the chutney. Hot oil wakes up the spices and gives the chutney its smell.

Warm a non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a little oil. Pour in half the batter and spread it into a thin round with the back of the ladle. Scatter on half the onion, drizzle a few drops of oil around the edge and cook until the underside is crisp and golden and the top looks dry, about 3 minutes. You do not need to flip it. Repeat with the rest.
Serve the pesarattu hot, with the chutney and the curd.
tip: A pinch of jaggery in the chutney is traditional, because allam pachadi is sweet, sour and hot. Pesarattu is often filled with a spoonful of upma, which is called an MLA pesarattu.
ingredients: a third for the batter, the rest for the chutney
finely chopped, for sprinkling on the dosa

name: Kerala prawn roast with green bean thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala chemmeen roast and beans thoran, served as a home lunch plate
about: Prawns tossed in a dark, glossy masala of slow-browned onion, tomato, ginger and black pepper, with a dry stir-fry of green beans and fresh coconut and a portion of red rice. It is the kind of plate you find at a Kerala home lunch. The prawns bring **lean protein, iodine and selenium**, and the beans and coconut bring fibre.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain. Red rice takes longer than white, so start it first.
Pat the prawns dry and toss them with the turmeric, a pinch of the salt and half the pepper.

Warm half the coconut oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and a splash of water and cook, stirring, until deep golden brown, about 10 minutes. Add a spoonful of water whenever it starts to catch. Browning the onion well is what makes a roast taste like a roast.

Add the ginger, half the curry leaves, the chili powder and the rest of the pepper and stir for a minute. Add the tomato and a splash of water and cook until it breaks down into a thick, jammy masala, about 8 minutes.
Add the prawns and toss for 3 to 4 minutes, until they curl and turn pink and the masala clings to them. Set aside.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the coconut oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Add the green beans, a pinch of salt and a splash of water, cover and cook for 5 minutes. Uncover, stir in the coconut, crushed with a spoonful of the onion and a pinch of turmeric, and cook for 1 minute more.
Serve the prawn roast and the thoran with the red rice.
tip: Cook the rice and brown the onion masala on Sunday night. At lunch, the prawns and thoran take 10 minutes. Keep the pan uncovered at the end of the thoran, since it is meant to be dry.
ingredients: Kerala matta rice, or any red rice
red chili powder, Kashmiri if you like it milder

name: Vegetable sambar with brown rice
inspiredBy: Tamil sambar, the everyday lentil and vegetable stew
about: Toor dal simmered with drumstick, pumpkin and spinach in a tangy tamarind broth, finished with a sizzling tempering of mustard seed, dried red chilies, hing and curry leaves. It is the soul of the Tamil table. The dal and vegetables bring **protein, fibre and folate** in one pot, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the dal and simmer it in a covered pot with plenty of water until completely soft, about 35 minutes (or 12 minutes in a pressure cooker). Mash it with the back of a spoon.
Meanwhile, rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.

In a second pot, simmer the onion, drumstick and pumpkin with the tamarind, sambar powder, salt and about 2 cups of water until the vegetables are tender but still holding their shape, about 12 minutes.
Stir the mashed dal and the spinach into the vegetables and simmer for 5 minutes, adding water as needed until the spinach has wilted and it is a pourable, soupy stew.

Now the tempering (thalippu), which gives sambar its fragrance. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the dried chilies, hing and curry leaves (stand back, they spit). The moment the leaves crackle, pour the sizzling oil into the sambar.
Serve the sambar over the rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch. Sambar thickens overnight, so add a splash of water when you reheat.
tip: Scrape the soft flesh of the drumstick off the tough pod with your teeth, and leave the pod on your plate. A small pinch of jaggery rounds off the tamarind nicely if you keep some in the pantry.
ingredients: cut into 5 cm lengths, frozen is fine
small shallots if you can find them, halved
roughly chopped, as in a keerai sambar

name: Kerala sardine curry with cabbage thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala mathi (sardine) curry, a sour red tamarind curry
about: Fresh sardines simmered in a sour, red chili and tamarind gravy with shallot, ginger and garlic, served with a dry cabbage and coconut thoran and red rice. It is a home classic of the Kerala coast. Sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3 fats and vitamin D** you can buy.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain.

Set aside a spoonful of the shallot, a clove of the garlic and a pinch of the turmeric for the thoran. Blitz the rest of the shallot, ginger and garlic with the chili powder, the rest of the turmeric and a splash of water into a rough red paste.
Warm half the coconut oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add half the curry leaves, then the paste, and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until it smells cooked and the oil begins to separate.

Stir in the tamarind, the salt and a cup of water and simmer for 5 minutes. Lay in the sardines, spoon the gravy over them, cover and cook gently for 8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and flakes easily. Shake the pan rather than stirring, so the fish stays whole.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Add the cabbage with a pinch of salt and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until crisp-tender, then stir in the coconut, crushed with a spoonful of the shallot, a clove of the garlic and a pinch of turmeric.
Serve the fish curry and the thoran with the rice.
tip: No fresh sardines? Atlantic mackerel steaks work well, or use one 120 g tin of sardines and warm them in the gravy for just 3 minutes.
ingredients: whole, cleaned and heads off, fresh or frozen
Kerala matta rice, or any red rice
small shallots if you can find them
red chili powder, Kashmiri if you like it milder

name: Egg hoppers with pol sambol
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan egg hoppers (egg appa), with a fermented brown rice batter
about: Lacy, bowl-shaped brown rice pancakes made from an overnight fermented batter, with a soft-set egg in the middle and a zingy pol sambol of fresh coconut, onion, chili and lemon. It is Sri Lanka's favourite breakfast. Two eggs bring **protein and choline** to the plate.
steps: The morning before, soak the brown rice in plenty of water for at least 6 hours. That evening, drain it and blend it with the cooked rice, coconut milk, curd, half the salt and just 2 tablespoons of water until completely smooth, like thick cream. Cover the bowl and leave it somewhere warm overnight, until the batter is bubbly and smells pleasantly sour. This is what gives hoppers their lacy edge.
In the morning, make the pol sambol: pound or pulse the coconut with the onion, chili powder, lemon juice and the rest of the salt until it is crumbly and bright red. It should be moist, not a paste.

Heat a small, deep non-stick pan (or a small wok with a lid) until it is very hot, then wipe it with a little of the oil. Pour in half the batter, then lift the pan and swirl so the batter climbs the sides and leaves a thicker pool in the middle.

Crack an egg into the middle, cover and cook over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until the edge is crisp and golden, the white is set and the yolk is still jammy. Slide the hopper out and repeat with the rest.
Eat the hoppers warm, tearing off the crisp edge and scooping up the egg with the sambol.
tip: A hopper pan (appachatti) makes the classic bowl shape, but a small deep non-stick pan does a fine job.
ingredients: soaked in water for at least 6 hours
a spoonful of cooked brown rice saved from Monday's sambar rice or Friday's kootu rice
finely chopped, red onion if you have it

name: Sri Lankan red lentil dhal with kale mallung and red rice
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan parippu with a kale mallung, in place of the usual gotu kola sambol
about: Creamy red lentils cooked with turmeric and a splash of coconut milk, finished with a mustard seed, dried chili and curry leaf tempering, alongside a quick kale mallung wilted with onion, turmeric and fresh coconut. It is Sri Lanka's everyday dhal (parippu) with a leafy side, a plate every home cook makes. The lentils bring **protein, iron and folate**, and the second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain.

Rinse the lentils and put them in a pot with most of the turmeric, half the onion, the garlic, half the salt and about 3 cups of water. Simmer, partly covered, until completely soft, about 20 minutes.
Stir in the coconut milk and simmer for 3 minutes more. Whisk briefly so the dhal turns creamy.

Now the tempering. Warm half the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the dried chilies and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit). Fry for 30 seconds and pour it over the dhal.

For the mallung, warm the rest of the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Add the rest of the onion and a pinch of turmeric and cook for 2 minutes, then add the kale and the rest of the salt and toss for 2 minutes, just until it wilts and stays bright green. Take it off the heat and stir in the coconut and the lemon juice.
Serve the dhal over the rice with the mallung alongside. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the mallung in a small container. Keep two spoonfuls of the dhal back for Saturday's rasam.
tip: Gotu kola is sold at some South Asian and Southeast Asian grocers. If you find it, make a raw sambol with it and the coconut instead of the mallung.
ingredients: stems removed, finely shredded, standing in for gotu kola

name: Mackerel ambul thiyal-style sour pepper fish with leek mallung and brown rice
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan ambul thiyal, which is normally made with tuna and goraka, here with mackerel and tamarind
about: Chunks of mackerel simmered dry in tamarind, black pepper, garlic and cinnamon until they are coated in a dark, tangy paste, with a quick leek and coconut mallung and brown rice. Ambul thiyal is a Sri Lankan southern-coast classic, normally made with tuna. Mackerel makes it a rich source of **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**.
steps: Rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.
Rub the fish with the tamarind, pepper, garlic, cinnamon and half the salt, and leave it for 10 minutes. The sourness tames the strong smell of the mackerel.

Put the fish in a pan with a little of the oil, the dried chilies, half the curry leaves and a quarter cup of water. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes, then uncover and cook until the liquid has cooked away and the fish is coated in a dark, almost dry paste, about 5 minutes. Turn the pieces gently once.

While the fish cooks, make the mallung. Warm the rest of the oil in a second pan, add the rest of the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and the green chili, then the leek, the turmeric and the rest of the salt. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the leek is soft and sweet.
Stir in the coconut and take the pan off the heat.
Serve the fish and the mallung over the rice.
tip: If goraka (a sour dried fruit) is at your grocer, soak a piece in warm water and use it in place of the tamarind.
ingredients: steaks or fillets, cut into chunks
gingelly oil, as in Sri Lankan cooking
white and pale green parts, sliced thin

name: Bisi bele bath-style lentil rice with pumpkin, spinach and peanuts
inspiredBy: Karnataka bisi bele bath ("hot lentil rice"), with brown rice and more greens
about: A one-pot Karnataka comfort dish of brown rice, toor dal, pumpkin and spinach cooked soft with tamarind and bisi bele bath spices, finished with a ghee, mustard seed and dried chili tempering and toasted peanuts. A bowl of curd on the side cools it. The dal and vegetables bring **protein and fibre**, and it makes two portions, so Saturday's lunch is done.
steps: Rinse the rice and the dal together. Put them in a heavy pot with about 4 cups of water and simmer, partly covered, until both are very soft and the mixture is porridge-like, about 40 minutes (15 minutes in a pressure cooker). Stir now and then so it does not stick.

Add the pumpkin, tamarind, bisi bele bath powder and salt, with another cup of water. Cook until the pumpkin is tender, about 12 minutes, then stir in the spinach and cook 3 minutes more, until everything melts together into a thick, spoonable stew.

Warm the ghee in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the peanuts and the dried chili and fry until the peanuts are golden, about 1 minute. Add the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit).
Pour the tempering, peanuts and all, over the pot and stir it in.
Serve in bowls with a bowl of curd on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of hot water when you reheat.
tip: Bisi bele bath should be loose and porridge-like, not dry, so stir in hot water until it falls off a spoon. A small pinch of jaggery is traditional if you keep some in the pantry.

name: Chettinad pepper chicken with foxtail millet
inspiredBy: Chettinad milagu kozhi (pepper chicken) from the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu
about: Chicken thighs slow-cooked in a freshly toasted and ground masala of black pepper, fennel, coriander seed and dried red chili with caramelized onion and a curd marinade, served over foxtail millet with a crisp onion and cucumber side. This is the peppery, fragrant cooking of the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu, and it is worth the weekend. The chicken brings **protein, niacin and B6**, and it makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Toast the peppercorns, coriander seed, half the fennel and the dried chilies in a dry pan over medium heat for about a minute, until they smell warm and toasty. Grind them to a fine powder in a spice grinder or mortar. This fresh masala is what makes Chettinad cooking taste the way it does.
Blitz the garlic and ginger with a splash of water into a smooth paste. Toss the chicken with half the paste, the curd and a pinch of the salt and leave it to marinate while you cook the onion.

Warm the oil in a wide, heavy pan over medium heat. Add the rest of the fennel seeds whole and let them sizzle for 10 seconds, then the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), then the onion, and cook until deep golden brown, about 12 minutes.
Stir in the rest of the garlic and ginger paste and cook for 2 minutes, until the raw smell is gone.

Add the marinated chicken, the ground masala and the rest of the salt, and stir well so every piece is coated. Pour in half a cup of water, cover and cook gently for 20 minutes, until the chicken is tender.

Meanwhile, rinse the millet and cook it in a little over twice its volume of water, covered, until fluffy, about 15 minutes. Toss the sliced cucumber with the few raw onion slices and a pinch of salt for the side.

Uncover the chicken and cook for 5 to 8 minutes more, stirring often, until the sauce clings to the chicken in a dark, almost dry masala. Serve over the millet with the cucumber and onion side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: For the real Chettinad flavour, use gingelly (sesame) oil in place of the canola. Make the masala powder in a double batch, since it keeps a month in a jar and is lovely on roasted vegetables.
ingredients: skinless thighs, bone out, cut into pieces
finely sliced, plus a few slices kept raw for the side

name: Kerala fish moilee with spinach thoran and red rice
inspiredBy: Kerala fish molee, a Syrian Christian coconut milk curry, with Spanish mackerel for seer fish
about: Chunks of fish in a light, gently spiced coconut gravy with ginger, green chili and curry leaves, finished with lemon and a sizzle of onion, alongside a green spinach thoran and red rice. Moilee is a mild, fragrant Kerala curry, traditionally made with seer fish. Spanish mackerel is from the same family, so it brings **omega-3 fats and B12**.
steps: Rinse the red rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain.
Rub the fish with the turmeric and half the salt and leave it for 10 minutes.

Warm half the oil in a wide pan over medium-low heat. Add half the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), then most of the onion, the ginger and the green chili and cook gently for 5 minutes, until soft and fragrant but not browned. Moilee is a pale curry.

Add the coconut milk and a quarter cup of water and bring to a bare simmer. Slide in the fish, cover and cook gently for 7 to 8 minutes, until it is just opaque, spooning the gravy over now and then. Do not boil hard, or the coconut milk may split. Stir in the lemon juice and take it off the heat.

For the thoran, warm the rest of the oil in a second pan. Add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the curry leaves and the last of the onion and cook for 1 minute. Spoon a little of this sizzling onion and curry leaf over the moilee, then add the spinach and the rest of the salt to the pan and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until wilted. Stir in the coconut.
Serve the moilee and the thoran with the red rice.
tip: Any firm white fish also makes a lovely, lighter moilee.
ingredients: steaks or fillets, cut into chunks, standing in for seer fish
Kerala matta rice, or any red rice

name: Foxtail millet upma with egg podimas
inspiredBy: Tamil thinai upma, made with foxtail millet in place of the usual semolina, with muttai podimas
about: A savoury, fluffy upma made with foxtail millet instead of semolina, with green beans and toasted peanuts, and soft onion-and-curry-leaf scrambled eggs (podimas) on the side. It is a Tamil tiffin favourite with a grain that keeps you full for hours. The millet and beans bring **fibre**, and the eggs bring **protein and choline**.
steps: Rinse the millet well and drain it. Toast it in a dry pot over medium heat for 2 minutes, until it smells nutty, then tip it into a bowl.

Warm the oil in the same pot. Add the mustard seeds, and when they pop, add the urad dal and the peanuts. Stir for about a minute, until the dal turns golden and the peanuts smell roasted. This is the tempering (thalippu), and the urad dal is what gives upma its nutty crunch.

Add the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), the green chili, ginger and two thirds of the onion. Cook until the onion is soft and glassy, about 4 minutes. Spoon a quarter of this mixture into a small bowl for the eggs.

Stir the green beans into the pot for 1 minute. Add the toasted millet, half the salt and a little over twice as much water as millet. Bring to a boil, then cover and cook on low until the water is absorbed and the millet is tender, about 15 minutes.

While the millet cooks, make the podimas. Warm a small non-stick pan, add the spoonful of onion mixture and the rest of the raw onion and cook for a minute. Beat in the eggs with the rest of the salt and stir gently until just set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Rest the upma covered for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork. Serve with the egg podimas and a bowl of curd.
tip: Make the upma the night before and reheat it with a splash of water while the eggs cook, or use a pressure cooker and have it ready in 10 minutes.

name: Lemon foxtail millet with peanuts and chickpeas, and cucumber pachadi
inspiredBy: Karnataka chitranna (lemon rice) made with foxtail millet, with chickpeas as in a Tamil sundal
about: Fluffy foxtail millet tossed with mustard seed, urad dal, peanuts, ginger and a good squeeze of lemon, with chickpeas folded in and a cooling cucumber pachadi on the side. It is a lunchbox favourite across Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The chickpeas and curd make it a **filling, protein-rich** lunch.
steps: Rinse the millet, drain it and cook it in a little over twice its volume of water with a pinch of the salt, covered, until tender and fluffy, about 15 minutes. Spread it on a plate for a few minutes so the grains stay separate.

Warm the oil in a wide pan. Add the mustard seeds, and when they pop, add the urad dal, the peanuts and the dried chili and fry until the dal is golden. This is the tempering (thalippu), and it is what makes lemon millet taste like lemon millet. Spoon a little of the tempering into a small cup and keep it for the pachadi.
Add the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), the ginger and turmeric to the pan and stir for 30 seconds. Add the chickpeas and warm them through for 2 minutes.
Fold in the millet and the rest of the salt, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the lemon juice. Adding the lemon off the heat keeps it fresh and bright.
Squeeze the grated cucumber dry and stir it into the curd with a pinch of salt, then stir in the reserved tempering. Serve the pachadi alongside the millet.

name: Moong dal and cabbage kootu with carrot poriyal and brown rice
inspiredBy: Tamil muttaikose kootu and carrot poriyal, the classic home lunch plate
about: A gentle, coconut-scented kootu of split moong dal and soft cabbage, alongside a sweet carrot poriyal tempered with mustard and urad dal, with brown rice and a bowl of curd. It is the sort of plate you would be served at a Tamil home lunch. The moong brings **protein, folate and iron**, and the carrot brings **vitamin A**.
steps: Rinse the brown rice and cook it in plenty of boiling water until tender, about 30 minutes, then drain.
Rinse the moong dal and simmer it with the turmeric, half the salt and about 3 cups of water until soft but not mushy, about 15 minutes.

Stir the cabbage into the dal and cook until it is soft and sweet, about 6 minutes. Crush half the coconut with the cumin and one of the dried chilies in a mortar into a rough paste, stir it in and simmer for 2 minutes. This is the kootu.

Now the tempering (thalippu). Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the urad dal, the other dried chili and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit) and fry until the dal is golden. Pour half over the kootu.

Stir the grated carrot into the rest of the tempering with the remaining salt and a splash of water. Cover and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until just tender, then uncover and stir in the rest of the coconut. This dry stir-fry is the poriyal.
Serve the kootu and the poriyal over the rice with the curd on the side.
tip: Use bottle gourd, ash gourd or zucchini in place of the cabbage for a different kootu.

name: Pepper rasam cup
inspiredBy: Tamil milagu rasam (pepper rasam)
about: A thin, tangy, peppery soup of tomato, tamarind, garlic and a little dal, with a mustard, dried chili and curry leaf tempering. Rasam is the South Indian cure for everything, and a hot cup in the afternoon is lovely. It has **vitamin C and lycopene** from the tomato.
steps: Mash the cooked dhal with a splash of hot water until it is smooth and thin.

Put the tomato, tamarind, half the garlic, half the pepper, half the cumin, the salt and 1 cup of water in a small pot. Simmer for 8 minutes, until the tomato has collapsed. Stir in the dhal and simmer 2 minutes.

Now the tempering. Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the rest of the cumin, pepper and garlic, the dried chili, the hing and the curry leaves (stand back, they spit), and pour it over the rasam. Sip it hot.
ingredients: two spoonfuls of leftover cooked dhal, or red lentils cooked soft
a piece of whole dried red chili

name: Moong kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka hesaru bele kosambari
about: A cool, crunchy Karnataka salad of soaked split moong dal, cucumber and coconut with lemon and a mustard seed tempering. It is a temple and festival favourite and it is light, with **protein and fibre**.
steps: Toss the soaked moong dal with the cucumber, coconut and finely chopped green chili in a bowl.
Warm the oil in a small pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the curry leaves for a few seconds and pour the sizzling oil over the salad.
Add the salt and lemon juice, toss and eat within the hour while the dal is still crunchy.
ingredients: moong dal, soaked in water for 1 to 2 hours and drained

name: Boiled peanut sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil verkadalai sundal
