about: Fresh peanuts simmered until tender and tossed with mustard seed, curry leaf, green chili and fresh coconut, a favourite street snack on the Tamil coast. It is hearty, with **protein and magnesium**.
steps: Soak the peanuts in cold water for 4 hours, then drain. Cover them with fresh water, add a pinch of the salt and simmer until tender, about 35 minutes. Drain them.
Warm the oil in a pan, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then the curry leaves and chopped green chili for a few seconds.
Add the peanuts and the rest of the salt and toss for 2 minutes. Off the heat, stir in the coconut and lemon juice.

name: Papaya with lemon
about: Ripe papaya in bite-sized chunks with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper, a soft, fragrant fruit snack. The papaya brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into chunks.
Squeeze the lemon over the top and add a pinch of freshly ground pepper.

name: Boiled egg with lunu miris
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan lunu miris
about: A hard-boiled egg halved and topped with lunu miris, the Sri Lankan relish of onion pounded with chili, lemon and salt. It is hot, sour and savoury, and it is a very easy snack. The egg brings **protein and choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 9 minutes, cool it in cold water, peel and halve it.
Pound the onion with the chili powder, lemon juice and salt into a wet red relish and spoon it over the egg.

name: Papaya with soaked almonds and lemon
about: Ripe papaya in bite-sized chunks with a few soaked almonds, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of black pepper. It is soft, sweet and a little crunchy, and it gives you **vitamin C, vitamin A and vitamin E**.
steps: Scoop out the seeds and cut the papaya into chunks. Drain the soaked almonds.
Squeeze the lemon over the papaya, scatter the almonds on top and add a pinch of freshly ground pepper.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight

name: Badam lassi
inspiredBy: South Indian badam paal, as a lassi
about: Cold yogurt blended with soaked almonds, a pinch of cardamom and a splash of water into a thick, cooling drink, a South Indian take on badam milk. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the yogurt brings calcium.
steps: Slip the skins off the soaked almonds so the lassi blends smooth. Put the curd, the almonds, the cardamom and about a quarter cup of cold water in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth and serve over ice.
tip: Blend in a little ripe papaya or a pinch of jaggery for a sweeter drink.
ingredients: soaked in water for a few hours or overnight and drained

name: South African oats with apricots, almonds and cinnamon
inspiredBy: South African oats porridge, with dried apricots and cinnamon
about: Creamy oats cooked in milk with chopped dried apricots and a good pinch of cinnamon, topped with toasted almonds. It is warm, gently sweet and ready in about 10 minutes. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the milk adds calcium and protein.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and nutty, about 3 minutes. Chop them roughly.
Put the oats, milk, apricots, cinnamon and salt in a small pot.
Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring often, until the oats are thick and creamy, about 6 minutes. Loosen with a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Spoon into a bowl and scatter the almonds over the top.
tip: Chop the apricots small so they melt into the porridge and sweeten it, with no sugar needed. Leave out the apricots and stir in a sliced ripe pear if you have no dried fruit.

name: Eggs in chakalaka with beans
inspiredBy: South African chakalaka, the spicy vegetable relish served at every braai, cooked into a breakfast skillet with beans and eggs
about: Eggs cooked until firm in a spicy tomato, pepper and carrot chakalaka with a few beans and a handful of spinach, the way South Africans love their baked beans and eggs. It is hearty, bright and a little hot. The eggs and beans bring **protein, choline and folate**.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, green pepper and carrot until soft and starting to colour, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, chakalaka spice and cayenne and cook for 1 minute, until it smells toasty.
Add the tomato, beans and salt and simmer, stirring, until the tomato is jammy, about 6 minutes. Stir in the spinach until just wilted.

Make two wells in the chakalaka and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook gently until the whites and the yolks are both firm, 8 to 10 minutes. Press a yolk gently with a spoon to check that it is not runny.
Toast the bread and serve it alongside for scooping up the eggs and the sauce.
tip: Cook the chakalaka (steps 1 to 3) the evening before, while the bobotie bakes or the umngqusho simmers. Reheat it in the morning, crack in the eggs and breakfast takes about 12 minutes.
ingredients: sugar beans or pinto beans, drained

name: Mabele sorghum porridge with amasi, guava, peanuts and sunflower seeds
inspiredBy: Mabele, the sorghum porridge of Botswana, Lesotho and South Africa, eaten soft with amasi (fermented milk), made here with whole sorghum cooked soft
about: A soft, slightly nutty sorghum porridge (mabele) topped with cold, tangy amasi, ripe guava and toasted peanuts and sunflower seeds. The sorghum, peanuts and seeds bring **iron, magnesium and vitamin E**, and the amasi adds calcium and protein.
steps: The night before, rinse the sorghum and soak it in plenty of cold water. Make enough for two mornings.

In the evening, drain the sorghum and put it in a pot with about three times as much fresh water and the salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer partly covered, stirring now and then, until the grains are tender and the porridge is thick, about 50 minutes. Top up with a splash of water if it gets dry. A pressure cooker does it in about 20 minutes.

Beat the porridge hard with a wooden spoon and mash some of the grains against the side of the pot, until it is soft and spoonable. This makes two portions, so cool both, cover and keep them in the fridge.

Next morning, toast the peanuts and sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Warm one portion with a splash of water, spoon it into a bowl and pour the amasi over it. Top with the guava and the toasted nuts and seeds.
The next day, warm the second portion and top it the same way.
tip: Cook it in the evening while dinner simmers, so breakfast is only a reheat. If you cannot find amasi, kefir or buttermilk is just as tangy. Use a ripe peach or a few strawberries when guava is not in season.
ingredients: plain kefir or buttermilk, for the amasi

name: Pilchards in tomato with soft pap and tomato and onion sambal
inspiredBy: South African pilchards and pap, the classic tinned fish lunch, with a fresh tomato and onion sambal
about: Canned pilchards warmed with onion, garlic and a handful of morogo-style greens, spooned over soft maize pap with a sharp tomato and onion sambal on the side. It is cheap, fast and a proper South African lunch. The pilchards bring **omega-3, vitamin B12 and calcium** from their soft bones.
steps: Make the sambal first so the flavours meet. Slice half the onion very thin and chop half the tomato. Toss them with the lemon juice, a pinch of cayenne, a pinch of salt and the cilantro, and leave it to sit.

Bring a pot of water to a boil, about five times the weight of the meal for a soft, spoonable pap, with a pinch of salt. Whisk in the cornmeal in a slow stream so there are no lumps. Turn the heat to low, cover and cook, stirring often, until the pap is thick and soft, about 15 minutes.
While the pap cooks, warm the oil in a small pan. Cook the rest of the onion and the garlic until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the remaining tomato and cook until saucy, about 3 minutes.
Tip in the pilchards with their sauce and break them up gently. Add the spinach and warm everything through until the spinach has just wilted, about 3 minutes.
Spoon the pap onto a plate, top with the pilchards and serve the sambal alongside.
tip: Use plain white cornmeal (whole-grain if you can find it), not masa harina or precooked arepa flour. Sardines in tomato sauce work if you cannot find pilchards.
ingredients: pilchards or sardines, with their tomato sauce
split between the sambal and the pan
half sliced thin for the sambal

name: Bobotie-inspired lentil and beef bake with turmeric rice and carrot sambal
inspiredBy: Cape Malay bobotie, spiced mince baked under an egg custard, with lentils sharing the work and brown rice for the usual yellow rice
about: Gently spiced beef and lentils with apricots and chutney, baked under a golden egg and milk custard, with turmeric brown rice and a bright carrot sambal. It is sweet, savoury and comforting, and it is even better the next day. The beef and lentils together bring **iron, zinc and plenty of protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 180C (350F). Rinse the rice and put it in a pot with plenty of water and half the turmeric. Simmer, covered, until tender, about 35 minutes, then drain. Make enough for two portions.
At the same time, simmer the lentils in plenty of water until just tender, about 25 minutes, and drain.
Warm the oil in a large pan. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, Cape Malay masala, cinnamon and the rest of the turmeric and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the beef and break it up as it browns, about 6 minutes. Stir in the lentils, chutney, apricots, half the lemon juice, salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 5 minutes, until moist but not wet.

Press the mixture into a baking dish and tuck the bay leaves on top. Beat the eggs with the milk and a pinch of salt and pour this over. Bake until the custard is set and lightly golden, about 25 minutes.
While it bakes, toss the grated carrot with the remaining lemon juice and a pinch of salt for the sambal.
Serve a portion of bobotie with the rice and the carrot sambal. This makes two portions, so pack the second for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well, or eat it cold.
tip: Use lean ground lamb if you like, which is also very Cape. For extra tang, serve a spoonful of chutney on the side.

name: Cape Malay-style mackerel and butternut curry with spinach
inspiredBy: Cape Malay fish curry, with tamarind for the sour note and butternut for sweetness
about: Chunks of mackerel simmered gently in a tomato and tamarind curry with sweet butternut and spinach, finished with lemon and cilantro. It is fragrant rather than fiery, with the sweet and sour balance the Cape does so well. The butternut adds **vitamin A**, and mackerel is a rich source of **omega-3, vitamin B12 and vitamin D**.
steps: Peel the butternut and cut it into 2 cm chunks. Cut the mackerel into big chunks, leaving the skin on, and sprinkle with half the salt and a little of the turmeric.
Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic, Cape Malay masala and the rest of the turmeric. Stir for 1 minute until it smells wonderful.
Add the tomato, tamarind, chutney and a mug of water, then add the butternut. Cover and simmer until it is nearly tender, about 12 minutes.

Nestle the mackerel into the sauce, cover and cook gently until it flakes, 6 to 8 minutes. Do not stir hard or the fish will break up. Fold in the spinach for the last 2 minutes, just until it wilts, then add the lemon juice, cilantro and the rest of the salt.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch and reheat it gently.
tip: Serve with rice or a roti for a bigger plate. Any oily fish works, such as sardines or fresh snoek if you have it.
ingredients: fillets with skin, cut in chunks

name: Zimbabwean beef stew with peanut greens and sadza
inspiredBy: Zimbabwean sadza ne nyama with muriwo une dovi, greens cooked in ground peanuts (a peanut butter sauce)
about: Slow-simmered beef in a tomato and onion gravy, with collard greens cooked in crushed roasted peanuts, and a modest portion of sadza to scoop it all up. It is the everyday Zimbabwean plate, and the greens make it so much more than meat and starch. Beef and greens together bring **iron, zinc and B12**, and the collards add calcium.
steps: Warm half the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in batches until deeply browned, about 8 minutes, and set aside.
In the same pot, cook two thirds of the onion until soft. Add the garlic, black pepper, bay leaves and cayenne, then the tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a sauce, about 6 minutes.

Return the beef to the pot with enough water to just cover it. Cover and simmer very gently until the beef is tender and the gravy is thick, about 90 minutes, or 35 minutes in a pressure cooker. Season with the salt near the end. This makes two portions.

For the greens, soften the rest of the onion in the remaining oil in a wide pan. Add the collards with a splash of water and cook, covered, for 6 minutes, then add the spinach and cook until both are silky and tender, about 4 more minutes. Stir in the crushed peanuts and a spoonful of the stew gravy and cook for 2 more minutes, until glossy and not wet.

For the sadza, bring water to a boil, about three times the weight of the meal. Stir a third of the meal with a splash of cold water to a slurry, whisk it into the boiling water and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the rest in handfuls, beating hard with a wooden spoon, then cover and cook on low for 5 minutes. Beat again until stiff and smooth.
Serve the sadza with the beef and the greens. Pack the second portion of stew and greens for tomorrow's lunch, and make a fresh small pot of sadza then, or reheat the leftover with a splash of water.
tip: A pressure cooker makes this a weeknight dish: 35 minutes for the beef. A spoonful of smooth peanut butter can stand in for the crushed peanuts. Collards stand in for the rape greens (kale-like) Zimbabweans use. Kale or chard work too, and amaranth leaves (morogo) are the traditional choice if you can find them.
ingredients: like Zimbabwean rape greens, ribs removed and sliced thin
whole-grain white mealie meal, for the sadza

name: Chakalaka and beans with boerewors-style beef patties and sweet potato
inspiredBy: South African chakalaka and beans, with lean beef patties seasoned like boerewors (coriander, clove and nutmeg) instead of the fatty sausage
about: A thick, spicy vegetable and bean stew, chakalaka, with juicy herb-and-spice beef patties seasoned like boerewors, and roasted sweet potato wedges to catch the sauce. It is the comfort food of any South African table. The beans and vegetables bring **fibre, folate and vitamin C**, and the sweet potato adds vitamin A.
steps: Cut the sweet potato into wedges and roast on a tray at 220C (425F) until soft and browned at the edges, about 25 minutes, turning once.
Mix the beef with the grated onion, boerewors spice, lemon juice and half the salt. The grated onion keeps lean beef juicy. Shape into patties and let them rest for 10 minutes.
Warm the oil in a wide pan. Cook the diced onion, green pepper and carrot until soft, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic, chakalaka spice and cayenne and cook for 1 minute.
Add the tomato and simmer until thick, about 10 minutes. Stir in the beans and the rest of the salt and cook until the chakalaka is thick and jammy, about 8 minutes.

Pan-fry the patties in a non-stick pan over medium heat, using a little of the oil, until well browned and cooked through to 71 C (160 F) inside, about 4 minutes per side. Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw beef.
Stir the cilantro into the chakalaka. Serve the patties on the beans with the sweet potato wedges alongside.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch. The patties are good cold or reheated in a pan.
tip: Ask for a lean grind, 95% lean, so the patties stay light. Lean ground lamb or turkey also work. Cook the chakalaka a day ahead: it only improves.
ingredients: 30 g grated for the patties, the rest diced
chopped, or use a can of crushed
pinto beans in place of sugar beans, drained

name: Umngqusho, samp and beans with lamb and greens
inspiredBy: Xhosa umngqusho, the slow-cooked samp and sugar bean dish, with a little lamb for flavour and greens folded in
about: Sugar beans and a little samp (dried hominy) simmered with lamb, onion, garlic and a little butter, finished with tomato, collard greens and cilantro. It is slow, filling food from the Eastern Cape. Beans and samp together bring **fibre, iron and folate**, the collards add calcium and the lamb adds zinc and B12.
steps: The night before, soak the samp in plenty of cold water. Drain it in the morning.

Melt the butter with the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Brown the lamb for about 6 minutes, then add the onion and cook until soft, about 6 minutes. Stir in the garlic, bay leaves, black pepper and cayenne.

Add the drained samp and enough water to cover by two finger widths. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently, stirring now and then and topping up the water, until the samp is very tender and creamy, about 2 hours, or 45 minutes in a pressure cooker.
With 30 minutes left, stir in the beans and tomato and cook uncovered, mashing a few beans against the side of the pot so they melt into the samp.
Fold in the collards and cook for 8 minutes, until silky and tender. Stir in the cilantro and the salt.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch. The pot keeps 4 days in the fridge, and freezes well.
tip: Real samp and sugar beans from a South African shop swap in by weight. Borlotti is the closest canned bean. Canned hominy, rinsed, also works: add it with the beans and the pot is ready in 40 minutes. Short on time? A pressure cooker makes dried samp a weeknight option.
ingredients: dried hominy, in place of samp, soaked overnight
pinto beans in place of sugar beans, canned, drained

name: Peri-peri chicken and livers with roasted butternut and spinach salad
inspiredBy: Mozambican and Portuguese frango piri-piri, with the roasted butternut salad you find at a South African braai
about: Chicken thighs and livers marinated in peri-peri, lemon and garlic and roasted until sticky and browned, with sweet roasted butternut, spinach, sliced onion and toasted pumpkin seeds. It is bold, smoky and bright, cooled with a lemony amasi drizzle, and the leftovers make a good cold plate tomorrow. The livers bring **iron, folate and choline**, the butternut and spinach add vitamin A and K, and the pumpkin seeds add zinc.
steps: Stir together the peri-peri sauce, half the lemon juice, the garlic, smoked paprika, half the oil and half the salt. Rub it all over the chicken thighs, and toss the trimmed livers in a spoonful of it too. Marinate the thighs for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, and keep the livers in the fridge until you need them.
Heat the oven to 220C (425F). Toss the butternut with the rest of the oil and salt on one tray. Put the chicken on another tray.

Roast the butternut until golden at the edges, about 30 minutes, turning once. Roast the chicken until it is browned and sticky at the edges and the juices run clear, 25 to 30 minutes, adding the livers to the tray for the last 8 minutes, until browned outside and just cooked through.
Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.

Toss the sliced onion with a squeeze of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt and leave it for 5 minutes to soften. Stir the rest of the lemon juice into the kefir with the cilantro to make a cooling amasi drizzle.
Pile the spinach on a plate, top with the warm butternut, the onion and the seeds. Serve the chicken and livers alongside, spoon the pan juices over them and drizzle with the amasi.
This makes two portions. Pack the second for tomorrow's lunch, with the spinach, seeds and amasi drizzle kept separate until you eat.
tip: Livers go grainy when reheated, so eat the leftover livers cold, sliced over the salad. Not a liver fan? Leave them out and add a little more chicken. Marinate overnight for the best flavour. Serve extra peri-peri at the table for people who like it hot, and use a mild sauce for kids.
ingredients: sliced thin, red if you have it
plain kefir or buttermilk, for the drizzle

name: Braaied mackerel with chutney glaze, sweet potato, greens and bean salad
inspiredBy: South African braaied snoek, basted with sweet chutney, butter and lemon, with mackerel standing in for snoek
about: Mackerel fillets brushed with a sticky chutney, lemon and garlic glaze and grilled hot, with sweet potatoes baked in foil, garlicky greens and a tangy bean and tomato salad. It is a Sunday braai at its best, and works on a grill or under the broiler. Mackerel gives you a big dose of **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Heat the grill (braai or broiler) until very hot. Wrap the sweet potatoes in foil with a pinch of salt and cook on the coals or at 200C (400F) until tender, about 40 minutes. A few minutes in the microwave first speeds it up.
Warm the butter, chutney, a spoonful of the lemon juice, half the garlic and the cayenne in a small pan until melted and runny, about 2 minutes.
Toss the beans, tomato, onion, oil, cilantro and half the lemon juice with a pinch of salt and let the salad sit while the fish cooks.
Warm a little of the oil in a pan and cook the collards with the rest of the garlic and a splash of water, covered, until silky and tender, about 8 minutes. Keep warm.

Pat the mackerel dry and season it with salt and pepper. Brush it with the glaze. Grill skin side down on a lightly oiled grid for about 4 minutes, brush again, then flip and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until it flakes. Under a broiler, cook skin side up for 6 to 7 minutes and skip the flip.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon juice over the fish and serve it with the sweet potatoes, the garlicky collards and the bean salad.
tip: Fresh snoek is the real thing if you can get it. Mackerel is richer and easier to find. Cook it fresh on the day, not as a leftover.
ingredients: a spoonful for the glaze, the rest for the salad and fish
minced, half for the glaze and half for the greens
pinto beans in place of sugar beans, drained

name: Guava with roasted peanuts
about: Sweet and slightly tart guava with a handful of roasted peanuts, the kind of snack you would grab from a South African fruit stall. Guava has more **vitamin C** than an orange, and the peanuts add protein and vitamin E.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges. The seeds are soft, so you can eat them.
Eat with the peanuts, in alternating bites.

name: Biltong with almonds
inspiredBy: South African biltong, the air-dried spiced beef eaten at every braai
about: Thin strips of dried, spiced beef with a handful of almonds, a salty and crunchy pairing. Biltong packs a lot of **protein and iron** into a small snack, and the almonds add vitamin E.
steps: Slice the biltong into thin strips if it is in a piece.
Eat a strip of biltong with a few almonds, or just alternate bites.
tip: Buy biltong at a South African shop or online. For jerky, pick the plainest, least sweet one, never teriyaki.

name: Amasi with mango
about: Cold, thick amasi (fermented milk) with sweet ripe mango. It brings **calcium and protein**, with vitamin A and vitamin C from the mango.
steps: Spoon the kefir into a bowl.
Top with the diced mango and eat it cold.
ingredients: plain kefir or buttermilk, for the amasi

name: Amasi with guava
about: Cold, tangy amasi (fermented milk) with soft, fragrant guava. It brings **calcium and protein**, and the guava adds more vitamin C than an orange.
steps: Spoon the kefir into a bowl.
Top with the diced guava and eat it cold.
ingredients: plain kefir or buttermilk, for the amasi

name: Dried apricots with almonds
about: Chewy Cape-style dried apricots with a handful of almonds, a snack that keeps in the bag all day. The apricots bring vitamin A and potassium, and the almonds add **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Put the apricots and almonds in a small bowl.
Eat them together so the sweet apricot balances the crunch.

name: Mielie with butter, lemon and chili
about: A braaied or boiled cob of sweet corn with a little butter, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, the way it is sold at roadside stalls. Roadside mielies are starchier; sweet corn is the closest cob here. It is a **whole-food starch** with fibre and folate.
steps: Bring a pot of salted water to a boil, or heat a grill until hot.
Boil the cob until the kernels are tender, about 8 minutes, or grill it, turning often, until it is charred in spots, about 12 minutes.
Rub the hot cob with the butter, squeeze over the lemon and finish with a pinch of cayenne.
ingredients: kernels cut from one large cob

name: Mango with lemon and chili
about: Ripe mango strips with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, a bright, sweet and spicy street-stall snack. It brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Cut the mango into strips.
Squeeze the lemon over it and dust with a pinch of cayenne.

name: Pilchards on toast with tomato
inspiredBy: South African pilchards on toast, a classic tinned-fish snack
about: Tinned pilchards mashed onto warm whole-wheat toast with sliced tomato, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, an old South African favourite. It is a quick hit of **omega-3, calcium and vitamin B12**, since the soft bones are edible.
steps: Toast the bread until golden and crisp.
Mash the pilchards lightly with a fork, bones and all, then spread them over the toast.
Top with the tomato, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of cayenne.
tip: The rest of the tin keeps 2 days, covered, in the fridge.
ingredients: pilchards or sardines, with their sauce

name: Peri-peri pumpkin seeds
about: Pumpkin seeds toasted with smoked paprika, cayenne and a squeeze of lemon, a crunchy bag-of-the-day snack. They are one of the best food sources of **magnesium and zinc**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until they puff and pop, about 4 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the smoked paprika, cayenne, salt and lemon juice. It sizzles and coats the seeds. Cool a minute before eating.

name: Dried apricots with toasted pumpkin seeds
about: Chewy dried apricots with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds, a sweet and crunchy bag-of-the-day snack. The apricots bring vitamin A and potassium, and the seeds add **zinc and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.
Eat them with the apricots, a few of each in every bite.

name: Mango with dried apricots
about: Fresh ripe mango with a few chewy dried apricots, a double dose of sweet and tangy fruit. It brings **vitamin A and vitamin C** and a good amount of potassium.
steps: Dice the mango into a bowl.
Chop the apricots small and scatter them over the mango.

name: Mango with toasted pumpkin seeds
about: Ripe mango with a handful of toasted pumpkin seeds, sweet and nutty. The mango brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**, and the seeds add zinc and magnesium.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan until they pop, about 3 minutes.
Dice the mango and scatter the seeds over it.

name: Chai-spiced oatmeal with banana and walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by masala chai, turned into a bowl of oatmeal
about: Creamy stovetop oats simmered in milk with cinnamon, cardamom, ginger and a pinch of clove, topped with sliced banana, walnuts and sunflower seeds. Warming rather than hot, it gives you **fibre, magnesium and a little omega-3** to start the day.
steps: Stir the oats, milk, cinnamon, cardamom, ginger, clove and pepper together in a small pot and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat.
Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring often, until the oats are thick and creamy. Add a splash of milk if you like it looser.
Spoon into a bowl, lay the sliced banana on top and scatter over the walnuts and sunflower seeds so they stay crunchy.
tip: Want it spicier? Add another pinch of ginger and black pepper. For a make-ahead version, soak the oats and spices in the milk in the fridge overnight, top in the morning and eat within 2 days.

name: Savoury masala oats with spinach and yogurt
inspiredBy: Inspired by Indian upma, made with oats instead of semolina
about: Oats toasted and cooked in milk with mustard seed, cumin, turmeric, tomato, spinach and a green chili, finished with lime and cilantro. A savoury, gently spicy breakfast with **protein, iron and folate** from the spinach, milk and yogurt, and lime to help you absorb the iron.
steps: Toast the oats and sunflower seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until they smell nutty. Tip them into a bowl.
Heat the oil in the same pan and add the mustard and cumin seeds. When the mustard seeds pop, add the onion and chili and cook for 3 minutes, until the onion is soft.
Stir in the turmeric and tomato and cook for 2 minutes, until the tomato softens. Add the milk and the salt and bring to a simmer.
Add the oats and spinach and stir for 3 to 4 minutes, adding water a little at a time, until thick and porridge-like.
Finish with the lime juice and cilantro, and spoon the cold yogurt on top. Taste and add more chili if you want more heat.
tip: Chop the onion and tomato the night before and this is about a 12-minute breakfast. Keep the chili seeds in for more heat, or leave the chili out and finish with a pinch of black pepper.
ingredients: washed, minced; start with less, or leave it out

name: Berbere scrambled eggs with crispy potatoes and spinach
inspiredBy: Inspired by Ethiopian enkulal firfir (spiced scrambled eggs)
about: Eggs scrambled until firm with onion, green chili and berbere, over crisp potato cubes and wilted spinach, with a cool lime yogurt on the side. A warming weekend breakfast with **protein, choline and potassium**, and it uses the berbere from Wednesday.
steps: Wash the potato, spinach and cilantro. Heat the oil in a wide non-stick skillet over medium heat, add the potato and half the salt, cover and cook for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until tender and golden at the edges.

Push the potatoes to one side. Add the onion and serrano and cook for 3 minutes, until soft, then stir in the berbere for 30 seconds, until fragrant. Fold in the spinach until it wilts. Wash your hands after cutting the chili and keep them away from your eyes.

Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt and wash your hands. Pour the eggs into the pan, turn the heat to medium-low and stir gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until the eggs are completely set and firm, with no runny bits left.
Stir the yogurt with the lime juice and spoon it alongside, then scatter with cilantro. Start with half the berbere if you like less heat; the yogurt cools it.
tip: No berbere? Use smoked paprika with a pinch of cumin and cayenne.
ingredients: washed, minced; start with less, or leave it out

name: Chai-spiced yogurt bowl with banana and walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by masala chai, as a yogurt bowl
about: Thick yogurt stirred with cinnamon, cardamom and ginger, topped with sliced banana, walnuts and sunflower seeds. A cool, no-cook version of the chai oatmeal with **protein, calcium and a little omega-3**.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the cinnamon, cardamom, ginger and pepper in a bowl until smooth.
Peel and slice the banana and lay it on top.
Scatter over the walnuts and sunflower seeds so they stay crunchy.
tip: Eat it straight away so the nuts stay crisp.

name: Piri-piri sardine and black bean salad with quinoa
inspiredBy: Inspired by Portuguese piri-piri, in a cold salad
about: Canned sardines and black beans on quinoa with tomato, cucumber and spinach, tossed in a lime piri-piri dressing of garlic, paprika and chili flakes. The sardines bring **omega-3, vitamin D and calcium** (from the soft bones) and the black beans bring fibre and iron.
steps: Rinse the quinoa and simmer it in plenty of water for 12 to 15 minutes, until tender. Drain, spread in a shallow container and cool within 1 hour.
Whisk the lime juice, oil, garlic, paprika, chili flakes and pepper in a large bowl. Taste and add more chili flakes for more heat.
Add the black beans, tomato, cucumber, onion, spinach and cooled quinoa and toss. Break the sardines into big pieces and fold them in last.
Keep any opened tin of sardines covered in the fridge and use it within 2 days. To pack it, use a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.
tip: Cook the quinoa the night before and this takes 10 minutes. Keep cooked quinoa no more than 3 days.

name: Chickpea and potato curry with spinach
inspiredBy: Inspired by Punjabi aloo chana
about: A comforting weeknight curry of chickpeas and potato in a tomato, ginger and garlic sauce, thickened with red lentils and finished with spinach, lime and cilantro, with a halved firm egg on top. Chickpeas, lentils and spinach bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Wash your hands. Put the eggs in a small pot (one for each portion), cover with cold water, bring to a boil and simmer for 10 minutes, until the yolks are fully firm. Cool them in cold water, then peel and halve one and keep the other in its shell in the fridge for tomorrow. Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then add the onion and cook for 5 minutes, until soft and golden.
Add the garlic, ginger and serrano and stir for 1 minute. Stir in the coriander, turmeric, Kashmiri chili and salt for 30 seconds, until fragrant. Wash your hands after cutting the chili.

Add the tomatoes, potato, red lentils and enough water to just cover the potato. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 15 to 18 minutes, stirring now and then, until the potato is tender and the lentils have melted into the sauce.

Stir in the chickpeas and heat through for 3 minutes. Add the spinach, garam masala and lime juice and stir until the spinach wilts. Taste: add more chili, or a pinch of cayenne, for more heat. The heat deepens in the leftovers.
Serve topped with the egg halves and the cilantro. If the heat is too much, a spoonful of cold yogurt from the fridge cools it.

Cool the second portion within 1 hour in a shallow container and refrigerate. Eat it within 3 days, reheating only the curry, once, until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F). Peel and halve the second egg and add it cold. Pack it in a cold bag with an ice pack if you carry it to work.
tip: Freeze the curry without the egg for up to 2 months: cool within 1 hour, thaw in the fridge, use within 2 days, never refreeze, and reheat to 74 °C (165 °F).
ingredients: washed, minced; start with less, or leave it out

name: Jerk-spiced chicken with mango salsa and coconut black beans
inspiredBy: Inspired by Jamaican jerk chicken with rice and peas
about: Chicken thighs rubbed with a fiery jerk paste of scallion, thyme, allspice, garlic and chili, roasted until juicy and served over coconut-simmered black beans with a cool mango and pepper salsa and a crunchy lime kale slaw. **Iron, folate, vitamin A and vitamin C** from the beans, mango, pepper and kale, and the heat is yours to set. It makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Mash most of the scallion, the garlic, serrano, thyme, allspice, cinnamon, pepper, half the salt, half the lime juice and the oil into a rough paste. Rub it over the chicken on a lined tray and leave it in the fridge while the oven heats, about 15 minutes. Never reuse the raw marinade.
Roast the chicken for 22 to 26 minutes, until it reaches 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece. Wash your hands and the board with hot soapy water after handling the raw chicken.
Meanwhile, warm the black beans gently in a small pot with the coconut milk and the remaining scallion for 5 minutes, mashing a few to thicken.

Make the salsa: stir the mango and red pepper with most of the remaining lime juice, the cilantro and a pinch of the salt. Massage the kale with the last of the lime juice and salt for a minute, until it softens.
Slice the chicken and serve it over the beans with the salsa and slaw. If the heat is too much, an extra spoonful of salsa cools it.

Cool the second portion of chicken, beans and salsa within 1 hour in separate shallow containers and refrigerate. Eat within 3 days, reheating the chicken and beans once until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F), and keeping the salsa and slaw cold. Pack in a cold bag with an ice pack.
tip: Wear gloves when you handle hot chilies. For a mild version, leave the chili out and use a pinch of black pepper and a little extra allspice. The heat deepens in the leftovers, so go easy the first night. Wash your hands after cutting chilies and keep them away from your eyes. A Scotch bonnet gives the classic heat if you can find one.
ingredients: washed, minced; start small, or leave it out

name: Berbere-spiced red lentils with cabbage, carrot and kale
inspiredBy: Inspired by Ethiopian misir wot, with potatoes as in dinich
about: Red lentils simmered slowly with onion, garlic, ginger and berbere until thick and glossy, with carrot, potato, cabbage and kale stirred in, a halved hard-cooked egg and a cooling spoonful of yogurt on top. It is **rich in plant protein, iron and folate**, with lime to help you absorb the iron, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Wash your hands. Put the eggs in a small pot (one for each portion), cover with cold water, bring to a boil and simmer for 10 minutes, until the yolks are fully firm. Cool in cold water, peel one and keep the other in its shell in the fridge for tomorrow. Meanwhile, cook the onion in a dry wide pot over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until it softens and starts to catch. Add the oil, garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the berbere and turmeric and cook for 30 seconds, then add the tomatoes. Start with half the berbere if you like less heat, and add more to taste at the end, or leave it out and use paprika.
Add the lentils, carrot, potato, cabbage, salt and enough water to cover by 2 cm. Simmer, partly covered, for 18 to 20 minutes, stirring often, until the lentils are soft and thick.
Stir in the kale and cook for 3 minutes, until wilted. Add the lime juice and taste for salt and heat. Serve with the halved egg and a spoonful of yogurt.

Cool the second portion within 1 hour in a shallow container and refrigerate. Eat within 3 days, reheating only the lentils once until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F). Peel and halve the second egg and add it and the yogurt cold.
tip: For a mild pot, use 2 g berbere and add a pinch of paprika. The heat deepens in the leftovers. Freeze the lentils without the egg and yogurt for up to 2 months: cool within 1 hour, thaw in the fridge, use within 2 days, never refreeze, and reheat to 74 °C (165 °F).

name: Moroccan-spiced salmon with chickpeas, tomatoes and kale
inspiredBy: Inspired by Moroccan chermoula fish
about: Salmon fillets over a skillet of chickpeas, tomatoes and kale, brushed with a chermoula of garlic, cumin, paprika, lime and cilantro. Salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, chickpeas and kale bring iron, folate and some calcium, and the chili is up to you. It makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Make the chermoula: stir the garlic, cilantro, lime juice, half the oil, cumin, paprika, coriander and chili flakes together. Spoon half into a small clean bowl for serving, then rub the rest over the salmon and put it in the fridge. Never reuse that raw marinade.

Heat the remaining oil in a wide skillet over medium heat. Cook the onion for 4 minutes, until soft. Add the turmeric, cinnamon and salt, then the tomatoes and chickpeas with a splash of water. Simmer for 8 minutes, until the tomatoes collapse into a sauce.

Stir in the kale and cook for 3 minutes, until wilted. Nestle the salmon on top, cover and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, until the fish flakes easily and reaches 70 °C (158 °F). Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw fish.
Spoon the rest of the chermoula over the top and serve it from the pan. Taste and add more chili flakes if you want more heat.

Cool the second portion within 1 hour in a shallow container and refrigerate. Eat it within 2 days, cold as a salad or reheated once until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F). Pack it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.

name: Sichuan-pepper beef and greens over quinoa
inspiredBy: Inspired by Sichuan stir-fried beef, with quinoa and more vegetables
about: Thin strips of lean beef stir-fried hot and fast with broccoli, cabbage and edamame in a garlicky ginger sauce, with toasted Sichuan peppercorns and chili for a tingling heat. The beef and greens bring **iron, zinc and vitamin K**, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the quinoa, simmer it in plenty of water for 12 to 15 minutes, drain and keep covered. Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan for 1 minute, until fragrant, then crush them.
Toss the beef with the ground peppercorns, pepper and half the soy sauce and leave it in the fridge for 10 minutes. Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw beef.

Heat half the oil in a wide pan or wok over high heat. Cook the beef in one layer for 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until browned and no pink is left in the thickest strip, 71 °C (160 °F) if you check with a thermometer. Move it to a plate.

Add the rest of the oil, then the broccoli with a splash of water and stir-fry for 3 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, scallion and chili flakes for 30 seconds, then the cabbage and frozen edamame for 2 to 3 minutes, until the edamame is steaming hot and the cabbage is tender-crisp.

Return the beef with the lime juice, the rest of the soy sauce and a splash of water, and toss for 1 minute. Taste and add more chili flakes for more heat; skip them for a mild version, because the Sichuan pepper tingles rather than burns. Serve over the quinoa.
Cool the second portion within 1 hour (quinoa in a separate shallow container) and refrigerate. Eat within 3 days, reheated once until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F).
ingredients: trimmed, sliced thinly across the grain

name: Goan-style mackerel in tamarind-tomato sauce with potato and green beans
inspiredBy: Inspired by Goan fish curry, with tamarind and no coconut
about: Atlantic mackerel simmered with potato and green beans in a sharp tamarind and tomato sauce with mustard seed, turmeric, coriander, ginger and chili, finished with kale and lime, over quinoa. Mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, the kale and green beans bring folate and vitamin K, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the quinoa, simmer it in plenty of water for 12 to 15 minutes, drain and keep covered. Meanwhile, heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and add the mustard seeds. When they pop, add the onion and cook for 4 minutes, until soft.

Add the garlic, ginger and serrano and stir for 1 minute, then the turmeric, coriander, cumin, Kashmiri chili and fenugreek for 30 seconds. Wash your hands after cutting chilies and keep them away from your eyes.
Stir the tamarind paste into a mug of warm water until it dissolves. Add it to the pot with the tomatoes, potato and salt. Simmer, covered, for 12 minutes, until the potato is nearly tender.

Add the green beans and cook for 3 minutes. Slide in the mackerel, cover and cook gently for 6 to 8 minutes, until the fish flakes easily and reaches 70 °C (158 °F). Wash your hands and the board after handling the raw fish.

Fold in the kale and cook for 2 minutes more, until just wilted, being careful not to break up the fish. Add the lime juice and top with cilantro. Taste: more lime sharpens it, more chili or a pinch of cayenne heats it. Serve over the quinoa.

Cool the second portion (quinoa separate) within 1 hour in shallow containers and refrigerate. Eat within 2 days. Add a splash of water and warm it gently, covered, once, until steaming hot, 74 °C (165 °F). Pack it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.
tip: Buy the mackerel last, keep it cold and cook it the day you buy it or the next. Frozen fillets work too: thaw them in the fridge, cook them within a day and never refreeze. Salmon works if mackerel is hard to find. The sauce deepens overnight, so go easy on the chili the first night.
ingredients: Atlantic (not king) mackerel fillets, skin on is fine, pin bones out, cut in 4 cm pieces
washed, trimmed, cut in 4 cm pieces
or a little extra lime juice if you cannot find it
washed, minced; start with less, or leave it out

name: Indonesian-style tempeh sambal with kale, red pepper and quinoa
inspiredBy: Inspired by Indonesian sambal tempeh
about: Golden pan-fried tempeh simmered with red pepper and kale in a thick chili-tomato sambal with ginger, garlic, coriander and lime, over quinoa. Tempeh brings **plant protein**, and the kale and sunflower seeds bring calcium and vitamin E.
steps: Rinse the quinoa, simmer it in plenty of water for 12 to 15 minutes, drain and keep covered. Meanwhile, heat half the oil in a wide pot over medium-high heat and brown the tempeh for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until golden on most sides. Move it to a plate.

Add the rest of the oil and the onion and cook for 4 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, serrano, coriander, cumin, paprika and turmeric and stir for 1 minute. Wash your hands after cutting chilies and keep them away from your eyes.
Stir in the tomatoes, red pepper, salt and a mug of water. Simmer uncovered for 10 minutes, until the pepper is soft and the sauce is thick.
Add the kale and tempeh and simmer for 5 minutes, until the kale is tender and the tempeh is steaming hot all the way through, 74 °C (165 °F).
Finish with the lime juice, sunflower seeds and cilantro. Taste, and add more chili or a pinch of cayenne for more heat. Serve over the quinoa.
tip: Tempeh blocks are usually about 240 g: wrap the rest and keep it in the fridge until its date, or freeze it. Keep tempeh cold until you cook it, and always cook it through.
ingredients: washed, minced; start with less, or leave it out

name: Chili-lime mango with sunflower seeds
about: Ripe mango chunks with lime and a dusting of chili, and a handful of sunflower seeds for crunch. Sweet, sharp and a little hot, with **vitamin C and magnesium**.
steps: Wash the mango, peel it and cut it into chunks, then toss with the lime juice and a pinch of chili flakes.
Eat with the sunflower seeds on the side.
ingredients: or less; add more to taste

name: Cucumber-mint raita with pepper and cucumber sticks
inspiredBy: Inspired by Indian raita
about: A cooling yogurt dip with grated cucumber, mint and toasted cumin, for dunking red pepper and cucumber sticks. **Calcium, protein and vitamin C**, and a good counter to a spicy day.
steps: Wash your hands and the vegetables. Stir the yogurt with the grated cucumber, mint, cumin, lime juice and salt.
Serve with the pepper and cucumber sticks. Keep it cold and eat it the same day.
ingredients: washed; half grated and squeezed dry, half cut in sticks

name: Mango and cucumber chaat with lime and chili
inspiredBy: Inspired by Indian fruit chaat
about: Diced mango and cucumber with red onion, mint, lime and a pinch of chili and cumin, in the style of an Indian fruit chaat. Juicy, sharp and a little hot, with **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Wash the mango, cucumber and mint. Peel and dice the mango, then toss it with the cucumber, onion and mint in a bowl.
Add the lime juice, chili flakes, cumin and salt and toss again.
Eat right away, or keep it covered in the fridge and eat within a day.
ingredients: or less; add more to taste

name: Cinnamon apple with peanut butter, walnuts and a pinch of chili
about: Crisp apple slices dusted with cinnamon and the faintest pinch of cayenne, with peanut butter to dip and a few walnuts. Sweet, warm and crunchy, with **fibre, vitamin E and a little omega-3**.
steps: Wash the apple and slice it. Toss the slices with the cinnamon (and chili, if using).
Dip the slices in the peanut butter and eat with the walnuts.
ingredients: smooth, unsalted if you can find it

name: Ginger-cardamom banana with walnuts
about: A banana sliced and dusted with ginger and cardamom, with a handful of walnuts. Mild and fragrant, with **potassium, vitamin B6 and a little omega-3**.
steps: Slice the banana and dust it with the ginger and cardamom.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Masala roasted chickpeas
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas tossed with cumin, coriander, amchur (dried green mango powder) or lime, and chili. A crisp, savoury snack with **fibre, iron and plant protein**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Pat the chickpeas very dry with a clean towel so they crisp.
Toss with the oil and spices on a tray and roast for 22 to 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crunchy. They firm up more as they cool.
Eat them warm or cooled. Keep the rest in a closed jar in the fridge for up to 3 days, and crisp them in a hot oven for 5 minutes before eating.
tip: Roast a double batch on Wednesday and keep the second half for Saturday.
ingredients: or a squeeze of lime at the end

name: Warm ginger-cardamom milk
inspiredBy: Inspired by masala chai
about: A mug of milk warmed with fresh ginger, cardamom and cinnamon, like a quick, unsweetened chai. A soothing end to a spicy day with **calcium, protein and B12**.
steps: Warm the milk with the ginger, cardamom and cinnamon in a small pot over medium-low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, until steaming but not boiling.
Strain into a mug and sip warm. Keep any extra in the fridge and drink it within a day.

name: Smoky sweet potato wedges with lime
about: Sweet potato wedges roasted until caramelised at the edges with smoked paprika, cumin and a squeeze of lime. Sweet, smoky and a little hot, with **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Toss the wedges with the oil, paprika, cumin, chili powder and salt on a lined tray.
Roast for 22 to 25 minutes, turning once, until tender inside and browned at the edges. Squeeze the lime over the top.
tip: Roast them alongside the chicken or the chickpeas to share the oven.

name: Cardamom yogurt with apple
about: Thick Greek yogurt with diced apple and a pinch of cardamom. Cool and creamy, with **protein and calcium**.
steps: Wash the apple, core it and dice it.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the apple and a pinch of cardamom.

name: Strawberry and walnut overnight oats
inspiredBy: Inspired by Swiss bircher muesli, with the first strawberries of the season
about: Rolled oats soaked overnight in milk, with half the strawberries mashed through so the whole jar turns blush pink, and walnuts on top for crunch. It gives you **fibre, protein and plant omega-3** before the day starts, with five minutes of work the night before.
steps: Wash your hands and the strawberries. Mash about half of the strawberries with a fork and slice the rest.
Stir the oats, milk, cinnamon and the mashed strawberries together in a jar until there are no dry patches. Put the lid on and refrigerate overnight.
In the morning, stir it up and loosen it with a splash of milk if it is too thick. Top with the sliced strawberries and the walnuts just before eating so they stay crunchy.
Keep the jar in the fridge and eat it within 2 days of making it.
tip: In a hurry, make it in a jar for the commute. Keep it cold in a bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.

name: Strawberry-rhubarb yogurt bowl with walnut oat crunch
inspiredBy: Inspired by an English strawberry and rhubarb fool, lightened up for breakfast
about: Rhubarb and strawberries simmered for a few minutes until jammy, spooned over thick yogurt with a crunch of toasted oats and walnuts. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Put the rhubarb, strawberries and cinnamon in a small pot with a spoonful of water. Cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 6 to 8 minutes, until the rhubarb is soft and the fruit is jammy. Tip it into a bowl so it cools a little.
While it simmers, toast the oats and walnuts in a dry skillet over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until golden and fragrant. Tip them onto a plate.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the warm fruit and scatter the crunch over the top.
Eat it the same day. The cooked fruit keeps 3 days in the fridge in a covered container if you want to make extra.
tip: The rhubarb is tart on purpose. If you like it sweeter, add a teaspoon of honey to the pot.
ingredients: washed, trimmed, sliced thin; leaves discarded

name: Asparagus and herb egg scramble with crisp new potatoes
inspiredBy: Inspired by a spring asparagus and egg brunch
about: Small potatoes crisped in the pan, then folded with snappy asparagus, spring onion, parsley and a whole egg and extra whites scrambled until fully set, with plenty of herbs. The egg brings **choline**, the whites add protein, and the asparagus adds folate and vitamin K.
steps: Put the diced potatoes in a skillet with the oil over medium heat. Cover and cook for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until tender and starting to turn golden.
Wash the asparagus, scallion and parsley. Add the asparagus and scallion to the pan and cook uncovered for 3 minutes, until the asparagus is bright green and just tender.
Beat the egg and egg whites with the salt and pepper and pour them over the vegetables. Stir gently over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until the eggs are completely set with no liquid left.
Fold in the parsley, scatter the sunflower seeds over the top and serve straight away.
tip: Potatoes boiled the night before and kept in the fridge? Skip step 1 and crisp them in the oil for 4 minutes, and the breakfast takes 10 minutes.
ingredients: small new potatoes, scrubbed and diced small
washed, woody ends snapped off, cut in short lengths
liquid egg whites, or the whites of two eggs

name: Canned salmon, egg and chickpea salad with fennel, orange and baby spinach
inspiredBy: Inspired by a Sicilian orange and fennel salad
about: Flaked salmon, a firm-cooked egg and chickpeas over shaved fennel, orange segments and baby spinach with a lemon-dill dressing. The salmon with its soft bones brings **omega-3, vitamin D and some calcium**, and the orange with the chickpeas helps your body take up the iron.
steps: Cover the egg with cold water in a small pot, bring to a boil and cook for 10 minutes so the yolk is completely firm. Cool it in cold water, then peel and quarter it. Wash the fennel, spinach and dill. Shave the fennel very thin and peel and segment the orange, catching any juice in a bowl.
Whisk the orange juice, lemon juice, oil, salt and pepper in the bowl. Add the onion and fennel and toss.
Add the chickpeas, spinach and dill and toss lightly. Flake the salmon over the top, add the egg and the sunflower seeds.
Cover and refrigerate any opened tin of salmon and use it within 2 days. If you pack this for lunch, carry it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.
tip: Spoon it onto a baked potato for a cold-evening version.
ingredients: drained, skin and bones mashed in

name: Minted pea soup with edamame, chickpeas and lemon yogurt
inspiredBy: Inspired by a classic English pea and mint soup
about: Sweet peas, carrot, a little onion and a handful of spinach simmered in stock and blended with fresh mint until silky, with edamame and chickpeas for body and a generous swirl of lemon yogurt. The peas, edamame and chickpeas together bring **fibre, folate and plant protein**, and the carrot and spinach add vitamin A.
steps: Wash the carrot and spinach, and dice the carrot. Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the onion for 4 minutes until soft and translucent.

Add the stock and the carrot, with a splash of water if the stock does not cover it, and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the frozen peas, edamame and half the chickpeas and simmer for 5 minutes more, until the peas and edamame are steaming hot all the way through.

Stir in the spinach and most of the mint until the spinach wilts, then blend until smooth with an immersion blender or in batches in a blender, holding the lid down with a towel. Add a little hot water if it is too thick to pour. Season with the salt, pepper and half the lemon juice.
Stir the yogurt with the rest of the lemon juice. Ladle the soup into a bowl, swirl the yogurt over it and top with the remaining chickpeas and mint.
tip: It is just as good cold on a warm day.

name: Herby quinoa salad with a firm egg, chickpeas and cucumber
inspiredBy: Inspired by Lebanese tabbouleh, with quinoa and chickpeas
about: Fluffy quinoa tossed with chickpeas, cucumber, radishes, carrot, spinach and a lot of dill and mint, topped with feta, a firm-cooked egg and sunflower seeds. Quinoa, chickpeas and egg make a **complete, filling lunch** with plenty of protein and fibre.
steps: Put the quinoa in a small pot with twice its volume of water. Bring to a boil, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes until the water is absorbed. Spread it on a plate to cool.
At the same time, cover the egg with cold water in another pot, bring to a boil and cook for 10 minutes so the yolk is completely firm. Cool it in cold water, then peel and halve it.
Whisk the lemon juice, oil and salt in a bowl. Add the cucumber, radishes, carrot, scallion, chickpeas, spinach, dill and mint, then the cooled quinoa, and toss.
Top with the egg, feta and sunflower seeds. If you pack this for lunch, keep it in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.
tip: Cook the quinoa the night before and chill it in a shallow container within 1 hour. Use it within 3 days.

name: Warm lentil salad with snap peas, carrot, dill, feta and flaked salmon
inspiredBy: Inspired by a French lentil salad
about: Green-brown lentils that hold their shape, tossed while still warm in a mustardy lemon dressing with crunchy snap peas, grated carrot, spring onion and plenty of herbs, with flaked canned salmon folded through. Lentils bring **iron and folate**, the salmon adds omega-3 and B12, and the lemon helps your body take up the iron.
steps: Rinse the lentils and put them in a pot with plenty of water, enough to cover by a good 5 cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until tender but still holding their shape. Drain.
Whisk the mustard, lemon juice, oil, salt and pepper in a large bowl. Tip in the warm lentils and toss so they soak up the dressing.
Wash the snap peas, carrot, scallion and herbs. Add them to the lentils with the feta and toss. Flake the salmon over the top and scatter the sunflower seeds on just before eating.

Put the second portion in a shallow container within 1 hour, without the sunflower seeds, and refrigerate. Eat it the next day, cold or at room temperature; it keeps 2 days at most because of the salmon. Cover and refrigerate any opened tin and use it within 2 days. If you pack it, use a cold bag with an ice pack and eat it the same day.
tip: Cook the lentils the night before and the salad takes 10 minutes.
ingredients: drained, skin and bones mashed in

name: Spring chicken pot with leeks, peas and barley
inspiredBy: Inspired by a French blanquette and a Scottish barley broth
about: Tender chicken thigh simmered with sweet leeks, carrots and pearl barley in a tarragon and mustard broth, with peas and spinach stirred in at the end and a squeeze of lemon. Barley, peas and spinach bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the chicken brings protein and B vitamins to a warm, cool-evening pot.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium-high heat. Add the chicken and brown it for 3 to 4 minutes, then lift it onto a plate. Wash your hands, the board and the knife with hot soapy water after handling the raw chicken.
Add the leeks, carrots and garlic to the pot with a pinch of the salt and cook for 4 minutes, until the leeks are soft. Stir in the mustard, tarragon and barley.

Pour in the broth with enough water to cover everything by 2 cm. Return the chicken, bring to a boil, then cover and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until the barley is tender and the chicken reads 74 °C (165 °F) in the thickest piece.

Stir in the peas and cook for 3 minutes, until they are steaming hot. Stir in the spinach until just wilted. Add the lemon juice, the rest of the salt, the pepper and most of the parsley. It should be a thick, spoonable stew; add a splash of water if it is too thick.

Serve in warm bowls with the rest of the parsley. Put the second portion in a shallow container within 1 hour and refrigerate. It keeps up to 3 days; reheat it to 74 °C (165 °F) until steaming, loosening with a splash of water.
tip: It thickens as it sits; add a splash of water or broth when you reheat it.
ingredients: trimmed of visible fat, cut in bite-size pieces

name: Green herb shakshuka with white beans
inspiredBy: Inspired by shakshuka, with a spring-green sauce instead of tomato
about: Eggs cooked in a bright green sauce of spinach, spring onion, parsley, dill and mint, with creamy white beans and a little feta. The eggs and beans bring **protein and choline**, and the spinach and herbs add iron, folate and vitamin K.
steps: Warm the oil in a deep skillet over medium heat. Cook the scallion and garlic with the cumin for 2 minutes, until soft and fragrant.

Add the spinach in handfuls and cook for 3 minutes, until wilted. Add the parsley, dill, mint, white beans and broth and simmer for 5 minutes. Mash about half the beans with a fork so the sauce turns creamy. Season with the salt, pepper and lemon juice.

Make two wells in the sauce and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook for 8 to 10 minutes on low, until the whites are set and the yolks are firm all the way through. Break the yolks with a spoon and keep cooking for a minute if any look soft.
Scatter the feta and the sunflower seeds over the top and serve in the skillet.
tip: Serve it with a bowl of sliced cucumbers on the side.

name: Trout and asparagus parcels with new potatoes and lemon-dill yogurt
inspiredBy: Inspired by the French way of cooking fish en papillote
about: A trout fillet baked in a sealed parchment parcel on thin-sliced new potatoes with carrot, asparagus, lemon and dill, so everything steams in its own juices. Trout brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the potatoes, carrot and asparagus add potassium, vitamin A and folate.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 °C (400 °F). Boil the potato slices in salted water for 5 minutes until just starting to soften, then drain. Buy the trout the day you cook it and keep it in the fridge until you start.

Cut a large sheet of parchment, fold it in half and open it flat. Pile the potatoes on one side with the carrot ribbons, garlic, scallion, half the oil and a pinch of the salt. Lay the asparagus on top.

Pat the trout dry and season it with the rest of the salt, pepper, half the lemon juice and half the dill. Place it on the vegetables, drizzle with the rest of the oil, fold the parchment over and crimp the edges tightly shut. Put the parcel on a tray. Wash your hands, the board and the plate that held the raw fish.
Bake for 18 to 20 minutes, until the trout flakes easily and reads 70 °C (158 °F) in the thickest part.
Stir the yogurt with the rest of the lemon juice and dill. Open the parcel carefully (the steam is hot) and spoon the yogurt over the top.
tip: Fresh fish is not a leftover. Cook it the day you buy it and eat it the same day.
ingredients: small new potatoes, scrubbed, sliced thin

name: Seared beef with salsa verde, roasted radishes and barley
inspiredBy: Inspired by Italian salsa verde over steak
about: Lean sirloin seared and sliced over chewy barley and roasted radishes, with a sharp, chunky salsa verde of parsley, mint, walnuts, garlic, lemon and mustard. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the lemon and parsley in the salsa help your body take up that iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 °C (425 °F). Toss the radishes and scallion with a third of the oil and a pinch of the salt on a tray and roast for 18 to 20 minutes, until browned at the edges and tender.
Rinse the barley. Simmer it in plenty of water with a pinch of salt for 25 minutes, until tender but still chewy. Drain well. Start it first, while the radishes roast.
Stir the parsley, mint, walnuts, garlic, lemon juice, mustard, half the remaining oil and a pinch of salt into a chunky salsa verde.

Pat the beef dry and season it with the rest of the salt and the pepper, then wash your hands, the board and the knife you used for the raw beef. Sear it in a hot skillet with the last of the oil for 4 to 6 minutes per side, until it reads 71 °C (160 °F) in the centre. Rest it for 3 minutes on a clean plate (never the one that held the raw steak), then slice it across the grain on the clean board.
Pile the barley and spinach on a plate, add the radishes and the beef, and spoon the salsa verde over everything.
tip: No barley? Quinoa works too and cooks in 12 minutes.

name: Seared salmon with minty pea and white bean smash and a radish-fennel salad
inspiredBy: Inspired by an English supper of salmon and crushed peas
about: Crisp-skinned salmon on a chunky smash of peas, edamame, white beans and mint, with a crunchy shaved radish and fennel salad on the side. Salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the peas and beans bring fibre and plant protein.
steps: Buy the salmon the day you cook it and keep it in the fridge until you start. Wash the radish, fennel, mint, dill and scallion. Toss the shaved radish and fennel with the dill, half the lemon juice, a teaspoon of the oil and a pinch of salt.

Put the peas and edamame in a pot with the beans and a splash of water. Cover and heat for 4 to 5 minutes, until the peas and edamame are steaming hot all the way through. Drain, then mash roughly with a fork, leaving some texture. Stir in the mint, scallion, half the remaining oil, the rest of the lemon and a pinch of salt.

Pat the salmon dry and season with the rest of the salt and the pepper. Heat the last of the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat and lay the salmon in skin-side down, then wash your hands, the board and the plate that held the raw fish. Cook for 5 minutes until the skin is crisp, flip and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, until it flakes and reads 70 °C (158 °F) in the thickest part.
Stir the yogurt with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of salt. Spoon the smash onto a plate, set the salmon on top, add the yogurt and sunflower seeds and serve the salad alongside.
tip: The salmon is cooked the day you buy it, never kept for later.

name: Spring lamb and white bean pot with carrots, leeks and peas
inspiredBy: Inspired by the French lamb stew navarin printanier
about: Lean lamb simmered slowly with new potatoes, white beans, carrots, leeks, mushrooms and thyme until the broth turns silky, with peas stirred in at the end. The lamb brings **iron and zinc**, and the beans and peas bring fibre. It is an unhurried weekend pot that tastes better the next day.
steps: Pat the lamb dry. Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the lamb in two batches for 5 minutes each, then lift it onto a plate. Wash your hands, the board and the knife with hot soapy water after handling the raw lamb.
Lower the heat and cook the onion, leeks, mushrooms and garlic for 6 minutes, until soft and the mushrooms have given up their liquid. Stir in the thyme and cook for 1 minute.

Return the lamb with its juices. Add the carrots, potatoes, bay leaf, broth and enough water to just cover everything. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for 40 minutes, until the lamb is tender and reads at least 71 °C (160 °F).
Add the white beans and cook for 10 minutes more. Stir in the peas and cook for 3 minutes, until steaming hot. Remove the bay leaf and season with the salt, pepper and lemon juice.

Serve in warm bowls scattered with the parsley. Put the second portion in a shallow container within 1 hour and refrigerate. It keeps up to 3 days; reheat it to 74 °C (165 °F) until steaming. It also freezes: cool within 2 hours, freeze up to 2 months, thaw in the fridge, use within 2 days, never refreeze.
tip: A pressure cooker does the lamb in 20 minutes.
ingredients: trimmed of visible fat, in bite-size cubes
small new potatoes, scrubbed and halved

name: Lemon-herb tofu with mushrooms, asparagus and minty crushed potatoes
inspiredBy: Inspired by an English crushed new potato supper, with seared tofu for the protein
about: Firm tofu seared until golden in lemon, garlic and mustard, on minty crushed new potatoes with mushrooms, asparagus and peas cooked in the same pan, and walnuts for crunch. Calcium-set tofu brings **protein and some calcium**, and the asparagus and peas add folate.
steps: Boil the potatoes in salted water for 15 to 18 minutes, until a knife slides in easily. Drain, return them to the pot and crush each one roughly with a fork. Fold in a third of the oil, the scallion, mint and a pinch of salt.
Whisk the mustard, garlic, half the lemon juice, a little of the salt and the pepper in a shallow dish. Press the tofu between clean towels for a few minutes, then turn it in the mixture.
Heat half the remaining oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Sear the tofu for 3 to 4 minutes per side, until golden and crisp at the edges. Lift onto a plate.

Add the rest of the oil and the mushrooms to the pan and cook for 4 minutes, until golden. Add the asparagus and peas and cook for 3 to 4 minutes more, turning, until the asparagus is bright green and just tender and the peas are steaming hot.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon over everything, scatter the walnuts on top and serve with the potatoes.
tip: Chicken breast works the same way if you prefer, cooked until it reads 74 °C (165 °F) in the centre.
ingredients: firm, calcium-set, patted dry and cut in thick slabs

name: Sugar snap peas and carrot sticks with lemony white bean dip
about: Crunchy snap peas and sweet carrot sticks for scooping through a creamy mash of white beans, lemon and parsley. A **high-fibre** snack with plant protein from the beans.
steps: Mash the white beans with the lemon juice, oil, salt and parsley with a fork until mostly smooth, adding a spoonful of water if it is stiff.
Wash the snap peas and carrot, trim the peas and cut the carrot into sticks, then serve with the dip. Keep leftover dip covered in the fridge and use it within 3 days.

name: Orange with walnuts
about: A juicy orange with a small handful of walnuts for crunch. The orange brings **vitamin C**, which helps your body take up iron from the day's meals, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Wash the orange, peel it and break it into segments.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Warm edamame with lemon, mint and sunflower seeds
about: Shelled edamame warmed through and tossed with lemon, mint, a pinch of salt and a few sunflower seeds. A snack of **plant protein, folate and vitamin E**.
steps: Put the frozen edamame in a bowl with a splash of water, cover and microwave for 2 minutes, until steaming hot all the way through, or simmer in a pot for 3 minutes. Drain well.
Toss with the lemon juice, mint, sunflower seeds and salt. Serve warm.

name: Kiwi with sunflower seeds
about: Two kiwi, halved to scoop with a spoon, and a small handful of sunflower seeds. The kiwi brings **vitamin C and fibre**, and the seeds bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Wash the kiwi, halve it and scoop it with a spoon.
Eat with the sunflower seeds.

name: Cucumber and radish with lemon-dill yogurt dip
about: Cool cucumber and peppery radish for dipping into thick yogurt with lemon and dill. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and it is a light, refreshing snack.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the lemon juice, dill and salt.
Wash and slice the cucumber and radishes and serve with the dip. Keep leftover dip covered in the fridge and use it within 2 days.

name: Strawberries with walnuts
about: A bowl of ripe strawberries with a small handful of walnuts. The berries bring **vitamin C**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Wash and hull the strawberries.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Smashed chickpeas on cucumber rounds with lemon and dill
about: Chickpeas lightly smashed with lemon, oil and dill, piled on thick cucumber rounds. A fresh, crunchy snack with **fibre and plant protein**.
steps: Smash the chickpeas roughly with a fork with the lemon juice, oil, dill and salt.
Wash and slice the cucumber, then spoon the chickpeas onto the rounds.

name: Sugar snap peas with lemon-mint yogurt dip
about: Sweet, crunchy snap peas for dipping into thick yogurt stirred with lemon and fresh mint. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the peas bring vitamin C and fibre.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the lemon juice, mint and salt.
Wash the snap peas, trim the ends and serve with the dip. Keep leftover dip covered in the fridge and use it within 2 days.

name: Kiwi and orange with walnuts
about: A kiwi and an orange cut up together, with a small handful of walnuts for crunch. The fruit brings **vitamin C and fibre**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Wash the kiwi and the orange. Peel both and cut them into bite-size pieces.
Eat with the walnuts.

name: Orange and strawberries with sunflower seeds
about: Orange segments and sliced strawberries with a small handful of sunflower seeds. The fruit brings **vitamin C**, and the seeds bring vitamin E and magnesium.
steps: Wash the orange and the strawberries. Peel the orange and break it into segments, and hull and slice the strawberries.
Eat with the sunflower seeds.

name: Radish and fennel pinzimonio
inspiredBy: Inspired by Tuscan pinzimonio
about: Crisp radishes and fennel cut into wedges for dipping into a little bowl of good olive oil with salt and pepper, the way Tuscans eat raw spring vegetables. The vegetables bring crunch and **vitamin C**, and the olive oil brings vitamin E.
steps: Wash the radishes and fennel. Halve the radishes and cut the fennel into thin wedges through the root so they hold together.
Pour the oil into a small dish and season it with the salt and pepper. Dip the vegetables as you eat.

name: Orange-ginger oatmeal with nuts and pumpkin seeds
about: Creamy oatmeal cooked in milk with a little fresh ginger and cinnamon, topped with a spoonful of Greek yogurt, juicy orange segments, toasted walnuts, almonds and pumpkin seeds. The oats and seeds bring **fibre, iron and magnesium**, the almonds bring vitamin E, the walnuts bring omega-3 fats, and the orange brings vitamin C.
steps: Wash the orange, then peel it and cut it into segments. Toast the walnuts, almonds and pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat until the pumpkin seeds puff and pop, about 3 minutes.
Stir the oats, milk, grated ginger, cinnamon and a splash of water together in a small pot and bring to a gentle simmer.
Cook, stirring, until thick and creamy, about 5 minutes.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the yogurt, orange segments, nuts and pumpkin seeds.
tip: Make it the night before: soak the oats in the milk in the fridge, then warm it in the morning. Eat soaked oats within 3 days.

name: Pineapple yogurt bowl with toasted oats and nuts
about: Thick Greek yogurt with sweet pineapple, a drizzle of honey, and a crunchy topping of toasted oats, almonds and walnuts. The yogurt brings **protein and calcium**, and the nuts bring vitamin E and omega-3 fats.
steps: Toast the oats, almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring, until golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes. Tip onto a plate to cool.
Wash the pineapple before cutting, then cut it into small chunks. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the pineapple.
Scatter over the crunchy topping and drizzle with the honey.
tip: Toast a few days of the oat topping at once and keep it in a jar.
ingredients: peeled, cored and cut into small chunks

name: Tomato and scallion egg scramble with spinach on whole-wheat toast
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese tomato and egg stir-fry
about: Eggs scrambled until completely firm with juicy tomato, scallion and a handful of spinach, piled on whole-wheat toast with a little soy and sesame, with a glass of milk and an orange on the side. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the spinach and tomato bring folate and vitamin C.
steps: Wash the tomato, spinach, scallion and orange, then chop the tomato and slice the scallion. Beat the eggs with the soy sauce. Peel the orange and cut it into segments.
Warm the oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high heat. Cook the tomato and most of the scallion until the tomato softens and the juices thicken, about 3 minutes. Add the spinach and stir until wilted.
Pour in the eggs and stir gently until completely set and no wet egg remains, about 2 minutes.
Pile onto the toast, drizzle with the sesame oil, scatter over the rest of the scallion and serve with the orange and a glass of milk.
ingredients: washed, peeled and cut into segments, on the side

name: Cold sesame noodle salad with salmon, edamame and crunchy veg
inspiredBy: Inspired by Chinese cold sesame noodles, with whole-wheat spaghetti and canned salmon
about: Whole-wheat noodles tossed in a soy, rice vinegar and sesame dressing with edamame, carrot, red pepper and kale, topped with flaked canned salmon. The salmon (soft bones and all) brings **omega-3, vitamin D and calcium**, and the edamame adds protein and folate.
steps: Boil the whole-wheat spaghetti (the noodles) in plenty of water until tender with a little bite, about 10 minutes. Add the frozen edamame for the last 3 minutes so it is steaming hot all the way through, then drain and rinse under cold water until cool.
Whisk the soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame oil and grated ginger in a large bowl.

Wash the carrot, red pepper, kale and scallion, then cut the carrot into matchsticks, the pepper into thin strips and slice the kale and scallion very thinly. Flake the salmon with a fork, keeping the soft bones.
Toss the noodles, edamame and vegetables in the dressing and let the kale soften for 5 minutes. Top with the salmon and sesame seeds.
Eat it the same day. If you pack it for lunch, keep it in a cold bag with an ice pack. Keep an opened tin of salmon covered in the fridge and use it within 2 days.
ingredients: whole-wheat spaghetti, used as the noodles
washed, stems removed, very thinly sliced
washed and cut into thin matchsticks
washed and cut into thin strips
