It's a slow weekend breakfast that makes two bowls, so Sunday morning is a reheat. Black rice and mung beans bring **fibre and plant protein**, and the egg and warm soy milk add **choline, calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Rinse the black glutinous rice for both servings (nếp cẩm, also sold as Thai black sticky rice, which roughly triples as it cooks) along with the mung beans, and soak them in separate bowls for at least 1 hour, or Friday night if you like. Plain black rice is not sticky enough for xôi.
Drain the rice and cook it in a small pot with 1½ times its volume of water, covered, over low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, until chewy and tender. Rest it with the lid on for 10 minutes.
While the rice cooks, rinse the peeled split mung beans and simmer them in plain water for 15 to 20 minutes, with no soaking, until they fall apart. Drain, add the salt and mash until smooth.

Soak the dried shrimp in warm water for 10 minutes, then chop finely. Toast the shrimp and peanuts together in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until fragrant, and crush them lightly. Toss the carrot and cucumber sticks with the lime juice, palm sugar and a pinch of salt and leave them for 15 minutes, until they turn tangy.

Boil one egg for 10 minutes, until the white and the yolk are firm, then cool it under cold water, peel and halve it. Fry the shallot rings in the oil until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes, and drain them on a paper towel.

Pile the rice into bowls, spoon the mung beans over it and top with the egg, the shrimp and peanut mix, the shallot and the scallion. Drizzle with the coconut milk and serve with the pickled carrot and cucumber, and a cup of warm soy milk.
Keep the second portion of rice and mung beans in the fridge. On Sunday, boil a fresh egg while the rice reheats with a splash of water, covered, until steaming.
tip: Add a spoon of crispy fried shallot on top if you have it, as many xôi stalls do.
ingredients: black glutinous rice (nếp cẩm), cooked weight, see step 2

name: Gỏi cuốn, shrimp summer rolls with a peanut dip
inspiredBy: Southern Vietnamese gỏi cuốn, the fresh rolls eaten with a peanut dip
about: Cool, chewy rice paper rolls packed with shrimp, seared tofu, thin rice noodles, crisp lettuce, carrot, mint and cilantro, with a smooth peanut and lime dip. Nothing here is cooked beyond the shrimp and tofu, so it's a fresh, light lunch. The shrimp and tofu bring **protein and calcium**, and the herbs add vitamin K.
steps: Soak the snapped noodles in a bowl of hot water for 10 minutes, until tender. Drain well and snip them into shorter lengths.

Poach the shrimp in simmering water for 2 to 3 minutes, until pink and curled. Drain, cool and cut each one in half lengthwise. Pat the tofu dry and sear the strips in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 2 minutes per side, until golden. Let them cool.

Make the dip: grind the peanuts with the garlic to a rough paste in a mortar or small food processor. Stir in the lime juice, fish sauce, palm sugar, the spoonful of coconut milk and a tablespoon of warm water until smooth and spoonable.

Dip one sheet of rice paper in warm water for 10 seconds, until just pliable, and lay it on a damp towel. Lay a few shrimp halves along the lower edge, then a bed of lettuce, herbs, carrot, tofu and noodles. Fold in the sides and roll it up snugly.
Repeat with the rest to make about 5 rolls and serve with the dip. If you're taking them to work, wrap them in a damp paper towel and then in plastic so they don't dry out or stick.
tip: Swap the shrimp for extra tofu.
ingredients: thin; snapped and soaked in hot water
calcium-set, check the label, cut into strips
ground to a paste with the garlic, for the dip

name: Đậu phụ sốt cà chua, tofu simmered in tomato with brown rice
inspiredBy: Northern Vietnamese đậu phụ sốt cà chua
about: Golden pan-fried tofu simmered in a sweet, tangy tomato sauce with a little minced chicken, shallot and cilantro, a staple of the northern Vietnamese family table. It's a quick, cheap lunch that tastes better than it sounds. The calcium-set tofu brings **a big share of your day's calcium**, and the tomatoes add vitamin C.
steps: Pat the tofu dry. Heat half the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and fry the slices for 2 to 3 minutes per side, until golden. Lift them out.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan with the shallot and garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the chicken and cook for 3 minutes, breaking it up, until no longer pink and it reaches 74 °C (165 °F).
Add the tomato wedges and cook, stirring, for 4 to 5 minutes, until they collapse into a thick sauce. Stir in the fish sauce, the salt and a splash of water.
Slide the tofu back into the sauce and simmer for 3 minutes, so it soaks up the flavour. The sauce should be tangy, savoury and a little sweet from the tomatoes.
Scatter on the scallion and cilantro. Serve over the brown rice with the cucumber slices on the side.
tip: A pinch of black pepper over the top is the traditional finish.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label, cut into thick slices

name: Thai red curry with chicken, tofu and gai lan
inspiredBy: Central Thai kaeng phet gai, with a quick fresh paste and extra vegetables
about: A fragrant red curry with a quick fresh paste of lemongrass, galangal, garlic, chili and shrimp paste, spiced with toasted coriander and cumin, and stirred through with chicken, tofu and gai lan in a little coconut milk with Thai basil on top. It makes two servings, so tomorrow's lunch is done. The coconut milk is just enough for flavour and richness, and the calcium-set tofu and gai lan make it **a good source of calcium**.
steps: Toast the coriander seed and cumin in a dry pan for 1 minute, until fragrant. Slice the lemongrass and galangal as finely as you can, tear the lime leaves, and blitz them with the garlic, chilies, shrimp paste, the toasted spices, the white pepper and 2 tablespoons of water in a mini chopper (or pound in a mortar) into a rough, fragrant paste.
Spoon the thick cream off the top of the coconut milk into a wide pot over medium heat and fry the paste for 2 minutes, until it smells wonderful and the oil starts to separate.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and about ½ cup (125 ml) of water for each serving. Add the tofu and the gai lan stems and simmer gently for 8 minutes.
Add the sliced chicken and simmer for 6 to 7 minutes, until it's just cooked through, then add the gai lan leaves for the last minute.
Stir in the fish sauce and palm sugar. Taste: it should be salty, a little sweet and properly hot. Take it off the heat and tear in the Thai basil.
Serve over the brown rice. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Swap the chicken for shrimp or extra tofu if you like. A spoon of ready-made red curry paste makes it a 20-minute dinner.
ingredients: stems and leaves, cut into 4 cm pieces
calcium-set, check the label, cut into cubes

name: Steamed salmon with lime, garlic and chili, with garlicky water spinach
inspiredBy: Central Thai pla neung manao, usually made with sea bass, here with salmon for its omega-3 fats
about: Salmon steamed gently over lemongrass and finished with a sharp, fiery sauce of lime, garlic, chili and cilantro, with garlicky water spinach and brown rice. It's all about the sauce, the sour, salty, sweet and hot every Thai table has. The salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the water spinach adds vitamin A and vitamin K.
steps: Bruise the lemongrass with the back of a knife and lay it in a steamer basket, or on a rack in a wide pot over 2 cm of water. Lay the salmon on top.
Cover and steam over a steady simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, until the salmon is just opaque and flakes at the thickest part.
While it steams, pound or finely chop half the garlic with the chili and the cilantro stems. Stir in the lime juice, fish sauce, palm sugar and 2 tablespoons of water until the sugar dissolves.

Heat the oil in a wok over high heat, fry the rest of the garlic for 20 seconds, then add the water spinach stems and stir-fry for 1 minute. Add the leaves and a splash of water for 1 to 2 minutes, until the leaves are wilted but the stems still snap.
Lift the salmon onto a plate, spoon the sauce over it and scatter on the cilantro leaves. Serve with the water spinach and the brown rice.
tip: The sauce is also excellent on steamed sea bass or cod, or spooned over tofu.
ingredients: divided between the sauce and the greens

name: Larb neua, Isaan beef herb salad in lettuce cups
inspiredBy: Isaan larb neua, with brown rice standing in for sticky rice
about: Minced lean beef cooked with only a splash of water, then tossed warm with lime, fish sauce, chili, toasted rice powder, shallot and handfuls of mint and cilantro. You scoop it into lettuce cups with raw yardlong beans and cucumber, so there's crunch in every bite, plus a plate of blanched gai lan on the side. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, the gai lan adds calcium, and the lime and the generous herbs add vitamin C and vitamin K.
steps: Spread about 2 tablespoons of the cooked brown rice in a dry pan over medium heat and stir for 8 to 10 minutes, until it's dry, golden and crunchy. Grind it to a coarse powder in a mortar or spice grinder.

Put the beef in a wide pan with a few tablespoons of water. Cook over medium heat, breaking it up with a spoon, for 6 to 7 minutes, until browned and cooked through and the pan is almost dry. Take it off the heat and let it cool for 2 minutes.
Toss the warm beef with the lime juice, fish sauce, chili flakes and half the rice powder. It should be sour first, then salty, then hot.
Stir in the shallot, scallion, mint and cilantro just before serving, so the herbs stay bright.
Bring a pot of water to a boil, blanch the gai lan stems for 1 minute, then add the leaves for 30 seconds. Drain well and squeeze a little lime over it.
Spoon into lettuce cups and serve with the blanched gai lan, raw yardlong beans, cucumber and the rest of the brown rice. Scatter on the rest of the rice powder.
Pack the second portion without the herbs and lettuce, and stir in fresh herbs tomorrow. The gai lan keeps in the fridge alongside it.
tip: Use minced chicken for larb gai. Isaan cooks often add a spoon of roasted chili flakes at the table.
ingredients: lean beef chuck, finely chopped or pulsed in a food processor
from your batch, with a spoonful toasted for the powder; the stand-in for sticky rice
blanched, stems and leaves cut into 4 cm pieces, served on the side

name: Cá thu kho tộ, caramel braised mackerel with greens
inspiredBy: Southern Vietnamese cá kho tộ, normally catfish in a clay pot, here with mackerel and less sugar
about: Chunks of mackerel simmered in a clay-pot style sauce of caramel, fish sauce, garlic, ginger and black pepper, with boiled water spinach and rice. It's sweet, salty and peppery, and the sauce is made for spooning over rice. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the water spinach adds vitamin A and vitamin K.
steps: Toss the fish with half the garlic, the shallot and a few grinds of black pepper and leave it for 10 minutes.

Make the caramel: put the palm sugar and a tablespoon of water in a small heavy pot over medium heat. Don't stir, just swirl the pot, for 3 to 4 minutes, until it turns a deep amber. Stand back and pour in about 100 ml (⅓ cup) of water, which will spit, and stir until the caramel dissolves.
Stir in the oil, the rest of the garlic, the ginger, the fish sauce and the chili, then slide in the fish and spoon the sauce over it.
Simmer gently, partly covered, for 10 minutes, turning the fish once, then uncover for the last 5 minutes so the sauce reduces to a glaze and the fish is cooked through and tender.
While it simmers, boil the water spinach for 1 to 2 minutes, until tender but still bright. Drain well.
Serve the fish and its sauce with the water spinach and brown rice, scattered with the scallion. Spoon a little of the sauce over the greens.
tip: Catfish or tilapia make the more traditional version.
ingredients: cut into 4 cm steaks or chunks

name: Gà nướng sả, lemongrass chicken on brown rice with pickles and nước chấm
inspiredBy: Southern Vietnamese cơm tấm nướng sả, made with chicken thigh and whole brown rice in place of broken rice
about: Thin slices of chicken thigh marinated in lemongrass, shallot and garlic and seared until the edges caramelize, on brown rice with quick-pickled carrot, cucumber, blanched water spinach and a spoonful of scallion oil. A small bowl of sweet, sour, salty nước chấm goes over the top. It's the classic Saigon rice plate, with less sugar and whole grain rice, and the chicken brings **protein and niacin** while the pickles keep it fresh.
steps: Slice the chicken thigh 4 mm thick. Mix it with the lemongrass, shallot, half the garlic, half the fish sauce, 4 g (about 1 tsp) of the palm sugar and a teaspoon of the oil. Leave it to marinate in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or overnight, and don't reuse the marinade.
Toss the carrot with a third of the lime juice, a pinch of the sugar and a tablespoon of water. Leave it for 15 minutes to turn tangy and crisp.

Make the nước chấm: whisk the rest of the lime juice, the rest of the fish sauce, about 3 g (¾ tsp) of the sugar, the rest of the garlic, the chili and 2 tablespoons of warm water until the sugar dissolves.
Make the scallion oil (mỡ hành): put the sliced scallion in a small bowl. Heat the rest of the oil until it shimmers, pour it over the scallion and let it sizzle.

Heat a cast iron or non-stick pan over high heat, or fire up the grill. Cook the chicken in batches for about 3 minutes per side, until the edges are browned and sticky and it reaches 74 °C (165 °F). Wash your hands and the board after the raw chicken. Blanch the water spinach for 1 minute and drain.
Plate the rice with the chicken, water spinach, pickled carrot and cucumber slices. Spoon the scallion oil over the rice and about 2 tablespoons of nước chấm over the plate, rather than drenching it.

For the second portion, cool the chicken quickly and keep it, the pickles and the sauce in the fridge (it keeps up to 3 days). Blanch both portions of water spinach tonight. In the morning, reheat the chicken in a hot pan until steaming hot (74 °C / 165 °F) and pack it with the rice, greens and pickles.
tip: The marinated chicken freezes well raw (thaw it in the fridge and use within 2 days), so you can make a double batch.
ingredients: sliced across the grain, 4 mm thick
divided between the marinade and the sauce
divided between the marinade, the pickle and the sauce
divided between the chicken and the scallion oil
divided between the pickle and the sauce

name: Phở bò with a slow broth, bean sprouts and a herb plate
inspiredBy: Vietnamese phở bò, Saigon style, with a lean cut of beef and a generous herb plate
about: Lean beef chuck simmered for a couple of hours with charred shallot and ginger, star anise, cinnamon and coriander seed until the broth is clear and fragrant, then ladled over rice noodles with a plate of bean sprouts, Thai basil, cilantro, lime and chili. It's the weekend project that makes the house smell wonderful and gives you two bowls. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the herb plate brings vitamin C.
steps: Char the shallots and ginger, cut side down, in a dry pan or under the broiler for 8 to 10 minutes, until blackened in spots. Rinse off any burnt bits.

Put the beef (and a few beef bones from the butcher, if you want a richer broth) in a big pot, cover with cold water, bring to a boil for 5 minutes and pour off the grey water. Rinse the beef and the pot, then cover the beef with about 1½ litres (6 cups) of fresh water for two servings.

Toast the star anise and coriander seed in a dry pan for about a minute, until fragrant. Add them to the pot with the charred shallots and ginger and the cinnamon. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then simmer gently, partly covered, for 1½ to 2 hours, until the beef is very tender.
Lift out the beef, let it cool a little and slice it thinly against the grain. Strain the broth, stir in the fish sauce and taste. It should be savoury and fragrant, not too salty.
Cook the noodles in boiling water as the package says, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Rinse and divide into big bowls.
Top the noodles with the beef and ladle over the boiling broth. Scatter on the scallion and cilantro.
Serve with a plate of bean sprouts, basil, lime wedges and chili for everyone to add as they like.
For tomorrow's bowl, keep the broth and sliced beef in the fridge, cook fresh noodles and bring the broth to a rolling boil.
tip: In a pressure cooker the broth takes 45 minutes. Without bones the broth is lighter and cleaner, which is how a lean phở is meant to taste.
ingredients: lean beef chuck or brisket, in one or two big pieces
about a 5 cm piece, unpeeled, halved lengthwise
a small cinnamon stick, or ¼ tsp ground in a tea ball

name: Lemongrass grilled mackerel with som tam
inspiredBy: Isaan pla ping and som tam Thai, with mackerel for the usual river fish and brown rice for sticky rice
about: A whole mackerel stuffed with lemongrass and grilled until the skin blisters, served with a pounded green papaya salad of lime, chili, garlic, tomato, beans, carrot, dried shrimp and peanuts. It's the Isaan way to eat a grilled fish, with a fiery, sour salad on the side. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the papaya salad adds vitamin C.
steps: Pat the mackerel dry and cut three slashes on each side. Stuff the cavity with the bruised lemongrass and one smashed garlic clove, and brush the skin with a little of the fish sauce. If you only find fillets, sandwich the lemongrass between two fillets and tie them with kitchen string.
Broil on a rack set close to the heat, or grill, for 7 to 8 minutes per side, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily at the thickest part. Mackerel is oily, so it needs no extra oil.

Make the som tam: soak the dried shrimp in warm water for 10 minutes. In a big bowl or mortar, pound the rest of the garlic, the chili and the shrimp to a rough paste. Add the yardlong beans and bruise them gently so they crack but keep their snap.

Add the tomato, papaya and carrot with the lime juice, the rest of the fish sauce and the palm sugar and toss, pounding lightly, until the sugar dissolves and the papaya just softens. Taste: it should be hot, sour, salty and a little sweet.
Scatter the peanuts over the salad. Serve the fish on a plate with the salad and the rice, and spoon some of the salad juices over the fish.
tip: Use sea bass or trout if you can't find mackerel. If green papaya is hard to find, shredded kohlrabi or cabbage works well.
ingredients: whole, gutted fish, listed as the edible weight, so buy one of about 300 g
from your batch, the stand-in for sticky rice

name: Pad kra pao gai, Thai basil chicken with a crispy fried egg
inspiredBy: Thai pad kra pao gai, with Thai basil in place of the usual holy basil
about: Minced chicken stir-fried hard and fast with a lot of garlic, chili, yardlong beans and a big handful of Thai basil, served over brown rice with a crispy fried egg on top. It's the dish Thai people order when they can't decide, and it takes 20 minutes. The chicken and egg bring **protein and choline**, and the Thai basil adds vitamin K.
steps: Pound or chop the garlic and chili into a rough, chunky paste. Stir the fish sauce, palm sugar and 2 tablespoons of water together in a small bowl.
Heat half the oil in a wok over high heat until it shimmers. Fry the garlic and chili paste for 20 seconds, until fragrant. Don't let the garlic brown.

Add the chicken and stir-fry hard for 2 minutes, breaking it up. Add the yardlong beans, the sauce and a splash of water, and cook for 2 minutes more, until the beans are bright and the chicken is cooked through but still moist.
Turn off the heat and stir in the Thai basil until it just wilts.

Heat the rest of the oil in a small non-stick pan until very hot. Crack in the egg and fry it for 3 to 4 minutes, flipping it for the last minute, until the white is crisp at the edges and the yolk is firm.
Serve the chicken over the brown rice with the fried egg on top and a squeeze of lime over everything.
tip: Cut back to one chili if you want it mild. Holy basil is the traditional herb if you can find it at an Asian market.
ingredients: divided between the stir-fry and the egg

name: Warm ginger soy milk
inspiredBy: Thai nam tao hu and Vietnamese sữa đậu nành
about: Fortified soy milk warmed with ginger and a little palm sugar, the way it's sold at breakfast stalls in Bangkok and Hanoi. It's a calming snack with **calcium and vitamin D**, if you pick a fortified one.
steps: Warm the soy milk with the ginger and sugar in a small pot over low heat for 5 minutes, without boiling.
Strain out the ginger, if you like, and sip warm.

name: Papaya with lime and roasted peanuts
about: Soft, sweet ripe papaya with a handful of crunchy roasted peanuts and a squeeze of lime. The peanuts bring **vitamin E and protein**, and the papaya brings vitamin C and folate.
steps: Scoop the papaya out of its skin, cut it into chunks and squeeze the lime over it.
Eat it with the peanuts alongside.

name: Papaya with lime and chili salt
about: Soft ripe papaya with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chili salt. It's sweet, sour, salty and hot, and brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Scoop the papaya out of its skin and cut it into chunks.
Mix the chili flakes and salt, squeeze the lime over the papaya and dip each piece in the mix.

name: Guava with chili salt
inspiredBy: Thai prik kleua, the chili salt that comes with street fruit
about: Crisp, fragrant guava dipped in the salty, hot mix that Thai street vendors sell with every fruit. A single guava has **more than a day's vitamin C** and plenty of fibre.
steps: Stir the salt and chili flakes together on a small plate.
Cut the guava into wedges, squeeze the lime over them and dip each one in the chili salt.

name: Guava with lime and salt
about: Crisp guava wedges with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt, a simple Vietnamese fruit snack. It's one of the best **vitamin C and fibre** snacks there is.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges.
Squeeze the lime over them and add a tiny pinch of salt.

name: Pineapple with lime and salt
about: Sweet pineapple chunks with a squeeze of lime and a tiny pinch of salt, which makes the sweetness taste brighter. The pineapple brings **vitamin C and manganese**.
steps: Cut the pineapple into chunks.
Squeeze the lime over them and add a tiny pinch of salt.

name: Pineapple with chili salt
about: Sweet, tangy pineapple with the little sprinkle of salt and chili that makes it taste like a street stall. It's high in **vitamin C and manganese**.
steps: Cut the pineapple into spears.
Mix the salt and chili flakes and sprinkle a little over the fruit.

name: Pineapple with mint and lime
about: Juicy pineapple chunks tossed with torn mint and a squeeze of lime. The mint makes it taste cool and fresh, and the pineapple brings **vitamin C and manganese**.
steps: Cut the pineapple into chunks.
Toss with the torn mint and lime juice.

name: Tào phớ, soft tofu with ginger syrup
inspiredBy: Vietnamese tào phớ, usually made with silken soy pudding
about: Warm, silky tofu in a light ginger syrup, a popular snack across Vietnam. The calcium-set silken tofu brings **calcium and plant protein**, and the ginger is warming.
steps: Simmer the ginger, palm sugar and about 50 ml of water in a small pot for 6 to 8 minutes, until it's a light syrup that coats a spoon.
Slide the silken tofu into a bowl and warm it for about 45 seconds in the microwave, or lower it into barely simmering water for 2 minutes. Don't stir it.
Spoon the ginger syrup over the tofu.
ingredients: calcium-set silken tofu, check the label

name: Chè đậu xanh, warm mung beans with coconut milk
inspiredBy: Vietnamese chè đậu xanh
about: A small bowl of soft, smooth mung beans simmered with ginger and a little coconut milk, a comforting Vietnamese sweet soup. You make two bowls at once, so the second is ready for another day. It brings **fibre, iron and folate**.
steps: Rinse about ¼ cup (50 g) of peeled split mung beans and simmer them with the ginger in about 6 times their volume of water for 15 to 20 minutes, with no soaking, until they fall apart.
Stir in the palm sugar and the coconut milk and warm through for 1 minute.
Serve one bowl warm. Keep the other in the fridge for up to 4 days and reheat with a splash of water.

name: Carrot and cucumber sticks with a peanut lime dip
about: Crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks with a smooth dip of peanut, garlic, lime and a spoonful of coconut milk, the same dip as the gỏi cuốn. It's a light snack with **fibre and vitamin A**.
steps: Cut the cucumber and carrot into sticks.
Grind the peanuts with the garlic to a paste, then stir in the lime juice, palm sugar, fish sauce, coconut milk and a spoonful of water, and use it for dunking.
ingredients: ground to a paste with the garlic

name: Guava with mint and lime
about: Crisp guava wedges tossed with torn mint and a squeeze of lime. The mint makes it taste cool and fresh, and the guava brings **vitamin C and plenty of fibre**.
steps: Cut the guava into wedges.
Toss with the torn mint and lime juice.

name: Apple-cinnamon porridge with toasted walnuts and yogurt
inspiredBy: Scottish porridge, with apple and cinnamon
about: Rolled oats simmered in milk with grated apple and cinnamon, finished with a little thick yogurt and a few crunchy toasted walnuts. The oats, milk and yogurt carry **protein and fibre**, and the walnuts and ground flax bring plant omega-3.
steps: Stir the oats, milk, grated apple, ground flax, cinnamon and a pinch of salt in a small pot over medium heat.
Simmer, stirring often, until the porridge is creamy and the apple has melted in, about 6 minutes.
While it cooks, toast the walnuts in a dry pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes, then chop them.
Pour the porridge into a bowl, drizzle with the honey, spoon the yogurt on top and scatter over the walnuts.
tip: Toast a jarful of walnuts on Sunday and they're ready all week. The apple and cinnamon can also go in the night before as overnight oats.

name: Huevos a la mexicana with black beans and warm tortillas
inspiredBy: Mexican huevos a la mexicana
about: Scrambled eggs cooked with tomato, onion, chili and browned mushrooms, served with black beans and warm corn tortillas. The eggs and beans together give you **protein, choline and B12 to start the day**.
steps: Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook the mushrooms until browned, about 4 minutes, then add the onion with the chili powder and cook until soft, 3 minutes more.
Add the tomato and a pinch of the salt and cook until the juices have thickened, about 4 minutes.
Pour in the eggs and stir slowly with a spatula until no runny egg is left, about 3 minutes.
Warm the beans in a small pot with the cumin and the rest of the salt, mashing a few. Heat the tortillas in a dry pan or directly over a flame.
Serve the eggs with the beans and tortillas, finished with the cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Huevos a la mexicana takes its name from the red tomato, white onion and green chili, so add a chopped fresh jalapeño or serrano with the onion if you have one.

name: Smoky roasted chickpeas with lemon
about: Crunchy chickpeas roasted until crisp with smoked paprika and finished with lemon. A **protein and fibre** snack you can eat by the handful.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the dry chickpeas with the oil, paprika and salt on a tray.
Roast, shaking the tray once, until crisp and deep golden, about 25 minutes.
Squeeze the lemon over them and let them cool a few minutes; they crisp as they cool.
tip: Make a double batch. They stay crisp in a jar for 2 days.

name: Apple with sharp cheddar and walnuts
about: Crisp apple slices with a few slices of sharp cheddar and a few walnuts, a British ploughman-style plate. The cheese brings **protein and calcium** and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Slice the apple and cheddar.
Arrange them on a plate with the walnuts.

name: White bean toast with za'atar and lemon
about: Whole-wheat toast piled with garlicky mashed white beans, olive oil, parsley and a good pinch of za'atar. Fibre, iron and **plant protein** in a few minutes.
steps: Mash the beans with the garlic, half the oil, the lemon juice and a grind of pepper.
Pile onto the toast, sprinkle with the za'atar and finish with the parsley and the rest of the oil.

name: Creamy garlic white beans on toast with poached eggs and mushrooms
inspiredBy: British beans on toast with poached eggs, made from scratch
about: Tender white beans simmered with garlic, thyme and a little smoked paprika, spooned onto thick toast with garlicky mushrooms and well-poached eggs. It is a proper **protein-rich** breakfast: beans, eggs and whole-wheat bread together bring fibre, iron, choline and B12.
steps: Warm half the oil in a small pot and soften the onion with half the garlic and the thyme until sweet, about 4 minutes. Stir in the smoked paprika for 20 seconds.
Add the beans, soy sauce and a good splash of water. Simmer, mashing a few beans against the side, until creamy and thick, about 8 minutes.
Meanwhile, cook the mushrooms in the rest of the oil over high heat until golden, about 5 minutes. Add the remaining garlic for the last minute and finish with the parsley and half the lemon juice.
Poach the eggs in barely simmering water, covered, until the white and the yolk are firm, 6 to 8 minutes. Toast the bread.
Spoon the beans over the toast, top with the mushrooms and the eggs, and finish with the rest of the lemon juice and a grind of pepper.
tip: Cook the beans on Sunday night. They keep 4 days in the fridge, so on the day you only warm them, poach the eggs and toast the bread.

name: Tamago and tofu rice bowl with sesame greens
inspiredBy: Japanese tamago-yaki and tofu donburi
about: Brown rice topped with a rolled soy-honey omelette, seared ginger tofu and mushrooms, sesame spinach and quick lemon-pickled carrot and onion. **Eggs and tofu together** make a high-protein bowl, and the calcium-set tofu brings calcium too.
steps: Rinse the rice, then simmer it covered in plenty of water until tender, about 35 minutes, and drain. A rice cooker does this without watching.
Toss the carrot and onion with the lemon juice and a pinch of the sesame seeds. Let them sit while you cook.

Whisk the eggs with half the soy sauce and the honey. Warm a little oil in a small non-stick pan over medium-low heat, pour in a thin layer of egg, and roll it up as it sets. Push it to one side, add a little more egg and roll again until all the egg is used. Slice the roll.

Sear the tofu in the rest of the oil over medium-high heat until golden on both sides, about 6 minutes. Add the mushrooms and cook until browned, 4 minutes more, then the ginger and the remaining soy sauce for the last minute.
Wilt the spinach in a splash of water, squeeze it dry and toss with the sesame oil and half the remaining sesame seeds.
Pile the rice in a bowl and arrange the tamago, tofu, greens and pickles on top. Finish with the last sesame seeds.
tip: Cook the rice on Sunday; it keeps 4 days in the fridge. Then the bowl comes together in about 15 minutes.

name: Black bean, mushroom and spinach enchiladas with red chili sauce
inspiredBy: Mexican enchiladas rojas, with black beans
about: Corn tortillas rolled around smoky black beans, browned mushrooms and wilted spinach, baked under a quick red chili and tomato sauce with a little melted cheddar and a cool lime yogurt crema. The beans and mushrooms bring **iron, folate and B vitamins**, and the lime in the crema helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Pull the stem and seeds out of the ancho chile, toast it in a dry pan for a few seconds a side until it smells fruity, then cover it with hot water to soak. Warm the oil in a pot and soften the onion with the garlic, about 5 minutes. Stir in the cumin and oregano for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes with their juice, the soaked ancho chile with a splash of its soaking water, and the salt. Simmer for 12 minutes, then blend until smooth. This is the sauce.

In a wide pan, cook the mushrooms over high heat until they release their water and brown, about 6 minutes. Add the beans with a few spoonfuls of the sauce and mash about half. Fold in the spinach and cook until it just wilts.

Warm the tortillas so they bend without cracking. Fill each with the bean mixture, roll tightly and lay seam side down in a baking dish. With only a tortilla or two in the dish, tear them into strips and layer them through the filling instead, like a tortilla casserole.
Pour the rest of the sauce over the top, scatter on the cheddar and bake until bubbling at the edges, about 15 minutes.
Stir the yogurt with the lime juice and a pinch of salt. Spoon it over the enchiladas and finish with the cilantro. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Make the sauce and the filling on Sunday. On Monday, warm the tortillas, roll and bake, so they don't go soggy overnight.

name: Misir wat with garlicky greens and flatbread
inspiredBy: Ethiopian misir wat and gomen
about: Red lentils slow-cooked with a mountain of onion, garlic, ginger and berbere until they turn into a thick, fragrant stew, served with soft garlicky greens and a piece of warm flatbread. The lentils and greens give you **iron, folate and plenty of protein**, and the lemon helps your body use the iron.
steps: Cook the onion in a dry heavy pot over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring, until it softens and starts to stick. Add half the oil and keep cooking until it is deep golden and jammy, about 10 more minutes.
Stir in half the garlic, half the ginger and the berbere. Cook for a minute until the pot smells rich and spicy, then add the tomatoes.

Add the lentils and plenty of water to cover by a finger. Simmer gently, stirring often and adding water if it gets too thick, until the lentils have collapsed into a thick stew, about 25 minutes. Season with half the salt.

For the greens, warm the remaining oil in a wide pan. Add the rest of the garlic and ginger for 30 seconds, then the kale with a splash of water and the remaining salt. Cook until tender, about 8 minutes, and finish with the lemon.
Serve the wat with the greens and the warm flatbread, and tear off pieces to scoop it up. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Berbere varies in heat, so start with less and add more once the lentils soften. Collards are the traditional green and work the same way as kale. If you find niter kibbeh (spiced butter) at an Ethiopian grocer, cook the onions in it for the real flavour.
ingredients: warmed; use injera if you have an Ethiopian grocer nearby

name: Minestrone with white beans, kale and brown rice
inspiredBy: Italian minestrone con riso, with white beans and kale
about: A thick Italian vegetable soup of carrot, kale and white beans, cooked with a little brown rice and finished with parmesan, parsley and a squeeze of lemon. The beans and rice together make a **complete, filling bowl** with plenty of fibre.
steps: Warm half the oil in a large pot and cook the onion and carrot until soft and sweet, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and rosemary for the last minute.
Add the tomatoes, rice and enough water to cover by about 5 cm (2 inches). Bring to a boil, then simmer for 35 minutes, until the rice is just tender.
Add the beans and kale, and simmer another 8 minutes, until the kale is silky. Mash a few beans against the side of the pot to thicken the broth. Season with the salt and pepper.
Stir in the lemon juice and half the parsley. Ladle into bowls and finish with the parmesan, the rest of the parsley and a drizzle of the remaining oil.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, adding a splash of water when you reheat it, since the rice keeps drinking.
tip: A pressure cooker has the rice soft in about 12 minutes. Keep the rind of a vegetarian parmesan wedge in the freezer and drop it in with the tomatoes for extra savoury depth.
ingredients: finely grated; pick one made with microbial (vegetarian) rennet

name: Toor dal tadka with spinach and brown rice
inspiredBy: Indian toor dal tadka and palak dal
about: Soft yellow pigeon pea dal wilted with spinach, finished with a sizzling tadka of cumin, mustard seed, garlic and chili in hot oil. Dal and rice together give you **complete protein, iron and folate**, and the lemon at the end brightens everything.
steps: Put the dal in a pot with the turmeric and plenty of water. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then simmer partly covered until completely soft, about 35 minutes. Whisk it smooth, adding hot water for a soupy, pourable texture.
While it cooks, simmer the rice in plenty of water until tender, about 30 minutes, and drain.
Stir half the salt into the dal and simmer 5 minutes. Stir in the spinach until it wilts.

For the tadka, warm the oil in a small pan until it shimmers. Add the mustard seeds; when they pop, add the cumin seeds, asafoetida, onion, garlic and ginger and cook until the onion is golden, about 4 minutes. Take off the heat and stir in the Kashmiri chili.
Pour the sizzling tadka over the dal, then stir in the lemon juice, the rest of the salt and the cilantro. Serve over the rice. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: A pressure cooker has the dal soft in about 15 minutes, and cooked dal freezes well. No Indian grocer nearby? Red lentils work the same way and are soft in about 20 minutes.
ingredients: rinsed until the water runs clear

name: Roast cauliflower and chickpea plate with labneh and za'atar pita
inspiredBy: Levantine roasted cauliflower with labneh and spiced chickpeas
about: Spiced roasted cauliflower and crisp chickpeas on a swoosh of lemony labneh, with a tomato and parsley salad, toasted almonds and warm za'atar pita. The chickpeas and labneh bring **protein and calcium**, and the lemon and tomato help you absorb the iron in the chickpeas.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the cauliflower with half the oil, the cumin, half the salt and the pepper on one tray, and the dry chickpeas with most of the rest on a second tray, so neither steams.
Roast both trays, stirring once, until the cauliflower is browned at the edges and the chickpeas are crisp, about 28 minutes.
Meanwhile, stir the labneh with half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and spread it on a plate.
Toss the tomato, parsley and onion with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt for the salad.
Brush the pita with the last of the oil, sprinkle with the za'atar and warm it in the oven for the last 3 minutes.

Pile the roasted vegetables and chickpeas on the labneh, scatter over the almonds and sumac, and serve with the salad and pita. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the labneh and salad in their own tubs.
tip: Warm the leftovers in the oven rather than the microwave to keep the crisp edges.

name: Lentil, mushroom and walnut shepherd's pie
inspiredBy: British shepherd's pie, made with lentils and walnuts, with miso for savoury depth
about: A rich filling of green lentils, mushrooms, carrot and walnuts in a savoury tomato gravy, topped with a creamy potato and cauliflower mash and a little cheddar baked until golden. The lentils bring **iron and plant protein**, and the walnuts add plant omega-3 and a meaty bite.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Simmer the lentils in plenty of water until just tender, about 22 minutes, then drain. At the same time, boil the potato and cauliflower in salted water until very soft, about 18 minutes, then drain and leave them in the colander to steam dry.
Warm the oil in a large pan and cook the mushrooms over high heat until the water cooks off and they brown, about 8 minutes. Add the onion and carrot and cook until soft, 6 minutes more.

Stir in the garlic and thyme, then the tomatoes, walnuts and miso. Add the lentils and a splash of water and simmer for 10 minutes into a thick, glossy filling. Season with pepper and spoon it into a baking dish.

Tip the potato and cauliflower back into the hot pot for a minute so the last of the steam escapes, then mash with the milk, the salt and a little pepper until smooth. Spread it over the filling and rake the top with a fork.
Scatter on the cheddar and bake until the top is golden and the edges are bubbling, about 25 minutes. Rest for 5 minutes and finish with the parsley.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Make the filling a day ahead. The flavour deepens overnight, and you only have to mash and bake.

name: Miso-glazed eggplant with ginger tofu and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese nasu dengaku, served as a rice bowl with tofu
about: Soft roasted eggplant glazed with sweet-salty miso, served with a scoop of brown rice with seared ginger tofu, sesame spinach and crunchy lemon-pickled onion. The tofu brings **protein, calcium and iron**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Rub the eggplant halves with half the oil and roast them cut side up until soft and golden, about 30 minutes. Meanwhile, simmer the rice in plenty of water until tender, about 35 minutes, and drain.
Stir the miso, honey and half the ginger with a spoonful of water. Brush most of it thickly over the eggplant and return it to the oven for 6 minutes, until glossy and caramelized at the edges.
Toss the onion with the lemon juice and a pinch of the sesame seeds, and set aside to soften.

Sear the tofu in the rest of the oil until golden on both sides, about 6 minutes. Turn the heat down, add the soy sauce and the remaining ginger, then brush the tofu with the rest of the glaze and turn it for a minute until glossy.
Wilt the spinach in a splash of water, squeeze dry and toss with the sesame oil.
Spoon the rice into a bowl and top with the eggplant, tofu, spinach and pickled onion. Finish with the rest of the sesame seeds.
tip: Start the rice first; everything else fits in the time it takes. Cook a double batch, cool the spare half within an hour and keep it in the fridge for Monday's tamago bowl.

name: Mango yogurt with lime and chili
about: Thick yogurt with juicy mango, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of chili, inspired by the way mango is eaten with lime and chili in Mexico. It is a cool, bright snack with **protein, calcium and vitamin C**.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and top with the mango.
Squeeze the lime over it and dust with the chili powder.
tip: Tajín, if you have it, is the classic Mexican finish.

name: Cardamom yogurt with honey, almonds and flax
about: Thick yogurt spiced with cardamom, with a spoonful of ground flax stirred in, sweetened with a little honey and topped with toasted almonds. A **protein and calcium** snack that feels like dessert, with plant omega-3 from the flax.
steps: Stir the cardamom, flax and half the honey into the yogurt.
Top with the toasted almonds and drizzle with the rest of the honey.

name: Labneh with olive oil, za'atar and warm pita
about: A swirl of tangy labneh with olive oil, lemon and za'atar, scooped up with warm whole-wheat pita wedges. It is a light Levantine snack with **calcium and protein**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the oven and cut it in wedges.
Spread the labneh in a shallow bowl, drizzle with the olive oil and lemon juice and sprinkle with the za'atar. Scoop it up with the pita.

name: Apple, oat and yogurt cup with cinnamon
about: Thick yogurt layered with grated apple, rolled oats and cinnamon, a no-cook cup that tastes like apple crumble. **Protein and fibre** for bigger days.
steps: Stir the oats into the yogurt with the cinnamon and honey.
Layer with the grated apple in a glass or bowl. Eat straight away, or leave for 15 minutes so the oats soften.

name: Chilled tofu with ginger, soy and sesame
about: A block of cold tofu dressed with grated ginger, a little soy sauce, lemon, toasted sesame and thin onion, like Japanese hiyayakko. It is a cool, savoury, **high-protein** snack that also brings calcium.
steps: Cut the tofu in a few slabs and set it on a plate.
Pile the ginger and onion on top, then drizzle with the soy sauce, lemon juice and sesame oil. Scatter with the sesame seeds.
tip: Ginger and a squeeze of lemon are the whole trick. Serve it straight from the fridge.

name: Toasted almonds with cumin and lime
about: Almonds toasted in a dry pan until fragrant, then tossed with cumin, a squeeze of lime and a tiny pinch of salt. A satisfying crunchy snack that brings **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, until they smell nutty and darken a shade, about 5 minutes.
Toss with the cumin, lime juice and salt while still warm, and let them cool a minute before eating.
tip: Toast a bigger batch on Sunday; plain, they keep a week in a jar. Add the cumin, lime and salt just before eating.

name: Boiled egg with za'atar and tomato
about: A boiled egg with a sprinkle of za'atar and olive oil, with juicy tomato wedges on the side, a classic Levantine snack. The egg brings **choline and B12**.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of simmering water and cook for 10 minutes until the white and the yolk are firm. Cool it under cold water, then peel.
Halve the egg, drizzle with the olive oil, and sprinkle with the za'atar and a pinch of salt. Serve with the tomato wedges.

name: Mango, oat and yogurt cup with lime
about: Thick yogurt layered with diced mango, rolled oats and a squeeze of lime, a no-cook cup that is bright and filling. **Protein and fibre** for bigger days.
steps: Stir the oats into the yogurt with the honey and lime juice.
Layer with the diced mango in a glass or bowl. Eat straight away, or leave for 15 minutes so the oats soften.

name: Moong and besan chilla with mint-peanut chutney and masala chai
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Gujarati besan chilla, with moong dal for more protein
about: Savoury lentil pancakes with spinach and onion, crisp at the edges and soft in the middle, with a sharp mint chutney thickened with roasted peanuts, a few soaked almonds on the side and a cup of cardamom chai. The **moong dal and besan together** bring plenty of protein, the milk in the chai brings calcium and vitamin B12, and the peanuts and almonds add vitamin E.
steps: The night before, rinse the moong dal and soak it in plenty of water for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Soak the almonds in a little water beside it.

Drain the dal and blitz it with the besan, half the lemon juice and enough water to make a pourable batter a little thicker than pancake batter. Stir in the onion, spinach, half the green chili, turmeric, chili powder, ajwain, cumin and salt.
For the chutney, dry-roast the peanuts until they smell nutty, then blitz them with the mint, the rest of the green chili and lemon juice and a splash of water until smooth and thick.

Heat a non-stick pan over medium heat and brush it with a little oil. Pour in a ladleful of batter and spread it thin and round. Cook until the underside is golden and the edges lift, about 3 minutes.
Brush a touch of oil on top, flip, and cook 2 minutes more until speckled brown. Repeat with the rest of the batter and keep the finished chillas warm under a plate.
For the chai, simmer the milk with the strong tea and cardamom for 3 or 4 minutes until it smells spicy and turns the colour of a caramel, then strain it into a mug and stir in the jaggery.
Serve the chillas with the chutney for dunking, the soaked almonds on the side and the chai alongside.
tip: Blend the dal and besan the night before and stir in the chopped vegetables in the morning, and breakfast takes 15 minutes. The plain batter keeps 2 days in the fridge and the chutney keeps 3.
ingredients: brewed strong, Assam or CTC if you can find it
soaked overnight with the moong and peeled, to eat on the side

name: Kanda poha with peanuts and peas, and a cup of masala chai
inspiredBy: Maharashtrian kanda poha, a breakfast Gujarat loves too, with the classic chai alongside
about: Fluffy flattened rice tossed with onion, turmeric, curry leaves, crunchy peanuts and sweet peas, finished with lemon, with a small bowl of thick dahi and a cup of ginger and cardamom chai alongside. The milk and dahi bring **calcium, vitamin B12** and protein, and the peanuts add a little vitamin E.
steps: Rinse the poha in a colander under cold water for a few seconds, just until it softens, then leave it to drain and puff for 10 minutes. Toss it gently with the turmeric, a pinch of salt and a pinch of the jaggery.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and add the mustard seeds. When they pop, add the peanuts and fry until golden, about 2 minutes.
Add the curry leaves and green chili, then the onion, and cook until soft and just turning golden, about 5 minutes. Add the peas and cook 2 minutes more.
Fold in the poha gently, so the flakes stay whole, and warm it through for 2 or 3 minutes. Finish with the lemon juice.

For the chai, simmer the milk with the strong tea, ginger and cardamom for 3 or 4 minutes, then strain it into a mug and stir in the rest of the jaggery. Serve the poha hot with the dahi and the chai.
tip: Rinse and drain the poha while the kettle boils and breakfast is on the table in 15 minutes.
ingredients: jada poha, from any Indian grocer
thick, strained dahi (hung curd), on the side
brewed strong, Assam or CTC if you can find it
a pinch goes in the poha, the rest in the chai

name: Idli with sambar and flax-peanut-sunflower chutney powder
inspiredBy: Tamil and Karnataka tiffin: idli, sambar and agase (flax) chutney powder
about: Soft steamed rice-and-urad idlis with a tangy sambar full of tomato and spinach and a spoonful of nutty seed and peanut chutney powder. It is a weekend project that makes two mornings, and the **toor, urad and flax together** bring protein, iron and plant omega-3 in a breakfast that tastes like a Chennai tiffin stop.
steps: The day before, soak the urad dal with the fenugreek seeds in one bowl and the rice in another, each in plenty of water, for 5 to 6 hours. Drain them and grind the urad to a fluffy, airy batter, then grind the rice coarse, like fine semolina.

Mix the two batters with your hand with half the salt, cover loosely and leave somewhere warm for 8 to 10 hours, until the batter has risen and smells pleasantly sour. In a cold kitchen, an oven with just the light on works.
Rinse the toor dal and cook it with the turmeric and plenty of water until completely soft, about 20 minutes in a pressure cooker or 45 in a covered pot. Mash it smooth.

For the sambar, heat half the oil in a pot, pop the mustard seeds, then add the hing, curry leaves and onion and cook until soft. Add the tomato, tamarind and sambar powder with enough water to make a loose, soupy sambar, and simmer until the tomato has broken down, about 12 minutes. Stir in the dal and the spinach, season with salt and simmer 5 minutes more, until the spinach is wilted and soft.

For the podi, dry-roast the flax, peanuts, sunflower seeds and sesame in a pan until the sesame turns golden and the nuts smell toasty, then cool and grind to a coarse powder with the chili powder and a pinch of salt. Loosen a spoonful with the rest of the oil when you serve, the way a Chennai tiffin shop does.
Steam the batter in an oiled idli mould for 12 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean.
Serve the idlis with the sambar and the podi. Pack the second portion for tomorrow, and re-steam the idlis for 3 minutes.
tip: At a lighter size you get about two idlis, and the sambar fills the bowl. A blender grinds a bigger batch better, so double it: the batter keeps 3 days in the fridge. No idli stand? Steam it in small oiled bowls.

name: Curd rice with chana dal kosambari and pomegranate
inspiredBy: Tamil thayir sadam with a Karnataka kosambari on the side
about: Soft, cool curd rice tempered with mustard, ginger and curry leaves, with a crunchy salad of soaked chana dal, carrot and coconut, and a few pomegranate seeds on top. The **dahi and chana dal together** bring about 30 g of protein, and the dahi brings calcium and vitamin B12.
steps: Soak the chana dal in water for 2 hours, then drain. Cook the rice with extra water until it is very soft and just breaking down, about 25 minutes, then mash it lightly and leave it to cool until warm.
Stir the dahi into the warm rice with a little salt, a splash of cold water to loosen it, and the ginger. It should be creamy, not stiff.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the hing, half the green chili and half the curry leaves for 20 seconds. Pour the tempering over the curd rice.
For the kosambari, toss the drained chana dal with the carrot, onion, coconut, cilantro, lemon juice, the rest of the green chili and a pinch of salt.
Spoon the curd rice into a bowl, scatter the pomegranate over it and serve the kosambari alongside.
tip: Soak the dal that morning and cook the rice the night before. Curd rice turns sour fast, so eat it the day you make it.
ingredients: thick, strained dahi (hung curd), loosened with a splash of milk

name: Rajma masala with brown basmati and kachumber
inspiredBy: Punjabi rajma chawal, finished with a little ghee
about: Kidney beans simmered in a thick onion and tomato masala until the gravy clings, with brown basmati and a crunchy cucumber and onion kachumber. Rajma is a **great iron source**, and the tomato in the masala and the lemon on the salad bring vitamin C that helps you absorb it. It is even better tomorrow, so lunch is made.
steps: Soak the rajma in plenty of water overnight, at least 8 hours. Drain, cover with fresh water and cook with a pinch of salt until completely soft, about 25 minutes in a pressure cooker or 75 in a covered pot.
Rinse the brown basmati and cook it with a bay leaf in plenty of salted water until tender, about 25 minutes, then drain.
Heat the oil in a wide pot and sizzle the cumin. Add most of the onion and cook until deep golden, about 10 minutes, stirring so it does not catch.

Add the ginger, garlic and green chili and cook for a minute, then the tomato, turmeric, Kashmiri chili and ground coriander. Cook until the tomato collapses and the oil starts to separate at the edges, about 8 minutes.

Tip in the rajma with a ladle of its cooking water. Simmer 15 minutes, mashing a few beans against the side of the pot so the gravy thickens, then stir in the garam masala, crushed kasuri methi, ghee and half the cilantro.

Toss the cucumber and the raw onion with the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and the rest of the cilantro. Serve the rajma over the rice with the kachumber alongside, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cook the soaked rajma in the pressure cooker the night before and the masala takes 30 minutes. At a lighter size, serve it with a few spoonfuls of rice, or a small roti instead.
ingredients: finely chopped, some set aside raw for the kachumber

name: Palak paneer with missi roti
inspiredBy: Punjabi palak paneer, with almond paste instead of cream, and Rajasthani missi roti
about: Soft cubes of paneer in a silky spinach gravy with ginger, garlic and a little almond for richness, scooped up with warm missi roti, a whole-wheat and besan flatbread. The paneer, dahi and besan bring good **protein and calcium**, and the spinach brings folate and vitamin K. Tomorrow's lunch is cooked too.
steps: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 1 minute, then plunge it into cold water and drain. Blitz it smooth with the green chili and the soaked almonds, using a splash of water.
Heat the oil in a pan and sizzle the cumin. Add the onion and cook until soft and golden, about 8 minutes, then add the ginger and garlic for a minute.
Stir in the tomato, turmeric, Kashmiri chili and ground coriander and cook until it breaks down into a jammy masala, about 6 minutes.

Pour in the spinach puree and simmer gently for 5 minutes. Do not boil it hard, or the green turns dull. Slide in the paneer cubes and warm them through for 3 minutes, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the whisked dahi, garam masala, crushed kasuri methi and salt.

For the missi rotis, mix the atta and besan with the ajwain, a pinch of salt and warm water into a soft dough, rest it 10 minutes, roll thin rounds and cook them on a hot dry pan until they puff and show brown spots. Brush with the ghee.
Serve the palak paneer with the hot missi rotis, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The dough keeps a day in the fridge, so you can roll it fresh for tomorrow's lunch.
ingredients: thick, strained dahi (hung curd), whisked smooth
soaked in hot water for 10 minutes, then peeled

name: Gujarati kadhi with moong khichdi and carrot-bean sambharo
inspiredBy: Gujarati kadhi khichdi with a warm sambharo of carrot and beans
about: A comforting plate of soft moong dal and rice khichdi, a tangy-sweet besan and dahi kadhi tempered with curry leaves, and a quick mustard-seed stir-fry of carrot and green beans with crushed peanuts. The moong, besan and dahi together give you **about 40 g of protein**, and it tastes even better the second day.
steps: Rinse the rice and soak it in water for 30 minutes, then drain. Cook it with the rinsed moong dal, half the turmeric, a pinch of salt and plenty of water until soft and porridge-like, about 35 minutes in a pot or 15 in a pressure cooker.

Whisk the dahi with the besan, the rest of the turmeric, half the ginger, half the green chili, the jaggery, salt and enough water to make a thin, pourable batter, until completely smooth. Heat it slowly, stirring, and simmer for 15 minutes until it thickens and the raw besan taste is gone.

For the kadhi tadka, heat half the oil, pop half the mustard seeds, then add the cumin, hing, curry leaves and Kashmiri chili for 20 seconds. Pour it into the kadhi and stir in half the cilantro and the lemon juice at the end.

For the sambharo, heat the rest of the oil in a pan, pop the remaining mustard seeds, then add the rest of the green chili and ginger. Toss in the green beans and carrot over high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, so they stay a little crunchy, then season with salt and scatter the crushed roasted peanuts over the top.
Serve the khichdi with the hot kadhi poured over, the sambharo alongside and the rest of the cilantro on top. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Day-old sour dahi makes a better kadhi. Keep the khichdi and the kadhi in separate containers, then warm the kadhi with a splash of water, because it thickens overnight.
ingredients: thick, strained dahi (hung curd), for the kadhi
stirred into the kadhi at the end
dry-roasted and crushed, for the sambharo

name: Rajasthani mixed dal with spinach and baked whole-wheat baati
inspiredBy: Rajasthani dal baati, with a lighter hand on the ghee and a Maharashtrian peanut-garlic chutney
about: Four lentils simmered together with spinach and a garlic and chili tadka, with golden whole-wheat baatis baked until crusty outside and tender inside, and a peanut-garlic chutney on the side. The mixed dals and spinach bring **protein, iron and folate**, and the squeeze of lemon helps you absorb the iron. It reheats well for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Rinse the four dals together and cook them with the turmeric, half the tomato and plenty of water until completely soft, about 25 minutes in a pressure cooker or 50 in a covered pot. Stir in the spinach for the last 3 minutes, then whisk everything smooth and season with salt and amchur.

Heat the oven to 200 C (400 F). Rub most of the ghee and the ajwain, with a pinch of salt, into the atta until it looks like damp crumbs and just holds when you squeeze a handful, then add just enough warm water to bring it to a firm dough. Shape it into tight balls, flatten the tops slightly and press a dent in the middle with your thumb.
Bake the baatis on a tray for about 25 minutes, turning them once halfway, until they are deep golden and sound hollow when tapped.

For the tadka, heat the oil and the rest of the ghee, sizzle the cumin, then add the garlic and green chili until the garlic is golden. Add the hing, the onion and the Kashmiri chili, cook until the onion is soft, about 6 minutes, then add the rest of the tomato for 2 minutes.

For the chutney, pound or blitz the roasted peanuts with the reserved garlic, a pinch of salt and a little of the lemon juice and water until it is a thick paste. Pour the tadka over the dal and squeeze in the rest of the lemon juice.

Break each hot baati in half, spoon plenty of dal over it and eat with the peanut-garlic chutney and the raw onion rings. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and re-warm the baatis in a hot oven or a dry pan.
tip: Cook the dal in the pressure cooker while the baatis bake, and nothing needs watching.
ingredients: most in the baati dough, the rest for the tadka
chopped, a handful kept raw as rings to serve
sliced, a few cloves kept for the chutney

name: Kala chana masala with whole-wheat roti and carrot-mint raita
inspiredBy: Punjabi and Rajasthani black chickpea curry
about: Nutty black chickpeas in a dark, tangy onion and tomato masala with a hint of amchur, with warm whole-wheat roti and a cooling carrot and mint raita. Kala chana is rich in **protein, iron and fibre**, and the raita brings calcium and vitamin B12. It reheats beautifully.
steps: Soak the kala chana in plenty of water overnight, at least 8 hours. Drain, cover with fresh water and cook with a pinch of salt until very tender, about 30 minutes in a pressure cooker or 90 in a covered pot. Keep the cooking water.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and sizzle the cumin. Add the onion and cook until deep golden, about 10 minutes, then add the ginger, garlic and green chili for a minute.
Stir in the tomato, turmeric, Kashmiri chili and ground coriander, and cook until the oil separates at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Add the chickpeas and a ladle of their water. Simmer 15 minutes, mashing a few against the side of the pan to thicken the gravy, then stir in the garam masala, amchur, salt and cilantro.
For the raita, whisk the dahi with the carrot, mint, kala namak and a pinch of salt.
For the rotis, mix the atta with warm water and a pinch of salt into a soft dough, rest it 10 minutes, roll thin rounds and cook them on a hot dry pan until they puff and show brown spots.
Serve the chana with the rotis and raita, and pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: At a lighter size, make one small, palm-sized roti. Soak the kala chana the night before and the pressure cooker does the rest.
ingredients: thick, strained dahi (hung curd), for the raita

name: Bisibele bath with ghee-fried cashews and coconut
inspiredBy: Karnataka bisibele bath, the hot lentil rice from Mysuru, made with more dal than rice
about: A Karnataka weekend special: toor and moong dal and rice cooked soft with carrot, beans, peas and tamarind, spiced with sambar powder, a pinch of cinnamon and clove, and topped with ghee-fried cashews and curry leaves. The dals and rice together bring **protein, iron and fibre**, and the tamarind and tomato give it a bright, sour edge. Lunch tomorrow is done.
steps: Rinse the toor and moong dal and the brown rice and cook them together with the turmeric and plenty of water until completely soft, about 30 minutes in a pressure cooker or 60 in a covered pot. Mash them together with the back of a ladle.

In a big pot, simmer the carrot, beans, peas, onion and tomato with the tamarind, sambar powder, cinnamon, cloves, half the grated coconut and a little salt in about a cup of water until the vegetables are tender, about 15 minutes.

Fold the dal and rice into the vegetables with enough hot water to make a thick, porridge-like consistency, and simmer for 10 minutes, stirring so it does not stick. It should flow slowly when you tilt the pot.
Heat the ghee in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, then fry the cashews until golden. Add the curry leaves and hing for 10 seconds and pour it sizzling over the bath.
Serve the bisibele bath hot, with the rest of the coconut scattered over it. Pack the second portion for tomorrow, and loosen it with a splash of hot water when you reheat it.
tip: Use bisibele bath powder if you find it, and skip the cinnamon and cloves. Cook the dal and rice in the pressure cooker while the vegetables simmer, so it all comes together at once.

name: Matar paneer in an almond-tomato gravy with missi roti
inspiredBy: Punjabi matar paneer, with an almond and tomato gravy
about: Soft paneer and sweet peas in a velvety onion, tomato and almond gravy finished with kasuri methi, with warm besan and whole-wheat missi roti. It is a slow-Sunday dinner, and the paneer and almonds bring **protein, calcium and vitamin E**, while the tomato brings vitamin C and lycopene.
steps: Heat the oil and half the ghee in a heavy pan and sizzle the cumin. Add the onion and cook gently until soft and pale golden, about 8 minutes, then add the ginger, garlic and green chili for a minute.
Add the tomato, turmeric, Kashmiri chili and ground coriander, cover and cook until completely soft, about 10 minutes.
Let the masala cool a little, then blitz it with the drained almonds and a splash of water until silky smooth. Pour it back into the pan and simmer 5 minutes.

Add the peas and simmer 4 minutes. Slide in the paneer cubes and warm them through for 3 minutes, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the whisked dahi, garam masala, cardamom, crushed kasuri methi, the rest of the ghee and half the cilantro. Season with salt.

For the missi rotis, mix the atta and besan with a pinch of salt and warm water into a soft dough, rest it 10 minutes, roll thin rounds and cook them on a hot dry pan until they puff and show brown spots.
Serve the matar paneer hot with the missi rotis and the rest of the cilantro on top.
tip: Make the gravy a day ahead, then warm it and add the paneer just before you eat. At a lighter size, one small, palm-sized roti is plenty.
ingredients: soaked in hot water for 15 minutes, then peeled
thick, strained dahi (hung curd), whisked smooth

name: Masala chaas with roasted cumin and mint
inspiredBy: Gujarati and Rajasthani masala chaas
about: Thin, cold spiced buttermilk with roasted cumin, mint, green chili and a pinch of black salt, the drink that rescues a hot afternoon all over western India. It is light and salty-sour, and the dahi brings **calcium and vitamin B12**.
steps: Dry-roast the cumin seeds in a small pan for 30 seconds until they smell toasty, then crush them.
Whisk the dahi with plenty of cold water until it is thin and pourable, like a smoothie.
Stir in the cumin, mint, cilantro, green chili, ginger, kala namak and salt. Pour over ice, or chill it for 15 minutes first.
ingredients: thick, strained dahi (hung curd), whisked with cold water until pourable

name: Haldi doodh with almonds
inspiredBy: haldi doodh, the turmeric milk many homes serve in the evening
about: Golden milk simmered with turmeric, ginger and black pepper, blended with a few almonds for a creamy finish and sweetened with a little jaggery. A warm evening cup with **calcium, vitamin B12** and a little vitamin E from the almonds.
steps: Blitz the peeled almonds with a third of the milk until smooth.
Warm the rest of the milk in a small pot with the turmeric, ginger, black pepper, cardamom and the almond paste. Simmer gently for 4 or 5 minutes and stir the pot often so the milk does not catch.
Stir in the jaggery until it melts, then pour into a mug and drink it warm.
ingredients: soaked in hot water for 10 minutes, then peeled

name: Moong sprouts chaat with tomato, onion and peanuts
inspiredBy: Delhi and Gujarati sprout chaat
about: Fresh moong sprouts tossed with tomato and onion, with lemon, chaat masala and a crunch of roasted peanuts. It is crunchy, tangy and cooling, with **protein and folate** from the sprouts and vitamin C from the lemon and tomato.
steps: Blanch the sprouts in boiling water for 30 to 60 seconds so they are tender but still crisp, then drain and cool under cold water.
Dry-roast the peanuts in a pan until they smell nutty, cool them and crush them coarsely.
Toss the sprouts with the tomato, onion, green chili, cilantro, lemon juice, chaat masala and kala namak.
Top with the peanuts just before you eat, so they stay crunchy.
tip: Cooking for small children, a pregnancy or anyone with a weaker immune system? Steam the sprouts for 4 or 5 minutes until hot right through, as Health Canada advises for them.
ingredients: moong sprouts, from the store or sprouted at home

name: Apple and pomegranate chaat with almonds and walnuts
inspiredBy: Delhi fruit chaat, with walnuts for crunch
about: Crisp apple and ruby pomegranate seeds tossed with lemon, chaat masala and black salt, with toasted almonds and walnuts on top. It is sweet, sour and salty all at once, and the almonds bring **vitamin E** and the walnuts a little plant omega-3.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan until they smell nutty, then chop them.
Toss the apple and pomegranate with the lemon juice, chaat masala and kala namak.
Scatter the nuts on top and eat straight away.

name: Til-alsi laddoo with almonds and walnuts
inspiredBy: North Indian winter til-alsi laddoo, bound with jaggery and a little ghee
about: Toasted sesame, sunflower seeds, flax, almonds and walnuts, ground coarse and bound with melted jaggery and a little ghee into two small laddoos, in the style of the North Indian winter til-alsi laddoo. The sunflower seeds and almonds bring **vitamin E**, the sesame adds calcium and iron, and the flax and walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Dry-roast the sesame and sunflower seeds in a pan until golden, then the ground flax for 1 minute until it smells nutty. Let everything cool, then pulse the seeds with the almonds and walnuts in a grinder a few times, to a coarse, slightly oily crumb.
Melt the jaggery and ghee together with no water and simmer until it foams, about 2 minutes.

Take the pan off the heat, stir in the crumb and the cardamom, and press it into two tight balls with oiled palms while it is still hot. If it won't hold, sprinkle in a teaspoon of warm milk and press again. They firm up as they cool.

name: Khaman dhokla with green chutney
inspiredBy: Gujarati khaman dhokla
about: Soft, spongy steamed besan cakes with a sizzling mustard and sesame tadka, with a cilantro and mint chutney on the side. It is a classic Gujarati snack with about **14 g of protein**, and a little dahi in the batter keeps it tender.
steps: Whisk the besan with the dahi, half the lemon juice, the ginger, half the green chili, salt and enough water to make a smooth, thick batter that falls off the spoon in a ribbon. Rest it for 10 minutes.
Stir the baking soda into the batter just before steaming, then pour it into a greased dish and steam it for 12 to 15 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean.
Blitz the cilantro and mint with the rest of the lemon juice, the rest of the green chili, the jaggery and a splash of water into a bright chutney.
Heat the oil, pop the mustard seeds, then add the sesame and curry leaves for 20 seconds and pour over the dhokla. Cut into squares and serve with the chutney.

name: Rice kheer with milk and almonds
inspiredBy: North Indian chawal ki kheer
about: Creamy rice pudding simmered slowly in milk with cardamom, jaggery and a few almonds. It is a gentle sweet treat that brings **calcium and vitamin B12**, and it feels like a festival day.
steps: Drain the soaked rice and crush it lightly with your fingers.
Simmer the rice in the milk over low heat, stirring often so it does not catch, until the grains are very soft and the kheer is creamy, about 35 minutes.
Stir in the jaggery off the heat, then the cardamom and almonds. Serve warm, or chill it. It thickens as it cools.
tip: At a lighter size it's a thinner, sippable kheer. Simmer it a few minutes longer if you like it thick.

name: Soya chunk tikka bites with lemon and onion rings
inspiredBy: North Indian soya chunk tikka, seared in a hot pan instead of a tandoor
about: Soya chunks marinated in lemon, ginger, garlic, ajwain and tikka spices, then seared until charred at the edges, with lemon and raw onion on the side. A high-protein snack with tikka-house flavour from a hot pan and **about 17 g of protein**, plus iron.
steps: Boil the soya chunks in plenty of water for 8 minutes until soft, then drain, rinse and squeeze out every drop of water. Tear any big ones in half.
Toss the chunks with the besan, half the lemon juice, the ginger, garlic, Kashmiri chili, ajwain, amchur, cumin, garam masala and salt. Leave them to marinate for at least 15 minutes.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan over medium-high heat and sear the chunks, turning now and then, until golden and charred at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Serve hot with the onion rings and the rest of the lemon juice squeezed over.
ingredients: sliced into thin rings, for serving

name: Moong dal kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka kosambari, the temple-festival salad
about: A fresh salad of soaked moong dal with cucumber, coconut and lemon, tempered with mustard and curry leaves. It is light, crunchy and cooling, with a surprising amount of **protein and folate** for a snack.
steps: Soak the moong dal in water for 2 hours until it swells and softens a little but still has a bite, then drain it well.
Toss the dal with the cucumber, coconut, cilantro, lemon juice, green chili and salt.
Heat the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, then add the curry leaves for 10 seconds and pour the tempering over the salad. Serve it the same day.

name: Cucumber and mint raita with roasted cumin
inspiredBy: North Indian raita, eaten by the bowl
about: A big, cooling bowl of thick dahi with grated cucumber, mint, roasted cumin and a pinch of black salt, eaten with a spoon. It is simple, tangy and **cooling**, and it brings protein, calcium and vitamin B12.
steps: Dry-roast the cumin seeds in a small pan for 30 seconds until they smell toasty, then crush them.
Whisk the dahi until smooth, then stir in the cucumber, mint, half the cumin and the kala namak.
Dust the top with the rest of the cumin and the chili powder, and eat it cold.
ingredients: grated, with the extra water squeezed out

name: Peanut, sunflower and flax chikki bites
inspiredBy: Gujarati and Lonavala peanut chikki, made as small bites with sunflower seeds and alsi (flax)
about: Roasted peanuts, sunflower seeds, sesame and ground flax tossed in hot jaggery and set into crisp little bites. It is crunchy and not too sweet, and the peanuts and sunflower seeds bring **vitamin E and niacin**, with plant omega-3 from the flax.
steps: Dry-roast the peanuts, sunflower seeds and sesame in a pan for a few minutes until they smell toasty, then stir in the ground flax for 30 seconds and tip everything into a bowl.

Melt the jaggery and ghee together in a small heavy pan over medium heat, stirring, until it bubbles, darkens a shade and a drop in cold water snaps, about 3 minutes. Watch it, because a small amount catches fast.
Take the pan off the heat, tip in the nuts and seeds and stir quickly until everything is coated. Drop small spoonfuls onto an oiled plate and leave them to cool and crisp, about 10 minutes.
tip: Make four or five servings at once. A bigger pan of jaggery is easier to cook, and the bites keep 2 weeks in a tin.

name: Thick yogurt with honey, walnuts and figs
inspiredBy: Greek yogurt with honey and walnuts, the taverna dessert that makes a fine breakfast
about: Thick yogurt with a drizzle of honey, toasted walnuts, chewy dried figs and a little ground flax, finished with a pinch of cinnamon. It takes five minutes, and the yogurt brings **protein, calcium and B12** while the walnuts and flax add plant omega-3.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Tip them onto a board and chop roughly.
Trim the stems off the figs and chop them small.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and stir in the ground flax.
Scatter over the figs and walnuts, drizzle with the honey and finish with a pinch of cinnamon.
tip: Toast a handful of walnuts on Sunday night and keep them in a jar, so weekday mornings are just spooning and drizzling.

name: Strapatsada, Greek tomato eggs, on toast
inspiredBy: Greek strapatsada, the tomato and egg scramble from the islands
about: Ripe tomatoes cooked down in olive oil until jammy, then scrambled with eggs and oregano and piled on toasted whole-wheat bread. **The eggs and the toast** make a proper protein breakfast, and the tomatoes bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat and soften the onion until translucent, about 3 minutes.

Add the grated tomato with a pinch of salt and cook, stirring now and then, until the juices have cooked off and it looks thick and jammy, about 7 minutes. Put the bread in the toaster while it bubbles.
Pour the beaten eggs into the pan and stir gently for 2 to 3 minutes, until they form creamy curds and no runny egg is left.
Stir in the oregano and Aleppo pepper, spoon over the toast and finish with black pepper.
tip: Stir in a few crumbles of feta at the end if you like. That is how many Greek cooks make it.

name: Ful medames with a boiled egg, tomato and tahini
inspiredBy: Levantine and Egyptian ful medames, the fava bean breakfast sold from carts across the region
about: Warm, half-mashed fava beans with garlic, lemon and cumin, topped with a halved boiled egg, chopped tomato, parsley and a swirl of tahini, with warm pita for scooping. Fava beans bring **iron, folate and plant protein**, and the lemon helps your body absorb the iron.
steps: Lower the egg into a small pot of boiling water and simmer for 10 minutes for a firm yolk. Cool it under cold running water, then peel and halve.

Meanwhile, tip the fava beans into another small pot with a few spoonfuls of water (or their cooking liquid, if you cooked them from dried), the garlic and the cumin. Warm gently, mashing about half the beans with a fork, until thick and steaming, about 5 minutes.
Take off the heat and stir in half the lemon juice, half the olive oil and the salt. Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spoon the ful into a shallow bowl and top with the egg, tomato and parsley. Drizzle with the tahini loosened with the rest of the lemon juice and a spoonful of water.
Finish with the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of Aleppo pepper, and serve with the warm pita.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday night, and the egg is already waiting for you. Using a can? Rinse the beans very well and taste before you salt: they usually need little or none.
ingredients: small brown ful beans, canned and well rinsed, or cooked from dried

name: Warm lentil salad with halloumi, blistered pepper and mint
inspiredBy: Greek and Cypriot lentil salads and grilled halloumi, with Levantine pomegranate molasses
about: Green lentils tossed warm with soft red pepper, mint, parsley and a tangy pomegranate dressing, topped with golden seared halloumi and toasted walnuts. The lentils carry the **protein and iron**, the halloumi adds more protein, and the lemon and pepper bring vitamin C to help you absorb the iron.
steps: Simmer the lentils in plenty of unsalted water until just tender but still holding their shape, about 20 minutes. Drain well.
While they cook, warm half the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the pepper strips until soft and blistered at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Whisk the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses, salt and the rest of the olive oil in a bowl. Toss the warm lentils with the dressing, onion, mint and parsley.
Sear the halloumi in a dry non-stick pan until golden, about 2 minutes a side. It is salty, so there is no need for more salt.
