Warm the tortilla in a dry pan, 30 seconds per side, until soft and a little toasty.
Lay the tortilla on a plate, spoon the tofu scramble on top, then the beans in salsa. Finish with avocado, cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Make the salsa ranchera the night before and the scramble comes together in 10 minutes. At Light, toast the half tortilla crisp as a tostada.
ingredients: calcium-set (check the label), pressed and crumbled

name: Black bean bowl with roasted sweet potato and cauliflower
inspiredBy: Mexican black bean and sweet potato tacos, rebuilt as a bowl that packs well
about: Chili-roasted sweet potato and cauliflower, black beans and quinoa under a pile of lime cabbage, pico de gallo and a pepita-lime crema. The beans, quinoa and pepita crema bring **close to 30 g of protein**, and the lime and tomato help your body take up the iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato and cauliflower with the oil, chili powder, cumin and a pinch of salt on a tray, and roast until tender and browned at the edges, about 25 minutes.
Meanwhile, cook the quinoa in twice its volume of lightly salted water, covered, for 15 minutes. Fluff it with a fork and let it steam off the heat for 5 minutes.
Toss the cabbage with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt. Mix the tomato, onion and half the cilantro into a quick pico de gallo, with a pinch of chili powder.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan until they pop. Blend half of them with the soy yogurt, a squeeze of lime and the rest of the cilantro into a green crema, and keep the rest whole for crunch.
Warm the beans with a splash of water. Build the bowl: quinoa, beans, sweet potato and cauliflower, cabbage and pico, then spoon the crema over the top and scatter with pepitas.
tip: Roast the sweet potato and cauliflower and cook the quinoa on Sunday, and the bowl takes 10 minutes to build. Keep the crema separate until you eat.
ingredients: for the cabbage and the crema

name: Soya and mushroom tinga tacos with chipotle, avocado and cabbage
inspiredBy: Tinga poblana, where soya chunks and oyster mushrooms stand in for the shredded chicken
about: A smoky, tangy tomato and chipotle sauce clinging to tender strips of soya chunks and oyster mushrooms, piled into warm corn tortillas with crunchy cabbage and creamy avocado. The soya and mushrooms bring **about 40 g of protein** and plenty of niacin and choline, and the lime and tomato help you absorb the iron.
steps: Cover the soya chunks with boiling water and let them soak for 10 minutes, or until they are soft all the way through. Drain, squeeze out the water, and tear them into rough shreds.
Blend the tomatoes, chopped onion, garlic, chipotle with its sauce, a squeeze of the lime, oregano, cumin and allspice until smooth.

Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the sliced onion until soft and starting to brown, about 8 minutes. Add the shredded soya and the mushrooms and cook for 6 minutes, until the mushrooms have given off their water and start to brown.

Pour in the blended sauce, add the bay leaf and the salt, and simmer, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and clings to the soya and mushrooms, about 15 minutes. Taste and add more chipotle if you want more heat.
Toss the cabbage with the rest of the lime juice and the cilantro. Warm the tortillas in a dry pan, about 30 seconds per side.

Pile the tinga into the warm tortillas with cabbage and avocado, and eat any extra filling with a fork, or serve it over rice. Pack the second portion of tinga (not the cabbage or avocado) for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The tinga freezes beautifully and tastes better the next day. Spoon it over rice or a baked potato if you run out of tortillas.
ingredients: half sliced into thin half-moons, half chopped
with a little of the adobo sauce
a little in the sauce, the rest on the cabbage

name: Peruvian quinoa chupe with white beans, camote and cancha-style hominy
inspiredBy: Peruvian chupe, a thick, creamy soup flavoured with ají amarillo, with quinoa and white beans in place of the usual egg and cheese
about: A thick, golden soup of quinoa, white beans, mushrooms, collards and sweet potato, spiced with ají amarillo and finished with a splash of soy beverage the way chupe gets its evaporated milk. A scatter of crunchy toasted hominy on top does the work of cancha, and the beans and quinoa bring **plenty of protein, iron and folate**.
steps: Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 6 minutes, then stir in the mushrooms, garlic, ají amarillo paste, cumin and oregano and cook for 3 minutes, until the mushrooms soften and it smells sweet and fruity.
Add the tomato and cook until it melts into the sauce, about 4 minutes.

Stir in the quinoa and sweet potato, then pour in enough water to cover everything by about 2 cm. Add the salt, bring to a boil, then simmer, covered, until the quinoa is cooked and the sweet potato is tender, about 15 minutes.
Add the white beans and the collards and simmer 5 more minutes, until the collards are tender. Mash a few beans against the side of the pot to thicken the soup.
Meanwhile, pat the hominy very dry and toast it in a dry pan over medium-high heat until golden and popping, 8 to 10 minutes, shaking the pan.

Turn the heat to low, stir in the soy beverage and warm it through without letting it boil. Finish with the lime juice and cilantro, and top your bowl with half the crunchy hominy. Save the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the rest of the hominy in a jar so it stays crunchy.
tip: Hominy is the closest stand-in for Peruvian choclo. Frozen choclo from a Latin grocer is better still. At Light, the topping is a spoonful of toasted hominy.
ingredients: stems removed, sliced into thin ribbons
canned, drained, all of it toasted for the topping
fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton)

name: Colombian-style beans with hogao, seared tempeh and roasted plantain
inspiredBy: Colombian frijoles with hogao and tajadas, a plant-based plate in the spirit of the bandeja
about: Creamy beans simmered in a tomato and onion hogao, served with garlicky seared tempeh, a small scoop of brown rice, a few slices of roasted plantain and sweet potato, and a few slices of avocado. The beans and tempeh bring **about 40 g of protein**, and the plantain adds the sweet note that makes the whole plate sing.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the plantain slices and the sweet potato wedges with a third of the oil and bake on a tray until caramelized and soft, about 25 minutes, flipping once.
Rinse the brown rice, then cook it in about twice its volume of lightly salted water, covered, for 35 to 40 minutes.

For the hogao, warm a third of the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add half the garlic, the cumin and the tomato and simmer until it breaks down into a thick, jammy sauce, about 10 minutes.
Add the beans and a splash of water, mash a few to thicken, and simmer for 10 minutes. Taste for salt and stir in the cilantro.
Meanwhile, stir the achiote paste into a splash of water with the rest of the garlic and a squeeze of lime. Rub it over the tempeh slices.
Warm the rest of the oil in a skillet and sear the tempeh until deep golden and crisp at the edges, about 3 minutes per side.
Serve the beans alongside a small scoop of rice with the tempeh, plantain, sweet potato and avocado on the side, and a squeeze of lime. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Colombian cooks use red cargamanto beans, but pintos or any red or pink bean work well. Cook about ½ cup of dry brown rice tonight and it covers this plate, Friday's picadillo and Saturday's feijoada. It keeps 4 days in the fridge. At Light, the rice is a spoonful or two.
ingredients: very ripe, peeled and sliced on the diagonal

name: Lentil, soya and mushroom picadillo with olives and raisins, brown rice and maduros
inspiredBy: Cuban picadillo, the sweet, salty, tangy ground-meat hash, with lentils and soya in place of the beef
about: Earthy lentils, soya and chopped mushrooms simmered with sweet potato, tomato, olives and raisins until it tastes like the sweet-and-salty picadillo you get in a Cuban kitchen. It brings **over 30 g of protein** and a big dose of iron, with the lime and tomato helping you absorb it.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the plantain with a third of the oil and a pinch of salt and bake on a tray until caramelized and soft, about 20 minutes, flipping once.

Cover the soya with boiling water and leave it to soak. Simmer the lentils in plenty of water until just tender, about 20 minutes, and drain. Warm the rice from Wednesday, or cook it in twice its volume of lightly salted water, covered, for 35 to 40 minutes.

Warm two thirds of the oil in a wide pan over medium heat and cook the onion and sweet potato until the onion is soft, about 6 minutes. Add the garlic, cumin, oregano and allspice and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Squeeze the soya dry and add it to the pan with the mushrooms and cook with the onions until the mushrooms give off their water and everything starts to colour, about 6 minutes.

Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down, about 8 minutes. Stir in the lentils, olives, raisins, bay leaf, salt and a splash of water, and simmer for 10 minutes, until thick and glossy but still a bit saucy. Finish with the lime juice.
Serve the picadillo alongside a small scoop of rice, with the maduros on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Use the brown rice from Wednesday. With the lentils cooked the night before, dinner takes 20 minutes. At Light, the rice is a spoonful or two.
ingredients: very ripe, peeled and sliced on the diagonal

name: Pozole verde with white beans, hominy and a pepita salsa verde
inspiredBy: Mexican pozole verde from Guerrero, with white beans and oyster mushrooms doing the work of the usual meat
about: Hominy, white beans and oyster mushrooms in a bright, green broth made from tomatillo, jalapeño, cilantro and toasted pepitas, with collards in place of the wild greens and crunchy cabbage and lime on top. The beans, mushrooms and pepitas bring **plenty of protein, iron and zinc**, and the lime and tomatillo help you absorb them.
steps: Simmer the tomatillos and jalapeño in a pot of water for 5 to 7 minutes, until they turn olive green and soft. Drain, saving a cup of the cooking water.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat until they puff up and pop, about 3 minutes. Set a spoonful aside for the top.
Blend the tomatillos, jalapeño, half the onion, garlic, most of the cilantro and the toasted pepitas with a splash of the cooking water until completely smooth.
Warm the oil in a pot over medium-high heat. Pour in the green sauce (it will spit) and fry for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens.

Add the hominy, white beans, mushrooms, collards, half the oregano, cumin, salt and about 500 ml of water. Simmer for 25 minutes, until the mushrooms and collards are tender and the broth is rich and slightly thickened.
Meanwhile, toss the cabbage with the diced onion and half the lime.

Ladle into bowls and top with the cabbage, reserved pepitas, the rest of the cilantro and a squeeze of lime. Sprinkle the rest of the oregano over each bowl. Pack the second portion (without the toppings) for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Reheat it with a splash of water, since the hominy drinks up the broth overnight. Add fresh cabbage and lime when you eat it.
ingredients: half in the sauce, half diced for the garnish
stems removed, sliced into thin ribbons

name: Feijoada-style black beans with smoky tofu, garlicky couve, orange and farofa
inspiredBy: Brazilian feijoada, with seared smoky tofu and soya "carne seca" in place of the usual smoked meats
about: A deep, rich pot of black beans simmered until silky, served with smoky seared tofu, garlicky collards, sweet orange slices to cut the richness, and a toasty corn and Brazil nut farofa. The beans, tofu and soya bring **about 40 g of protein**, and the orange and collards help your body use the iron.
steps: Warm the brown rice from Wednesday, or rinse it and cook it in twice its volume of lightly salted water, covered, for 35 to 40 minutes, while you start the beans.
Cover the soya chunks with boiling water and soak for 10 minutes, until soft all the way through. Drain, squeeze dry and tear into small, rough shreds.

Warm a third of the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat and cook half the onion until soft, about 5 minutes. Add half the garlic, the tomato, the bay leaf, cumin, pepper and the soya shreds and cook for 3 minutes, until the tomato melts.

Add the black beans and enough water to cover them by about 2 cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer, partly covered, for 45 minutes, until the broth is dark and thick. Mash about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pot to make it silky, and add the salt.

Meanwhile, rub the tofu with the smoked paprika, a clove of garlic, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt and let it sit for 15 minutes. Sear it in a third of the oil over medium-high heat until deep golden and crusty, about 4 minutes per side. Keep it warm and lay it on top of the beans when you serve, so the crust stays crisp.

For the couve, warm half the remaining oil in a wide pan over high heat. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, then add the collards and a pinch of salt and toss until bright green and just tender, about 4 minutes. Finish with the rest of the lime.

For the farofa, cook the remaining onion in the rest of the oil until golden, about 5 minutes. Add the masarepa and chopped Brazil nuts and stir over medium heat until it smells toasty and looks like sandy crumbs, about 3 minutes. Season with a pinch of salt.

Serve the feijoada alongside a small scoop of rice, with the tofu on top, the couve, orange slices and farofa. Pack the second portion of beans, tofu and couve for tomorrow's lunch, with the farofa in a jar so it stays crisp, and slice a fresh orange tomorrow.
tip: Classic farofa uses manioc flour, but toasted masarepa gives you the same sandy crunch. At Light the farofa is a spoonful. If you have time, soak and cook 70 g of dry black beans per serving instead of using canned: soak overnight, then simmer for 1 hour.
ingredients: calcium-set, pressed and cut in 2 cm slabs
half for the beans, half for the farofa
for the beans, the tofu and the couve
stems removed, sliced into thin ribbons

name: Enchiladas rojas with pinto beans, a smoky spiced tempeh crumble and collards
inspiredBy: Mexican enchiladas rojas, made as enchiladas montadas (layered) with pintos and a smoky spiced tempeh crumble
about: Corn tortillas dipped in red sauce and layered with pinto beans, collard greens, mushrooms and a spicy tempeh crumble, baked under a deep red guajillo sauce and finished with a cool soy crema and crunchy pepitas. The pintos, tempeh and mushrooms bring **about 40 g of protein**, and the collards bring a good dose of calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Toast the guajillo chiles in a dry pan for 20 seconds per side, until fragrant, then soak them in hot water for 10 minutes.

Blend the soaked chiles with the tomato, half the onion, most of the garlic, half the cumin, half the oregano, a squeeze of the lime and a splash of the soaking water until smooth. Fry the sauce in a little of the oil for 5 minutes, until it darkens, and season with salt.

For the tempeh crumble, warm the rest of the oil in a pan and crumble in the tempeh. Cook until it starts to brown, about 4 minutes. Add the rest of the onion and garlic, the smoked paprika, a spoonful of the red sauce, the rest of the cumin and oregano, and the rest of the lime juice, and cook for 3 more minutes, until it clings together.
Stir in the mushrooms and collards and cook until the mushrooms release their water and the collards wilt, about 6 minutes. Add the pinto beans and mash roughly with the back of the spoon.

Warm the tortillas in a dry pan until pliable, dip each in the red sauce and tear it in half. Spread a little sauce in a baking dish, then layer half the tortillas, half the filling, the rest of the tortillas and the rest of the filling. Pour the remaining sauce over the top.
Bake for 15 minutes, until bubbling at the edges. Top with the soy crema, toasted pepitas and cabbage.
tip: Make the sauce and the filling on Saturday and Sunday dinner is 20 minutes of layering and baking. For rolled enchiladas, make 4 small ones and serve the extra filling on the side. At Light there is only about one tortilla, so layer it thin and serve the rest as a bean bowl.
ingredients: half in the sauce, half in the filling
stirred with a squeeze of lime for crema
in the sauce, the tempeh crumble and the crema

name: Jícama and orange cup with pepitas, lime and chile
inspiredBy: Mexican street fruit and jícama cups with lime and chile
about: Crunchy jícama sticks and juicy orange segments, tossed with lime and chile, with a handful of toasted pepitas for crunch and protein. It brings **most of a day's vitamin C**, plus a good bit of fibre and magnesium.
steps: Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat until they puff up and start to pop, about 2 minutes.
Peel the jícama and cut it into thin sticks. Peel the orange and break it into segments.
Toss the jícama and orange with the lime juice, a dusting of chili powder and a pinch of salt. Scatter with the pepitas and eat right away.

name: Toasted almonds with lime and chile
inspiredBy: Mexican cacahuates con limón y chile, made here with almonds
about: Almonds toasted until golden and fragrant, then tossed with lime and chile. A small handful is one of the best everyday sources of **vitamin E**, with calcium and magnesium too.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, until golden and fragrant, about 4 minutes.
Toss with the chili powder and salt while still warm, and let them cool a few minutes to crisp up. Add the lime just before you eat.

name: Chía fresca with lime and pineapple
inspiredBy: Mexican agua de chía, a cool lime drink thickened with chia
about: Chia seeds soaked in cold water with lots of lime and a little fresh pineapple until they plump up into little pearls. It is a very Mexican way to get **plant omega-3, calcium and fibre**, and it is wonderfully refreshing.
steps: Use a ripe, sweet pineapple, since it is the only sweetener. Blend it with about 300 ml of cold water until smooth, and strain it if you like it clear.

Stir in the chia and let it sit for 5 minutes, then stir again so it doesn't clump. Add the lime juice and a few ice cubes. Let it stand for 10 more minutes, until the seeds are plump and the drink is slightly thick, and stir before you drink it.
tip: Taste before adding the chia, and add more pineapple if it is tart. A jug keeps 2 days in the fridge.
ingredients: blended with the water until smooth

name: Achiote tofu bites with seared pineapple
inspiredBy: Mexican street-taco flavours, with achiote-marinated tofu and seared pineapple
about: Cubes of tofu marinated in achiote, guajillo and pineapple, then seared until the edges caramelize, with sweet seared pineapple on the side. It is a snack you can build a meal around, with **about 15 g of protein** and plenty of calcium from the calcium-set tofu.
steps: Blend half the pineapple with the achiote paste, the soaked guajillo, garlic, half the lime juice, cumin, oregano and salt until smooth. Toss the tofu cubes in the marinade and leave them for at least 15 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Lift the tofu from the marinade and sear it, turning now and then, until the edges are dark and sticky, about 8 minutes. Add the leftover marinade for the last minute so it glazes.
Sear the rest of the pineapple, cut in chunks, in the same pan for 2 minutes per side, until caramelized.
Pile the tofu and pineapple on a plate and scatter with the onion, cilantro and the rest of the lime juice.
tip: Marinate the tofu the night before and it takes 15 minutes. The tofu is great cold on a tortilla the next day.
ingredients: calcium-set, pressed and cut in 2 cm cubes
half blended into the marinade, half seared
stem and seeds removed, soaked in hot water for 10 minutes

name: Licuado de plátano with oats, almonds and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Mexican licuado de avena con plátano, the blender shake sold at every market stall
about: A thick banana licuado blended with oats, almonds, chia and cinnamon, made with a big glass of fortified soy beverage. It carries your **vitamin B12 and calcium** along with about 13 g of protein, and it tastes like a milkshake.
steps: Add the soy beverage, banana, oats, almonds, chia and cinnamon to a blender with a few ice cubes.
Blend until completely smooth, about 1 minute. Drink right away, or let it sit 5 minutes so the oats and chia thicken it a bit.
ingredients: fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton)

name: Soy yogurt with orange, almonds, Brazil nuts and chia
inspiredBy: the fruit-and-yogurt cups at Mexican markets
about: Plain soy yogurt topped with juicy orange segments, toasted almonds, a chopped Brazil nut and a spoonful of chia. It is cool and tangy with a good crunch, and it gives you **about 8 g of protein** and a good dose of selenium.
steps: Toast the sliced almonds and the chopped Brazil nuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, about 2 minutes.
Stir the chia and cinnamon into the soy yogurt. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the chia softens.
Spoon into a bowl, top with the orange segments and the toasted nuts.

name: Chipotle soya tostadas with cabbage
inspiredBy: Mexican tostadas de tinga, crisp tortillas under smoky chipotle soya
about: Crisp baked corn tortillas topped with a quick smoky chipotle and tomato soya, crunchy cabbage and a squeeze of lime. It is a snack with **about 17 g of protein**, so it makes a hungry afternoon feel properly handled.
steps: Cover the soya with boiling water and soak for 10 minutes. Drain, squeeze dry and tear into small shreds.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Lay the tortillas on a tray and bake until crisp and golden, about 8 minutes, flipping once.
Warm the oil in a small pan and cook the onion and garlic until soft, about 4 minutes. Add the soya, tomato, chipotle, oregano, cumin and salt and simmer until thick and saucy, about 8 minutes.
Spoon the soya onto the tostadas and top with the cabbage and a squeeze of lime.

name: Crispy tempeh with lime and chile
inspiredBy: Mexican chicharrón, the crunchy, salty, chile-and-lime snack, made here with tempeh
about: Tempeh cut into thin strips and pan-fried until crunchy at the edges, then tossed with lime, chile and garlic. It is salty and crisp like chicharrón, with **about 14 g of protein** and a good dose of iron.
steps: Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the tempeh strips in a single layer and cook, turning now and then, until deep golden and crisp at the edges, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic for the last 30 seconds, then take the pan off the heat and toss with the lime juice, chili powder and salt.
Pile on a plate with the onion and cilantro and eat while still warm.

name: Black bean and avocado tostadas with lime
inspiredBy: Mexican tostadas de frijol, crisp corn tortillas piled with refried beans and avocado
about: Crisp baked corn tortillas topped with warm mashed black beans, creamy avocado and a squeeze of lime. They are crunchy, creamy and satisfying, with **about 12 g of protein** and plenty of fibre.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Lay the tortillas on a tray and bake until crisp and golden, about 8 minutes, flipping once.
Warm the oil in a small pan and cook the garlic for 30 seconds. Add the beans, cumin, chili powder, salt and a splash of water, and mash until thick and creamy, about 4 minutes.
Spread the beans on the warm tostadas, top with the avocado, cilantro and a squeeze of lime.

name: Chipotle black bean dip with jícama and tortilla wedges
inspiredBy: Mexican frijoles negros refritos, blended into a dip
about: A smoky, creamy black bean dip with a little chipotle and lime, scooped with crunchy jícama sticks and baked corn tortilla wedges. It is a snack that actually fills you up, with **11 g of protein** and lots of fibre.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Cut the tortilla into wedges, spread them on a tray and bake until crisp, about 8 minutes.
Blend the beans, chipotle, lime juice, garlic, oil, cumin and salt with a splash of water until smooth and creamy.
Serve the dip with the jícama sticks and the warm tortilla wedges.
tip: The dip keeps 4 days in the fridge, so make a bigger batch and snack from it.

name: Toasted pepitas with lime and chile
inspiredBy: Mexican pepitas tostadas con limón y chile, a snack bag staple from Oaxaca to Mexico City
about: Pepitas toasted until they puff and pop, then tossed with lime and chile. A handful brings **magnesium, zinc and iron**, and the crunch hits the spot when you want something salty.
steps: Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, until they puff up and start to pop, about 3 minutes.
Toss with the lime juice, chili powder and salt while still warm. Let them cool and crisp up for a few minutes before eating.

name: Overnight oats with soy beverage, ground flax, walnuts and figs
inspiredBy: Greek and Levantine fig and walnut breakfasts, as an overnight jar
about: Rolled oats soaked overnight in cinnamon soy beverage with chopped dried figs, ground flax and wheat germ, then topped with toasted walnuts for crunch. The figs melt into the oats and sweeten them, so you need no sugar. The fortified soy beverage brings **vitamin B12 and calcium**, and the flax and walnuts bring plant omega-3. Wheat germ adds **vitamin E and choline**.
steps: The night before, chop the figs and stir them into a jar with the oats, ground flax, wheat germ, cinnamon, salt and about ¾ cup of the soy beverage. It should look a little runny, since the oats, flax and wheat germ drink it up.
Cover and refrigerate overnight so the oats turn thick and creamy.
In the morning, give it a stir. It should be thick and spoonable, and a splash more soy beverage loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until you can smell them, then chop roughly.
Top the oats with the walnuts and drink the rest of the soy beverage alongside.
tip: Toast a week of walnuts on Sunday and keep them in a jar. Mix two oat jars at once, they keep for 3 days in the fridge.
ingredients: fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton); about ¾ cup in the jar, the rest to drink alongside

name: Ful medames with lemon, tomato and parsley
inspiredBy: Egyptian ful medames and the Lebanese ful that mixes in a few chickpeas
about: Warm, garlicky fava beans and a few chickpeas mashed roughly with cumin and lemon, then topped with chopped tomato, onion and parsley and a good drizzle of olive oil, the way it is eaten in Cairo. You scoop it up with warm pita. The beans bring **iron and folate**, and the tomato and lemon help you absorb that iron.
steps: Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the fava beans and chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water, the garlic and the cumin, stirring now and then, until steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork, leaving some whole beans for texture. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Spoon the beans into a shallow bowl. Drizzle with the rest of the olive oil, then pile on the tomato, onion and parsley and dust with Aleppo pepper.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster and tear it up to scoop.
tip: A pinch of chili flakes or a few chopped pickles on top is very welcome.
ingredients: cooked from dried, or a tin with no salt added, drained

name: Chickpea fatteh with garlicky soy yogurt, tahini and toasted walnuts
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian fattet hummus, with plain soy yogurt in place of the usual dairy yogurt
about: Warm chickpeas piled over crisp toasted pita, drenched in a cool, garlicky sauce of plain soy yogurt, tahini and lemon, and finished with sizzled walnuts, almonds and parsley. It is the traditional yogurt fatteh made plant-based, with hemp hearts blended into the sauce. The chickpeas and soy yogurt bring **protein and calcium**, the walnuts and hemp bring plant omega-3, and the glass of fortified soy beverage alongside adds **vitamin B12**.
steps: Tear the pita into bite-size pieces and toast them in a dry pan or a hot oven until golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the cumin and a splash of water until steaming, about 5 minutes.
Mash the garlic with the salt, then blend or whisk it with the soy yogurt, tahini, hemp hearts and lemon juice until smooth. Thin with a spoonful of cold water if it is stiff.
Sizzle the walnuts and almonds in the olive oil for 1 to 2 minutes, until they smell toasty. Watch them, they scorch quickly.

Layer the pita in a bowl, spoon the chickpeas and a splash of the warm cooking water over it, pour on the yogurt sauce and finish with the hot nuts and oil, the parsley, sumac and Aleppo pepper. Warm the soy beverage with a pinch of cinnamon and drink it alongside.
tip: On a weekday, toast the pita and make the sauce the night before. In the morning it takes 10 minutes.
ingredients: fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton), a glass, warmed, to drink alongside

name: Hummus bowl with roasted baharat tofu and seitan, cauliflower and tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese hummus plates, with spiced roasted tofu and seitan where the meat would go
about: Thick, lemony hummus spread in a bowl and topped with crisp-edged tofu and seitan roasted with baharat, roasted cauliflower, a chopped cucumber and tomato salad and toasted almonds. Think of the hummus plates in Beirut, with tofu and seitan where the spiced meat would be. The calcium-set tofu and chickpeas bring **protein, iron and calcium**, and the cauliflower adds choline.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Pat the tofu dry, cut it and the seitan into cubes and toss with half the canola oil, the baharat and a pinch of salt. Toss the cauliflower florets with the rest of the canola oil and a pinch of salt. Roast both on a tray for 20 minutes, turning once, until the tofu and seitan edges are crisp and the cauliflower is browned.

Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water for 3 minutes. Blend them with the tahini, half the lemon juice, the garlic, cumin and a few spoonfuls of ice water, in a mini processor if you have one, for a full 2 minutes until very smooth and creamy.
Chop the cucumber, tomato and parsley and toss with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes.
Spread the hummus in a wide bowl, make a dip in the middle and drizzle in the olive oil.
Pile the tofu, seitan, cauliflower and salad on top, scatter over the almonds and dust with za'atar. Warm pita on the side is welcome.
tip: Monday's lunch is easiest made on Sunday: roast the tofu, seitan and cauliflower and blend the hummus, then pack them separately. A double batch of hummus blends smoother and keeps 4 days in the fridge.

name: Horiatiki with marinated tofu "feta" and white beans
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, as it is eaten on fasting days, with tofu in place of feta
about: A Greek village salad of ripe tomato, cucumber, pepper, olives and capers under a slab of lemony oregano tofu, with white beans and pita to make it a meal. It is the kind of thing Greek cooks put together on fasting days, when there is no cheese. The tofu brings **calcium and protein**, and the white beans bring iron and fibre.
steps: Press the tofu between towels for 10 minutes, then lay the slab in a shallow dish and spoon over half the lemon juice, half the vinegar, half the oregano and a good pinch of salt. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or leave it in the fridge in the morning or overnight.
Cut the tomato into wedges, the cucumber into thick half-moons and the pepper into rings, and slice the onion thinly.
Toss the vegetables with the white beans, olives, capers, the rest of the lemon juice and vinegar and most of the olive oil.
Spoon the salad onto a plate and set the tofu on top like a slab of feta. Drizzle with the last of the oil, the marinade and the rest of the oregano.
Toast the pita and tear it up to mop the juices.
tip: Marinate the tofu the night before or in the morning, it tastes much better after a few hours. Crumble it with your hands if you want it to look more like feta.
ingredients: pressed, cut in a thick slab

name: Mujaddara hamra with caramelized onions and lemony cabbage salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese mujaddara hamra, the bulgur version, with malfouf salad
about: Brown lentils and bulgur cooked together with cumin, topped with deep golden onions, and served with a crunchy lemon, garlic and mint cabbage and carrot salad. It is the Lebanese Lenten classic, plain food done properly. The lentils and bulgur together bring **protein, iron and fibre**, and the lemony salad helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Rinse the lentils, cover with plenty of water and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes, until nearly tender but still holding their shape. Drain, saving the cooking water.

While the lentils simmer, slice the onions thin. Cook them in the canola oil over medium heat, stirring every few minutes and adding a splash of water if they catch, for 25 minutes, until deep golden and sweet. Take out a third and keep it for the top.
Stir the cumin and baharat into the onions left in the pot for 30 seconds, then add the bulgur, the lentils, the salt and enough of the lentil water to cover by about 2 cm.
Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes, until the water is gone. Rest off the heat for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Shred the cabbage finely and grate the carrot. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and toss it with the cabbage, carrot, lemon juice, olive oil and torn mint.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes. Serve the mujaddara topped with the reserved onions and the almonds, with the cabbage salad on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Keep the cabbage salad in a separate container so it stays crunchy for tomorrow.

name: Gigantes plaki, giant white beans baked in tomato, dill and parsley
inspiredBy: Greek gigantes plaki, made with canned beans so it works on a weeknight
about: Creamy white beans baked in a sweet-sharp tomato sauce with celery, carrot, red pepper, chard and dill until the edges blister. It is Greek Lenten cooking at its best, and it tastes even better the next day. The beans bring **iron, calcium and fibre**, and a squeeze of lemon at the end helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C. Warm the olive oil in a wide ovenproof pan and cook the chopped onion, celery, pepper and diced carrot for 8 minutes, until soft.
Stir in the garlic, paprika and oregano for 30 seconds, then add the passata, bay leaf, salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 10 minutes, until the sauce thickens.
Fold in the white beans, the chopped chard, half the dill and half the parsley, and slide the pan into the oven for 20 to 25 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling and the edges are browned.
Finish with the lemon juice and the rest of the herbs. Serve with crusty bread or warm pita if you like. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cannellini work well here, and canned giant beans from a Greek grocer are even better. If you cook dried giant beans, soak them overnight and simmer them for about an hour before they go into the sauce.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added

name: Seitan, mushroom and cauliflower shawarma plate with garlic sauce and pickled carrot
inspiredBy: Lebanese shawarma, with seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower for the meat and a tofu garlic sauce for the toum
about: Baharat-spiced seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower roasted on one tray until the edges crisp, piled on a plate with a fluffy tofu garlic sauce, tomato, parsley and tangy pickled carrot, with warm pita on the side to scoop. It has the smoky, garlicky shawarma-stand flavour without the spit. The seitan and tofu together bring **protein, selenium and calcium**, and the vitamin D mushrooms add **vitamin D**.
steps: Heat the oven to 230 C. Cut the seitan into thin strips. Toss them with the baharat, paprika, cumin, half the lemon juice, half the garlic (mashed), half the canola oil and a good pinch of salt. Let them sit while the oven heats.
Meanwhile, toss the carrot ribbons with the vinegar and a pinch of salt and leave them to pickle.
Blend the tofu with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and a splash of cold water until fluffy and white, like toum.

Spread the seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower on one big tray (two if they crowd), drizzle the mushrooms and cauliflower with the rest of the oil, season them with a pinch of salt and roast for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once, until browned and crisp at the edges.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Pile the seitan, mushrooms and cauliflower on a plate with the garlic sauce, tomato, parsley and the drained pickled carrot, and eat with the warm pita.
tip: Double the tofu garlic sauce, it keeps 4 days in the fridge and is good on the falafel too.
ingredients: sliced; sold as vitamin D mushrooms. Plain white mushrooms work, with less vitamin D

name: Baked chickpea and fava falafel in pita with roasted cauliflower and tahini sauce
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Egyptian falafel and ta'ameya, made with chickpeas and fava and baked instead of fried
about: Green, herby chickpea and fava falafel baked until crisp outside and fluffy inside, with warm pita, tahini sauce, a fresh tomato, cucumber and carrot salad and a side of roasted cauliflower. It has all the flavour of the street-stall version with a lot less oil. The chickpeas and fava beans bring **protein, iron and zinc**, and the cauliflower adds choline and vitamin C.
steps: The night before, cover the dried chickpeas and fava beans with plenty of cold water and soak for 12 hours. Drain well and, if you used whole fava beans, slip off the skins. Split, peeled fava beans skip this step.

Heat the oven to 220 C. Pulse the soaked chickpeas and fava beans (double the amount for two portions) in a food processor with the onion, garlic, parsley, cumin, coriander and most of the salt until it looks like coarse couscous, not paste. Rest for 15 minutes so the beans bind.

Shape the mixture into 12 small patties (6 per portion). Toss the cauliflower florets with a third of the canola oil and a pinch of salt and spread them on a big tray. Put a second tray in the oven to preheat, then brush it with the remaining oil, set the falafel on it and brush the tops too.
Bake both trays for 25 minutes, turning the falafel once, until the falafel are deep golden and the cauliflower is browned at the edges.
Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice and enough cold water to make a pourable sauce.

Dice the tomato and cucumber and toss with the grated carrot. Warm the pita, open it and tuck in a few falafel with some salad and tahini sauce. Eat the rest of the falafel, salad and cauliflower on the plate with the remaining sauce. Pack the second portion and the sauce for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: The beans must be soaked from dry. Canned ones turn to mush and the falafel fall apart. Leftover falafel are not good cold: reheat them for 8 minutes at 200 C and pack the tahini sauce separately.
ingredients: dried fava beans, peeled if you can find them, soaked overnight

name: Adas bi hamod, lemony lentil and chard soup with toasted pita
inspiredBy: Lebanese adas bi hamod, the lentil soup with chard and lemon
about: A thick Lebanese lentil soup with silky chard, garlic and plenty of lemon, topped with crisp toasted pita and a swirl of olive oil. It is bright, sour and deeply comforting, and a Lenten favourite. The lentils bring **protein, iron and folate**, and the chard adds vitamins A and K.
steps: Rinse the lentils. Warm the canola oil in a big pot and cook the chopped onion for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, cumin and coriander and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the lentils and plenty of water, enough to cover them by about 5 cm. Bring to a boil, then simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until the lentils are completely soft and falling apart.
Slice the chard stems thin and chop the leaves. Add the stems and cook for 5 minutes, then add the leaves for 3 minutes more, until silky.

Mash some of the soup against the side of the pot with a spoon, or give it a few pulses with a stick blender, so it is thick but still has texture. Add the salt and the lemon juice. It should taste distinctly sour.
Tear the pita into pieces and toast in a dry pan until golden and crisp, about 4 minutes.
Ladle the soup into bowls and top with the pita, the parsley, a drizzle of the olive oil and a pinch of Aleppo pepper. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the pita in a separate bag.
tip: Thin the leftovers with a splash of water when you reheat them. The soup thickens overnight.

name: Lenten chard and mushroom pie with tofu "feta"
inspiredBy: Greek hortopita and manitaropita, the Lenten (nistisimi) pies made with oil and no dairy
about: Crisp layers of oil-brushed phyllo around a lemony filling of chard, mushrooms, dill and herby crumbled tofu. It is the kind of fasting-season pie Greek families bake with no cheese or egg. The tofu brings **calcium and protein**, and the vitamin D mushrooms add **vitamin D** and niacin.
steps: Heat the oven to 190 C. Chop the chard, stems and all, and cook it in a dry pot over medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, until wilted. Tip it into a colander, cool for a few minutes, then squeeze out as much water as you can.

Cook the chopped onion and mushrooms in the olive oil for 8 minutes, until soft and the liquid has cooked off. Crumble the tofu into a big bowl with the lemon juice, oregano and most of the salt and let it stand while the chard drains.
Mix the chard, onion and mushrooms into the tofu with the dill, parsley, nutmeg, pepper and the rest of the salt. Taste, it should be bright and well seasoned.
Brush a baking dish with some of the canola oil. Lay in half the phyllo sheets, brushing each one lightly with oil, then spread the filling over.
Cover with the remaining phyllo, again brushing each sheet. Tuck in the edges, brush the top generously, and score the top layers into squares with a sharp knife.
Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until deep golden and crisp. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Thaw frozen phyllo in the fridge overnight, so move the box from the freezer on Friday night. Keep the sheets under a damp towel while you work so they do not dry out and crack. Short on sheets? Skip the bottom layer and scrunch all the phyllo loosely over the filling, brushing as you go. Leftovers crisp up in a hot oven.
ingredients: finely chopped; sold as vitamin D mushrooms. Plain white mushrooms work, with less vitamin D

name: Sicilian caponata with white beans and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Sicilian caponata with a Levantine pomegranate molasses twist, served warm over white beans as a main
about: A sweet-sharp Sicilian eggplant stew with celery, olives, capers and toasted almonds, spooned warm over creamy white beans and chickpeas. It is Sicily's answer to ratatouille, with a bit of agrodolce bite. The beans and almonds bring **protein and calcium**, and the eggplant adds fibre.
steps: Toss the eggplant cubes with the canola oil and a pinch of salt, spread them on a tray and cover with foil. Roast at 220 C for 10 minutes, then take off the foil and roast 15 minutes more, until browned and soft. Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes and chop.
Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a wide pan and cook the onion, celery and pepper for 8 minutes, until soft.
Add the passata, olives and capers and simmer for 10 minutes.
Stir in the roasted eggplant, the vinegar and the pomegranate molasses and simmer for 5 minutes, until glossy. It should taste sweet and sharp at once.
Warm the white beans and chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water and a pinch of salt.
Spoon the beans into a bowl, top with the caponata and the almonds, and serve with toasted bread if you like.
tip: Caponata tastes even better made ahead. It keeps 4 days in the fridge, so you can cook it on Saturday and just warm the beans on Sunday.
ingredients: passata or tomato sauce, no salt added
from a tin, no salt added, drained

name: Muhammara with cucumber sticks and pita
inspiredBy: Aleppo muhammara, the Syrian walnut and pepper dip
about: A smoky, tangy red pepper and walnut dip from Aleppo, with a hit of pomegranate molasses and Aleppo pepper, scooped up with cool cucumber and crisp pita. The walnuts bring **plant omega-3 and vitamin E**.
steps: Roast the pepper under a hot grill or over a flame for 10 to 15 minutes, turning, until the skin is blackened. Peel, seed and chop.
Toast the pita until dry and crisp, then break up half of it. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes. (Double the amounts for two portions.)
Blitz the pepper, walnuts, the broken pita, garlic, cumin, Aleppo pepper, lemon juice, pomegranate molasses and half the olive oil to a thick, rough paste. Season with the salt.
Spoon into a bowl, drizzle with the rest of the oil and serve with the cucumber sticks and the rest of the pita.
tip: This makes two portions, one for Monday and one for Thursday. Drained jarred roasted red peppers skip the first step.

name: Fig, flax and wheat germ shake with soy beverage
inspiredBy: the fig and date milk shakes of Egypt and the Levant
about: A thick, creamy shake of soft dried figs, fortified soy beverage, ground flax and wheat germ, spiced with cinnamon. Fig and date milk shakes are a classic cooler in Egypt and the Levant. A glass brings **vitamin B12, calcium and plant omega-3**, with vitamin E and selenium from the wheat germ.
steps: Soak the figs in a little hot water for 10 minutes if they are firm, then snip off the stems.
Blend the soy beverage, figs, ground flax, wheat germ and half the cinnamon until completely smooth, 1 to 2 minutes.
Pour into a tall glass and dust with the rest of the cinnamon.
ingredients: fortified with B12 and calcium (check the carton)

name: Lupini beans with lemon, mint and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: Egyptian and Levantine termis, the lupini bean snack
about: Plump, salty-sharp lupini beans, tossed with lemon, olive oil, fresh mint and a pinch of chili. They are a street snack from Cairo to Beirut. A bowl is one of the most **protein-rich** snacks you can eat.
steps: Drain the lupini and soak them in fresh cold water for 10 minutes to take the edge off the brine, then drain again.
Toss with the lemon juice, olive oil, torn mint and Aleppo pepper.
Serve with a lemon wedge. Squeeze each bean out of its skin with your teeth.
tip: Look for jarred lupini at Italian or Middle Eastern grocers, or at Costco.

name: Warm edamame with lemon and sumac
inspiredBy: warm green fava beans (ful akhdar) with lemon, as sold in spring across the Levant
about: Warm shelled green soybeans tossed with lemon, a pinch of sumac and a little salt, the way fresh green fava beans are eaten across the Levant in spring. A big bowl is a very **protein-rich** snack, with fibre and folate too.
steps: Simmer the frozen edamame in salted water for 3 to 4 minutes, until tender, then drain well.
Toss with the lemon juice, olive oil and sumac while still warm.

name: Roasted peanuts with cumin and lemon
inspiredBy: the roasted peanuts sold from carts in Cairo and Beirut
about: Warm dry-roasted peanuts tossed with cumin, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of Aleppo pepper. Roasted peanuts are a favourite nibble all over the Levant and Egypt. The peanuts bring **protein, niacin and vitamin E**.
steps: Warm the peanuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes until fragrant.
Toss with the lemon juice, cumin and Aleppo pepper and eat warm.

name: Dried figs with toasted almonds
inspiredBy: the figs and nuts plate of Syria and Greece
about: Chewy, jammy dried figs with a handful of warm toasted almonds and a pinch of cinnamon. A figs-and-nuts plate is the simplest sweet in Syria and Greece. The almonds bring **vitamin E and calcium**, and the figs bring potassium and fibre.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan for 3 minutes, until fragrant.
Serve with the figs and a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Spiced seitan bites with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: the crispy shawarma-pan bits of Lebanon, made with seitan
about: Little cubes of baharat-spiced seitan seared until crisp at the edges, tossed with lemon, parsley and a drizzle of tahini. Think of the crispy bits at the bottom of the shawarma pan. A serving brings **plenty of protein and selenium**.
steps: Cut the seitan into small cubes and toss with the baharat.
Sear in the canola oil over high heat for 5 to 6 minutes, turning, until browned and crisp at the edges.
Toss with the lemon juice, parsley and a drizzle of tahini loosened with a spoonful of water.

name: Garlicky seitan tawook skewers with tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese shish tawook, with seitan in place of chicken
about: Seitan cubes marinated in lemon, garlic and paprika, threaded on skewers and seared until golden, with a juicy tomato on the side. It is the shish tawook marinade on a plant-based protein. Seitan is a very **protein-dense** snack, and it brings selenium and niacin too.
steps: Cut the seitan into cubes and toss with the lemon juice, mashed garlic, paprika, salt and a spoonful of the canola oil. Leave for 10 minutes.
Thread onto skewers and sear in a hot pan with the rest of the oil for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until golden on all sides.
Serve with the tomato cut in wedges and a scatter of parsley.

name: Seitan skewers with kafta spices, onion and parsley
inspiredBy: the flavours of Lebanese and Syrian kafta (grated onion, parsley and baharat) on seitan
about: Seitan cubes rubbed with grated onion, parsley and baharat, threaded on skewers and seared until golden. It has the flavours of the kafta grilled all over Lebanon and Syria. Seitan is a very **protein-dense** snack, with selenium and niacin too.
steps: Cut the seitan into bite-size cubes. Grate the onion and mix the pulp and juice with the chopped parsley, baharat and salt, then rub it all over the seitan and leave for 10 minutes.
Thread onto skewers.
Sear in the canola oil over medium-high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, turning, until golden and the onion catches at the edges. Squeeze over the lemon.

name: Hummus with carrot and cucumber sticks
inspiredBy: Lebanese hummus bil tahini, the everyday mezze
about: Creamy, lemony chickpea hummus with a swirl of olive oil, scooped up with crunchy carrot and cucumber sticks. It is the everyday mezze snack of Lebanon. The chickpeas and tahini bring **protein, iron and calcium**.
steps: Blend the chickpeas with the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, cumin, salt and a few spoonfuls of cold water until very smooth.
Spoon into a bowl, make a dip in the middle and drizzle in the olive oil.
Cut the carrot and cucumber into sticks and serve alongside.

name: Roasted chickpeas with cumin and za'atar
inspiredBy: leblebi, the roasted chickpeas sold across the eastern Mediterranean
about: Crisp, crunchy chickpeas roasted with cumin and za'atar until they rattle. A snack bowl with the tangy, herby bite of za'atar. The chickpeas bring **protein and iron**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Dry the chickpeas very well in a clean towel.
Toss with the canola oil, cumin and salt and roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray twice, until crisp.
Toss with the za'atar while still warm.

name: Egg sauce with greens and pan-grilled ripe plantain
inspiredBy: Nigerian egg sauce, with collards folded in and the plantain cooked in very little oil
about: Soft eggs stirred through a thick tomato, onion and pepper sauce with a little collard greens, served with golden slices of ripe plantain. It is savoury and sweet on one plate, and quick when the sauce base is made ahead. The eggs bring protein and **choline**, and the plantain adds potassium and vitamin A.
steps: Make the sauce base up to two days ahead. Warm half the oil in a pan, soften the onion and pepper for 4 minutes, then add the tomato and chili. Cook, stirring now and then, until the tomato has broken down into a thick, jammy sauce, about 8 minutes. Chill it.

On the day, peel the plantain and slice it on an angle into thick coins. Brush a non-stick pan with a little of the remaining oil and cook the plantain over medium heat until deep golden and soft, about 3 minutes on each side. Set it aside.
Add the rest of the oil to the pan and warm the sauce through. Stir in the collards with a splash of water and cook until tender, about 3 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the salt, pour them over the sauce and stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes. Serve right away with the plantain.
tip: The sauce base keeps for two days in the fridge, so a double batch covers two mornings. Boiled yam is the other classic partner for egg sauce, and ground crayfish is a traditional addition if you have it. Leave out the chili for a mild version.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Moi moi, steamed black-eyed pea pudding, with avocado and orange
inspiredBy: Nigerian moi moi, steamed in ramekins instead of leaves
about: A soft, savoury pudding of black-eyed peas blended with sweet peppers and onion, with half a boiled egg tucked in the middle, served with creamy avocado and a few orange segments. It makes two portions, and the second is just as good reheated the next morning. The peas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the avocado brings vitamin E.
steps: On Saturday night, cover the peas with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak overnight.

On Sunday evening, drain the peas and rub handfuls between your palms under water to loosen the skins. Pour off the skins as they float up and repeat until most are gone. It takes about 10 minutes and gives the pale, smooth moi moi you are after.
Hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes, then cool, peel and halve them.

Blend the peas with the pepper, tomato, onion, chili, dried shrimp and a splash of water until you have a thick batter that drops off the spoon in a slow ribbon. Stir in the vegetable oil, palm oil and salt.

Ladle the batter into lightly oiled ramekins or foil cups, filling them about three quarters full, and press half an egg into the middle of each. For two portions that is four ramekins. Cover tightly with foil.

Stand the cups on a rack in a wide pot with a finger of simmering water, put the lid on and steam for about 40 minutes, topping up the water if it runs low. It is done when it is firm like set custard and a knife comes out clean. Cool and chill.

On Tuesday morning, reheat two ramekins for 2 minutes in the microwave or 10 minutes in a steamer and serve with the avocado and orange. Keep the other two for Wednesday. Moi moi keeps for three days in the fridge.
tip: Skins-on moi moi is darker, grittier and firmer, so it is worth the ten minutes to rub them off. A spoon of fresh pepper sauce or a little millet pap (ogi) on the side is the traditional partner. Foil cups or a muffin tin work if you do not have ramekins.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Spiced millet koko with yogurt, banana and groundnuts
inspiredBy: Hausa koko, the ginger and clove millet porridge of northern Nigeria and Ghana, with yogurt in the spirit of nono, the fermented milk
about: A thick, creamy millet porridge warmed with fresh ginger, clove and black pepper, topped with a big spoonful of cool yogurt, sliced banana and a crunch of chopped roasted groundnuts. It is gentle, a little sweet and keeps you full all morning. Millet is a whole grain with plenty of **magnesium and fibre**, and the yogurt adds protein and calcium.
steps: The evening before, rinse the millet and leave it to soak in plenty of cold water. This is optional, but it cuts the cooking time nearly in half.

Drain the millet and tip it into a pot with about three times as much fresh water, the grated ginger, clove, black pepper and salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring often so it does not catch.
Cook until the grains have burst and the porridge is thick and creamy, about 15 minutes after soaking, or 25 if you skipped it. Add a splash of water if it gets stiff.
For a smoother, more traditional pap, mash it hard with the back of a spoon or give it a few pulses with a stick blender.

Cook the porridge the evening before and chill it, so breakfast is only a reheat. In the morning, warm one portion with a splash of water and spoon it into a bowl. Top with the cool yogurt, the sliced banana and the chopped groundnuts.
Reheat the second portion the next morning in the same way and add the toppings fresh.
tip: Koko is often eaten with akara or bread. For more kick, add extra ginger. Groundnuts are what West Africans call peanuts.

name: Nigerian-style salad with black-eyed peas, corn and avocado
inspiredBy: Nigerian party salad, with black-eyed peas in place of baked beans and a lime and mustard dressing in place of salad cream
about: A big, crunchy bowl of shredded cabbage, tomato, carrot and sweet corn with seasoned black-eyed peas and ripe avocado, in a tangy lime and mustard dressing. It is cool, filling and needs almost no cooking. The peas bring protein, **iron and fibre**, and the raw vegetables bring vitamin C.
steps: If you are starting from dried peas, soak them overnight, then simmer in unsalted water until tender but not mushy, about 40 minutes. Cook a big batch on Sunday and they keep for four days. Drain well.
While the peas are still warm, toss them with a third of the onion, half the lime juice and the salt so they take on the flavour. Let them cool.
Shred the cabbage very finely, chop the tomato and grate the carrot. Slice the rest of the onion into thin rings.
Whisk the rest of the lime juice with the mustard and oil until creamy.
Toss the peas with the cabbage, tomato, carrot, corn and onion in a big bowl. Top with the avocado and spoon the dressing over just before eating.
tip: Canned sardines or a boiled egg are popular additions in Nigeria. Pack the dressing separately if you take it to work.
ingredients: soaked and boiled until tender (or about three times the dry weight in canned)
kernels cut from the cob, or canned

name: Suya-spiced beef with cucumber and collard slaw and sweet potato
inspiredBy: Hausa suya, the peppery peanut-spiced grilled beef of northern Nigeria, with sweet potato in place of bread
about: Thin strips of beef rubbed with a warm, nutty yaji spice mix of ground groundnuts, paprika, cayenne, ginger, garlic and onion, grilled until the edges char, and served with a crunchy cucumber and collard slaw and soft sweet potato. It is hot, savoury and bright with lime. The beef brings **iron and zinc**, and the sweet potato brings vitamin A.
steps: Put the flank steak in the freezer for 20 minutes so it firms up, then cut it across the grain into very thin strips.
Grind the groundnuts to a coarse powder with the paprika, cayenne, garlic powder, onion powder and ground ginger, in a spice grinder or with a mortar. This is your yaji.
Toss the beef in the oil. Add about two thirds of the yaji, mix well and leave for 15 minutes while you cook the sweet potato.
Boil the sweet potato wedges in salted water until just tender, about 12 minutes, and drain well.

Heat a heavy pan over medium-high heat, or heat the broiler. Cook the beef in a single layer for 2 to 3 minutes on each side, until browned at the edges and just cooked through. Do not crowd the pan or it will steam, and watch the peanut coating, which scorches fast.
Slice the cucumber, collards and onion as thinly as you can, chop the tomato and toss with the lime juice. Let it sit for a few minutes so the collards soften.
Serve the beef on the slaw with the sweet potato and a sprinkle of the remaining yaji.
tip: Slice and season the beef the night before and boil the sweet potato with another meal, and lunch is a 10-minute job. Skewers are lovely if you have them. Use less cayenne for a milder version.
ingredients: flank steak, cut as thin as you can

name: Egusi soup with smoked mackerel and bitter greens, with boiled yam
inspiredBy: Nigerian egusi soup, with collards and mustard greens standing in for bitterleaf or ugwu, and smoked mackerel for smoked fish
about: A thick, nutty soup of ground melon seeds cooked in red palm oil with onion, chili and dried shrimp, loaded with collards and mustard greens and finished with flakes of smoked mackerel, served with soft boiled yam. It makes two portions and reheats well. The mackerel brings **omega-3 and B12**, the melon seeds bring magnesium and zinc, and the collards bring calcium.
steps: Peel the yam, cut it into chunks and boil in salted water until tender, 15 to 20 minutes. Drain.

Warm the palm oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook for 4 minutes, then stir in the garlic, chili and the ground dried shrimp. Let the shrimp sizzle in the oil for a minute so it loses its raw smell.

Stir in the tomato paste and half a cup of water and bring it to a simmer. Grind the melon seeds to a fine powder (or use pre-ground egusi from an African grocery) and stir them with a few spoonfuls of water to a thick paste. Spoon lumps of it into the pot, cover and cook on low for 8 minutes, until it sets into soft curds.
Pour in about another cup of water for two portions, stir gently and simmer for 8 minutes. It should be a thick soup, not a thin one.
Stir in the collards and mustard greens and cook until tender, 8 to 10 minutes.
Flake in the smoked mackerel and warm it through for 2 minutes. Taste before adding any salt.
Serve with the yam, mashed with a fork if you like. Pack the second portion for tomorrow and loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: Pumpkin leaves (ugwu) or frozen bitterleaf are the traditional greens if you can find them at an African grocery, and the same trip will find ground crayfish, ground egusi and iru. Without them, mustard greens give the bitter edge.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili
only if needed, the fish is salty

name: Chicken yassa with steamed millet
inspiredBy: Senegalese yassa poulet, with millet in place of the usual white rice
about: Chicken thighs marinated in lime juice, mustard and a mountain of onions, grilled for char, then simmered in the onions until they melt into a sweet and tangy sauce, over fluffy millet. It makes two portions, and the tangy onions taste even better on the second day. The onions and lime bring **vitamin C**, and the millet adds magnesium and fibre.
steps: The night before or that morning, slice the onions. Set aside a small handful of the sliced onion in the fridge for the top, away from the chicken. Mix the rest with the lime juice, vinegar, mustard, crushed garlic, chili, black pepper and half the salt, add the chicken, turn to coat and leave it in the fridge for at least 30 minutes and no more than 12 hours.

Lift the chicken out of the marinade, keeping the onions, and pat it dry. Broil it on a tray for about 4 minutes on each side, until it is nicely charred at the edges. It does not need to be cooked through.
Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the marinated onions and the carrot and cook them, stirring often, until soft, golden and jammy, about 15 minutes.
Nestle the chicken into the onions with a splash of water, cover and simmer gently until it is cooked through and the sauce is thick, about 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, rinse the millet and simmer it in about two and a half times as much salted water, covered, until the water is absorbed and the grains are tender, 15 to 20 minutes. Rest it for 5 minutes, then fluff with a fork.

Serve the chicken and onion sauce over the millet, topped with the raw onion you set aside and the parsley. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Millet turns stiff in the fridge, so add a splash of water and a squeeze of lime when you reheat it.
tip: Marinate the night before or that morning, since much longer in lime and the chicken goes soft. Dijon mustard is the traditional choice. In Senegal yassa is often served with rice, and fish yassa made with a firm white fish is just as good.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Groundnut stew with beef, sweet potato and collards
inspiredBy: Senegalese mafe and Ghanaian groundnut soup, with collards for the greens
about: Tender beef and soft sweet potato in a thick, savoury groundnut and tomato sauce with ginger, garlic and chili, with collards stirred in at the end and a squeeze of lime to cut the richness. It is rich without needing much oil, and it makes two portions. Groundnuts are a great source of **vitamin E**, and the sweet potato and collards add vitamin A, calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef in batches until well coloured on all sides. Set it aside.

Lower the heat and soften the chopped onion with the ginger, garlic and chili for 5 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste for a minute, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it darkens and thickens, about 8 minutes.
Return the beef to the pot with a mug of water and the salt. Cover and simmer gently until the beef is tender, about 60 minutes (or 25 minutes in a pressure cooker).
Add the sweet potato and enough water to nearly cover. Simmer for 12 minutes, until it is soft.

Blend the groundnuts with a ladle of the hot broth until completely smooth, then stir it into the pot along with the collards. Simmer very gently for 10 more minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and glossy. Do not let it boil hard or the groundnuts can catch.
Stir in the lime juice and taste for salt. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The stew thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water.
tip: Cassava is the other classic here. Natural peanut butter, stirred in with the broth, is a fine shortcut for the blended groundnuts, and chicken thighs cook in half the time.
ingredients: flank steak, cut in bite-size pieces
scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Grilled tilapia with onion and chili sauce, boiled cassava and stewed greens
inspiredBy: Ivorian poisson braisé, grilled fish with an onion, tomato and chili sauce, with cassava in place of attiéké and Sierra Leone-style stewed greens
about: Tilapia fillets rubbed with ginger and garlic and broiled until golden, with a tangy raw onion, tomato and chili sauce, soft boiled cassava and collards and mustard greens stewed with a little palm oil and dried shrimp. It is simple, bold and quick to put together. The fish brings lean protein, B12 and selenium, and the greens bring **calcium and vitamin K**.
steps: Peel the cassava, cut it into chunks and cut out the woody core. Boil in salted water until completely soft, about 20 minutes, then drain.
For the sauce, slice half the onion very thinly and chop the tomato and chili. Toss with the lime juice and a pinch of salt and let it sit while you cook. It should be sharp, juicy and fresh.
Grate the garlic and half the ginger and rub them over the tilapia with the vegetable oil and a pinch of salt. Lay the fillets on a tray lined with oiled foil.
Heat the broiler to high. Broil the fish for about 4 minutes without turning, until it is opaque and flakes easily. Thin fillets cook fast, so watch them.

Meanwhile warm the palm oil in a pan, chop the rest of the onion and soften it with the rest of the ginger and the ground dried shrimp for 3 minutes, letting the shrimp sizzle. Add the collards and mustard greens with a splash of water, cover and cook until tender and glossy, about 8 minutes.
Serve the fish with the cassava, the greens and a big spoonful of the onion sauce.
tip: Boiled yam or plantain are the other classic partners. A whole fish grilled over charcoal is the real thing, and you would need about 450 g for one portion. Leave the chili out of the sauce for a mild version.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Red-red, black-eyed pea stew with pan-fried ripe plantain and egg
inspiredBy: Ghanaian red-red, with the plantain pan-fried in very little oil instead of deep-fried
about: Black-eyed peas simmered until creamy in a deep red palm oil, tomato, onion and ginger sauce, with sweet pan-fried plantain and a boiled egg on the side. It is the classic Ghanaian comfort plate, and it makes two portions. The peas are a great source of **folate, iron and fibre**.
steps: Soak the peas overnight in plenty of cold water. Drain, cover with fresh water and simmer until completely soft, about 45 minutes (or 15 in a pressure cooker). Do not salt them until they are tender. Keep a mug of the cooking water.
Blend the pepper with half the onion and the tomato. Chop the rest of the onion finely.

Warm the palm oil gently in a wide pot, then soften the chopped onion with the ginger, chili and the ground dried shrimp for about 5 minutes. Add the tomato paste and cook for a minute, then the blended tomato mixture.
Cook, stirring, until the sauce turns a deep red and the oil starts to separate, about 12 minutes. This is where the name comes from.
Stir in the drained peas, the salt and a good splash of the cooking water. Simmer for 15 minutes, mashing a few peas against the side of the pot to thicken the stew.

While it simmers, hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes. Slice the plantain into thick coins, toss with the vegetable oil and a pinch of salt and cook in a non-stick pan over medium heat for about 4 minutes on each side, until caramelized at the edges.

Serve the peas with the plantain, a halved egg and a few slices of avocado. Pack the second portion of stew for tomorrow. At lunch, pan-sear fresh plantain for 8 minutes while you reheat the stew, as plantain is never as good reheated.
tip: Many cooks add a little fried fish on top. A spoonful of gari is the other traditional topping. Two cans of drained black-eyed peas will save you the simmering time.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Thieboudienne-inspired fish and vegetable rice
inspiredBy: Senegalese thieboudienne, with brown rice cooked in the fish and vegetable broth
about: Fish seasoned with a parsley, garlic, chili and lime paste, laid over brown rice cooked in a rich tomato broth with sweet potato and cabbage. It is Senegal's national dish, simplified for a home kitchen, and it makes two portions. The sweet potato and cabbage add **vitamin A and fibre**, and the fish brings lean protein.
steps: Rinse the rice and soak it in cold water for 30 minutes. Brown rice is chewier than the broken rice used in Senegal, so the soak helps.
Make the paste (called rof): crush or blitz the parsley, garlic, half the onion, the chili, half the lime juice and a pinch of salt into a rough paste.
Cut a few slashes in each fish fillet and press about half of the paste into them. Let the fish sit in the fridge while you start the sauce.

Heat half the oil in a large, heavy pot and soften the remaining onion for 5 minutes, along with the ground dried shrimp. Stir in the tomato paste and fry until it darkens to brick red, about 4 minutes. Add the rest of the paste and about 3 cups of water for the two portions, bring to a boil and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the sweet potato, tomato and cabbage and simmer for 15 minutes, until the sweet potato is tender. Lift the vegetables out onto a plate and keep them warm.

Ladle off all but about 1½ cups of the broth for the two portions and keep it hot to spoon over at the table. Drain the rice and stir it into the broth left in the pot. Cover and cook very gently, stirring once or twice, until the rice is tender and has soaked up the broth, 35 to 40 minutes.

While the rice finishes, warm the rest of the oil in a pan and sear one fillet for 3 minutes on each side. Lay it on the rice with half the vegetables and finish with the rest of the lime juice and some of the hot broth.

Pack the second portion of rice and vegetables for tomorrow's lunch and keep the second fillet raw in the fridge. Tomorrow, sear it fresh for 3 minutes a side while you reheat the rice with a splash of water.
tip: White rice or broken rice gives the soft, broth-soaked texture and the crispy bottom. Snapper or cod work as well as haddock, and mackerel makes a richer pot. Cassava and eggplant are classic additions.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Goat and yam pepper soup with collards
inspiredBy: Nigerian goat pepper soup, a clear, fiery broth with ginger and warm spices, with yam and collards added to make it a meal
about: A clear, peppery goat broth warmed with ginger, garlic, scotch bonnet, black pepper, nutmeg, clove and allspice, with soft chunks of yam and collards added at the end. It is light, spicy and deeply comforting. The goat brings protein, iron and zinc, the collards bring **calcium and vitamin K**, and the yam brings potassium.
steps: Blend the onion, ginger, garlic and chili with a splash of water into a rough paste.

Put the goat in a pot with the paste, black pepper, nutmeg, clove, allspice and salt and cover with water by a few centimetres. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam and simmer gently until the goat is tender, about 60 minutes (or 25 in a pressure cooker), skimming off any fat that rises.
Add the yam and simmer for another 15 minutes, until the yam is tender and the broth has thickened slightly.
Stir in the collards and simmer for 6 minutes, until tender. Squeeze in the lime juice and taste for salt and heat.
Serve very hot, in a big bowl.
tip: The weight is for boneless goat. If you buy it on the bone, as most cooks do, buy about 250 g and take the bones into the pot. Look for goat at a halal butcher or a Caribbean or African market, and use lamb or chicken thighs if you cannot find it. A teaspoon of ready-made pepper soup spice from the African grocery can replace the ground spices, and a few basil leaves stand in for scent leaf. Goat comes in bigger packs, so make a double pot and freeze the second bowl.
ingredients: about ½ scotch bonnet or habanero, or another hot red chili

name: Groundnut and sesame bites
inspiredBy: Hausa kuli-kuli, the crunchy groundnut snack, here with sesame and without the pressing and frying
about: Roasted groundnuts pounded with toasted sesame (benne) seeds, fresh ginger and a little chili into nutty, crumbly little balls with a crunch of sesame. The sesame brings **calcium** and the groundnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 2 minutes.
Grind half the groundnuts in a spice grinder or mortar until they turn oily and start to clump. Roughly crush the other half so some pieces stay coarse.
Mix both with the sesame seeds, ginger, chili and salt, squeeze into small balls and press firmly so they hold together. Eat right away or keep for a day.

name: Orange and roasted groundnuts
about: A juicy orange with a handful of roasted groundnuts, the street snack you will find all over Accra and Lagos. Sweet, salty and crunchy. The orange brings **vitamin C** and the groundnuts bring vitamin E.
steps: Peel the orange, break it into segments and eat it with the groundnuts.

name: Orange yogurt with toasted sesame
about: Thick yogurt with juicy orange segments and a spoonful of toasted sesame (benne) seeds. Cool, sweet and crunchy. The yogurt and sesame together bring **calcium and protein**.
steps: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan until golden, about 2 minutes.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the orange segments and scatter the sesame seeds over.

name: Roasted corn with fresh coconut
about: A large cob of corn roasted until charred in spots, eaten with chunks of fresh coconut, the pairing sold from roadside stalls in Ghana and Nigeria. Sweet, smoky and chewy. Corn brings fibre and B vitamins, and the coconut brings **crunch and fibre**.
steps: Roast the cob over a gas flame, on a hot grill or in a dry heavy pan, turning often, for about 10 minutes, until charred in spots. Sprinkle with the salt and eat it with the coconut chunks.

name: Avocado with tomato and lime
about: Half a ripe avocado with chopped tomato, a squeeze of lime and a pinch of salt. It is creamy, juicy and sharp, the way avocado is eaten across Ghana and Nigeria. Avocado brings **vitamin E**, fibre and potassium.
steps: Halve the avocado and chop the tomato. Spoon the tomato over the avocado, squeeze over the lime juice and sprinkle with the salt.

name: Sardines and tomato on warm yam slices
about: Warm slices of boiled yam topped with canned sardines, chopped tomato, a little onion and chili. Canned sardines are a staple pantry food across West Africa. Sardines eaten with their soft bones bring omega-3, **calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Slice the yam into thick rounds and boil in salted water until tender, about 12 minutes. Drain. If you have leftover boiled yam, just warm it.
Chop the tomato, onion and chili and mix with the lime juice. Top the warm yam with the sardines, broken into chunks, and the tomato mixture.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, with the soft bones
scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Roasted groundnuts
about: A handful of roasted groundnuts, the simplest snack in West Africa, sold in little twists of paper on every corner. Crunchy and satisfying, with protein and plenty of **vitamin E**.
steps: Sprinkle the groundnuts with a pinch of salt if they are unsalted, and eat them as they are.

name: Ripe banana and roasted groundnuts
about: A ripe banana with a handful of roasted groundnuts, a simple, filling pairing sold at roadsides across Ghana. The banana brings **potassium** and the groundnuts bring protein and vitamin E.
steps: Peel the banana and eat it with the groundnuts.

name: Fresh coconut and roasted groundnuts
about: Chunks of fresh coconut with a handful of roasted groundnuts, a roadside favourite in Ghana. Sweet, crunchy and filling. The groundnuts bring protein and **vitamin E**.
steps: Crack the coconut, pry out the flesh and cut it into chunks. Eat it with the groundnuts.

name: Boiled egg with tomato and fresh pepper
about: A hard-boiled egg with juicy tomato, a little thinly sliced onion and chopped chili and salt. Fresh, hot and simple, and a good source of protein and **choline**.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 8 minutes, then cool and peel it.
Slice the egg and tomato onto a plate, scatter with the onion and chili and sprinkle with the salt.
ingredients: scotch bonnet or habanero (produce aisle), or another hot red chili

name: Akara, black-eyed pea fritters, pan-fried
inspiredBy: Nigerian akara, pan-fried in a little oil instead of deep-fried
about: Little golden fritters of blended black-eyed peas, onion and chili, pan-fried in just a little oil until crisp outside and fluffy inside. Akara is eaten for breakfast and as a snack across Nigeria and Ghana. The peas bring **iron, folate and fibre**.
steps: Soak the peas in plenty of cold water for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Rub them between your palms to loosen the skins and rinse most of them away.
Blend the peas with the onion, chili, salt and just enough cold water to make a thick, fluffy batter. Beat it hard with a spoon for a minute to add air.
